items.title: Step-up authentication: how to right-size authentication to risk
items.summary: Not every action a user takes in an application carries the same risk. Viewing an account balance in a banking application isn’t the same as wiring several thousand dollars to a new payee. In practice, though, many applications ask users to prove their identity once at sign-in and then treat every action the same from that point on, whether that sign-in used a password alone or included multi-factor authentication (MFA). That creates a tension: if the sign-in is strict enough for the most sensitive operation, everyday tasks carry unnecessary friction. If it’s easy enough for everyday tasks, the most sensitive operations might not be protected well enough. Even a strong sign-in from hours earlier says little about who is at the keyboard when a high-risk request arrives. Amazon Cognito now resolves that trade-off by supporting step-up authentication, which records the authentication assurance level and the methods used, and including both in the JSON web tokens (JWTs) it issues. You ask for a target assurance level when a user signs in. Amazon Cognito returns the level the user reached in an acr claim (authentication context class reference) and the methods they completed in an amr claim (authentication methods reference). These claims are part of the OpenID Connect Core specification , so your application can reason about authentication strength in a standard way and match it to the potential risk of what the user is trying to do. In this post, I explain how the claims support step-up authentication and walk through four patterns that put them to use: transaction-level step-up in a banking app, varying risk postures across a portfolio of applications, step-up enforced on API and SDK sign-in, and authentication assurance carried across a federated third-party OpenID Connect (OIDC) identity provider. You can request authentication levels through Amazon Cognito managed login using the standard OIDC acr_values and max_age parameters, and through the SDK and API using the USER_AUTH flow with TARGET_ACR_VALUES and MAX_AGE . Requesting step-up authentication requires the Essentials or Plus feature plan . ; For the complete list of features, behaviors, and limitations, see the Authentication levels with ACR and AMR claims . What ACR and AMR tell your application Amazon Cognito defines four assurance levels, and the factor combinations that satisfy each one are fixed. You can use the default names as is or rename the level URIs to fit your organization’s own naming scheme. Renaming changes only the label. If you need to relate Amazon Cognito levels to a framework such as NIST SP 800-63 or eIDAS , make that mapping in your application. The following are the default Amazon Cognito defined levels. Level 1 ( urn:cognito:loa:1 ) is password only. Level 2 ( urn:cognito:loa:2 ) is a single one-time password (OTP) over SMS or email. Level 3 ( urn:cognito:loa:3 ) is a passkey on its own, or a password combined with an SMS or email OTP. Level 4 ( urn:cognito:loa:4 ) is the highest: a password with a time-based one-time password (TOTP) code from an authenticator app. Amazon Cognito assigns the highest level the user’s completed factors fully satisfy, so a user who signs in with a password and a TOTP code lands at level 4, even though they also met the assurance requirements for every level below it. Four claims in the token facilitate a step-up decision. The acr claim is the level the sign-in reached and is what your application compares against what the operation requires. The amr claim lists the methods behind that level, so you can confirm a specific factor was used. The auth_time claim records when the user last authenticated interactively and is what max_age is measured against. The iat claim only records when the token was issued, so a refreshed token carries a new iat but keeps its old auth_time . Finally, send a nonce in the request and verify it on the returned ID token, so the result is tied to the request you made. The following is an example access token for a user completing a level 4 authentication. Notice the four claims I’ve discussed: acr , amr , auth_time , and iat . { "sub": "387173a0-60c1-700a-4a02-e84b49bcc7a9", "iss": "https://cognito-idp. .amazonaws.com/ _123abc", "aud": "123abcn2ci4a99a4ieno123abc", "exp": 1445470140, "iat": 499163700, "auth_time": -446666160, "token_use": "access", "acr": "urn:cognito:loa:4", "amr": ["pwd", "otp", "mfa"], "email": "marty@example.com", "cognito:username": "387173a0-60c1-700a-4a02-e84b49bcc7a9" } Two important behaviors are worth understanding before you build on this. First, a token refresh preserves the acr and amr values, so a user who reached level 4 keeps level 4 across refreshes and isn’t asked to prove it again on every rotation. Second, a refresh doesn’t reset the auth_time claim. That field records when the user interactively authenticated, not from a non-interactive token refresh. This is what lets you reason about freshness of authentication separately from assurance strength. At a high level, every step-up interaction in this post follows the same loop: the application checks the token it already holds, redirects for a stronger level only when the operation requires more than the user has, and re-validates the acr claim on the freshly issued token before it proceeds. The following diagram provides a general step-up authentication flow. Figure 1: General step-up authentication flow to access a sensitive operation How you request a level, and what stays your responsibility The request side is deliberately straightforward. On managed login you add acr_values and optionally max_age to the or endpoint. In the SDK and API, you pass TARGET_ACR_VALUES and MAX_AGE in the USER_AUTH flow of the API. Both acr_values and TARGET_ACR_VALUES accept an ordered list of target levels. The same parameters work whether you’re setting the level for an initial sign-in or raising the level of a user who is already signed in; the patterns later in this post show both. Amazon Cognito acts only on what you send. It doesn’t infer the level you meant, so if you omit the parameter or request the wrong level, the user might not be stepped up the way you intended. That points to the part your application and API owns: what assurance authentication level is needed. Amazon Cognito issues a token that honestly reports the level the user reached based on what your application requested. For example, deciding that a given operation requires an assurance level 3, checking the token’s acr against that requirement, and refusing the operation when it falls short is enforcement your application and API performs. Amazon Cognito produces the evidence; your code acts on it. In practice, that means checking the token you already hold before you redirect, so you don’t send a user to re-authenticate who already meets the bar, and validating the acr and auth_time claims on the tokens Amazon Cognito returns before you grant access. Amazon Cognito computes these claims itself, so you can’t customize, add to, or suppress them with a pre-token-generation Lambda trigger. There is one more detail that saves debugging time later. If you rename your acr level URIs after tokens have already been issued, an older token might carry an acr value that no longer matches any configured level. Amazon Cognito treats that as an unrecognized level rather than an error. It still honors the token’s amr values and prompts only for factors not already present, without crediting any particular level. The amr list, in other words, remains meaningful even when a renamed level string goes stale. See Configuring ACR level names to learn how to configure this. With the claims and the division of responsibility in place, the following four patterns show how they work in practice. Each one applies the same loop from Figure 1 to a different situation: a single application, a portfolio of applications, API-driven sign-in, and federation. Pattern 1: Transaction-level step-up in a banking app Consider a retail banking application. Signing in and viewing balances is routine, and the bank is comfortable requiring a moderate assurance level for it. Moving money is considered a privileged action, and a large transfer deserves stronger proof that the person at the keyboard is really the account holder. The bank sets its baseline at level 2, so a user signs in with a one-time code over SMS or email and can see balances, statements, and pending transactions. When that same user initiates a transfer above $1,000, the application’s own policy says the operation requires level 4. Before it shows the transfer initiation screen, the application inspects the acr claim in the token it already holds. The user authenticated at level 2, level 2 is below the required level 4, so the application redirects the user to managed login with acr_values=urn:cognito:loa:4 . GET https://auth.example-bank.com/oauth2/authorize ?response_type=code &client_id=abc123def456 &redirect_uri=https://app.example-bank.com/callback &scope=openid &acr_values=urn:cognito:loa:4 Amazon Cognito now requires the user to complete a factor combination that satisfies level 4, for example entering their password and then a TOTP code from their authenticator app. When authentication finishes, Amazon Cognito issues fresh tokens with acr set to urn:cognito:loa:4 , amr set to ["pwd", "otp", "mfa"] , and a fresh updated auth_time claim. The application validates that the new token meets its requirement and only then lets the transfer proceed. A transfer under the threshold never triggers any of this, so the everyday experience stays light and the friction lands exactly where the risk is. The application logic reads naturally, here’s a pseudo JavaScript snippet: // Use your own URIs here, if different than defaults. const ACR_RANK = { "urn:cognito:loa:1": 1, "urn:cognito:loa:2": 2, "urn:cognito:loa:3": 3, "urn:cognito:loa:4": 4, }; const REQUIRED_LEVEL = "urn:cognito:loa:4"; const HIGH_VALUE_THRESHOLD = 1000; function canAuthorizeTransfer(accessTokenClaims, amount) { if (amount < HIGH_VALUE_THRESHOLD) { return true; // baseline session is sufficient } // High-value transfer: require level 4. // An unrecognized acr ranks 0, so it never passes. const achieved = ACR_RANK[accessTokenClaims.acr] ?? 0; return achieved >= ACR_RANK[REQUIRED_LEVEL]; } You can extend the same idea to freshness. A bank might accept a level 4 session for a high-value transfer only if the user authenticated within the last 5 minutes, which you express by adding max_age=300 to the request. Amazon Cognito compares that window against the auth_time claim in the access token and reauthenticates the user if the window has passed, even if the token was refreshed seconds ago. Pattern 2: A portfolio of applications with different risk postures Assurance levels are just as useful across a set of applications as they are within one. Suppose an organization runs five applications from a single Amazon Cognito user pool using managed login, and each one carries a different risk posture. An internal cafeteria menu is low risk, so it’s fine with level 1, password only. An employee directory and an expense viewer hold personal data but nothing that moves money, so they require level 2: a one-time code over SMS or email on top of the password. A source code portal warrants a passkey or a password plus a one-time code, which is level 3. The production financial console is the crown jewel, so it demands level 4: a password with a TOTP code. Each application requests its own floor by setting acr_values to the level that matches its risk, and each validates the acr claim on the returned token before granting access. Because the applications share a user pool, managed login keeps a single sign-on (SSO) session across them. A user who has already reached level 4 for the financial console is redirected to managed login when they open another application, finds the existing session, and receives tokens for that application without another prompt, provided the application doesn’t send a max_age that the session has outlived. Each application then compares levels by rank, so a level 4 token satisfies a level 2 floor. Someone who signed in at level 1 for the cafeteria menu, on the other hand, is stepped up the first time they open the expense viewer, because level 1 doesn’t meet the level 2 floor that the application enforces. The user pool stays single and central; the assurance requirement travels with each application’s own policy. Renaming the level URIs helps here. If the organization already classifies systems against an internal assurance standard, it can set AcrConfiguration on the user pool so that, say, level 3 reports as urn:example-corp:assurance:standard and level 4 as urn:example-corp:assurance:high . The factor combinations behind each level stay fixed; only the names change, so every application validates against strings its developers already recognize. Pattern 3: Step-up on API and SDK sign-in Managed login covers browser-based flows, including federation, but plenty of clients authenticate directly against the Amazon Cognito API, and the same assurance model applies there, such as using the USER_AUTH flow with the InitiateAuth API. This matters for a mobile app, a desktop client, or a service that drives sign-in programmatically and needs to raise assurance before a sensitive call. Take a mobile trading app that signs its users in with the SDK. A user opens the app with a password and reaches level 1, which is enough to browse watchlists and market data. When they place a trade, the app’s policy requires level 4. Because the app authenticates through the API rather than a browser redirect, it starts a new USER_AUTH flow and passes the access token it already holds along with TARGET_ACR_VALUES , requesting the level it needs. Amazon Cognito drives the user through a factor combination that satisfies level 4, then returns tokens whose acr claim the app validates before it submits the order. The InitiateAuth request would look similar to the following API call. { "AuthFlow": "USER_AUTH", "ClientId": "abc123def456", "AuthParameters": { "USERNAME": "user@example.com", "ACCESS_TOKEN": "eyJraWQiOi...", "TARGET_ACR_VALUES": "urn:cognito:loa:4", "MAX_AGE": "300" } } Passing the access token the app already holds lets Amazon Cognito step the user up from the factors in that token; without it, Amazon Cognito authenticates the user from scratch. The MAX_AGE parameter behaves the same way it does on managed login. It ties the requirement to auth_time , so a trade placed after the window elapses forces a fresh authentication even if the app refreshed its tokens in the meantime. One behavior specific to the API path is worth knowing when you test on a lower Cognito feature plan. If you request step-up through InitiateAuth on a user pool that isn’t on the Essentials or Plus plan, the API returns a FeatureUnavailableInTierException . Managed login handles the same situation differently: the authorize endpoint silently ignores acr_values and proceeds with normal authentication rather than raising an error. Pattern 4: Carrying assurance across a federated OIDC identity provider The three patterns so far assume Amazon Cognito is where the user authenticates and the authoritative source for the identity. Many organizations federate sign-in to a third-party OIDC provider, so the person proving who they are is doing it against an external identity provider (IdP), while Amazon Cognito brokers the session. The assurance model follows them there. When your application requests a level, it sends acr_values and optionally max_age to the Amazon Cognito authorize endpoint exactly as before. If that user is configured to federate through an OIDC IdP, Amazon Cognito sends the authorization request to that IdP on the user’s behalf. It translates the level you requested into the acr value the IdP expects, using the mapping you configured, and passes max_age along with it. A standards-compliant OIDC IdP honors acr_values the same way Amazon Cognito does: it drives the user through an authentication that satisfies the requested level, and it returns its own acr value describing what the user reached. max_age carries forward in the same way, so a freshness requirement is enforced at the provider that actually authenticates the user rather than being lost at the broker. Keep in mind that this is only supported with OIDC identity providers. The request is unchanged from the application’s point of view. It still directs to Amazon Cognito: GET https://auth.example.com/oauth2/authorize ?response_type=code &client_id=abc123def456 &redirect_uri=https://app.example.com/callback &scope=openid &identity_provider=PartnerOIDC &acr_values=urn:cognito:loa:3 &max_age=300 The interaction gains a third participant, the downstream IdP, but the assurance requirement is persisted through the entire federated authentication flow as shown in figure 2. Figure 2: Federation with an OIDC third-party IdP, persisting the acr_values and max_age request parameters The value that comes back from a partner IdP won’t use Amazon Cognito’s level URIs, so this lets you map the provider’s acr values onto its own levels with the AcrMapping field on the OIDC IdP configuration. A partner IdP that reports, say, https://partner.example/assurance/strong can be mapped to Amazon Cognito level 3 ( urn:cognito:loa:3) , so that by the time the token reaches your application the acr claim speaks the same vocabulary regardless of whether the user authenticated locally or through a federated provider. Your resource server keeps a single enforcement rule and authorization logic and doesn’t need to have special handling depending on where the user ultimately authenticated. See Step-up authentication for federated users to learn how to map external OIDC IdP acr levels to Cognito. This is the same pattern that RFC 9470 , the OAuth 2.0 Step Up Authentication Challenge Protocol, describes: the assurance level is requested at the edge of your application, travels through Amazon Cognito to whatever provider authenticates the user, and returns normalized to a vocabulary your code already understands. A user federating from a corporate IdP and a user signing in against the same user pool directly both arrive at your resource server carrying an acr claim that means the same thing. Conclusion In this post, I showed you how the acr and amr claims in Amazon Cognito let you match authentication strength to the risk of what a user is doing, instead of settling for one bar at the front door. Your application requests a target level with acr_values and max_age (or TARGET_ACR_VALUES and MAX_AGE in the USER_AUTH flow), Amazon Cognito reports the level reached and the methods used, and your application enforces what each operation requires. The four patterns, from a banking transfer to a federated third-party IdP, follow that same loop, and one enforcement rule at your resource server covers every sign-in path. The larger shift is that assurance is now something Amazon Cognito expresses in a standard way and your application reasons about directly, without building your own step-up tracking. To get started, move your user pool to the Essentials or Plus feature plan, decide the level each operation requires, and add acr_values to your existing authorize requests. For the complete parameter reference and federated behavior, see the Amazon Cognito Developer Guide . If you have questions about this post, contact AWS Support or start a new thread on AWS re:Post . Abrom Douglas III Abrom is a Senior Solutions Architect within AWS Identity with over 20 years of software engineering and security experience, specializing in identity and access management. He loves speaking with customers about how identity and access management can provide secure outcomes that enable both business and technology initiatives. In his free time, he enjoys cheering for Arsenal FC, photography, travel, volunteering, and competing in duathlons.

  "urn:cognito:loa:2": 2,
  "urn:cognito:loa:3": 3,
  "urn:cognito:loa:4": 4,

The factor combinations behind each level stay fixed; only the names change, so every application validates against strings its developers already recognize.

Pattern 3: Step-up on API and SDK sign-in

Managed login covers browser-based flows, including federation, but plenty of clients authenticate directly against the Amazon Cognito API, and the same assurance model applies there, such as using the USER_AUTH flow with the InitiateAuth API. This matters for a mobile app, a desktop client, or a service that drives sign-in programmatically and needs to raise assurance before a sensitive call.

Take a mobile trading app that signs its users in with the SDK. A user opens the app with a password and reaches level 1, which is enough to browse watchlists and market data. When they place a trade, the app’s policy requires level 4. Because the app authenticates through the API rather than a browser redirect, it starts a new USER_AUTH flow and passes the access token it already holds along with TARGET_ACR_VALUES, requesting the level it needs. Amazon Cognito drives the user through a factor combination that satisfies level 4, then returns tokens whose acr claim the app validates before it submits the order. The InitiateAuth request would look similar to the following API call.

{
  "AuthFlow": "USER_AUTH",
  "ClientId": "abc123def456",
  "AuthParameters": {
    "USERNAME": "user@example.com",
    "ACCESS_TOKEN": "eyJraWQiOi...",
    "TARGET_ACR_VALUES": "urn:cognito:loa:4",
    "MAX_AGE": "300"
  }
}

Passing the access token the app already holds lets Amazon Cognito step the user up from the factors in that token; without it, Amazon Cognito authenticates the user from scratch. The MAX_AGE parameter behaves the same way it does on managed login. It ties the requirement to auth_time, so a trade placed after the window elapses forces a fresh authentication even if the app refreshed its tokens in the meantime. One behavior specific to the API path is worth knowing when you test on a lower Cognito feature plan. If you request step-up through InitiateAuth on a user pool that isn’t on the Essentials or Plus plan, the API returns a FeatureUnavailableInTierException. Managed login handles the same situation differently: the authorize endpoint silently ignores acr_values and proceeds with normal authentication rather than raising an error.

Pattern 4: Carrying assurance across a federated OIDC identity provider

The three patterns so far assume Amazon Cognito is where the user authenticates and the authoritative source for the identity. Many organizations federate sign-in to a third-party OIDC provider, so the person proving who they are is doing it against an external identity provider (IdP), while Amazon Cognito brokers the session. The assurance model follows them there.

When your application requests a level, it sends acr_values and optionally max_age to the Amazon Cognito authorize endpoint exactly as before. If that user is configured to federate through an OIDC IdP, Amazon Cognito sends the authorization request to that IdP on the user’s behalf. It translates the level you requested into the acr value the IdP expects, using the mapping you configured, and passes max_age along with it. A standards-compliant OIDC IdP honors acr_values the same way Amazon Cognito does: it drives the user through an authentication that satisfies the requested level, and it returns its own acr value describing what the user reached. max_age carries forward in the same way, so a freshness requirement is enforced at the provider that actually authenticates the user rather than being lost at the broker. Keep in mind that this is only supported with OIDC identity providers.

The request is unchanged from the application’s point of view. It still directs to Amazon Cognito:

GET https://auth.example.com/oauth2/authorize
  ?response_type=code
  &client_id=abc123def456
  &redirect_uri=https://app.example.com/callback
  &scope=openid
  &identity_provider=PartnerOIDC
  &acr_values=urn:cognito:loa:3
  &max_age=300

The interaction gains a third participant, the downstream IdP, but the assurance requirement is persisted through the entire federated authentication flow as shown in figure 2.

Figure 2: Federation with an OIDC third-party IdP, persisting the acr_values and max_age request parameters

The value that comes back from a partner IdP won’t use Amazon Cognito’s level URIs, so this lets you map the provider’s acr values onto its own levels with the AcrMapping field on the OIDC IdP configuration. A partner IdP that reports, say, https://partner.example/assurance/strong can be mapped to Amazon Cognito level 3 (urn:cognito:loa:3), so that by the time the token reaches your application the acr claim speaks the same vocabulary regardless of whether the user authenticated locally or through a federated provider. Your resource server keeps a single enforcement rule and authorization logic and doesn’t need to have special handling depending on where the user ultimately authenticated. See Step-up authentication for federated users to learn how to map external OIDC IdP acr levels to Cognito.

This is the same pattern that RFC 9470, the OAuth 2.0 Step Up Authentication Challenge Protocol, describes: the assurance level is requested at the edge of your application, travels through Amazon Cognito to whatever provider authenticates the user, and returns normalized to a vocabulary your code already understands. A user federating from a corporate IdP and a user signing in against the same user pool directly both arrive at your resource server carrying an acr claim that means the same thing.

Conclusion

In this post, I showed you how the acr and amr claims in Amazon Cognito let you match authentication strength to the risk of what a user is doing, instead of settling for one bar at the front door. Your application requests a target level with acr_values and max_age (or TARGET_ACR_VALUES and MAX_AGE in the USER_AUTH flow), Amazon Cognito reports the level reached and the methods used, and your application enforces what each operation requires. The four patterns, from a banking transfer to a federated third-party IdP, follow that same loop, and one enforcement rule at your resource server covers every sign-in path.

The larger shift is that assurance is now something Amazon Cognito expresses in a standard way and your application reasons about directly, without building your own step-up tracking. To get started, move your user pool to the Essentials or Plus feature plan, decide the level each operation requires, and add acr_values to your existing authorize requests. For the complete parameter reference and federated behavior, see the Amazon Cognito Developer Guide.

If you have questions about this post, contact AWS Support or start a new thread on AWS re:Post.

items.summary: TL;DR: Two critical vulnerabilities in NGINX’s HTTP/2 implementation, CVE-2026-123633 and CVE-2026-123007, could allow unauthenticated attackers to execute code remotely on affected servers. Both vulnerabilities carry a CVSS v4.0 score of 9.2 and require HTTP/2 to be enabled. Organizations should identify affected NGINX deployments and apply available security updates immediately. items.title: NGINX2Root: Five nginx Flaws, Led by CVE-2026-123007. How to Find, Mitigate, and Patch Now
items.summary: Executive Summary NGINX2Root is a set of five nginx vulnerabilities disclosed on November 18, 2026. The lead flaw, CVE-2026-123007, is a memory corruption bug in the way nginx handles HTTP/2 connections. F5, which maintains nginx, rates it 9.2 under CVSS v4.0 and 8.1 under CVSS v3.1. An attacker with no credentials can crash nginx worker processes, and researchers have demonstrated remote code execution with the privileges of the nginx worker. Where the worker runs without root privileges, an attacker would need an additional escalation path to gain root. This could involve chaining the NGINX vulnerability with a suitable local privilege-escalation flaw. Unpatched builds of NGINX Open Source from 1.9.5 through 1.31.8, and unpatched NGINX Plus builds, are in scope when HTTP/2 is enabled. Fixes shipped in NGINX Open Source 1.30.7 and 1.31.9, and turning off HTTP/2 closes this exposure where patching has to wait. A separate Linux kernel flaw that the researchers used to go from the worker account to root has no patch yet. Start with internet-facing nginx servers that accept HTTP/2, and assign an owner and a deadline to every system still unpatched. What’s at Risk A Flaw in nginx Could Hand Attackers the Front Door to Your Applications. nginx is often the first system a web request reaches. It runs as a web server, a reverse proxy (a server that passes requests to the applications behind it), a load balancer, and the entry point to Kubernetes clusters. CVE-2026-123007 is in nginx’s own HTTP/2 code, so no application behind it has to be at fault. HTTP/2 lets a client tell the server how much data it is allowed to send. nginx can lose count of that allowance when a client cancels requests at the right moment. The bad count later makes nginx copy memory it should not touch. F5 says the result is typically a crash of the nginx worker, the process that handles live traffic. F5 also says code execution is possible where ASLR, the memory-address randomization that makes exploits harder, is disabled or bypassed. Xint , the team that named NGINX2Root, reports doing exactly that: it leaked memory addresses and then ran commands as the nginx worker over a public HTTPS port. In Qualys TRU’s assessment, three outcomes matter to the business: Exposure of traffic and keys. Code running in the worker can read requests and responses after nginx decrypts them, including passwords and session tokens. It may also expose TLS private keys that are held in software and accessible to the worker. A foothold behind the perimeter. Backend systems usually trust the proxy in front of them. An attacker on that proxy starts from a trusted position. Outages. A failed attempt can still crash workers and drop connections. Workers normally run under a restricted account. An attacker gets whatever privileges the worker actually has, so if it already runs as root, no further escalation is needed in that environment. Where it does not, the researchers chained a separate flaw in the Linux kernel’s SCTP code to get root. SCTP is a network protocol, like TCP, that the kernel supports. They report root on the host, including from nginx running inside a Docker container. That kernel flaw has no CVE and no patch yet, so patching nginx removes the remote entry point but not the step to root. NGINX2Root covers four more nginx flaws. F5 scores all five 9.2 under CVSS v4.0 and 8.1 under CVSS v3.1, and the same nginx releases fix them. Each needs a different configuration: CVE CONFIGURATION THAT PUTS A SERVER IN SCOPE DOES TURNING OFF HTTP/2 HELP? CVE-2026-123007 HTTP/2 enabled Yes CVE-2026-123633 HTTP/2 for clients, requests passed to a backend, and a worker running low on connections Yes CVE-2026-123634 Proxying where the backend server name contains variables, plus an SSI or mirror subrequest that looks up the same name No CVE-2026-121810 HTTP/3 enabled No CVE-2026-113425 nginx used as a mail proxy No The rest of this post focuses on CVE-2026-123007, the flaw with the widest reach. Are You Affected? A system is in scope only when both conditions are true. For an attack to work, the attacker must also be able to open an HTTP/2 connection to nginx itself. CONDITION AFFECTED NOT AFFECTED NGINX BUILD Unpatched NGINX Open Source 1.9.5 through 1.31.8. Unpatched NGINX Plus: 37.0.0 before 37.0.8.1, 37.1.0 before 37.3.0.1, and R33 and later R-series releases NGINX Open Source 1.30.7 and 1.31.9. Releases before 1.9.5, which predate HTTP/2 support. Builds compiled without the HTTP/2 module. Any vendor build that contains the fix HTTP/2 Turned on for at least one listener, with http2 on ; or with http2 on a listen line Not turned on for any listener F5 notes that it did not evaluate versions past End of Technical Support. F5 also lists BIG-IP, BIG-IQ, and F5OS as not vulnerable in its advisory . The checks below come from the researchers’ write-up. Run them on the nginx host. The first shows whether the build includes HTTP/2. The second shows whether the configuration turns it on. nginx -V 2>&1 | grep -o — ‘–with-http_v2_module’ sudo nginx -T 2>&1 | sed ‘s/#.*//’ | grep -nE ‘listen[[:space:]].*http2|^[[:space:]]*http2[[:space:]]+on[[:space:]]*;’ Run this one from outside your network. ALPN protocol: h2 means the server accepts HTTP/2 from the internet. openssl s_client -connect HOST:443 -servername HOST -alpn h2 &1 | grep -E ‘ALPN protocol:|No ALPN negotiated’ nginx also ships inside other software. Status as of November 18, 2026: WHERE NGINX RUNS STATUS F5 NGINX INGRESS CONTROLLER Release 5.8.0 builds on NGINX Open Source 1.31.9. For NGINX Plus images, confirm the build against F5’s advisory F5 NGINX GATEWAY FABRIC Release 2.9.0 moves to NGINX Open Source 1.31.9. For NGINX Plus images, confirm the build against F5’s advisory COMMUNITY INGRESS-NGINX FOR KUBERNETES Archived in March 2026. The project states it will ship no further security fixes LINUX DISTRIBUTION PACKAGES Ubuntu and Debian list their nginx packages as vulnerable, with no fixed package yet OFFICIAL DOCKER IMAGE Mainline tags now point to 1.31.9. Running containers stay on the old build until you pull and redeploy OTHER PRODUCTS THAT BUNDLE NGINX Potentially affected. Verify the bundled nginx version, vendor backports, and whether the vulnerable feature is enabled Three cautions when scoping: Do not rely on nginx -v alone. Distributions often fix a flaw without changing the nginx version number. Compare the full package version with the distribution’s advisory. Check where the HTTP/2 connection ends. If a CDN or load balancer handles HTTP/2 in front of nginx, an outside test only reaches that device. Test the nginx port directly. Use internet exposure to order the work, not to close findings. An internal nginx with HTTP/2 on is still reachable by an attacker who is already inside the network. Exploitation Status As of November 18, 2026, we have not seen public confirmation of exploitation in the wild. Working exploit code is public. The team behind NGINX2Root also reports its own exploit working over public IP addresses on AWS, GCP, and Azure, and is holding back the final steps. The public exploit is hard to use. It sends a very large number of HTTP/2 control messages over one long-lived connection for several minutes, has to reach nginx directly, and depends on a specific memory-copy routine in the standard Linux C library on 64-bit Intel and AMD processors. These limits slow mass exploitation. In Qualys TRU’s assessment, they do not protect a specific internet-facing server from a capable attacker, and other techniques may follow. What to Do Now Updating nginx is the only complete fix. F5 released fixed builds on November 18, 2026. PRODUCT AFFECTED FIXED BUILD NGINX OPEN SOURCE, MAINLINE 1.31.0 through 1.31.8 1.31.9 NGINX OPEN SOURCE, STABLE 1.30.0 through 1.30.6 1.30.7 NGINX OPEN SOURCE, OLDER BRANCHES 1.9.5 through 1.29.x None listed. Move to 1.30.7 or 1.31.9, or use a vendor package that contains the fix NGINX PLUS 37.1 AND LATER 37.1.0 before 37.3.0.1 37.3.0.1 NGINX PLUS 37.0 37.0.0 before 37.0.8.1 37.0.8.1 NGINX PLUS R-SERIES R34 through R36 in F5’s advisory, R33 and later in the CVE record None listed. Move to a fixed 37.x build Linux distributions publish on their own schedules. As of November 18, 2026, Ubuntu and Debian had not shipped fixed packages. Use your vendor’s advisory to identify the fixed package and confirm it addresses CVE-2026-123007. Restart nginx after you update. A reload applies configuration changes but keeps the old program running, so the flaw stays in memory until a restart. If you cannot patch today, turn off HTTP/2 on every affected listener. F5 states the flaw affects only configurations that use HTTP/2, and the researchers recommend this as a temporary measure. For the exact steps, see nginx’s documentation for the http2 directive , CERT-EU’s advisory , and section 3.3 of the researchers’ write-up . Clients fall back to HTTP/1.1. Services that need HTTP/2, such as gRPC, will stop working, so test first. This covers CVE-2026-123007 and CVE-2026-123633 only, and it does not replace the patch. Advice for Risk and Vulnerability Management Teams Qualys TRU’s advice for the teams running this response: Do not let the score set the deadline: Under CVSS v3.1 this flaw is 8.1, which many remediation policies file as High. Public exploit code and a server that faces the internet matter more than the number. Handle vulnerable nginx deployments with externally reachable HTTP/2 as an emergency. Close findings on evidence: A server is done when the fixed build is installed, nginx has been restarted, and the vendor’s advisory confirms the package covers all five CVEs. Report patched, temporarily mitigated, not exposed by configuration, and unknown as separate states, and do not count unknown as safe. Fix the template as well as the server: Update container images, Helm charts, machine images, and autoscaling templates. Otherwise the next scale-out or failover brings the vulnerable build back. Put an end date on every workaround: Turning off HTTP/2 covers two of the five flaws, and the next configuration push can undo it. Record who owns each exception and when it ends. Decide what to do with nginx that will not get a fix: The community ingress-nginx project is archived, and the older NGINX Plus R-series branches have no fixed build listed, although fixed NGINX Plus 37.x releases exist. These need a migration plan or a signed risk acceptance. Treat privilege escalation flaws as part of this response: Where the worker runs without root privileges, an attacker would need an additional escalation path to gain root. The newly disclosed SCTP flaw is one such path, and any other local privilege-escalation flaw that can be exploited from the worker’s context could serve the same purpose. Patch known local privilege-escalation flaws on nginx hosts, in the kernel and elsewhere, with the same urgency. A current kernel does not mean the SCTP flaw is fixed, because that flaw has no patch yet. How Qualys Can Help Inventory nginx Installations with Qualys CSAM Qualys CyberSecurity Asset Management (CSAM) lists every asset with nginx installed, along with the version of each installation, so teams can quickly scope NGINX2Root remediation. Because NGINX Open Source 1.9.5 through 1.31.8 is affected, the version tells you which installations are in range. It does not tell you whether HTTP/2 is turned on or whether a Linux distribution has backported the fix, so check those separately. nginx bundled in containers, Kubernetes ingress controllers, and appliances may not appear in a standard inventory, so check those separately too. Assets With nginx in the Affected Range Use the following CSAM query to identify potentially affected NGINX Open Source installations on the stable, mainline, and older branches for further assessment. It uses two ranges because 1.31.0 through 1.31.8 are affected even though they are higher than the fixed 1.30.7. software:(name:”nginx” AND ( (version>=1.9.5 AND version<1.30.7) OR (version>=1.31.0 AND version<1.31.9) )) Detection VMDR QIDs Qualys is releasing the following detection QIDs. We will add distribution-specific detection QIDs to this blog as they are released. QID Detection Title Release 736231 NGINX Open Source Multiple Security Vulnerabilities (K000164058) TBD By EOD 389654 F5 NGINX Plus Multiple Security Vulnerabilities (K000164058) TBD By EOD
items.summary_html:
Executive Summary

NGINX2Root is a set of five nginx vulnerabilities disclosed on November 18, 2026. The lead flaw, CVE-2026-123007, is a memory corruption bug in the way nginx handles HTTP/2 connections. F5, which maintains nginx, rates it 9.2 under CVSS v4.0 and 8.1 under CVSS v3.1. An attacker with no credentials can crash nginx worker processes, and researchers have demonstrated remote code execution with the privileges of the nginx worker. Where the worker runs without root privileges, an attacker would need an additional escalation path to gain root. This could involve chaining the NGINX vulnerability with a suitable local privilege-escalation flaw.

Unpatched builds of NGINX Open Source from 1.9.5 through 1.31.8, and unpatched NGINX Plus builds, are in scope when HTTP/2 is enabled. Fixes shipped in NGINX Open Source 1.30.7 and 1.31.9, and turning off HTTP/2 closes this exposure where patching has to wait. A separate Linux kernel flaw that the researchers used to go from the worker account to root has no patch yet. Start with internet-facing nginx servers that accept HTTP/2, and assign an owner and a deadline to every system still unpatched.

What’s at Risk

A Flaw in nginx Could Hand Attackers the Front Door to Your Applications. nginx is often the first system a web request reaches. It runs as a web server, a reverse proxy (a server that passes requests to the applications behind it), a load balancer, and the entry point to Kubernetes clusters. CVE-2026-123007 is in nginx’s own HTTP/2 code, so no application behind it has to be at fault.

HTTP/2 lets a client tell the server how much data it is allowed to send. nginx can lose count of that allowance when a client cancels requests at the right moment. The bad count later makes nginx copy memory it should not touch.

F5 says the result is typically a crash of the nginx worker, the process that handles live traffic. F5 also says code execution is possible where ASLR, the memory-address randomization that makes exploits harder, is disabled or bypassed. Xint, the team that named NGINX2Root, reports doing exactly that: it leaked memory addresses and then ran commands as the nginx worker over a public HTTPS port.

In Qualys TRU’s assessment, three outcomes matter to the business:

  • Exposure of traffic and keys. Code running in the worker can read requests and responses after nginx decrypts them, including passwords and session tokens. It may also expose TLS private keys that are held in software and accessible to the worker.
  • A foothold behind the perimeter. Backend systems usually trust the proxy in front of them. An attacker on that proxy starts from a trusted position.
  • Outages. A failed attempt can still crash workers and drop connections.

Workers normally run under a restricted account. An attacker gets whatever privileges the worker actually has, so if it already runs as root, no further escalation is needed in that environment. Where it does not, the researchers chained a separate flaw in the Linux kernel’s SCTP code to get root. SCTP is a network protocol, like TCP, that the kernel supports. They report root on the host, including from nginx running inside a Docker container. That kernel flaw has no CVE and no patch yet, so patching nginx removes the remote entry point but not the step to root.

NGINX2Root covers four more nginx flaws. F5 scores all five 9.2 under CVSS v4.0 and 8.1 under CVSS v3.1, and the same nginx releases fix them. Each needs a different configuration:

CVECONFIGURATION THAT PUTS A SERVER IN SCOPEDOES TURNING OFF HTTP/2 HELP?CVE-2026-123007HTTP/2 enabledYesCVE-2026-123633HTTP/2 for clients, requests passed to a backend, and a worker running low on connectionsYesCVE-2026-123634Proxying where the backend server name contains variables, plus an SSI or mirror subrequest that looks up the same nameNoCVE-2026-121810HTTP/3 enabledNoCVE-2026-113425nginx used as a mail proxyNo

The rest of this post focuses on CVE-2026-123007, the flaw with the widest reach.

Are You Affected?

A system is in scope only when both conditions are true. For an attack to work, the attacker must also be able to open an HTTP/2 connection to nginx itself.

CONDITIONAFFECTEDNOT AFFECTEDNGINX BUILDUnpatched NGINX Open Source 1.9.5 through 1.31.8. Unpatched NGINX Plus: 37.0.0 before 37.0.8.1, 37.1.0 before 37.3.0.1, and R33 and later R-series releasesNGINX Open Source 1.30.7 and 1.31.9. Releases before 1.9.5, which predate HTTP/2 support. Builds compiled without the HTTP/2 module. Any vendor build that contains the fixHTTP/2Turned on for at least one listener, with http2 on; or with http2 on a listen lineNot turned on for any listener

F5 notes that it did not evaluate versions past End of Technical Support. F5 also lists BIG-IP, BIG-IQ, and F5OS as not vulnerable in its advisory.

The checks below come from the researchers’ write-up. Run them on the nginx host. The first shows whether the build includes HTTP/2. The second shows whether the configuration turns it on.

nginx -V 2>&1 | grep -o — ‘–with-http_v2_module’

sudo nginx -T 2>&1 | sed ‘s/#.*//’ | grep -nE ‘listen[[:space:]].*http2|^[[:space:]]*http2[[:space:]]+on[[:space:]]*;’

Run this one from outside your network. ALPN protocol: h2 means the server accepts HTTP/2 from the internet.

openssl s_client -connect HOST:443 -servername HOST -alpn h2 &1 | grep -E ‘ALPN protocol:|No ALPN negotiated’

nginx also ships inside other software. Status as of November 18, 2026:

WHERE NGINX RUNSSTATUSF5 NGINX INGRESS CONTROLLERRelease 5.8.0 builds on NGINX Open Source 1.31.9. For NGINX Plus images, confirm the build against F5’s advisoryF5 NGINX GATEWAY FABRICRelease 2.9.0 moves to NGINX Open Source 1.31.9. For NGINX Plus images, confirm the build against F5’s advisoryCOMMUNITY INGRESS-NGINXFOR KUBERNETESArchived in March 2026. The project states it will ship no further security fixesLINUX DISTRIBUTION PACKAGESUbuntu and Debian list their nginx packages as vulnerable, with no fixed package yetOFFICIAL DOCKER IMAGEMainline tags now point to 1.31.9. Running containers stay on the old build until you pull and redeployOTHER PRODUCTS THAT BUNDLE NGINXPotentially affected. Verify the bundled nginx version, vendor backports, and whether the vulnerable feature is enabled

Three cautions when scoping:

  • Do not rely on nginx -v alone. Distributions often fix a flaw without changing the nginx version number. Compare the full package version with the distribution’s advisory.
  • Check where the HTTP/2 connection ends. If a CDN or load balancer handles HTTP/2 in front of nginx, an outside test only reaches that device. Test the nginx port directly.
  • Use internet exposure to order the work, not to close findings. An internal nginx with HTTP/2 on is still reachable by an attacker who is already inside the network.
Exploitation Status

As of November 18, 2026, we have not seen public confirmation of exploitation in the wild.

Working exploit code is public. The team behind NGINX2Root also reports its own exploit working over public IP addresses on AWS, GCP, and Azure, and is holding back the final steps.

The public exploit is hard to use. It sends a very large number of HTTP/2 control messages over one long-lived connection for several minutes, has to reach nginx directly, and depends on a specific memory-copy routine in the standard Linux C library on 64-bit Intel and AMD processors.

These limits slow mass exploitation. In Qualys TRU’s assessment, they do not protect a specific internet-facing server from a capable attacker, and other techniques may follow.

What to Do Now

Updating nginx is the only complete fix. F5 released fixed builds on November 18, 2026.

PRODUCTAFFECTEDFIXED BUILDNGINX OPEN SOURCE, MAINLINE1.31.0 through 1.31.81.31.9NGINX OPEN SOURCE, STABLE1.30.0 through 1.30.61.30.7NGINX OPEN SOURCE, OLDER BRANCHES1.9.5 through 1.29.xNone listed. Move to 1.30.7 or 1.31.9, or use a vendor package that contains the fixNGINX PLUS 37.1 AND LATER37.1.0 before 37.3.0.137.3.0.1NGINX PLUS 37.037.0.0 before 37.0.8.137.0.8.1NGINX PLUS R-SERIESR34 through R36 in F5’s advisory, R33 and later in the CVE recordNone listed. Move to a fixed 37.x build

Linux distributions publish on their own schedules. As of November 18, 2026, Ubuntu and Debian had not shipped fixed packages. Use your vendor’s advisory to identify the fixed package and confirm it addresses CVE-2026-123007.

Restart nginx after you update. A reload applies configuration changes but keeps the old program running, so the flaw stays in memory until a restart.

If you cannot patch today, turn off HTTP/2 on every affected listener. F5 states the flaw affects only configurations that use HTTP/2, and the researchers recommend this as a temporary measure. For the exact steps, see nginx’s documentation for the http2 directive, CERT-EU’s advisory, and section 3.3 of the researchers’ write-up. Clients fall back to HTTP/1.1. Services that need HTTP/2, such as gRPC, will stop working, so test first. This covers CVE-2026-123007 and CVE-2026-123633 only, and it does not replace the patch.

Advice for Risk and Vulnerability Management Teams

Qualys TRU’s advice for the teams running this response:

  • Do not let the score set the deadline: Under CVSS v3.1 this flaw is 8.1, which many remediation policies file as High. Public exploit code and a server that faces the internet matter more than the number. Handle vulnerable nginx deployments with externally reachable HTTP/2 as an emergency.
  • Close findings on evidence: A server is done when the fixed build is installed, nginx has been restarted, and the vendor’s advisory confirms the package covers all five CVEs. Report patched, temporarily mitigated, not exposed by configuration, and unknown as separate states, and do not count unknown as safe.
  • Fix the template as well as the server: Update container images, Helm charts, machine images, and autoscaling templates. Otherwise the next scale-out or failover brings the vulnerable build back.
  • Put an end date on every workaround: Turning off HTTP/2 covers two of the five flaws, and the next configuration push can undo it. Record who owns each exception and when it ends.
  • Decide what to do with nginx that will not get a fix: The community ingress-nginx project is archived, and the older NGINX Plus R-series branches have no fixed build listed, although fixed NGINX Plus 37.x releases exist. These need a migration plan or a signed risk acceptance.
  • Treat privilege escalation flaws as part of this response: Where the worker runs without root privileges, an attacker would need an additional escalation path to gain root. The newly disclosed SCTP flaw is one such path, and any other local privilege-escalation flaw that can be exploited from the worker’s context could serve the same purpose. Patch known local privilege-escalation flaws on nginx hosts, in the kernel and elsewhere, with the same urgency. A current kernel does not mean the SCTP flaw is fixed, because that flaw has no patch yet.
How Qualys Can Help

Inventory nginx Installations with Qualys CSAM

Qualys CyberSecurity Asset Management (CSAM) lists every asset with nginx installed, along with the version of each installation, so teams can quickly scope NGINX2Root remediation. Because NGINX Open Source 1.9.5 through 1.31.8 is affected, the version tells you which installations are in range. It does not tell you whether HTTP/2 is turned on or whether a Linux distribution has backported the fix, so check those separately. nginx bundled in containers, Kubernetes ingress controllers, and appliances may not appear in a standard inventory, so check those separately too.

Assets With nginx in the Affected Range

Use the following CSAM query to identify potentially affected NGINX Open Source installations on the stable, mainline, and older branches for further assessment. It uses two ranges because 1.31.0 through 1.31.8 are affected even though they are higher than the fixed 1.30.7.

software:(name:”nginx” AND ( (version>=1.9.5 AND version<1.30.7) OR (version>=1.31.0 AND version<1.31.9) ))

Qualys is releasing the following detection QIDs. We will add distribution-specific detection QIDs to this blog as they are released.

items.title: Detecting cross-cloud lateral movement with AWS Security Hub
items.summary: Most organizations run a multicloud estate, and so do the attackers targeting them. An adversary who compromises an identity in one provider follows that identity wherever it leads, including across a federated trust into a second cloud service provider. The signals enumerating this scenario are rarely missing; the problem is that they live in separate consoles, in different schemas, owned by different teams. No one has visibility into the whole picture, so no one can decide what to fix first. AWS Security Hub addresses prioritization and triage with exposure findings. Security Hub correlates reachability, blast radius, vulnerabilities, misconfigurations, and effective permissions, providing a strong correlation layer with an attack-path visualization, providing the context needed to generate risks from findings. That analysis now extends to Microsoft Azure. Security Hub records and analyzes your Azure resources with the same correlation engine used for Amazon Web Services (AWS) resources. The resulting details and meta-data land in the same console, ranked in the same queue, providing holistic, multicloud visibility into your security risks. In this blog post, you learn how to configure the Azure integration for Security Hub and use exposure findings to prioritize attack paths across both clouds from one console. We follow a realistic scenario: a compromised identity that threatens both an Azure and an AWS environment through a shared, federated identity plane. We show you how the critical exposures along that path are presented as ranked findings that you can triage together, and we map each one to the MITRE ATT&CK framework. We also cover the prerequisites that teams commonly overlook. Why prioritizing multicloud risk is difficult Consider an organization whose Microsoft Entra ID tenant is federated into an AWS account, so identities in the tenant can assume an AWS role. This is an ordinary and intentional configuration used to avoid having to manage a second set of credentials. It also means the two clouds share an identity plane: a single compromised Entra identity is both an Azure threat and—through the federation—an AWS threat. An attacker exploits this, but the defensive signals land in different places: Where the risk lives Traditionally visible in Owned by Weak Entra identity controls: over-privileged identities, no multi-factor authentication (MFA), vulnerable conditional access policies (CAP) Entra ID and Microsoft Defender for Cloud Identity team Internet-reachable Azure host with admin rights Defender for Cloud Azure platform team Federated trust into AWS AWS Identity and Access Management (IAM) Cloud security team Sensitive data and over-exposed resources in AWS AWS security tooling Cloud security team Each team sees one fragment, and in isolation each fragment appears low severity. You see the risk only when you correlate all of it together and discover the same identity plane ties the attack path together. Exposure findings provide that severity within AWS; extending it to Azure closes the multicloud visibility gap. How the Azure integration works You create the Azure connector in the AWS Management Console for Security Hub. It authenticates to your Entra ID tenant through an application registration, records and evaluates your Azure resource configurations, and streams Microsoft Defender for Cloud alerts and Entra ID audit logs through an Azure Event Hubs namespace. Your Azure resources then flow into the same correlation engine that analyzes signals from AWS Security Hub Cloud Security Posture Management (CSPM) , Amazon Inspector , Amazon Macie , and Amazon GuardDuty . That engine produces two kinds of findings: Control findings against standards such as the CIS Microsoft Azure Foundations Benchmark. Exposure findings , which are ranked, attack-path findings that correlate traits such as reachability, effective permissions, and misconfiguration, with a severity based on how discoverable and exploitable the risk is. Both use the Open Cybersecurity Schema Framework (OCSF) and appear in the same console as your AWS findings. However, one filtering detail matters: because Security Hub produces the finding, its top-level cloud.provider is AWS, while the evaluated resource carries resources[].provider = Azure . Filter on resources.provider to scope to a single cloud. Prerequisites To follow along with this post, you need: An AWS account with Security Hub enabled. If you use a delegated administrator account for Security Hub, create the connector there, in the AWS Region where you aggregate findings. An Entra ID tenant with a Microsoft Azure subscription. You need privileges in Azure to create an application registration, assign roles at the tenant root management group, and create a subscription-level diagnostic setting. The Azure CLI, authenticated to the target subscription with az login command. Activity log export. Azure resource recordings are change-driven and depend on activity logs reaching the event hub that the connector reads. The onboarding process assigns an Azure policy to create the required diagnostic setting, but it only remediates existing subscriptions after you create a remediation task. If the connector reports healthy status but resources never appear, run az monitor diagnostic-settings subscription list to confirm the export exists, and create a remediation task if the list is empty. Configuration The following steps detail how to connect your Azure environment to Security Hub v2: Registering the Azure application, establishing federated identity credentials, and assigning the roles required for AWS to evaluate your Azure resources. Step 1: Create the Azure connector in Security Hub The first step in this configuration is to create the Azure connector in Security Hub. The connector establishes trust with your Azure tenant and defines which subscriptions and regions Security Hub v2 will evaluate. Open the Security Hub console and choose Integrations . Choose Create Azure connector . Enter your Azure Tenant ID and the Application (client) ID of the application registration you created for the integration. For Subscriptions and Regions , select all. Attack paths cross subscription and Region boundaries, so partial coverage leaves blind spots where a compromised identity can pivot unseen. Scope to specific IDs or Regions only when data-residency rules require it. Run the generated setup script in your Azure environment, then choose Create connector . Include the global region scope. Controls that evaluate Entra ID and Microsoft Graph resources require it, and those identity exposures are central to this scenario. If you also create an Amazon Inspector or Security Hub CSPM connector for the same tenant, keep its subscriptions and regions consistent with this one. Step 2: Verify the connector and its recording activity Health status alone doesn’t tell you whether recording is flowing. Confirm both. AWS Command Line interface (AWS CLI) command 1: Verify connector health and recording state aws securityhub list-connectors-v2 --region \ --query "Connectors[?ProviderSummary.ProviderName=='AZURE']" --output json aws securityhub get-resources-v2 --region --max-results 50 \ --filters '{"CompositeFilters":[{"StringFilters":[{"FieldName":"ResourceType", "Filter":{"Value":"microsoft.compute/virtualmachines","Comparison":"EQUALS"}}]}], "CompositeOperator":"AND"}' \ --query "Resources[].{id:ResourceId, captured:ResourceDetailCaptureTimeDt}" --output table Step 3: Query exposure findings for Azure resources Scope to Azure by filtering on the resource provider. AWS CLI command 2: Retrieve exposure findings for Azure resources ​​aws securityhub get-findings-v2 --region --max-results 50 \ --filters '{"CompositeFilters":[ {"StringFilters":[{"FieldName":"resources.provider","Filter":{"Value":"Azure","Comparison":"EQUALS"}}]}, {"StringFilters":[{"FieldName":"metadata.product.feature.uid","Filter":{"Value":"security-hub/Exposure","Comparison":"EQUALS"}}]}], "CompositeOperator":"AND"}' \ --query "Findings[].{sev:severity, title:finding_info.title}" --output table​ Step 4 (optional): Add Amazon Inspector for Azure vulnerability scanning To add vulnerability findings for Azure virtual machines (VMs), function apps, or container registry images, create an Amazon Inspector connector for the same tenant. VM scanning requires each target VM to have a system-assigned managed identity, which you can enforce with an Azure Policy. Figure 1 shows a correctly configured Azure integration inside Security Hub, with vulnerability management and posture management deployed. Figure 1: Successful configuration of the Azure integration with Security Hub Step 5: Prerequisites for Microsoft Azure See the AWS documentation for the prerequisites for Microsoft Azure . Walk-through: Prioritizing a cross-cloud attack path In this example, the organization has one identity plane across two clouds, comprising a Microsoft Entra ID tenant with a federated trust into an AWS account. An adversary who compromises the right Entra identity gains an initial foothold in Azure and a path into AWS, because both clouds trust the same identity plane. The following sections trace that path. Each step is a real, high-severity exposure finding that Security Hub ranked on its own. The point of the walk-through is to demonstrate a real-life scenario and examine all findings in one unified security console. Phase 1: A compromised identity (Azure) ATT&CK: Phishing (T1566), Valid Accounts: Cloud Accounts (T1078.004) The path begins with an Entra identity that is both over-privileged and unprotected. You’ll find this in the Security Hub console under Exposures , where Security Hub raises it as an identity exposure finding and maps the attack path stemming from it: Potential Unauthorized Access: Azure RBAC user with administrative access has MFA disabled (high). It correlates the user, the role assignment that grants administrative access, and the organization. The tenant’s authorization policies let an attacker broaden that foothold, and Security Hub CSPM reports each policy as a failed control (high): Microsoft Entra ID authorization policies should prohibit default users from registering applications…should restrict user consent for applications , and Azure authorization policies should restrict guest invitations to admin roles only . Each finding expands what a single compromised, non-privileged identity can do without an administrator. Phase 2: Foothold and privilege escalation (Azure) ATT&CK: Exploit Public-Facing Application (T1190), Valid Accounts: Cloud Accounts (T1078.004) The tenant contains an internet-reachable VM whose network security group allows inbound from any address, and whose attached identity holds administrative rights over the subscription. Security Hub surfaces this under Exposures , correlating reachability and effective permissions into one finding that shows why it matters: anyone reaching the VM inherits admin control of the subscription.: Potential Initial Access: Potentially internet reachable Azure virtual machine with open network security group has administrative access (high). It correlates the VM, the role assignment, the network security group, and the public IP address. The finding’s analysis reads like an attack path. The resource “may be reachable from the public internet,” “overly permissive network security group (NSG) rules allow unintended inbound access,” and “the Owner or Contributor role grants extensive permissions… enabling a threat actor to escalate privileges.” Security Hub evaluates this from configuration and network-path modeling, so it surfaces whether or not the VM is running. Figure 2 shows the correlated attack path for that virtual machine. Figure 2: An Azure attack-path exposure, analyzed by the same correlation engine as AWS exposures The cross-cloud bridge: Federation into AWS The tenant from Phases 1 and 2 is federated into the AWS account through an IAM SAML identity provider. As shown in Figure 2, a role trusts that provider and grants read access to every bucket in Amazon Simple Storage Service (Amazon S3) . This trust is what expands the risk across clouds from the same adversary: a compromised Entra identity can assume this role and reach AWS data. This one hop lives in IAM rather than in Security Hub. Security Hub doesn’t not raise a finding for a role that trusts your own federated identity provider. Confirming it is a normal investigative pivot: the role trusts a SAML identity provider that represents your Entra tenant, the same tenant whose exposures you triaged when you added Amazon Inspector in Step 4. Figure 3: The federated trust that links the two clouds through a shared identity plane Phase 3: The impact (AWS) ATT&CK: Data from Cloud Storage (T1530), Transfer Data to Cloud Account (T1537) On the AWS side, the correlation engine has already categorized the resources this identity can reach. Under Exposures in the Security Hub console, the sensitive-data objective surfaces this finding because that reachable set includes data at risk; a compromised identity could destroy it: Potential Sensitive Data Destruction: S3 bucket has sensitive data and versioning disabled and Object Lock disabled and MFA delete disabled (high). A Macie finding, The S3 object contains personal information , is a contributing signal, and the control S3 general purpose buckets should be encrypted at rest with AWS KMS keys fails alongside it. The same account carries related AWS attack-path exposures. Two examples are Potential Resource Hijacking: Internet reachable EC2 instance with open security group has software vulnerabilities with limited effective permissions and Potential Unauthorized Access: IAM user has weak password policies . In the exposure queue, these sit next to the Azure findings, ranked by the same severity model. Prioritizing across both clouds in the console Here is the operational benefit. An analyst is notified of generated exposure findings and opens the dashboard and filters to High severity. In one prioritized list, without switching tools or opening a ticket for another team, they see the Azure admin identity without MFA, the internet-reachable Azure VM with subscription-admin rights, and the AWS sensitive data exposure. Together, these show the full scope of what a single vector, sharing an identity plane, might target. The analyst confirms the connecting federation with one pivot into IAM. The multicloud triage that used to require two products and two teams now occurs in one place. Figure 4 shows that single ranked queue. Figure 4: Cross-cloud exposure prioritization in a single console Phase-to-exposure summary The following table traces each phase of the attack path to its MITRE ATT&CK techniques, the cloud where it plays out, and the ranked Security Hub exposure that surfaces it — following the pivot from Azure into AWS across the shared identity plane. Phase ATT&CK Cloud Ranked exposure in Security Hub 1. Compromised identity T1566, T1078.004 Azure Potential Unauthorized Access: Azure RBAC user with administrative access has MFA disabled (High) 2. Foothold and privilege escalation T1190, T1078.004 Azure Potential Initial Access: internet reachable Azure VM with open NSG has administrative access (High) 2.1 Bridge T1550 (Use Alternate Authentication Material) Azure to AWS Federated trust, confirmed in AWS IAM (shared identity plane) 3. Data objective T1530, T1537 AWS Potential Sensitive Data Destruction: S3 bucket has sensitive data… (High), plus Macie Conclusion A cross-cloud attack is difficult to prioritize because signals are generated across separate consoles, schemas, and teams. In this post, you saw how the Azure integration for AWS Security Hub brings Azure resources into the same exposure engine and the same queue as your AWS resources. One analyst can prioritize an attack path that spans a compromised Microsoft Entra ID identity, across a federated trust, to sensitive data in Amazon S3, without leaving Security Hub. To recap why this workflow is practical and effective: Security Hub records and analyzes your Azure security findings and displays them in the same unified console as your AWS resources, and produces ranked, attack-path exposure findings for both clouds. Findings from both clouds share the OCSF schema, so you filter, group, and prioritize them in one place. Filter on resources.provider to scope an individual cloud. Security Hub correlates signals into attack paths within each cloud. The analysis creates a cross-cloud narrative, such as a shared federated identity plane, while co-locating ranked correlation findings across both Azure and AWS, creating efficient scoping and remediations. Confirm your prerequisites. Include the global region scope for Entra ID controls, know that sign-in log signals require an Entra ID P1 or P2 license, and confirm that the subscription diagnostic setting that exports Activity Logs to the connector’s event hub is in place. A connector can report a healthy status while it records nothing. To get started, see Enabling Microsoft Azure integration in Security Hub and Exposure findings in Security Hub . If you have questions about this post, contact AWS Support or start a new thread on AWS re:Post . Kyle Shields Kyle is a Security Specialist Solutions Architect focused on threat detection and incident response at AWS. Today, he’s focused on helping enterprise AWS customers adopt and operationalize AWS Security Incident Response and improve their security posture. Marshall Jones Marshall is a Worldwide Security Specialist Solutions Architect at AWS. His background is in AWS consulting and security architecture and focused on a variety of security domains including edge, threat detection, and compliance. Today, he’s focused on helping enterprise AWS customers adopt and operationalize AWS security services to increase security effectiveness and reduce risk.

items.title: Outage or attack? Don’t let social media fill in the gaps
items.summary: Your banking app won’t load. Someone posts that an airline is having computer problems. Then you see a screenshot showing trouble at a cloud provider. By the time you’ve scrolled through a few more posts, someone is telling you to withdraw cash and prepare for a nationwide blackout. That is quite a journey from an error message. Recent technology disruptions have provided plenty of material for this kind of speculation. As CNN describes , real outages have become mixed up with exaggerated reports, unrelated events, and conspiracy theories about what might happen next. A routine emergency alert test was even folded into the narrative. The outages are real and so is the inconvenience. The problem with reporting on computer failures is how quickly “the system is down” becomes “the system is under attack.” Non-malicious causes include faulty software updates, configuration mistakes, equipment failures, power interruptions, and damaged cables. Cyberattacks can also disrupt services by overwhelming them with traffic or using ransomware to make systems unusable. From the outside, both can have you staring at much the same unhelpful error message. There has been a lot of this recently. So much so that US Secretary of State Marco Rubio felt the need to dismiss widespread concerns that the recent tech outages in the past week are connected. What actually went down During an outage, users want immediate answers, but investigators need time to establish what’s gone wrong. In that information vacuum, speculation thrives. Let’s have a look at some recent events: European refrigeration attacks disrupted cooling systems at some businesses. Separately, monitoring systems at three French blood-storage sites were affected, but staff intervened before any blood products or samples were compromised. Microsoft 365 outage was caused by a latent software defect in networking gateways. Several organizations lost a full day of work. The FAA nationwide ground stop in the US due to a telecommunications failure that disrupted some air traffic control communications. The ground stop led to thousands of flight cancellations and delays are ongoing. JPMorgan Chase and knock-on banking problems were caused by a software bug in an on-premises hardware system that slowed transaction processing. The issue delayed transactions; no lasting damage has been reported. Optimizely Web Experimentation supply-chain attack served malicious code on 178 popular websites. The issue was fixed rapidly, but visitors may have been exposed to malicious code that infected their devices. There is an important distinction between outages caused by bugs and those caused by attacks, but the cause alone doesn’t tell us how disruptive an incident will be. A technical failure can cause enormous problems without an attacker being involved. And an attack can cause harm without producing a spectacular outage. We should judge the cause and the consequences separately and not assume that the most visible disruption must be the most sinister. How social media amplifies the alarm These things happen all the time, and sometimes the impact is bigger than at other times. That’s not a reason to panic or assume they’re all part of a big conspiracy. The recent claims that the US was about to face a 90-day blackout are a good example. Combined with social media algorithms, these incidents can quickly pull people who show an interest in these incidents into a vortex of bad news, making it feel as if the end of the world is just around the corner. A feed full of outages is not evidence of an approaching “bugalypse.” Before accepting that explanation, ask what connects the incidents beyond the fact that they appeared in your feed. The 90-day blackout claim shows how quickly genuine events can be turned into evidence for a much bigger story. Social media users turned a routine US emergency alert test into a prediction of a 90-day blackout . Some posts pointed to the Microsoft outage and FAA ground stop as evidence that the disaster was already unfolding. Others misrepresented military contingency planning as advance knowledge of an imminent crisis. In reality, the alert was a scheduled test, and the Federal Emergency Management Agency (FEMA) explicitly said there were “no blackouts, no secret emergencies.” The test went ahead without the predicted catastrophe. That is the problem: Genuine disruptions were being used to support a much larger claim for which there was no evidence. Where AI fits in AI is helping both software vendors and attackers find more bugs. That can mean larger updates from Microsoft, Google, and others, covering more vulnerabilities at a faster pace. AI can also help attackers find ways to exploit those vulnerabilities, putting pressure on security teams and consumers to install those patches as soon as possible. Reports of misaligned AI agents can make it harder to see how AI can work both ways. That’s because the balance in cybersecurity isn’t where we want it to be yet. But in other fields, AI is helping scientists and researchers make large strides. For an example of AI doing something genuinely useful, look at protein research . Determining a protein’s three-dimensional structure experimentally can take years. AlphaFold can often generate a useful prediction in minutes or hours, and its freely accessible database contains predictions for more than 200 million protein structures. Those models still need expert scrutiny and, where necessary, experimental validation. But they give researchers a starting point at a speed and scale that laboratory work alone could not match. What to do You can take cybersecurity seriously without treating every error message as a warning of impending disaster. An outage deserves an explanation. An attack deserves investigation. Neither benefits from speculation presented as fact. Companies need to explain what they know, what they’re still investigating, and what customers should do. Those of us reporting on these incidents have a responsibility to make those distinctions clear and not connect the dots before we know whether there is a connection. As readers, we can pause before sharing the next alarming prediction. Does it offer evidence, or just a collection of things that happened around the same time? Is there something useful we should do, or is someone simply giving us another reason to keep scrolling? Keep your software updated. Protect your devices . Have a backup plan for services you depend on. But don’t let someone else’s take on things fill the gaps in what is known. Scammers know more about you than you think.
