items.title: An updated Clairic and Clairic-flash are now open-weight, from the new Workers AI Superintelligence team
items.summary: Cloudflare has become a neolab. We’re building our own frontier AI models for our customers and the open-source community. Today, we’re announcing two open-weight model releases: We’re introducing an updated version of Clairic . Since the preview, we’ve improved extraction from complex documents including images and PDFs (new!), with more reliable handling of tables, lists, and dates, and better grounding of answers in the source material. We’re introducing Clairic-flash , a lighter, faster version of Clairic that delivers strong extraction and prediction performance in a compact, 9-billion-parameter model. Both extraction models are hosted on Workers AI and full open weights are available on Hugging Face . We’re also excited to re-introduce ourselves as the Workers AI superintelligence team, the frontier AI research team behind Clef , Clairic, and lots more in the works. This team is working quickly to push the AI frontier and build useful models for Cloudflare’s customers and the open source community. A new version of Clairic: redesigned after the preview release Since announcing Clairic in preview, we have received a ton of use cases and helpful feedback on how customers wanted to use an extraction model. We heard about use cases ranging from extracting data from images like receipts to reading values from support tickets. We knew that we wanted extraction to be the clear focus for the model, so it had to excel at reading from unstructured data. We decided to go back to the drawing board with Clairic and redesigned our architecture, differentiating this new version of Clairic from our preview release. For ordinary text and number extraction fields, we now use parallel slot autoregressive generation instead of a single forward pass. Each field uses the tokens it has already written to choose its next token, then stops at its own end marker. All the fields advance together in the serving batch, still giving lightning-fast latency per request. This boosted our accuracy in extraction for both text and images, and the trade-off in accuracy offsets the small latency cost. For computation, estimation, and extraction use cases, we trained special heads that can handle estimates, forecasts, durations, calculated dates, and explicit arithmetic. Although the model architecture evolved, we kept the parts of the typed API interface that make the answers useful: confidence scores, character spans, and probabilities are still intact with every request. The model is still incredibly fast and cheap. From the evals below, you can see how our newer versions of Clairic have greatly improved on extraction across text, images, PDFs, and more. Eval Clairic-preview Clairic Clairic-flash D1.2 + OCR ScaleDown Fresh text fields, 96 requests 295/336 335/336 328/336 304/336 259/336 Internal eval (mchen) - mixed-input fields, 36 requests 207/226 221/226 213/226 116/226 156/226 Tracked customer assertions, 139 request shapes 1,033/1,263 1,263/1,263 1,263/1,263 973/1,263 653/1,263 Synthetic receipt fields in text and images 369/576 576/576 576/576 397/576 280/576 There are no public extraction benchmarks yet, but we ran our internal evals for other emerging extraction models on the market, such as Liquid AI’s D1.2 (pipelined with Apple Vision for optical character recognition) and Scaledown’s Extract . Our Clairic models excel across extraction use cases, but take these evals as directional guidance since they are self-reported. We wanted to show an illustrative picture of how Clairic is performing across generalized extraction use cases and celebrate the fact that other companies are releasing extraction models as well — confirming our original hypothesis that extraction was a pain point for LLM users because of the cost, latency, and accuracy. But is it fast? We ran latency tests for Clairic and Clairic-flash, measuring complete HTTP response from a self-hosted server, including all fields in the request. Even with the redesigned architecture, you can expect responses in under one second — much faster than typical LLM responses for similar workloads. Eval set Requests per model Clairic p50 / p95 Clairic-flash p50 / p95 Fresh text fields 96 358 / 736 ms 155 / 328 ms Fresh image fields 48 453 / 976 ms 305 / 605 ms Commercial leases 180 691 / 803 ms 379 / 519 ms Loan pricing 600 395 / 407 ms 188 / 192 ms Traffic forecasting 114 532 / 585 ms 243 / 261 ms Expense audit, development 60 632 / 742 ms 393 / 512 ms Better extraction for images and PDFs In our preview blog post , Clairic read a photo of a receipt. Now the Clairic family of models can read PDFs too, so you can ask for the supplier, line items, and total in one request, even when they appear on different pages. You can include up to four images or PDF pages in total, and line items can come back as rows that keep each description, quantity, and price together. Due to Clairic’s new architecture, image reading accuracy has improved from 207 errors to 0 on our internal benchmarks, explicitly covering text and images. Promotional pricing on Clairic for a limited time When we first launched our preview endpoint of Clairic at @cf/cloudflare/clairic , we hosted the 9B variant as it was faster and easier to train, at the preview price of $0.10 per M input tokens. We’re now moving the 9B model to the @cf/cloudflare/clairic-flash endpoint and the 27B model will live at @cf/cloudflare/clairic . The 27B Clairic model will be priced at $0.24 per M input tokens, while the 9B Clairic-flash model will be priced at $0.10 per M input tokens. Although the model does technically generate output tokens, we decided to keep the System One pricing principles and are only charging on input tokens: we eat the cost of the output token generation. In order to make this a seamless swap, we’re offering a promotional discount on Clairic — until December 1, 2026, both Clairic and Clairic-flash will cost $0.10 per M input tokens. This means you get to try out the higher quality variant of Clairic at the same price. If your applications are hooked up to the Clairic endpoint that we released in preview, you will automatically benefit from the better extraction capabilities of our new model, which we’re rolling out in place. If you’d like to move more cost-sensitive workloads to the cheaper 9B Clairic-flash variant, we encourage you to do so. On December 1, we’ll be ending the promotional discount for Clairic and pricing will resume at $0.24 per M input tokens instead of the discounted $0.10 per M input tokens. Clairic and Clairic-flash (new) are open-weight Both Clairic models are now open-weight on Hugging Face as well. We have seen an outpouring of experiments and tuned models from our release of Clef, and we’re happy to continue supporting teams and research with our open-weight release of Clairic. Our mission with these System One models is to help people augment their expensive LLM usage with smaller, faster, cheaper models that are purpose-built for a specific task. We hope that releasing these models open-weight encourages others to experiment and build on our ideas as well. Try them out Clairic and Clairic-flash are available on Workers AI as @cf/cloudflare/clairic and @cf/cloudflare/clairic-flash . The developer documentation has the full API schemas, which remain unchanged from our preview endpoint. We’re also publishing the open-weight releases for Clairic and Clairic-flash on Hugging Face. The team behind these models — the Workers AI superintelligence team — is just getting started, and growing fast to push frontier AI research at Cloudflare. Join us early and help shape what the superintelligence team becomes.

items.title: Threat Hunting On The Network: An Active Search for Risks on the Wire
items.summary: All threat hunters are looking for evidence of nefarious activity, hopefully before an incident happens. Threat hunting on the network involves actively searching through packet data for malicious activity. Threat hunting on an endpoint depends more heavily on logs. Think of it as on the wire (or in the air) versus on a host itself. Don’t worry, you don’t have to look through every packet in a pcap file. That would make your head explode! We would like to think our firewalls and Intrusion Detection/Prevention Systems (IDS or IPS) are blocking all evil traffic from coming in, but those appliances have limits. Adversaries evolve their techniques faster than the static signatures used on our perimeter defenses. Updates from vendors and threat intelligence feeds can’t keep up. A network threat hunter looks for patterns beyond specific byte sequences, file hashes, and documented signature exploits. In contrast to signatures, behavior analysis lets network threat hunters draw insights from network baselines to understand expected protocols and traffic flows. Threat actors may change their techniques and procedures, but they still have fundamental network behaviors. Signature-Based vs Behavioral Analysis in Threat Hunting Common Data Sources NetFlow or Internet Protocol Flow Information Export (IPFIX) records Every switch, router, firewall, VPN appliance, IDS/IPS, or other network device capable of exporting flow data should be sending these flow records to the SIEM. HTTP/HTTPs Proxy logs for TLS/HTTP headers VPN appliance logs for external connections to internal resources Full packet captures Pcap files captured from taps or SPAN sessions. My Favorite Tools NetFlow/IPFIX/logs > SIEM (Wazuh or Graylog) for aggregation and metadata Logs and/or packets > Elasticsearch > Kibana for log analysis and visualization Packets > Zeek > RITA by Active Countermeasures for full packet capture, indexing, alerting, and search Packets > Arkime for full packet capture, indexing, and search Packets > Wireshark or TShark for deep analysis A Few Additional Indicators Unusual port usage: services running on non-standard ports. DNS anomalies: DGA domains, DNS tunneling, or excessive NXDOMAIN responses. Failed authentication attempts: brute force indicators across multiple systems. Certificate anomalies: mismatched common names or short validity periods. TLS/SSL anomalies: weak ciphers, unusual JA3/JA4+ hashes, or certificate chain issues. My Favorite Methodologies Crown jewel analysis — Focus on protecting most critical assets and data. Hypothesis-driven hunting — Form theories about potential threats and test them. Kill chain mapping — Identify which attack phase the indicators belong to. Assumed breach methodology — Operate as though compromise has already occurred. Take advantage of established frameworks: MITRE ATT&CK®, Pyramid of Pain, PEAK. A good network threat hunter is also looking at internal traffic. Is Susie in Accounting supposed to be using SSH to access a server in another country? No. What about Brad in Marketing? Is it normal for him to download multi-gigabyte files from a server in the data center? Maybe. At three o’clock in the morning? Probably not. Finally, don’t be afraid to dive in. Threat hunting is not just for the most experienced cybersecurity analysts. Start with a single protocol and tools you already have to build confidence.

items.title: Critical NGINX HTTP/2 Vulnerabilities (CVE-2026-123633 and CVE-2026-123007): What Imperva Customers Need to Know
items.summary: Published November 18, 2026. We will update this post as new information becomes available. What happened Today, F5 released security updates for two critical vulnerabilities in NGINX, the open-source web server and reverse proxy that sits in front of an estimated 225 million websites. Researchers from Wiz Research, Ikotas Labs, Metnir, Rapid7, and Xint independently found the flaws and reported them to F5 as part of a coordinated disclosure. Both issues are memory-safety bugs in how NGINX handles HTTP/2 traffic. Each is rated Critical (CVSS 4.0 score of 9.2) and can allow an unauthenticated attacker to execute code on the server: CVE-2026-123633 is a use-after-free in HTTP/2 connection handling. It affects reverse-proxy processing when available connection slots run low, and affects NGINX OSS from 1.19.7. CVE-2026-123007 is an integer underflow in HTTP/2 flow-control accounting (send_window). Researchers demonstrated code execution against NGINX serving ordinary static files, with no backend application or third-party module involved. It affects NGINX versions going back to 1.9.5, released in 2015. Successful exploitation could let an attacker run commands, steal sensitive data, tamper with websites, or disrupt services. Because one NGINX deployment often fronts several applications, the impact can reach multiple sites and APIs. The flaws are in NGINX itself, so applications with secure code can still be exposed. Both require HTTP/2 to be enabled on the affected NGINX server. Are you affected? You are potentially exposed if you run NGINX OSS or NGINX Plus anywhere in your environment with HTTP/2 enabled and reachable by untrusted clients. This includes NGINX acting as a reverse proxy, load balancer, ingress controller, or origin web server. What have we learned so far? According to our initial analysis, Cloud WAF and WAF gateway protect out of the box against both vulnerabilities. We continue to monitor the situation, including the publication of further technical details and any reports of exploitation, and will update this post and our protections as needed. As an extra safety protection, you can choose to mitigate such attacks with Cloud WAF by choosing the HTTP/2 “client to Imperva” only option for your site. With this option, HTTP/2 is used only between the client and Imperva. Traffic from Imperva to your origin does not use HTTP/2, so attackers cannot reach the vulnerable HTTP/2 code path on your NGINX servers through Imperva. Your visitors keep the performance benefits of HTTP/2 at the edge, and your origin is protected from this attack vector while you patch. Patch your NGINX servers The mitigation above buys you time; it is not a replacement for patching. Upgrade to a fixed release as soon as you can: Product Fixed releases NGINX OSS 1.30.7 (stable), 1.31.9 (mainline) NGINX Plus (CVE-2026-123633) 37.0.7.1, 37.2.0.1 NGINX Plus (CVE-2026-123007) 37.0.8.1, 37.3.0.1 If you have questions, please contact our support team.

items.title: Java4Shell (CVE-2026-114938): What You Need to Know and How Imperva Protects You
items.summary: Published November 18, 2026. We will update this post as new information becomes available. On November 17, 2026, security firm Calif publicly disclosed Java4Shell ( CVE-2026-114938 ), a critical memory-corruption vulnerability in the Base64 decoder of OpenJDK, the most widely used Java runtime. The OpenJDK Vulnerability Group published a fix the same day. Because Java runs a large share of enterprise applications, and because the flaw sits in the runtime rather than in a library, many organizations will need to act. Imperva is providing protection to Cloud WAF, Imperva for AWS and Imperva for Google Cloud customers today. Manual mitigation instructions for Imperva WAF Gateway customers are available. In addition, a new Imperva WAF Gateway version with dedicated protection is about to be released in the next following days. Details are below, but first, the vulnerability itself. What is Java4Shell? Base64 is a common way of representing binary data as text. Applications use it in authentication headers, tokens, file uploads and API messages, so Java services often decode Base64 that came straight from the network. To decode Base64 faster, OpenJDK uses specialized CPU instructions on supported processors. The hand-written machine code that handles the final characters of the input miscalculates how much data to write when the input ends in padding. As a result, the decoder writes beyond the end of its output buffer on the Java heap. Java then rejects the malformed input, but neighboring objects may already be corrupted. With careful exploitation, an unauthenticated remote attacker could leak memory contents or achieve remote code execution. Working exploits have been demonstrated against several widely used Java applications in their default configurations, including identity, CI/CD, collaboration and artifact-management platforms, as well as sample applications built on popular frameworks. A Java client that connects to a malicious TLS server can also be compromised, so the issue is not limited to servers that accept inbound requests. There is no universal exploit. Each target application requires its own tailored approach, and an unsuccessful attempt can crash the Java process. That should not be read as reassurance: the researchers report that they found the bug in about an hour and built the first working exploit in a few more. Severity The vulnerability is rated 9.2 (Critical) under CVSS 4.0. The OpenJDK advisory lists a CVSS 3.1 score of 8.1. The two scores use different scales and are not directly comparable. Who is affected? According to the OpenJDK advisory dated November 17, 2026, CVE-2026-114938 affects Java 17, 21, 25 and 27. For Java 17, the affected range begins at 17.0.6. Java 8 and 11 are not listed in the advisory, although Oracle lists its Java 8 performance build (8u511b33-perf) as vulnerable. Because the issue is in OpenJDK code, distributions built from it are also affected, including Amazon Corretto, Eclipse Temurin, Microsoft Build of OpenJDK, Azul Zulu, BellSoft Liberica, SAP SapMachine, Red Hat OpenJDK, Oracle OpenJDK, Oracle Java SE and Oracle GraalVM for JDK. The vulnerable code is hardware-specific. It requires an x86-64 processor with AVX-512 VBMI support, which includes Intel Xeon (Ice Lake and newer) and AMD EPYC and Ryzen (Zen 4 and newer). ARM64 processors are not affected. Many applications bundle their own Java runtime, so checking the system-wide Java installation is not enough. What you should do Patch. Update your Java runtime to the fixed build from your Java vendor, and then restart every Java process. This is the only complete remediation. Replacing files on disk does not change a JVM that is already running. Rebuild container images on a patched base image, and ask vendors of third-party products with bundled runtimes for updates. Inventory. Identify every Java runtime in your environment, including containers and bundled runtimes, and check which of them run on x86-64 hosts with AVX-512 VBMI. Because the flaw is in the JDK, dependency scanners that look for vulnerable libraries will not find it. Use a temporary JVM option if you cannot patch immediately. Start OpenJDK with -XX:-UseBASE64Intrinsics , which disables hardware-accelerated Base64 handling, or with -XX:UseAVX=2 , which disables AVX-512. Use the second option on x86-64 hosts only, since OpenJDK on ARM does not recognize it and will fail to start. Both require a restart, may affect performance for Base64-heavy workloads, and should be tested first. Neither replaces patching. Be careful with proof-of-concept code. Repositories using the CVE identifier are already appearing, and fake exploits are a common way to spread malware after high-profile disclosures. Review any code before running it, and never run it on production systems. How Imperva protects you Starting today, November 18, Imperva Cloud WAF, Imperva for AWS and Imperva for Google Cloud customers are protected against attempts to exploit CVE-2026-114938 in common base64 input fields. If you have a custom Java application running a vulnerable version exposed to the internet, you are advised to contact our support team for further guidance. Manual mitigation instructions for Imperva WAF Gateway customers are available. In addition, a new Imperva WAF Gateway version with dedicated protection is about to be released in the next following days. We will publish the version number and upgrade instructions in the release notes and update this post when it is released. A web application firewall is a valuable layer of defense, especially while patching is under way, but it does not replace patching. Exploitation depends on how each application uses Base64, and the fix for this vulnerability is in the Java runtime itself. We strongly recommend that you apply your Java vendor’s update as well. What’s next We continue to monitor the situation , including the publication of further technical details and any reports of exploitation, and will update this post and our protections as needed. If you have questions, please contact our support team.

There is no universal exploit. Each target application requires its own tailored approach, and an unsuccessful attempt can crash the Java process.   • Use a temporary JVM option if you cannot patch immediately. Start OpenJDK with -XX:-UseBASE64Intrinsics, which disables hardware-accelerated Base64 handling, or with -XX:UseAVX=2, which disables AVX-512. Use the second option on x86-64 hosts only, since OpenJDK on ARM does not recognize it and will fail to start. Exploitation depends on how each application uses Base64, and the fix for this vulnerability is in the Java runtime itself. We strongly recommend that you apply your Java vendor’s update as well.

Book Review: "Chip War"
items.summary: "Chip War: The Fight for the World's Most Critical Technology" by Chris Miller is a fascinating book on the history of semiconductors and how these tiny pieces of silicon became one of the most strategically important technologies in the world. The book walks through the early days of transistor development at Bell Labs, the rise of Silicon Valley and companies like Intel, and the eventual globalization of semiconductor manufacturing. I listened to the book on Audible at ~$15 for 12 hours. I give the book 6 out of 10 stars for being a fantastic history on the evolution of computer hardware, and how fragile the underpinning economy is in today's world. I'd highly recommend Chip War to engineers, security professionals, and anyone interested in understanding why semiconductors have become such a critical component of modern economic and national security. What I found particularly interesting was how closely the development of computing technology was tied to military competition, economic policy, and American technological dominance during the Cold War. The book actually paints a fantastic picture of the chip war being the evolution of the Cold War through an economic and trade perspective. Miller does a fantastic job explaining how an industry that started with a handful of American engineers eventually evolved into an incredibly complex global supply chain, involving companies like TI, TSMC, ASML, Huawei and Samsung, where only a few organizations possess the knowledge and equipment necessary to manufacture the world's most advanced chips. In my typical style, the following are the chapters of the book: Part 1: Cold War Chips Chapter 1: From Steel to Silicon Chapter 2: The Switch Chapter 3: Noyce, Kilby, and the Integrated Circuit Chapter 4: Liftoff Chapter 5: Mortars and Mass Production Chapter 6: "I...WANT...TO...GET...RICH" Part 2: The Circuity of the American World Chapter 7: Soviet Silicon Valley Chapter 8: "Copy It" Chapter 9: The Transistor Salesman Chapter 10: "Transistor Girls" Chapter 11: Precision Strike Chapter 12: Supply Chain Statecraft Chapter 13: Intel's Revolutionaries Chapter 14: The Pentagon's Offset Strategy Part 3: Leadership Lost? Chapter 15: "That Competition Is Tough" Chapter 16: "At War With Japan" Chapter 17: "Shipping Junk" Chapter 18: The Crude Oil of the 1980s Chapter 19: Death Spiral Chapter 20: The Japan That Can Say No Part 4: America Resurgent Chapter 21: The Potato Chip King Chapter 22: Disrupting Intel Chapter 23: "My Enemy's Enemy": The Rise of Korea Chapter 24: "This Is The Future" Chapter 25: The KGB's Directorate T Chapter 26: "Weapons of Mass Destruction": The Impact of the Offset Chapter 27: War Hero Chapter 28: "The Cold War Is Over and You Have Won" Part 5: Integrated Circuits, Integrated World? Chapter 29: "We Want a Semiconductor Industry in Taiwan" Chapter 30: "All People Must Make Semiconductors" Chapter 31: "Sharing God's Love with the Chinese" Chapter 32: "Lithography Wars" Chapter 33: "The Innovator's Dilemma" Chapter 34: "Running Faster?" Part 6: Offshoring Innovation? Chapter 35: "Real Men Hav Fabs" Chapter 36: The Fabless Revolution Chapter 37: Morris Chang's Grand Alliance Chapter 38: Apple Silicon Chapter 39: EUV Chapter 40: "There Is No Plan B" Chapter 41: How Intel Forgot Innovation Part 7: China's Challenge Chapter 42: Made in China Chapter 43: "Call Forth the Assault" Chapter 44: Technology Transfer Chapter 45: "Mergers Are Bound to Happen" Chapter 46: The Rise of Huawei Chapter 47: The 5G Future Chapter 48: The Next Offset Part 8: The Chip Choke Chapter 49: "Everything We're Competing On" Chapter 50: Fujian Jinhua Chapter 51: The Assault on Huawei Chapter 52: China's Sputnik Moment? Chapter 53: Shortages and Supply Chains Chapter 54: The Taiwan Dilemma Conclusion Perhaps the most important takeaway from this book is just how fragile and strategically important the semiconductor supply chain has become. Taiwan plays an enormous role in advanced chip manufacturing, making the growing geopolitical tensions between China and the United States particularly concerning. The book also offers some excellent lessons on technological innovation, industrial policy, and how decades of investment and specialized engineering create competitive advantages that are extremely difficult to replicate. While this isn't necessarily a technical book about semiconductor engineering, it provides an incredible amount of historical and geopolitical context for anyone working in technology. One of my favorite historical facts was on the discussion of Morre's Law and how it's common understanding has changed over time. Today, Morre's Law is often paraphrased as computing power doubling every year or two, but Gordon Moore's original observation was actually about the number of components that could git on an integrated circuit initially doubling doubling annually before later changing that prediction to doubling every two years. I just found it really interesting how this relatively specific observation about semiconductor manufacturing eventually evolved into a much broader "law" around the exponential growth of computing technology. The following is a video of Chris Miller discussing some of this history and where this has gone since the release of the book

Conclusion

Perhaps the most important takeaway from this book is just how fragile and strategically important the semiconductor supply chain has become. Taiwan plays an enormous role in advanced chip manufacturing, making the growing geopolitical tensions between China and the United States particularly concerning. The book also offers some excellent lessons on technological innovation, industrial policy, and how decades of investment and specialized engineering create competitive advantages that are extremely difficult to replicate. While this isn't necessarily a technical book about semiconductor engineering, it provides an incredible amount of historical and geopolitical context for anyone working in technology. One of my favorite historical facts was on the discussion of Morre's Law and how it's common understanding has changed over time. Today, Morre's Law is often paraphrased as computing power doubling every year or two, but Gordon Moore's original observation was actually about the number of components that could git on an integrated circuit initially doubling doubling annually before later changing that prediction to doubling every two years. I just found it really interesting how this relatively specific observation about semiconductor manufacturing eventually evolved into a much broader "law" around the exponential growth of computing technology. items.title: Hackers Use GhostMap eBPF Rootkit to Hide IronWorm Malware From Linux Security Tools
items.summary: Hackers are using a Linux rootkit called GhostMap to hide IronWorm malware from tools administrators rely on to inspect running systems. The rootkit can make selected processes, files, and network sockets disappear from routine listings without removing them. In one test, a malware listener vanished from /proc/net/tcp but remained visible to ss , a Linux utility that reads socket information through a different interface. GhostMap is the concealment component, not the entire implant. IronWorm is Rust-based malware delivered through compromised software packages. Earlier reporting on the IronWorm supply chain attack documented its focus on developer secrets, including credentials and API keys. The new research examined what happens after installation, when a Linux service starts the implant and the rootkit begins changing what local tools can see. Researchers Dolev Mizrahi and Ivan Kosarev from Aqua Security (Aquasec) identified GhostMap in examined IronWorm and Atomic Arch payloads. Their November 17 report found evidence that both payloads used the same rootkit implementation, but did not establish that the two campaigns had the same operator. Hackers Use GhostMap eBPF Rootkit Aqua examined the executable bundled with weavedb-sdk@0.45.3 . When the researchers ran it with root privileges, it copied itself into /var/lib and created a persistent systemd service. The process launched by that service loaded GhostMap. That distinction matters for investigators: following only the original installer’s child processes would have missed the process that loaded the rootkit. The test did not demonstrate privilege escalation or an unprivileged loading path. GhostMap abuses eBPF, short for extended Berkeley Packet Filter, a Linux feature that lets small programs run at selected points in the kernel. Aqua counted 13 programs and 10 maps, which hold data the programs use. Two delivery channels (Source – Aquasec) As earlier coverage of LinkPro’s Linux rootkit activity shows, GhostMap is not the first malware to abuse eBPF for concealment. Aqua’s contribution was to measure exactly what disappeared and what remained observable. In six altered directory listings, Aqua found that changing one byte was enough to make the reader skip selected records. The entries were still in memory, and the amount of data returned did not change. Test processes dropped out of ps output but remained accessible through their known /proc/PID paths. When the rootkit stopped, the processes appeared in the listings again. The socket tests exposed another limit. IronWorm’s local collector disappeared from /proc/net/tcp in all three checks, but the tested build of ss still showed the listener each time, without identifying its owning process. The collector stored test records in an extended file attribute called user.d . Aqua verified local storage but did not observe successful external delivery or authenticated remote command execution. Detecting GhostMap and Investigating Exposed Linux Hosts Aqua also found matching eBPF program and map names in the Atomic Arch sample. Earlier coverage of the Atomic Arch supply chain traced that campaign to compromised Arch User Repository build scripts. The overlap gives defenders a reason to look beyond npm package names, but Aqua’s detailed concealment and detection tests apply to the examined IronWorm specimen. Tracee, Aqua’s open-source runtime security tool, flagged three eBPF programs with application-memory write capabilities when they attached. It also retained all 48 directory-reader calls in the test. This demonstrated detection, not prevention. Reporting on SANSAR Linux mining malware illustrates a similar lesson: a normal-looking system reading does not mean the activity behind it has stopped. On potentially exposed hosts, investigators should compare process listings with retained execution records and known /proc/PID paths. They should also review unexpected systemd services and eBPF attachments, then preserve executable metadata, including extended attributes, before removing suspect components. A matching hash identifies a specific artifact; a path or attribute name alone does not confirm infection. items.title: Hackers Use Hidden Cron Jobs to Reinstall Malware on Firewalls and Routers Every 5 Minutes
items.summary: A Linux botnet is hiding in a place most network teams never look: the scheduled jobs on their firewalls, routers and switches. If a responder kills the malware and deletes the file, a hidden cron job downloads it again within five minutes. The botnet is called Evooo1Bot. FortiGuard Labs first described it on August 13, 2026. It goes after internet-facing devices such as routers, firewalls, IP cameras, phone systems and storage boxes. The malware reuses the attack engine from the leaked Mirai source code, and its authors have added encrypted control traffic, a password-guessing scanner and a proxy feature. Analysts at Eclypsium noted this weakness in a November 17 report. They warned that killing the process does not clean a compromised device when a scheduled job quietly puts the malware back. Many teams treat that step as the end of cleanup, and that is where this botnet wins. Hackers Use Hidden Cron Jobs Cron is the standard Linux job scheduler. It runs tasks at set times, and many network operating systems are built on Linux, so they include it. The legitimate jobs on a firewall are usually small. They rotate logs, clean up files and run health checks. Evooo1Bot abuses this. One bot command, !persist , installs several ways to stay on the device at once. The cron entry runs every five minutes. It uses wget or curl to download a script and pipes it straight into a shell. If the bot process is killed and the binary is deleted, the next five-minute mark pulls everything back. The cron job is only one layer. The same command also creates a systemd service with the harmless-sounding name “Apache HTTPD Cache Manager,” an init script, an /etc/rc.local entry and a login script under /etc/profile.d/ . Removing the cron line alone leaves those in place. The malware also lowers its priority for the system’s out-of-memory killer and keeps the watchdog file open, so a hardware reboot is less likely to interrupt it. Cron is not how the botnet gets in. According to FortiGuard, it spreads by exploiting known flaws in devices from D-Link, Tenda, NETGEAR, Telesquare and others, and by guessing SSH passwords. All the exploit callbacks pointed to one loader address. Once inside, the bot can turn a device into a SOCKS proxy. FortiGuard called that the most important feature, because the attacker can hide behind your device and move deeper into your network. This is not a one-off trick. Flare researchers described the SSHStalker botnet in February 2026. It uses a cron job that runs every minute and restarts the malware if it disappears. Our earlier report on a legacy IRC botnet campaign showed how that one-minute watchdog brings bots back in about 60 seconds. How Defenders Can Find and Remove Hidden Jobs Appliances are easy to miss. Admins work in the vendor’s command line, and configuration tools track the vendor settings, not the Linux crontab underneath. Endpoint agents usually do not run on these devices. As we have seen when hackers target edge devices , that blind spot is exactly why attackers like them. Eclypsium advises starting in the device’s Linux shell. On Arista EOS, the bash command opens one. On Cisco NX-OS, the bash shell must be enabled first, and many deployments leave it off. If you cannot enable it, record that cron was not inspected. Do not record the device as clean. Read the scheduler files directly. Check /etc/crontab , /etc/cron.d/ , the hourly, daily, weekly and monthly folders, and the spool files under /var/spool/cron/ . Do not rely on crontab -l alone. An attacker with root can write straight into the spool folder without ever running that command. The spool path also differs by Linux family, so check both /var/spool/cron/crontabs/ and /var/spool/cron/ . Then search for risky patterns. A curl or wget command piped into sh or bash points to Evooo1Bot. References to /dev/tcp , nc or ncat suggest a reverse shell, and a long base64 string suggests a hidden command. Jobs that run every minute or at boot deserve a closer look, but some vendors run their own frequent jobs, so treat those as suspicious and not proof. Any job that downloads and runs code should go to incident response. Order matters during cleanup. Save a copy of the cron file and its timestamps, remove the cron entry first, and only then kill the process. Doing it the other way gives the scheduler another chance to run. After that, check the other startup spots, and look at vendor schedulers such as NX-OS EEM applets or Arista event handlers, which are not cron. Eclypsium also warned that it has not tested whether a cron entry survives a reboot or upgrade on every platform. Patching helps stop the first break-in, but it will not remove a job that is already there. In the stealthy PEERSTITCH malware implant case, attackers also relied on weak visibility inside firewalls. A Linux botnet is hiding in a place most network teams never look: the scheduled jobs on their firewalls, routers and switches.

If a responder kills the malware and deletes the file, a hidden cron job downloads it again within five minutes. The botnet is called Evooo1Bot. FortiGuard Labs first described it on August 13, 2026.

It goes after internet-facing devices such as routers, firewalls, IP cameras, phone systems and storage boxes.

The malware reuses the attack engine from the leaked Mirai source code, and its authors have added encrypted control traffic, a password-guessing scanner and a proxy feature.

Analysts at Eclypsium noted this weakness in a November 17 report. They warned that killing the process does not clean a compromised device when a scheduled job quietly puts the malware back. Many teams treat that step as the end of cleanup, and that is where this botnet wins.

Hackers Use Hidden Cron Jobs

Cron is the standard Linux job scheduler. It runs tasks at set times, and many network operating systems are built on Linux, so they include it. The legitimate jobs on a firewall are usually small. They rotate logs, clean up files and run health checks.

Evooo1Bot abuses this. One bot command, !persist, installs several ways to stay on the device at once. The cron entry runs every five minutes.

It uses wget or curl to download a script and pipes it straight into a shell. If the bot process is killed and the binary is deleted, the next five-minute mark pulls everything back.

The cron job is only one layer. The same command also creates a systemd service with the harmless-sounding name “Apache HTTPD Cache Manager,” an init script, an /etc/rc.local entry and a login script under /etc/profile.d/.

Removing the cron line alone leaves those in place. The malware also lowers its priority for the system’s out-of-memory killer and keeps the watchdog file open, so a hardware reboot is less likely to interrupt it.

Cron is not how the botnet gets in. According to FortiGuard, it spreads by exploiting known flaws in devices from D-Link, Tenda, NETGEAR, Telesquare and others, and by guessing SSH passwords.

All the exploit callbacks pointed to one loader address. Once inside, the bot can turn a device into a SOCKS proxy. FortiGuard called that the most important feature, because the attacker can hide behind your device and move deeper into your network.

This is not a one-off trick. Flare researchers described the SSHStalker botnet in February 2026. It uses a cron job that runs every minute and restarts the malware if it disappears.

Our earlier report on a legacy IRC botnet campaign showed how that one-minute watchdog brings bots back in about 60 seconds.

How Defenders Can Find and Remove Hidden Jobs

Appliances are easy to miss. Admins work in the vendor’s command line, and configuration tools track the vendor settings, not the Linux crontab underneath.

Endpoint agents usually do not run on these devices. As we have seen when hackers target edge devices, that blind spot is exactly why attackers like them.

Eclypsium advises starting in the device’s Linux shell. On Arista EOS, the bash command opens one. On Cisco NX-OS, the bash shell must be enabled first, and many deployments leave it off. If you cannot enable it, record that cron was not inspected. Do not record the device as clean.

Read the scheduler files directly. Check /etc/crontab, /etc/cron.d/, the hourly, daily, weekly and monthly folders, and the spool files under /var/spool/cron/.

Do not rely on crontab -l alone. An attacker with root can write straight into the spool folder without ever running that command. The spool path also differs by Linux family, so check both /var/spool/cron/crontabs/ and /var/spool/cron/.

Then search for risky patterns. A curl or wget command piped into sh or bash points to Evooo1Bot. References to /dev/tcp, nc or ncat suggest a reverse shell, and a long base64 string suggests a hidden command.

Jobs that run every minute or at boot deserve a closer look, but some vendors run their own frequent jobs, so treat those as suspicious and not proof. Any job that downloads and runs code should go to incident response.

Order matters during cleanup. Save a copy of the cron file and its timestamps, remove the cron entry first, and only then kill the process. Doing it the other way gives the scheduler another chance to run.

After that, check the other startup spots, and look at vendor schedulers such as NX-OS EEM applets or Arista event handlers, which are not cron. Eclypsium also warned that it has not tested whether a cron entry survives a reboot or upgrade on every platform.

Patching helps stop the first break-in, but it will not remove a job that is already there. In the stealthy PEERSTITCH malware implant case, attackers also relied on weak visibility inside firewalls.

items.summary: A small one. The rest of our binaries now carry their version the way Gadget does, two latent bugs in Idun are gone, found by building against a GLib with its runtime checks enabled, and the XNU agent stopped sleeping through two kinds of wakeups. Version metadata In 17.27.0, Gadget started embedding its name, version and architectures, readable through BinaryMetadata.from_file() without loading it. frida-server, frida-portal, frida-inject and gum-graft now do the same, so tools can tell which one they have without running it. The embedding moved into a generator in our release engineering tooling, shared by frida-core and frida-gum. Idun The GLib in the binaries we ship is built without runtime checks, which hid two bugs. They surfaced when building against a distro’s GLib, where those checks are typically enabled. When talking to a jailed iOS device, our client for the Instruments process control service is told when a process terminates. The notification carries the pid as an NSNumber , which we read as if it were a GObject. Without runtime checks, GLib hands back the pointer without looking at its type, so this happened to work. With them it returns NULL , and we crashed. A handful of enum properties were also never installed there, as GLib rejects a property whose default is not a member of its enum. Barebone Getting the XNU agent’s tests to run reliably on CI turned up two lost wakeups, both a matter of ordering. The agent injected into a process sampled its wake word after testing the predicate, so a wake landing in between left it asleep with work already queued. And when that agent rang the kernel half’s bell before the kernel half’s loop had blocked, the wake was lost and the queued frame stranded. A test that wedges on CI now fails within a time budget and dumps the host’s stacks and the guest’s registers, rather than hanging the job. Enjoy! A small one. The rest of our binaries now carry their version the way Gadget does, two latent bugs in Idun are gone, found by building against a GLib with its runtime checks enabled, and the XNU agent stopped sleeping through two kinds of wakeups.

Version metadata

In 17.27.0, Gadget started embedding its name, version and architectures, readable through BinaryMetadata.from_file() without loading it. frida-server, frida-portal, frida-inject and gum-graft now do the same, so tools can tell which one they have without running it. The embedding moved into a generator in our release engineering tooling, shared by frida-core and frida-gum.

Idun

The GLib in the binaries we ship is built without runtime checks, which hid two bugs. They surfaced when building against a distro’s GLib, where those checks are typically enabled.

When talking to a jailed iOS device, our client for the Instruments process control service is told when a process terminates. The notification carries the pid as an NSNumber, which we read as if it were a GObject. Without runtime checks, GLib hands back the pointer without looking at its type, so this happened to work. With them it returns NULL, and we crashed.

A handful of enum properties were also never installed there, as GLib rejects a property whose default is not a member of its enum.

Barebone

Getting the XNU agent’s tests to run reliably on CI turned up two lost wakeups, both a matter of ordering. The agent injected into a process sampled its wake word after testing the predicate, so a wake landing in between left it asleep with work already queued. And when that agent rang the kernel half’s bell before the kernel half’s loop had blocked, the wake was lost and the queued frame stranded. A test that wedges on CI now fails within a time budget and dumps the host’s stacks and the guest’s registers, rather than hanging the job.

Enjoy!

items.summary: Executive Summary Security teams have never had better visibility into their assets, vulnerabilities, and threats. What they lack is the speed to act on it. Frontier AI models are surfacing vulnerabilities faster than ever, attackers are using the same models to exploit them within hours, and most remediation still depends on scans, tickets, and change windows. That operating model is the AI-native Risk Operations Center (AI-ROC). On October 13, 2026, Microsoft released the largest Patch Tuesday in its history, fixing 1,414 vulnerabilities . That is more than seven times the 193 vulnerabilities Microsoft fixed in October 2025. One of the new vulnerabilities was already being exploited, and the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA) set a deadline of just three days to patch it. At ROCon Americas 2026, we made the case that most organizations are focused on the wrong question. Knowing how many exposures you have is no longer useful on its own. What matters is how quickly you can turn those exposures into verified risk reduction. The Vulnerability Surge Has Outpaced Remediation Over the last twenty years, the security industry has gotten very good at finding things. Organizations now have more data on assets, vulnerabilities, misconfigurations, threat intelligence, and alerts than ever before. The ability to fix what matters has not kept up. Frontier AI has made that gap much wider. These models are not creating new vulnerabilities. They are surfacing flaws that already existed in code, and they are doing it much faster than before. The last two Patch Tuesdays, with 974 vulnerabilities in September and more than 1,400 in October, show how fast this is moving. Attackers have access to the same AI tools and are using them to weaponize new vulnerabilities within hours. In September, two of the vulnerabilities Microsoft disclosed were already being exploited before a patch was available. The way most organizations remediate has barely changed. A scanner detects the vulnerability, a second tool adds asset context, a third ranks it, an attack simulation tool tests it, and a ticket is created in the hope that someone fixes it within a 30- or 60-day service-level agreement (SLA). Each of those handoffs adds time, and risk only goes down when the fix is actually applied. This process was not built for attackers who move in hours. What the Surge Means for Security Teams Remediation timelines are shrinking from weeks to days, but the resources to meet them are not keeping pace. SLAs are moving from weeks to days. The 30- and 60-day SLAs most programs were built around no longer match the threat. Critical vulnerabilities now need to be patched in days, and mandates from CISA and CERT-In, the Indian Computer Emergency Response Team, can require remediation in as little as 12 to 24 hours . Exploitation is how most breaches now start. The Verizon 2026 Data Breach Investigations Report found that vulnerability exploitation was the leading way attackers got in, while the median time to patch grew to 43 days. Budgets and headcount are not keeping pace. Only 15% of security leaders expect their budgets to grow by more than 10%. Hiring more analysts is not a realistic answer. There are too many findings to fix. One large Qualys customer had 62.5 million findings. No team has the time or budget to work through that many. The Ideal Operating Model for Exposure Management None of this is a new problem. Exposure management still comes down to the same basics of visibility, prioritization, and remediation. What has changed is the speed at which each of them has to happen. Detection must happen in real time. New exposures should be identified as soon as a vulnerability is disclosed, not after the next scheduled scan. Prioritization must be based on proof. Risk scores tell you what could be dangerous. Teams need to know whether an attacker can actually reach and exploit the vulnerability in their environment. Remediation must take hours, not a month. Low-risk fixes should be automated, and every fix should be checked to confirm it worked. These steps also need to run on one platform. Every handoff between separate tools and teams adds delay, and that delay is the window attackers use. Qualys calls this operating model the Risk Operations Center (ROC). When AI agents handle the time-sensitive work at each stage, it becomes an AI-native ROC, or AI-ROC. How Qualys Operationalizes the AI-ROC The Qualys AI-ROC brings this operating model together on the Qualys Enterprise TruRisk Management Platform. It pulls in every asset and exposure across cloud, on-premises, operational technology (OT), Internet of Things (IoT), mobile, and AI environments, enriches them with threat intelligence and business context, and then prioritizes and remediates the risk that matters. Three AI agents handle the work that has to happen at machine speed: Agent Insta for detection, Agent Val for validation, and Agent Sara for remediation. AI-Speed Detection with InstaScan With traditional scanning, a vendor has to write a detection signature, roll it out, and then customers have to rescan their environment. That can take a day or two before a team even knows it is affected. InstaScan, powered by Agent Insta , monitors vendor advisories around the clock and matches them against the asset and software data customers already have. No new scan is needed. After the October release, Agent Insta customers had detections within five minutes . Hyper-Prioritization with TruConfirm Even after applying threat intelligence and business context, a large organization can still be left with hundreds of thousands of findings. TruConfirm, powered by Agent Val , tests whether those findings can actually be exploited in the customer’s environment, using production-safe payloads that never download malware. For the customer mentioned above, this reduced 62.5 million findings to 60,000 that were confirmed exploitable. Zero-Day Remediation with TruRisk Eliminate Detection and prioritization only matter if the risk gets fixed. Before launching TruRisk Eliminate with TruConfidence, we kept asking why teams were not remediating faster. Automation was not the blocker, since patch automation tools have existed for years. Confidence was. Teams did not know whether they were choosing the right fix, whether a patch would crash a business application, or whether compensating controls already covered the risk. TruRisk Eliminate with TruConfidence is built to answer those questions and to be the system of record and system of action for cyber risk reduction. It takes prioritized findings from Qualys or third-party tools and recommends the right fix for each one. A patch reliability score shows how likely a patch is to deploy without issues, and integrations with firewalls and other controls show when a compensating control already covers the risk. Patching is not always the answer. If a company has moved from Zoom to Microsoft Teams and a Zoom zero-day is disclosed, the right action is to uninstall Zoom rather than patch it. Agent Sara plans the rollout. Low-impact updates such as browsers and standalone utilities are patched automatically with no reboot required. Production workloads are patched in rings, starting in a lab environment, with health monitoring through partners like Dynatrace. If CPU, memory, or network indicators show a problem, Agent Sara stops the rollout and rolls the patch back. When a patch is not safe to deploy, Agent Sara applies a mitigation instead. Trust Is Built Into the AI-ROC As soon as agents start remediating, security and IT teams ask the same four questions. The AI-ROC answers each one with a setting the team controls. What breaks if the agent gets it wrong? Every patch carries an AI reliability score based on real-world deployments. Dependency and downtime impact are known before anything is approved, and rollback is staged in advance. Can we start small and prove it? Deployment waves let teams start with zero-touch automation for low-impact fixes, use ring-based rollouts for everything else, and keep tighter control over their most critical systems. Each team decides where to start. How do I know why it did that? ROCky, the Qualys conversational AI interface, and every agent show their reasoning, including the threat, the affected asset, any compensating control, and the TruConfirm evidence behind each action. Can I take the wheel back? Each wave can have its own approval gate. Rollback happens automatically if a service degrades, and nothing is marked closed until it has been revalidated. Policy, risk appetite, confidence thresholds, approval gates, and exceptions stay with the security team, and the agents work within those boundaries. Autonomy is not something teams have to take on faith. They control how much of it to use, and the program can grow with the environment instead of with headcount. How the Three Agents Handle a Zero-Day At ROCon, we walked through how the agents worked together on CVE-2026-81963, a Windows vulnerability from the September Patch Tuesday that CISA added to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities (KEV) Catalog on the same day. Agent Insta detected it in the customer’s environment within minutes of disclosure. Agent Val confirmed it was exploitable on the customer’s assets. Agent Sara saw that the patch required a reboot and already had a low reliability score, so it deployed to the lab environment first. When health indicators showed issues, Agent Sara rolled the patch back and applied a temporary mitigation, reducing the risk without the patch ever reaching production. What Comes Next for the AI-ROC Organizations can adopt the AI-ROC in stages. The journey begins with AI-speed detection, then extends CTEM across every tool already in use, moves to autonomous risk elimination, and finally quantifies cyber risk in business terms for the chief information security officer (CISO), the chief financial officer (CFO), and the board. Each stage builds on the one before it, so teams see results early while working toward a fully autonomous program. The AI-ROC will continue to grow with the attack surface. As applications, AI systems, and more advanced attack techniques create new kinds of exposure, they will come into the same platform, the same risk view, and the same agent-driven workflows. Agentic ROC Studio and the Future of Agentic AI in Risk Operations The next step is Agentic ROC Studio, a concept Qualys is building toward. Every security team has its own runbooks, its own tools, and its own way of working, and no set of prebuilt agents can cover all of it. Agentic ROC Studio is designed to let teams build agents around how they already operate. A team would describe what an agent should do in plain language, choose the tools it is allowed to use, and have it running in minutes, with no scripting required. These agents would work alongside the Qualys AI agents for exposure, threat, patch, and compliance, and connect to third-party tools and agents across security, IT, cloud, and identity to run as one cross-domain workflow. That is where agentic AI in risk operations is headed: a digital workforce that takes on the repetitive work across the entire risk program, while the security team sets the rules and stays in the loop. Conclusion Frontier AI has changed the pace of vulnerability management. Record Patch Tuesdays have arrived for two consecutive months; attackers can weaponize new flaws within hours, and the SLAs most programs were built on no longer hold. Adding more scanners, more findings, and more tickets will not close that gap. What closes it is an operating model built for AI speed. That means detecting new vulnerabilities as soon as they are disclosed, proving which ones can be exploited, and remediating them autonomously with safeguards that let teams trust the results. The AI-ROC brings all of this together on one platform, with AI agents doing the work at machine speed and security teams in control of every decision that matters. Every tool on the market can tell you how many exposures you have. The organizations that stay ahead in the frontier AI era will be the ones that can answer a harder question: how quickly can we turn exposure into verified risk reduction? At ROCon, we walked through how the agents worked together on CVE-2026-81963, a Windows vulnerability from the September Patch Tuesday that CISA added to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities (KEV) Catalog on the same day. Agent Insta detected it in the customer’s environment within minutes of disclosure. Agent Val confirmed it was exploitable on the customer’s assets. Agent Sara saw that the patch required a reboot and already had a low reliability score, so it deployed to the lab environment first. When health indicators showed issues, Agent Sara rolled the patch back and applied a temporary mitigation, reducing the risk without the patch ever reaching production.

What Comes Next for the AI-ROC

Organizations can adopt the AI-ROC in stages. The journey begins with AI-speed detection, then extends CTEM across every tool already in use, moves to autonomous risk elimination, and finally quantifies cyber risk in business terms for the chief information security officer (CISO), the chief financial officer (CFO), and the board. Each stage builds on the one before it, so teams see results early while working toward a fully autonomous program.

The AI-ROC will continue to grow with the attack surface. As applications, AI systems, and more advanced attack techniques create new kinds of exposure, they will come into the same platform, the same risk view, and the same agent-driven workflows.

Agentic ROC Studio and the Future of Agentic AI in Risk Operations

The next step is Agentic ROC Studio, a concept Qualys is building toward. Every security team has its own runbooks, its own tools, and its own way of working, and no set of prebuilt agents can cover all of it. Agentic ROC Studio is designed to let teams build agents around how they already operate. A team would describe what an agent should do in plain language, choose the tools it is allowed to use, and have it running in minutes, with no scripting required.

These agents would work alongside the Qualys AI agents for exposure, threat, patch, and compliance, and connect to third-party tools and agents across security, IT, cloud, and identity to run as one cross-domain workflow. That is where agentic AI in risk operations is headed: a digital workforce that takes on the repetitive work across the entire risk program, while the security team sets the rules and stays in the loop.

Conclusion

Frontier AI has changed the pace of vulnerability management. Record Patch Tuesdays have arrived for two consecutive months; attackers can weaponize new flaws within hours, and the SLAs most programs were built on no longer hold. Adding more scanners, more findings, and more tickets will not close that gap.

What closes it is an operating model built for AI speed. That means detecting new vulnerabilities as soon as they are disclosed, proving which ones can be exploited, and remediating them autonomously with safeguards that let teams trust the results. The AI-ROC brings all of this together on one platform, with AI agents doing the work at machine speed and security teams in control of every decision that matters.

Every tool on the market can tell you how many exposures you have. The organizations that stay ahead in the frontier AI era will be the ones that can answer a harder question: how quickly can we turn exposure into verified risk reduction?

Ready to see how the Qualys AI-ROC detects, validates, and remediates exposures at AI speed? Watch the full session from ROCon Americas 2026, then try it in your own environment with a free 30-day trial of Qualys Enterprise TruRisk Management (ETM).

What Do the Three Agents Do?

Can the Agents Patch Without Approval?

Only within the boundaries the team sets. Low-impact updates can be zero-touch. Each wave can have its own approval gate. Rollback is automatic if a service degrades. Nothing is marked closed until it has been revalidated.

items.title: AI Hacking Framework CyberStrikeAI Runs 221 Tool Executions Without Human Approval
items.summary: An exposed CyberStrikeAI workspace recorded 221 tool executions in a single session on November 16, 2026. The logs show no human decision at the framework’s tool approval gate, and the saved configuration later showed that the gate had been switched off. A person still directed the AI agent through chat. The difference matters: telling an agent what to do is not the same as approving each action before it runs. CyberStrikeAI is an open-source penetration testing framework, not a newly discovered malware family. It connects a language model to security tools and stores their results. Earlier reporting on CyberStrikeAI multi-agent activity described a separate case involving 44 agents. In the November 16 session, every recorded tool call came from one main agent, even though the workspace was configured in supervisor mode. Researchers from huntback identified the exposed workspace and examined its conversation database, diagnostic log and application source. Their CyberStrikeAI workspace investigation did not establish who operated the framework or whether the testing was authorized. The researchers reviewed the artifacts without running recovered programs, replaying requests or contacting the services under test. AI Hacking Framework CyberStrikeAI The runtime logged 240 tool calls, but only 221 had execution IDs that matched entries in the database’s execution table. The other 19 were local actions, such as updating plans and reading files, that did not receive those IDs. Of the stored executions, 209 were marked completed and 12 failed. A completed status meant the tool finished running, not that the action it attempted succeeded. Some completed runs returned authentication or application errors. The database recorded four approval rejections, all issued by an automated reviewer after it failed to get a response from its model. None was a human decision. At 09:48:15 UTC, the saved configuration showed approval enforcement was off. Huntback could not determine who changed the setting and found no evidence that the AI agent bypassed the control on its own. The operator later asked the agent to list potentially harmful write and delete actions for review, then approved the proposed items in chat. That approval did not restore the software control that could stop a tool call before execution. The repeated instructions also distinguish this session from cases covered in the FBI’s ARTEX security warning , where some intrusions reached privileged access in under three hours. What the CyberStrikeAI Session Actually Proved The strongest evidence was that a compute service returned node and job data. The retained outputs did not establish that the agent gained a shell, reached an internal network, breached a data lake or made a destructive database change. A search result showing at least 10,000 matches did not establish that 10,000 records were downloaded. Likewise, a script reported collecting 260 node entries, but it did not check for duplicates, and researchers did not recover the full list. The agent entered nine findings in the database, but those were not nine independently verified vulnerabilities. A newly generated wallet did not prove that someone else’s credentials were stolen, and a catalogue of available tools did not establish permission to run them. As coverage of AI attack automation trends shows, agents can drive real tool activity. Investigators still need returned data and system logs to verify what that activity achieved. For security teams running AI agents, the clearest detection opportunity is the sequence: reviewer errors, a change to approval settings and renewed tool activity. Huntback also recommends checking whether file servers or backup routes expose conversation databases, uploaded documents or runtime logs, even when the main application requires authentication. items.title: ClamAV 1.5.5 & 1.4.7 security patch release
items.summary: Today, we are publishing the 1.5.5 and 1.4.7 security patch versions . The release files for the patch versions are available for download on the ClamAV downloads page, on the GitHub Release page , and through Docker Hub with both Alpine and Debian containers. The images on Docker Hub may not be immediately available on release day.
items.summary_html:
Today, we are publishing the 1.5.5 and 1.4.7 security patch versions.  

The release files for the patch versions are available for download on the ClamAV downloads page, on the GitHub Release page, and through Docker Hub with both Alpine and Debian containers. The images on Docker Hub may not be immediately available on release day. Continue reading to learn what changed in each version. 


1.5.5

ClamAV 1.5.5 is a patch release with the following fixes:

  • CVE-2026-76422: Fixed Rust-to-C logging so rendered messages are passed as data rather than as C format strings. Crafted input could otherwise cause a crash, disclose process memory, or corrupt memory when attacker-controlled text was logged.

    This issue affects ClamAV 0.105.0 through 1.5.4. The fix is included in 1.4.7 and 1.5.5.

    Thank you to Feng Xue for identifying this issue.

  • CVE-2026-76411: Fixed URL canonicalization length accounting that could write beyond a stack buffer while scanning crafted email with full-hash phishing database entries loaded.

    This issue affects ClamAV 0.94 through 1.5.4. The fix is included in 1.4.7 and 1.5.5.

    Thank you to Feng Xue for identifying this issue.

  • CVE-2026-76415: Fixed yC executable unpacker offset validation that could underflow and read beyond a heap buffer while scanning a malformed file.

    This issue affects ClamAV 0.96 through 1.5.4. The fix is included in 1.4.7 and 1.5.5.

    Thank you to Nebula Security for identifying this issue.

  • CVE-2026-76414: Bounded CHM directory traversal to prevent cyclic directory data from causing an infinite scan loop and denial of service.

    This issue affects ClamAV 0.100.0 through 1.5.4. The fix is included in 1.4.7 and 1.5.5.

    Thank you to Nebula Security for identifying this issue.

  • CVE-2026-76416: Validated InstallShield file table counts and offsets, and applied scan time limits, to prevent malformed archives from pinning a scan worker.

    This issue affects ClamAV 0.96 through 1.5.4. The fix is included in 1.4.7 and 1.5.5.

    Thank you to Nebula Security for identifying this issue.

  • CVE-2026-76417: Fixed OLE2 property traversal recursion accounting to prevent a deeply nested crafted document from exhausting the process stack.

    This issue affects ClamAV 0.71 through 1.5.4. The fix is included in 1.4.7 and 1.5.5.

    Thank you to Nebula Security for identifying this issue.

  • CVE-2026-76421: Validated LZX match offsets before narrowing them to prevent a malformed CHM archive from causing an out-of-bounds heap write.

    This issue affects ClamAV 0.80 through 1.5.4. The fix is included in 1.4.7 and 1.5.5.

    Thank you to Feng Xue and XGPT of ThreatBook for identifying this issue.

  • CVE-2026-76430: Bounded UPX decompression and PE rebuilding output to prevent malformed packed executables from causing out-of-bounds heap writes.

    This issue affects ClamAV 0.94.1 through 1.5.4. The fix is included in 1.4.7 and 1.5.5.

    Thank you to Feng Xue and, independently, Nicola Ruaro for identifying this issue.

  • CVE-2026-76516: Enforced file-count and scan-size limits before XAR extraction writes to prevent crafted archives from exhausting temporary storage.

    This issue affects ClamAV 0.98 through 1.5.4. The fix is included in 1.4.7 and 1.5.5.

    Thank you to DieHardMan 300 for identifying this issue.

  • CVE-2026-76515: Bounded OLE2 directory-chain traversal and applied scan time limits to prevent crafted documents from causing excessive CPU use.

    This issue affects ClamAV 0.98.1 through 1.5.4. The fix is included in 1.4.7 and 1.5.5.

    Thank you to Ziyue Wang, Liyi Zhou, Strick, Maurice, and Chenchen Yu of Disproof AI Lab, University of Sydney, for identifying this issue.

  • Tightened the built-in HTML file type signatures so XML and custom elements whose names merely start with an HTML tag name are not classified as HTML.

  • Sigtool now retries after a delay when building a database archive whose MD5 hash begins with 00, preserving compatibility with ClamAV 1.1 through 1.4.

  • Restored clamsubmit sample submissions after the service changed its presigned-upload endpoint from GET to POST. The client now preserves the session, CSRF token, and referer, handles optional S3 ACL fields, and reports HTTP or malformed-response errors instead of crashing.

    The fix is included in 1.4.7 and 1.5.5.

  • Improved compatibility with OpenSSL 4 and reduced hashing overhead by reusing digest implementations fetched from a long-lived private library context. Also read opaque ASN1_TIME values through supported accessors instead of accessing OpenSSL internals directly.

    Thank you to Seweryn Chlewicki and Sebastian Andrzej Siewior for these improvements.

  • Upgraded the Rust anyhow and rand dependencies to resolve the RUSTSEC-2026-0190 and RUSTSEC-2026-0097 advisories.

    This issue affects ClamAV 0.94.1 through 1.5.4. The fix is included in 1.4.7 and 1.5.5.

    Thank you to Feng Xue and, independently, Nicola Ruaro for identifying this issue.

    This issue affects ClamAV 0.98 through 1.5.4. The fix is included in 1.4.7 and 1.5.5.

    Thank you to DieHardMan 300 for identifying this issue.

    Thank you to Ziyue Wang, Liyi Zhou, Strick, Maurice, and Chenchen Yu of Disproof AI Lab, University of Sydney, for identifying this issue.

  • Fixed clamd shutdown cleanup so the server thread does not close listening descriptors owned by clamd, preventing duplicate closes.

  • Fixed Rust CDIFF handling so a borrowed file descriptor remains owned by the calling C code, preventing the descriptor from being closed twice.

items.title: NGINX HTTP/2 Flaws Could Allow Memory Corruption and Remote Code Execution on Web Servers
items.summary: Two critical vulnerabilities in NGINX could let remote attackers run code on vulnerable web servers without logging in. The flaws, tracked as CVE-2026-123633 and CVE-2026-123007, were disclosed on November 18, 2026. Both require NGINX to accept HTTP/2 connections from clients, but the conditions differ. One affects certain reverse proxy setups, while the other can affect a server that does nothing more than serve static files. The bugs are in NGINX itself, not the websites or APIs behind it. NGINX often handles HTTPS and routes incoming requests to several applications. That means a single vulnerable proxy can put multiple services at risk even when their application code is secure. Depending on what the NGINX process can access, a successful attack could expose sensitive data, alter website content, or interrupt service. Wiz Research named Ikotas Labs, Metnir, Rapid7, and Xint as independent finders across the two disclosures. Both flaws carry a critical score of 9.2 under the CVSS 4.0 severity scale. The findings show that remote code execution is possible under the reported conditions. They do not, on their own, establish that attackers have used either flaw against production systems. Netcraft counted more than 225 million sites using NGINX in its September 2026 web server survey. That figure shows how widely the software is used, not how many sites are vulnerable. Exposure depends on the installed version and how the server handles HTTP/2. Multiple sites can also share the same NGINX deployment, so a site count is not a count of affected servers. These are separate from the NGINX flaws F5 disclosed in October . An organization that applied those fixes may still need another update. F5 lists NGINX Open Source 1.31.8 as affected by CVE-2026-123633, so running a build newer than October’s security release does not mean it contains the November fixes. NGINX HTTP/2 Vulnerabilities In its advisory for CVE-2026-123633 , F5 describes a use-after-free bug, which means a worker process can reuse memory after it has been released. The issue affects setups where NGINX accepts HTTP/2 client connections and forwards requests to a backend. F5 says the worker must also be running low on available connections. The flaw can crash the worker or, under certain conditions, let an attacker run code. CVE-2026-123007 has a wider reach. It affects NGINX Open Source releases dating back to 1.9.5, which shipped in 2015. In its disclosure report , Wiz said it demonstrated code execution on an NGINX server serving ordinary static files, with no backend application or third-party modules. A basic site should therefore be part of the patch review, not just API gateways and reverse proxies. The two November bugs are also distinct from the NGINX HTTP/2 proxy and gRPC vulnerability patched in June , which depended on a different set of configuration options. For this update, administrators should check whether NGINX accepts HTTP/2 from clients. Checking only the protocol NGINX uses to reach a backend can miss the client-facing exposure. Fixed NGINX versions The fixes for both flaws are listed for NGINX Open Source 1.31.9 on the mainline branch and 1.30.7 on the stable branch. For NGINX Plus, the minimum fixed builds differ by CVE. CVE Product Affected versions First fixed versions CVE-2026-123633 NGINX Open Source 1.19.7–1.30.6 and 1.31.0–1.31.8 1.30.7 (stable), 1.31.9 (mainline) CVE-2026-123633 NGINX Plus 37.x 37.0.0–37.0.6.1 and 37.1.0–37.2.0 37.0.7.1 and 37.2.0.1 CVE-2026-123007 NGINX Open Source 1.9.5–1.30.6 and 1.31.0–1.31.8 1.30.7 (stable), 1.31.9 (mainline) CVE-2026-123007 NGINX Plus 37.x 37.0.0–37.0.7.1 and 37.1.0–37.2.0.1 37.0.8.1 and 37.3.0.1 Both CVEs NGINX Plus R-series R34–R36 No fix listed for these releases. Upgrade to a 37.x build that fixes both CVEs. Administrators should check F5’s CVE-2026-123007 advisory alongside the CVE-2026-123633 advisory and choose a build that covers both. If the current branch has no fix listed, F5 recommends moving to one that does. Start with internet-facing servers, then check internal proxies and static sites. For NGINX installed through a Linux distribution or bundled with another product, check the supplier’s security notice for the package or image that contains both fixes. After updating, verify the version actually running on every instance. A configuration reload alone does not replace the running NGINX binary, so restart the service or roll out replacement containers as appropriate. If a fixed build is not yet available through your update channel, temporarily turn off client-facing HTTP/2 on affected listeners where the service can tolerate the change. Afterward, test from the client side to confirm the endpoint no longer accepts HTTP/2, and check that websites and APIs still work. Disabling HTTP/2 reduces exposure to these two flaws, but it does not fix the underlying bugs. Install the security update before turning the protocol back on. CVEProductAffected versionsFirst fixed versionsCVE-2026-123633NGINX Open Source1.19.7–1.30.6 and 1.31.0–1.31.81.30.7 (stable), 1.31.9 (mainline)CVE-2026-123633NGINX Plus 37.x37.0.0–37.0.6.1 and 37.1.0–37.2.037.0.7.1 and 37.2.0.1CVE-2026-123007NGINX Open Source1.9.5–1.30.6 and 1.31.0–1.31.81.30.7 (stable), 1.31.9 (mainline)CVE-2026-123007NGINX Plus 37.x37.0.0–37.0.7.1 and 37.1.0–37.2.0.137.0.8.1 and 37.3.0.1Both CVEsNGINX Plus R-seriesR34–R36No fix listed for these releases. Upgrade to a 37.x build that fixes both CVEs.

Administrators should check F5’s CVE-2026-123007 advisory alongside the CVE-2026-123633 advisory and choose a build that covers both. If the current branch has no fix listed, F5 recommends moving to one that does.

Start with internet-facing servers, then check internal proxies and static sites. For NGINX installed through a Linux distribution or bundled with another product, check the supplier’s security notice for the package or image that contains both fixes.

After updating, verify the version actually running on every instance. A configuration reload alone does not replace the running NGINX binary, so restart the service or roll out replacement containers as appropriate.

If a fixed build is not yet available through your update channel, temporarily turn off client-facing HTTP/2 on affected listeners where the service can tolerate the change.

Afterward, test from the client side to confirm the endpoint no longer accepts HTTP/2, and check that websites and APIs still work. Disabling HTTP/2 reduces exposure to these two flaws, but it does not fix the underlying bugs. Install the security update before turning the protocol back on.
