items.title: SpyCloud’s 2027 Forecast: Attackers Will Exploit Trusted Access, From Hijacked Sessions to AI Agents
items.summary: Austin, TX, USA, November 17th, 2026, CyberNewswire New predictions drawn from SpyCloud’s research teams and a survey of security professionals show why stolen sessions, API keys, and vendor connections will drive the most damaging attacks in 2027. SpyCloud , the leader in identity threat protection, today released its SpyCloud 2026 Forecast Report , outlining several predictions for 2027 drawn from the company’s experts across security research, product, investigations, and data science, plus a survey of 50 security professionals at large enterprises. The predictions are ordered by expert confidence, with the most certain listed first. AI is speeding up attackers and defenders alike, but organizations are adopting it faster than they can govern it. Attackers are using that gap to automate phishing and evolve malware, shortening their path to the access they want. “The clearest pattern heading into 2027 is that attackers are gaining access through vectors that organizations already trust: active employee sessions, vendor connections, and even insider threats,” said Aurora Johnson, Director, Threat Research & Intelligence at SpyCloud . “Security measures like multifactor authentication are good, but defenders need to be mindful that they’re not enough these days. Criminals have developed new tactics to effectively bypass these protections.” Cybersecurity Threats SpyCloud Anticipates in 2027 Attackers will keep slipping past MFA by taking over the session or the device it trusts. SpyCloud experts expect phishing kits to keep moving to methods MFA does not stop, including device code phishing and relay attacks, also known as adversary-in-the-middle (AiTM) attacks.Some attackers will skip the kit altogether and work inside the victim’s own browser through browser-in-the-middle (BitM) attacks, and the kits that remain will keep adapting. The API keys and tokens behind AI tools and agents will become attackers’ next favorite target. WardenStealer and Aoki , two commodity infostealers, already collect the tokens, keys, and session cookies that AI coding tools store on developer machines, and SpyCloud has recaptured more than 127,000 WardenStealer infections since August. Stolen AI access retains much of its reach after a password reset, and criminals already sell it well below list price. These non-human identity (NHI) credentials will only grow more valuable as AI tools and agents reach more enterprise systems. The most damaging compromises will come through access the organization already trusts, from a vendor integration to an employee insider threat. Attackers keep reaching big targets through connections granted long ago. SpyCloud experts expect the next wave to include both negligent and potentially malicious insiders, and integrations that still hold admin scope years after someone approved them. In the survey, 68% of security professionals reported being affected by a breach at a vendor, contractor, or SaaS provider. Fraudsters will stitch together convincing identities from real stolen data and AI-generated faces, voices and documents. Stolen personal data is plentiful, and AI makes it cheaper to turn into a believable face, voice, or document. Experts expect fraud cases to become harder to identify and crack as these identities improve and AI agents open accounts at volume. Only 6% of survey respondents have seen this activity, so this call runs ahead of what most teams see today. Attackers will start phishing AI agents the same way they have always phished people. AI agents now hold as many tokens, keys, and sessions as the people they work beside, and they read tickets, logs, and résumés all day without anyone checking each one. Early signs include malicious skills on an AI agent marketplace that tell agents to download infostealer malware. In SpyCloud’s 2026 Identity Threat Report , 91% of security leaders said their organizations used AI tools or agents with access to internal systems. Threat actor groups will keep changing names and members, and their conversations will keep hopping between chat apps. As forums are taken down, only to resurface under new names, more cybercriminal activity is moving to chat apps that are free, feature-rich, and easy to join. SpyCloud experts agree the conversation will stay on chat apps but are split on where. Some expect Telegram to hold, while others expect a move to invite-only platforms such as Session, SimpleX and Matrix, which is why SpyCloud rates this call medium-confidence. Fully autonomous attacks will grab the headlines in 2027, but ordinary attacks running faster will do most of the damage. Familiar attacks built on stolen sessions, tokens, and vendor connections will keep doing the most damage, with AI making them cheaper and quicker to run, even if autonomous attacks take the spotlight. Autonomous attacks have not yet shown up in SpyCloud’s recaptured data, so SpyCloud rates that half of the call low-confidence. Of the security professionals surveyed, 46% expect attackers to gain ground in the first half of 2027. Several of these predictions point to the same shift in what attackers want: not just employee passwords, but the tokens, keys, and service accounts that connect SaaS platforms, vendors, and AI tools. “With the proliferation of more SaaS and less on-prem services, NHIs have become as valuable if not more valuable than everyday traditional username/email password pairs,” said Joe Roosen, Senior Director, Security Research at SpyCloud . “Because of this, commodity infostealers will pivot to seeking out NHIs as a preference.” Security Implications of AI Driven Threats Drawing on more than one trillion recaptured identity assets, SpyCloud helps organizations identify compromised identities and automate remediation before stolen access can enable session hijacking, account takeover, ransomware, fraud, and other cyberattacks. “AI is making familiar attacks faster and easier to scale,” said Jason Lancaster, Chief Investigations Officer at SpyCloud . “Stolen sessions, API keys, and tokens already give criminals access to business systems, and as AI tools and agents hold more of those credentials, organizations need greater visibility into what has been exposed and the ability to remediate compromised access before attackers can exploit it.” To read the full insights and report users can visit spycloud.com . About SpyCloud SpyCloud transforms recaptured darknet data to disrupt cybercrime. Its automated identity threat protection solutions use advanced analytics and AI to accelerate investigations and protect workforce, consumer, and supplier identities from the threats that matter most: authentication bypass, session hijacking, malicious insiders, account takeover, ransomware, and fraud. Its data from malware-infected devices, successful phishes, combolists, and third-party breaches also powers many popular dark web monitoring and identity theft protection offerings. Customers include 7 of the Fortune 10, along with hundreds of global enterprises, mid-sized companies, and government agencies worldwide. Headquartered in Austin, TX, SpyCloud is home to more than 250 cybersecurity experts whose mission is to protect businesses and consumers from the stolen identity data criminals are using to target them now. items.title: Armornet Debuts AI Security for the Code and Vendors Companies Trust
items.summary: Grand Rapids, Michigan, November 18th, 2026, CyberNewswire Startup shows teams the vendors they rely on, keeps a live risk score on each one and secures the software supply chain from end to end Armornet , an AI cybersecurity company, is accepting teams into the private alpha of its platform, which gives an automatically discovered, continuous view of the vendors a company’s teams relies on. Procurement and risk review each vendor at signing. First- and third-party engineering teams ship thousands of lines of code a day. As that code changes, so does how teams use each vendor and where that vendor stands on breaches, exploits and patching. The review done at signing captures none of it. After teams connect their version control, compliance and workspace tools, Armornet lists the vendors and packages they rely on and how they use them. Armornet’s Agent Mesh monitors everything from package installs to the breach notifications, counting each block and response against the vendor’s risk score. Open-source malware grew 75% in 2025, according to Sonatype’s 2026 State of the Software Supply Chain report. In May, GitHub said a hacking group took about 3,800 of its internal repositories through a poisoned code-editor extension on an employee’s device. “A vendor review is a snapshot, but vendor risk changes every day. Breaches, exploits and patches keep coming, and the teams relying on that vendor are typically the last to find out,” said Tony Ramos, founder and CEO of Armornet. “Armornet gives procurement, security and engineering teams one shared, continuously monitored record of each vendor they rely on, so everyone works from the same picture.” To enhance developer security skillsets, Armornet offers a growing suite of free-to-play, open-source cybersecurity games. Designed for a range of experience levels, the games turn real-world cybersecurity concepts and software supply chain threats into interactive, hands-on challenges. Anyone can play at armornet.io/breach . Teams can request alpha access at armornet.io/alpha . About Armornet Armornet is an AI cybersecurity company focused on securing the software supply chain, bringing visibility and control of the code, tools and third parties that introduce risk into an organization. The Grand Rapids, Michigan-based company was founded in 2026. Learn more at armornet.io . Contact Head of Product Kaitlyn Melendez Armornet kaitlyn@armornet.io

items.title: How Cloudflare WAF helps protect against Java4Shell (CVE-2026-114938)
items.summary: On November 17, 2026, the security research company Calif disclosed Java4Shell (CVE-2026-114938) , a memory-corruption vulnerability in the Base64 decoder of OpenJDK, the most widely used Java runtime. Under the Common Vulnerability Scoring System (CVSS) 4.0, it scores 9.2 out of 10 (Critical). The flaw affects Java. OpenJDK published a security advisory and Oracle released patched builds in its November 2026 Critical Patch Update the same day, at 21:00 UTC. The vulnerability lets a remote attacker with no credentials send malformed Base64 data to a Java application and overwrite memory next to the decoded output. Calif turned that overwrite into a leak of heap memory, similar to Heartbleed , and into remote code execution. Calif demonstrated pre-authentication remote code execution against Keycloak, Atlassian Jira, Atlassian Confluence, JFrog Artifactory, Jenkins and PingFederate in their default configurations, and post-authentication remote code execution against Apache Kafka, Apache Solr, Elasticsearch, Gerrit, and Spinnaker. Cloudflare has released a new set of rules in the Cloudflare Managed Ruleset designed to detect malformed Base64 input patterns associated with this vulnerability. The rules are available on Pro, Business and Enterprise plans and are enabled by default with the Log action because malformed input and some benign application-specific token formats can resemble exploitation attempts. Blocking by default could therefore disrupt legitimate traffic. Customers can review matching requests in Security Events now and change the rules action to Block once they confirm it does not affect legitimate traffic. The WAF is an additional layer of defense, not a replacement for the patch. Java4Shell can be reached through paths a WAF does not see, like outbound TLS responses, and the only complete fix is to update the Java runtime. Our analysts continue to monitor attack activity and will update the rules as new techniques and variations appear. You can track rule changes in the WAF changelog and get more information on how the vulnerability develops on the dedicated Cloudflare Zero Wire briefing . We have seen no indication so far that Java4Shell was exploited on Cloudflare infrastructure. What we know about the vulnerability Base64 is a common way to represent binary data as text. Java applications decode Base64 when they process authentication headers, tokens, file uploads and many network messages. To decode it faster, OpenJDK replaces frequently used code with specialized machine code, called intrinsics. On supported x86-64 processors, the Base64 intrinsic uses AVX-512 instructions to process 64 bytes at a time. The bug sits in the handwritten assembly that handles the final characters of the input. When the tail of the input contains padding characters (=) in a position where valid Base64 never places them, the routine calculates a negative output length. That invalid length turns into a full 64-byte write. For a 65-character input, made of 64 characters followed by a single =, OpenJDK allocates a 50-byte output array and then writes 62 bytes past its end. Java eventually rejects the input as invalid and throws an exception. By then, the neighboring memory has already been overwritten. An application's own input validation does not help, because the corruption happens inside the decoder before the application can reject the data. The simplest trigger is 64 A characters followed by =. On OpenJDK 17, the trigger needs 128 characters followed by =, because the threshold for the fast code path is higher. Exploitation is not point-and-shoot. The overwritten bytes are mostly fixed values, and the attacker controls only where the write lands. To build a working exploit, Calif arranged the Java heap so that the overflow enlarged neighboring arrays, which gave them first a way to read heap memory and then a way to write chosen bytes. Each target application requires its own exploit chain. Calif reported developing its first working local exploit in about three hours with the help of AI agents, so we expect other attackers to build exploit chains quickly. Who is affected Java4Shell affects a system only when all the following conditions are true: Condition Details Java runtime OpenJDK 17.0.6 or newer, including distributions built from OpenJDK: Amazon Corretto, Eclipse Temurin, Microsoft Build of OpenJDK, Azul Zulu, BellSoft Liberica, SAP SapMachine, Red Hat OpenJDK, Oracle OpenJDK, Oracle Java SE and Oracle GraalVM for JDK. Check Oracle's advisory for the exact list of affected Oracle builds. Processor x86-64 with AVX-512 VBMI support, such as Intel Xeon Ice Lake, Sapphire Rapids, Emerald Rapids and Granite Rapids, or AMD EPYC and Ryzen Zen 4 or newer. ARM64 processors are not affected. Input The application decodes attacker-controlled Base64 data with the standard Java decoder. Many applications bundle their own Java runtime, and container images ship with a fixed Java Development Kit (JDK). Upgrading the system Java package does not update those copies, and it does not replace a Java virtual machine (JVM) that is already running. Every updated service needs a restart. Mitigate if you cannot patch right away If you cannot update immediately, Calif documents two JVM startup flags that remove the vulnerable code path: -XX:-UseBASE64Intrinsics disables hardware-accelerated Base64 encoding and decoding. -XX:UseAVX=2 disables AVX-512. Apply this flag only on x86-64 hosts. OpenJDK on ARM does not recognize it and will fail to start. Both flags require a restart and may reduce performance for workloads that decode large amounts of Base64. They buy time while you patch. They do not replace the update. Protect your infrastructure while you patch Patching every Java runtime takes time, especially when JDKs are bundled inside applications and container images. Cloudflare WAF can reduce your exposure while you patch. A new managed rule, available on paid plans and enabled in Log mode by default, detects the malformed Base64 input that triggers Java4Shell. For Business and Enterprise customers, WAF attack score adds a machine learning layer that scores each request for remote code execution payloads, which helps catch variations and bypass attempts that signature-based rules can miss. New managed rules Protection for paid plans has been released as part of the Cloudflare Managed Ruleset (Ruleset ID efb7b8c949ac4650a09736fc376e9aee). The rule is enabled by default with the Log action, because blocking by default could cause false positives on legitimate Base64 traffic. To review its matches, go to Security > Security Analytics > Events and filter by the rule ID. If the matches are not legitimate traffic, change the rule action to Block: go to Security > Settings, edit the Cloudflare Managed Ruleset, search for CVE-2026-114938 and set the rule action to Block. Alternatively, you can follow the link to review your configuration on the Zero Wire briefing. Rule description Rule ID Java4Shell - Malformed Base64 Header - CVE-2026-114938 5de9b20a45ea45d3841919ab4d718bf4 Java4Shell - Malformed Base64 Query Value - CVE-2026-114938 46bb4172813e471ea62d31c02337b51d Java4Shell - Malformed Base64 Body Value - CVE-2026-114938 d4dc3f71f1bc44a0811ae570e5e5836c Java4Shell - Malformed Base64 Path Segment - CVE-2026-114938 0dceaf0684b54fd0b085fcfb6fd6f152 Java4Shell - Malformed Base64url JWT Component - CVE-2026-114938 0ddd0eb664a040779f2f19065a25d991 Java4Shell - Malformed Base64 WebAuthn Value - CVE-2026-114938 4fce1ea79a614c07a27348d167d74ebb We are working on a rule for the Cloudflare Free Managed Ruleset and will update this post when it is available. A WAF can block the exploit when the malformed Base64 arrives in an HTTP request that passes through Cloudflare. It cannot block every path to the vulnerable decoder, including: Encoded or nested data. The Base64 value may be wrapped inside another encoding or compressed format that the application unpacks before decoding. Non-HTTP protocols. Some affected products, such as the Apache Kafka broker, accept traffic over their own protocols. Outbound connections. Calif also shared a client-side exploit: a Java program that opens a TLS connection to a malicious server can be compromised, even if it exposes no service of its own. Traffic that bypasses Cloudflare. This includes internal traffic between services. Adding defense-in-depth with WAF attack score While the managed rule is the primary way to block malformed Base64 triggers at the edge, Cloudflare WAF Attack Score (and specifically its remote code execution sub-score cf.waf.score.rce available on Enterprise plans) can offer an additional, complementary layer of protection. Because CVE-2026-114938 (Java4Shell) is a binary heap-corruption vulnerability, an attacker rarely achieves full, reliable remote code execution with a single 65-byte (or 129-byte) trigger string alone. On the wire, that initial trigger looks like an opaque, malformed Base64 string containing heap-corruption bytes rather than traditional web-layer injection syntax. As a result, machine learning models trained on application-layer injection patterns will not flag the raw Base64 trigger in isolation. Instead, turning a bounded JVM heap overflow into remote code execution over HTTP almost always requires a multi-stage or multi-parameter exploit chain, which creates more fingerprints that WAF Attack Score can inspect and flag, including: Heap Grooming and Triggering: To corrupt a predictable adjacent object on the JVM heap (such as a String or byte[] length header), attackers often send repetitive parameters or headers alongside the malformed Base64 payload to shape memory layout before triggering the out-of-bounds write. Second-Stage Payloads: Once heap corruption gives the attacker control over execution flow or object references, the exploit still needs commands, scripts, or Java gadgets to run. If an exploit chain pairs the initial heap-corruption trigger with a second-stage payload such as shell execution primitives (/bin/sh -c, cmd.exe, reverse-shell strings) or Java class-loading gadgets (java.lang.Runtime, ProcessBuilder, serialized object streams) tucked into another header, query parameter, or request body, cf.waf.score.rce can detect and score that secondary payload as malicious. Post-Exploitation Activity: Even if an initial heap-read or corruption request slips past edge filters, subsequent HTTP requests attempting to interact with an in-memory webshell or pass OS commands to the compromised JVM remain directly visible to WAF Attack Score. Deploy protections and patch Because sophisticated in-memory exploits can still execute raw shellcode or manipulate bytecode without ever sending plaintext shell commands over HTTP, WAF Attack Score should be used alongside explicit Base64 rules and JVM patching. You can find more information on how to deploy Managed rules and attack score in our WAF guide , but in a nutshell: 1. Set the CVE-2026-114938 rule in the Cloudflare Managed Ruleset (Pro plan and above) to Block. It is enabled in Log mode by default, so review its matches in Security Events first. Use the links on the Cloudflare Zero Wire page to review your rules status. 2. Layer Attack Score to get ML-based remote code execution (RCE) detection: create a custom rule blocking or challenging requests with a low RCE attack score (for example, cf.waf.score.rce le 20 on Enterprise plans, or cf.waf.score.class eq "attack" on Business plans) to catch multi-stage exploit chains and post-exploitation command traffic. 3. Remediate at runtime: Upgrade to patched OpenJDK builds (or set -XX:+UnlockDiagnosticVMOptions -XX:-UseBASE64Intrinsics as a temporary workaround) to eliminate the vulnerable AVX-512 code path entirely. Follow the OpenJDK advisory and Oracle's Critical Patch Update and install your Java vendor's fixed release as soon as possible. For a prompt you can give an AI agent to inventory your Java runtimes, see the Java4Shell page on Cloudflare Zero Wire . Impact on Cloudflare infrastructure Cloudflare also runs Java, so when Java4Shell was disclosed we checked our own systems. The vulnerability can only be triggered in specific hardware configurations, namely a x86-64 processor that supports AVX-512 VBMI, so a system is exposed only when both are true. Our investigation found that the majority of our Java workloads are not scheduled on vulnerable systems; we took immediate action to protect the remainder. About an hour after the patches were published, we began rolling out a JVM startup option that turns off the accelerated Base64 routine containing the bug on all Java workloads, so decoding falls back to the standard implementation. To be safe, we are rolling out our patched configuration to all machines, regardless of hardware as a precaution. We have seen no indication so far that Java4Shell was exploited on Cloudflare infrastructure. Update every Java runtime now Java4Shell turns a performance optimization in the Java runtime into a path to remote code execution, and with technical details now public, we expect exploit attempts to follow quickly. The fix is to update every Java runtime and restart the services that use it. While you patch, review the new managed rule's matches and switch it to Block if you are on a paid plan and use attack score to catch remote code execution payloads that signatures may miss. Our WAF analysts will continue to update protections as new techniques emerge. Follow the WAF changelog for rule updates and the Java4Shell page on Cloudflare Zero Wire for the latest on this vulnerability.
items.summary_html:
On November 17, 2026, the security research company Calif disclosed Java4Shell (CVE-2026-114938), a memory-corruption vulnerability in the Base64 decoder of OpenJDK, the most widely used Java runtime. Under the Common Vulnerability Scoring System (CVSS) 4.0, it scores 9.2 out of 10 (Critical). The flaw affects Java. OpenJDK published a security advisory and Oracle released patched builds in its November 2026 Critical Patch Update the same day, at 21:00 UTC.

The vulnerability lets a remote attacker with no credentials send malformed Base64 data to a Java application and overwrite memory next to the decoded output. Calif turned that overwrite into a leak of heap memory, similar to Heartbleed, and into remote code execution. Calif demonstrated pre-authentication remote code execution against Keycloak, Atlassian Jira, Atlassian Confluence, JFrog Artifactory, Jenkins and PingFederate in their default configurations, and post-authentication remote code execution against Apache Kafka, Apache Solr, Elasticsearch, Gerrit, and Spinnaker.

Cloudflare has released a new set of rules in the Cloudflare Managed Ruleset designed to detect malformed Base64 input patterns associated with this vulnerability. The rules are available on Pro, Business and Enterprise plans and are enabled by default with the Log action because malformed input and some benign application-specific token formats can resemble exploitation attempts. Blocking by default could therefore disrupt legitimate traffic. Customers can review matching requests in Security Events now and change the rules action to Block once they confirm it does not affect legitimate traffic. 

The WAF is an additional layer of defense, not a replacement for the patch. Java4Shell can be reached through paths a WAF does not see, like outbound TLS responses, and the only complete fix is to update the Java runtime. Our analysts continue to monitor attack activity and will update the rules as new techniques and variations appear. You can track rule changes in the WAF changelog and get more information on how the vulnerability develops on the dedicated Cloudflare Zero Wire briefing.

We have seen no indication so far that Java4Shell was exploited on Cloudflare infrastructure.

What we know about the vulnerability

Base64 is a common way to represent binary data as text. Java applications decode Base64 when they process authentication headers, tokens, file uploads and many network messages. To decode it faster, OpenJDK replaces frequently used code with specialized machine code, called intrinsics. On supported x86-64 processors, the Base64 intrinsic uses AVX-512 instructions to process 64 bytes at a time.

The bug sits in the handwritten assembly that handles the final characters of the input. When the tail of the input contains padding characters (=) in a position where valid Base64 never places them, the routine calculates a negative output length. That invalid length turns into a full 64-byte write. For a 65-character input, made of 64 characters followed by a single =, OpenJDK allocates a 50-byte output array and then writes 62 bytes past its end.

Java eventually rejects the input as invalid and throws an exception. By then, the neighboring memory has already been overwritten. An application's own input validation does not help, because the corruption happens inside the decoder before the application can reject the data.

The simplest trigger is 64 A characters followed by =. On OpenJDK 17, the trigger needs 128 characters followed by =, because the threshold for the fast code path is higher.

Exploitation is not point-and-shoot. The overwritten bytes are mostly fixed values, and the attacker controls only where the write lands. To build a working exploit, Calif arranged the Java heap so that the overflow enlarged neighboring arrays, which gave them first a way to read heap memory and then a way to write chosen bytes. Each target application requires its own exploit chain. Calif reported developing its first working local exploit in about three hours with the help of AI agents, so we expect other attackers to build exploit chains quickly.

Who is affected

Java4Shell affects a system only when all the following conditions are true:

Condition

Details

Java runtime

OpenJDK 17.0.6 or newer, including distributions built from OpenJDK: Amazon Corretto, Eclipse Temurin, Microsoft Build of OpenJDK, Azul Zulu, BellSoft Liberica, SAP SapMachine, Red Hat OpenJDK, Oracle OpenJDK, Oracle Java SE and Oracle GraalVM for JDK.

Check Oracle's advisory for the exact list of affected Oracle builds.

Processor

x86-64 with AVX-512 VBMI support, such as Intel Xeon Ice Lake, Sapphire Rapids, Emerald Rapids and Granite Rapids, or AMD EPYC and Ryzen Zen 4 or newer. ARM64 processors are not affected.

Input

The application decodes attacker-controlled Base64 data with the standard Java decoder.

Many applications bundle their own Java runtime, and container images ship with a fixed Java Development Kit (JDK). Upgrading the system Java package does not update those copies, and it does not replace a Java virtual machine (JVM) that is already running. Every updated service needs a restart.

Mitigate if you cannot patch right away

If you cannot update immediately, Calif documents two JVM startup flags that remove the vulnerable code path:

  • -XX:-UseBASE64Intrinsics disables hardware-accelerated Base64 encoding and decoding.
  • -XX:UseAVX=2 disables AVX-512. Apply this flag only on x86-64 hosts. OpenJDK on ARM does not recognize it and will fail to start.

Both flags require a restart and may reduce performance for workloads that decode large amounts of Base64. They buy time while you patch. They do not replace the update.

Protect your infrastructure while you patch

Patching every Java runtime takes time, especially when JDKs are bundled inside applications and container images. Cloudflare WAF can reduce your exposure while you patch. A new managed rule, available on paid plans and enabled in Log mode by default, detects the malformed Base64 input that triggers Java4Shell. For Business and Enterprise customers, WAF attack score adds a machine learning layer that scores each request for remote code execution payloads, which helps catch variations and bypass attempts that signature-based rules can miss.

New managed rules

Protection for paid plans has been released as part of the Cloudflare Managed Ruleset (Ruleset ID efb7b8c949ac4650a09736fc376e9aee). The rule is enabled by default with the Log action, because blocking by default could cause false positives on legitimate Base64 traffic. To review its matches, go to Security > Security Analytics > Events and filter by the rule ID. If the matches are not legitimate traffic, change the rule action to Block: go to Security > Settings, edit the Cloudflare Managed Ruleset, search for CVE-2026-114938 and set the rule action to Block. Alternatively, you can follow the link to review your configuration on the Zero Wire briefing.

Rule description

Rule ID

Java4Shell - Malformed Base64 Header - CVE-2026-114938

5de9b20a45ea45d3841919ab4d718bf4

Java4Shell - Malformed Base64 Query Value - CVE-2026-114938

46bb4172813e471ea62d31c02337b51d

Java4Shell - Malformed Base64 Body Value - CVE-2026-114938

d4dc3f71f1bc44a0811ae570e5e5836c

Java4Shell - Malformed Base64 Path Segment - CVE-2026-114938

0dceaf0684b54fd0b085fcfb6fd6f152

Java4Shell - Malformed Base64url JWT Component - CVE-2026-114938

0ddd0eb664a040779f2f19065a25d991

Java4Shell - Malformed Base64 WebAuthn Value - CVE-2026-114938

4fce1ea79a614c07a27348d167d74ebb

We are working on a rule for the Cloudflare Free Managed Ruleset and will update this post when it is available.

A WAF can block the exploit when the malformed Base64 arrives in an HTTP request that passes through Cloudflare. It cannot block every path to the vulnerable decoder, including:

  • Encoded or nested data. The Base64 value may be wrapped inside another encoding or compressed format that the application unpacks before decoding.
  • Non-HTTP protocols. Some affected products, such as the Apache Kafka broker, accept traffic over their own protocols.
  • Outbound connections. Calif also shared a client-side exploit: a Java program that opens a TLS connection to a malicious server can be compromised, even if it exposes no service of its own.
  • Traffic that bypasses Cloudflare. This includes internal traffic between services.
Adding defense-in-depth with WAF attack score

While the managed rule is the primary way to block malformed Base64 triggers at the edge, Cloudflare WAF Attack Score (and specifically its remote code execution sub-score cf.waf.score.rce available on Enterprise plans) can offer an additional, complementary layer of protection.

Because CVE-2026-114938 (Java4Shell) is a binary heap-corruption vulnerability, an attacker rarely achieves full, reliable remote code execution with a single 65-byte (or 129-byte) trigger string alone. On the wire, that initial trigger looks like an opaque, malformed Base64 string containing heap-corruption bytes rather than traditional web-layer injection syntax. As a result, machine learning models trained on application-layer injection patterns will not flag the raw Base64 trigger in isolation.

Instead, turning a bounded JVM heap overflow into remote code execution over HTTP almost always requires a multi-stage or multi-parameter exploit chain, which creates more fingerprints that WAF Attack Score can inspect and flag, including:

  • Heap Grooming and Triggering: To corrupt a predictable adjacent object on the JVM heap (such as a String or byte[] length header), attackers often send repetitive parameters or headers alongside the malformed Base64 payload to shape memory layout before triggering the out-of-bounds write.
  • Second-Stage Payloads: Once heap corruption gives the attacker control over execution flow or object references, the exploit still needs commands, scripts, or Java gadgets to run. If an exploit chain pairs the initial heap-corruption trigger with a second-stage payload such as shell execution primitives (/bin/sh -c, cmd.exe, reverse-shell strings) or Java class-loading gadgets (java.lang.Runtime, ProcessBuilder, serialized object streams) tucked into another header, query parameter, or request body, cf.waf.score.rce can detect and score that secondary payload as malicious.
  • Post-Exploitation Activity: Even if an initial heap-read or corruption request slips past edge filters, subsequent HTTP requests attempting to interact with an in-memory webshell or pass OS commands to the compromised JVM remain directly visible to WAF Attack Score.
Deploy protections and patch

Because sophisticated in-memory exploits can still execute raw shellcode or manipulate bytecode without ever sending plaintext shell commands over HTTP, WAF Attack Score should be used alongside explicit Base64 rules and JVM patching.

You can find more information on how to deploy Managed rules and attack score in our WAF guide, but in a nutshell:

1. Set the CVE-2026-114938 rule in the Cloudflare Managed Ruleset (Pro plan and above) to Block. It is enabled in Log mode by default, so review its matches in Security Events first. Use the links on the Cloudflare Zero Wire page to review your rules status.

2. Layer Attack Score to get ML-based remote code execution (RCE) detection: create a custom rule blocking or challenging requests with a low RCE attack score (for example, cf.waf.score.rce le 20 on Enterprise plans, or cf.waf.score.class eq "attack" on Business plans) to catch multi-stage exploit chains and post-exploitation command traffic.

3. Remediate at runtime: Upgrade to patched OpenJDK builds (or set -XX:+UnlockDiagnosticVMOptions -XX:-UseBASE64Intrinsics as a temporary workaround) to eliminate the vulnerable AVX-512 code path entirely. Follow the OpenJDK advisory and Oracle's Critical Patch Update and install your Java vendor's fixed release as soon as possible. For a prompt you can give an AI agent to inventory your Java runtimes, see the Java4Shell page on Cloudflare Zero Wire.

items.title: OX Security Launches OX Radar and Response Center to Show Companies Which Cyber Threats Actually Affect Them
items.summary: New York, United States, November 18th, 2026, CyberNewswire New technology monitors critical vulnerabilities and supply chain threats, automatically assessing customer exposure and guiding remediation OX Security , a leader in AI-native application protection, today announced the launch of OX Radar and Response Center, giving security teams one place to track high-priority cyber threats, determine whether their organizations are affected, and manage remediation. OX Radar continuously monitors emerging vulnerabilities, compromised software dependencies, and actively exploited threats. Integrated with OX Security’s application security platform, the Response Center automatically checks supported threats against customer environments, identifying affected assets and providing the context and guidance needed to respond. Separately, a publicly accessible OX Radar threat feed provides broader security research and findings across the software and AI supply chain. When a major vulnerability or supply chain attack emerges, security teams often spend hours searching advisories, checking inventories, and correlating findings across tools to answer the question that matters most: Are we affected? As new software and AI components proliferate, investigating every potential threat manually is becoming increasingly impractical. “The question isn’t just whether a new threat is dangerous. It’s whether it’s dangerous to you,” said Neatsun Ziv, CEO and co-founder of OX Security. “AI is accelerating software development, expanding the supply chain, and generating more security alerts than teams can realistically investigate. Security teams need to know immediately which threats affect their organization, which don’t, and what action is required.” From Breaking Threats to Customer Action To help security teams stay ahead of threats requiring urgent attention, OX Radar scans CVE databases, known-exploited vulnerability catalogs, security advisories, and vendor research approximately every 10 minutes. The customer-facing capabilities focus on high-priority threats, including compromised or malicious dependencies, exploited vulnerabilities, and critical-severity CVEs. The Response Center connects supported OX Radar threats to each customer’s environment, checking whether vulnerable components are present and assessing their exploitability. It combines intelligence from the U.S. Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA) and the European Union Agency for Cybersecurity (ENISA) Known Exploited Vulnerabilities (KEV) catalogs, EPSS exploit predictions, and VEX exploitability status with OX Security’s AI-generated exploit checks and runtime visibility to determine whether vulnerable libraries are affected. Through the Response Center, security teams can: Track threats: Follow high-priority incidents as new intelligence and findings emerge. Assess exposure: Identify affected assets and examine supporting evidence. Prioritize risk: Evaluate severity, exploitation, code usage, and reachability. Manage remediation: Access safe versions and guidance, and create or track tickets and fix pull requests. Document response: Maintain records of findings and remediation activity. For each supported incident, the Response Center indicates whether a vulnerability has been detected in the customer’s environment, provides evidence of its potential exploitability, and incorporates available VEX information to help teams determine whether action is required. Teams can also initiate investigations using a CVE identifier, GitHub Security Advisory identifier, or advisory URL. Expanding Threat Visibility Through Public Research Alongside the customer-facing capabilities, OX Security is introducing a publicly accessible OX Radar threat feed with a broader catalog of security findings. Powered by OX Security’s independent research and scanning, the feed analyzes newly published npm and PyPI packages, AI skills, and Model Context Protocol (MCP) servers. OX Security will continue expanding the range of threats assessed against customer environments, bringing more findings from its public research into the Response Center over time. Availability OX Radar and Response Center are available to OX Security customers as part of OX Security’s AI-Native Application Protection Platform (AINAPP). The broader OX Radar research feed is publicly accessible through the OX Security website. About OX Security OX Security is the first AI-Native Application Protection Platform built to secure software from prompt to production runtime. Its platform includes VibeSec, OX Code, OX Cloud, and OX Agentic Pentester, giving security teams a unified system for securing AI-driven development, applications, and cloud environments. Contact Head of Communications Jillian Jones OX Security jillian.jones@ox.security

New York, United States, November 18th, 2026, CyberNewswire

New technology monitors critical vulnerabilities and supply chain threats, automatically assessing customer exposure and guiding remediation

OX Security, a leader in AI-native application protection, today announced the launch of OX Radar and Response Center, giving security teams one place to track high-priority cyber threats, determine whether their organizations are affected, and manage remediation.

OX Radar continuously monitors emerging vulnerabilities, compromised software dependencies, and actively exploited threats.

Integrated with OX Security’s application security platform, the Response Center automatically checks supported threats against customer environments, identifying affected assets and providing the context and guidance needed to respond.

Separately, a publicly accessible OX Radar threat feed provides broader security research and findings across the software and AI supply chain.

When a major vulnerability or supply chain attack emerges, security teams often spend hours searching advisories, checking inventories, and correlating findings across tools to answer the question that matters most: Are we affected? As new software and AI components proliferate, investigating every potential threat manually is becoming increasingly impractical.

“The question isn’t just whether a new threat is dangerous. It’s whether it’s dangerous to you,” said Neatsun Ziv, CEO and co-founder of OX Security. “AI is accelerating software development, expanding the supply chain, and generating more security alerts than teams can realistically investigate.

Security teams need to know immediately which threats affect their organization, which don’t, and what action is required.”

From Breaking Threats to Customer Action

To help security teams stay ahead of threats requiring urgent attention, OX Radar scans CVE databases, known-exploited vulnerability catalogs, security advisories, and vendor research approximately every 10 minutes.

The customer-facing capabilities focus on high-priority threats, including compromised or malicious dependencies, exploited vulnerabilities, and critical-severity CVEs.

The Response Center connects supported OX Radar threats to each customer’s environment, checking whether vulnerable components are present and assessing their exploitability.

It combines intelligence from the U.S. Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA) and the European Union Agency for Cybersecurity (ENISA) Known Exploited Vulnerabilities (KEV) catalogs, EPSS exploit predictions, and VEX exploitability status with OX Security’s AI-generated exploit checks and runtime visibility to determine whether vulnerable libraries are affected.

Through the Response Center, security teams can:

  • Track threats: Follow high-priority incidents as new intelligence and findings emerge.
  • Assess exposure: Identify affected assets and examine supporting evidence.
  • Prioritize risk: Evaluate severity, exploitation, code usage, and reachability.
  • Manage remediation: Access safe versions and guidance, and create or track tickets and fix pull requests.
  • Document response: Maintain records of findings and remediation activity.

For each supported incident, the Response Center indicates whether a vulnerability has been detected in the customer’s environment, provides evidence of its potential exploitability, and incorporates available VEX information to help teams determine whether action is required.

Teams can also initiate investigations using a CVE identifier, GitHub Security Advisory identifier, or advisory URL.

Expanding Threat Visibility Through Public Research

Alongside the customer-facing capabilities, OX Security is introducing a publicly accessible OX Radar threat feed with a broader catalog of security findings.

Powered by OX Security’s independent research and scanning, the feed analyzes newly published npm and PyPI packages, AI skills, and Model Context Protocol (MCP) servers.

OX Security will continue expanding the range of threats assessed against customer environments, bringing more findings from its public research into the Response Center over time.

Availability

OX Radar and Response Center are available to OX Security customers as part of OX Security’s AI-Native Application Protection Platform (AINAPP). The broader OX Radar research feed is publicly accessible through the OX Security website.

About OX Security

OX Security is the first AI-Native Application Protection Platform built to secure software from prompt to production runtime.

Its platform includes VibeSec, OX Code, OX Cloud, and OX Agentic Pentester, giving security teams a unified system for securing AI-driven development, applications, and cloud environments.

Contact

Head of Communications

Jillian Jones

OX Security

jillian.jones@ox.security

items.title: Microsoft Unveils Windows Server 2028 With Hundreds of Security Protections Enabled by Default
items.summary: Microsoft has released Windows Server 2028 in public preview. The biggest change is that a new server now starts in a locked-down state rather than an open one. Hundreds of security settings are on from the first boot, so admins no longer need to harden the system by hand after setup. Microsoft announced the release on November 17, 2026. For years, Windows Server shipped in a “compatible by default” form. Admins had to apply the Security Baseline or their own scripts to secure it. Until that work was done, every new server ran in a weaker state, and the gap was easy to miss. In its Hardened Server Core announcement , Microsoft says this approach is changing. Admins now start from a hardened setup and relax only what a workload needs. Layer What is hardened Identity and authentication Kerberos is preferred over NTLM. LSASS is protected. Strong passwords and account lockout are on. Consumer accounts are not allowed. Network exposure SMB signing and encryption are on. The firewall is on in every profile. Legacy name resolution and unauthenticated RPC are off. Cryptography TLS is limited to modern cipher suites. Key exchange is hybrid post-quantum (ML-KEM). Stored keys get strong protection. Privilege and admin access Admins must approve elevation. Powerful rights stay with Administrators. Guests cannot sign in. Installers cannot elevate on their own. Platform and code integrity The sign-in process runs only Microsoft-signed code. Signature validation is stricter. The paging file is encrypted. Remote access and observability RDP needs NLA and TLS. WinRM blocks Basic, Digest and unencrypted traffic. Advanced audit records command lines. PowerShell script block logging is on. Event logs are larger. Hardened Settings in Windows Server 2028 The change starts with Windows Server Insider Preview build 29706, where Server Core installs hardened. The settings line up with industry benchmarks such as CIS and DISA STIG. This closes the window in which a freshly deployed server sits exposed while it waits to be hardened. Microsoft grouped the settings by layer, and it says they were validated together so they work as a set. On identity, Kerberos is preferred over NTLM, LSASS is protected, and strong passwords and account lockout are on. Consumer accounts are not allowed. On the network side, the server talks only over signed, encrypted, and authenticated channels. SMB signing and encryption are on, and the firewall runs in every profile. Legacy name resolution and unauthenticated RPC are off. Cryptography also gets stronger. TLS is limited to modern cipher suites, and key exchange uses hybrid post-quantum protection with ML-KEM. Admins must approve privilege elevation, and Guests cannot sign in. The sign-in process runs only Microsoft-signed code, and the paging file is encrypted. For remote access, RDP needs NLA and TLS. WinRM blocks Basic and Digest logins and unencrypted traffic. Audit logs now record command lines, PowerShell script block logging is on, and event logs are larger. These choices target problems that defenders have seen for years. Cyber Security News has covered how Windows SMB client flaws let intruders take over Active Directory when relay protections are weak. Many of those cases worked because SMB signing was optional on most servers. A proof-of-concept for CVE-2026-24294 showed the same pattern. It gave SYSTEM-level access on a default Windows Server 2025 install where signing was not enforced. Microsoft fixed that path in March 2026. The research still warned that as long as NTLM stays common and signing stays optional, new tricks will keep appearing. Turning on signing, encryption, and Kerberos preference at install time removes much of that room. It also matches the advice researchers keep repeating. Cymulate noted that turning off NTLM alone is not enough and that anti-relay protections must be enforced on every service. Microsoft delivers the hardened values as policy in the HKLM\SOFTWARE\Policies hive wherever a component supports it. Policy wins over local settings, so a script or installer cannot quietly weaken a default. In Microsoft’s test, trying to turn on WinRM Basic authentication was refused because policy controls it.Admins keep control. OSConfig, Group Policy or another management tool can manage the settings, and whichever tool sets a value owns it. One surprise is that gpresult and RSOP report these settings as Not Configured. The defaults are built into the image, so there is no policy file for those tools to read. A new PowerShell module called MSHardenedPolicyEval ships in the box. The Get-MSHardenedPolicyScore cmdlet scores the server by category. In Microsoft’s example output, the server passed 191 of 237 checks, an overall score of 80.59 percent. Restore-MSHardenedPolicy removes hardened values for one category or the whole server. Set-MSHardenedPolicy applies them again. Both support -WhatIf, so admins can preview a change before making it. Microsoft warns that names may change in later previews, and that scores below 100 percent are expected on this build. Microsoft says some things that worked on Windows Server 2025 may break. Older protocols, legacy authentication, and some management tools and scripts are the likely trouble spots. Teams should test apps and admin tooling against the hardened setup first. They should relax only the specific setting a workload needs. Some protections are also still missing from this preview. These include NTLM blocking, Secure Boot and DMA protection requirements, kernel shadow stacks, and Windows Protected Print. Print and RPC hardening is also on the list, along with extra settings such as the logon banner. The wider release adds more protection. Trusted Launch helps guarantee boot integrity across virtual machine fleets. Confidential VM support begins a path toward integrity-protected runtimes on supported hardware. Microsoft is also working on automatic certificate management and post-quantum cryptography. Windows Server 2028 also adds native NVMe storage by default, along with NVMe over TCP and RDMA. Intune management for Windows Server is in preview, and Windows Admin Center Virtualization Mode is now generally available. Microsoft further plans AI inference on local servers, with AMD Instinct MI350P cards in preview from the first half of 2027. The preview is open through the Windows Server Insider Program. Teams that want early access and direct contact with engineers can apply to the Windows Server Technology Adoption Program at aka.ms/WSTAP. Admins should try the build in a lab, score it, and report any workload that breaks. Microsoft says this feedback will shape the defaults before general availability. For now, keep patching current servers and enforce SMB signing and Kerberos where possible. Doing so will make a move to Windows Server 2028 much smoother when it arrives.

A proof-of-concept for CVE-2026-24294 showed the same pattern. It gave SYSTEM-level access on a default Windows Server 2025 install where signing was not enforced. Microsoft fixed that path in March 2026.

The research still warned that as long as NTLM stays common and signing stays optional, new tricks will keep appearing. Turning on signing, encryption, and Kerberos preference at install time removes much of that room. It also matches the advice researchers keep repeating.

Cymulate noted that turning off NTLM alone is not enough and that anti-relay protections must be enforced on every service. Microsoft delivers the hardened values as policy in the HKLM\SOFTWARE\Policies hive wherever a component supports it. Policy wins over local settings, so a script or installer cannot quietly weaken a default.

In Microsoft’s test, trying to turn on WinRM Basic authentication was refused because policy controls it.Admins keep control. OSConfig, Group Policy or another management tool can manage the settings, and whichever tool sets a value owns it. One surprise is that gpresult and RSOP report these settings as Not Configured.

The defaults are built into the image, so there is no policy file for those tools to read. A new PowerShell module called MSHardenedPolicyEval ships in the box. The Get-MSHardenedPolicyScore cmdlet scores the server by category. In Microsoft’s example output, the server passed 191 of 237 checks, an overall score of 80.59 percent.

Restore-MSHardenedPolicy removes hardened values for one category or the whole server. Set-MSHardenedPolicy applies them again. Both support -WhatIf, so admins can preview a change before making it.

Microsoft warns that names may change in later previews, and that scores below 100 percent are expected on this build. Microsoft says some things that worked on Windows Server 2025 may break. Older protocols, legacy authentication, and some management tools and scripts are the likely trouble spots.

Teams should test apps and admin tooling against the hardened setup first. They should relax only the specific setting a workload needs.

Some protections are also still missing from this preview. These include NTLM blocking, Secure Boot and DMA protection requirements, kernel shadow stacks, and Windows Protected Print. Print and RPC hardening is also on the list, along with extra settings such as the logon banner.

The wider release adds more protection. Trusted Launch helps guarantee boot integrity across virtual machine fleets. Confidential VM support begins a path toward integrity-protected runtimes on supported hardware.

Microsoft is also working on automatic certificate management and post-quantum cryptography. Windows Server 2028 also adds native NVMe storage by default, along with NVMe over TCP and RDMA. Intune management for Windows Server is in preview, and Windows Admin Center Virtualization Mode is now generally available.

Microsoft further plans AI inference on local servers, with AMD Instinct MI350P cards in preview from the first half of 2027. The preview is open through the Windows Server Insider Program. Teams that want early access and direct contact with engineers can apply to the Windows Server Technology Adoption Program at aka.ms/WSTAP.

Admins should try the build in a lab, score it, and report any workload that breaks. Microsoft says this feedback will shape the defaults before general availability.

For now, keep patching current servers and enforce SMB signing and Kerberos where possible. Doing so will make a move to Windows Server 2028 much smoother when it arrives.

items.title: New Hello Again Attack Bypasses Windows Hello and BitLocker PIN Lockout Protection
items.summary: Researchers have shown that someone with a laptop and a few cheap parts can guess a Windows Hello PIN in about 40 hours. With the lockout working as designed, the same job would take 69 days. The same trick also cuts the worst-case time to crack a default 6-digit BitLocker startup PIN from 19 years to 20 days. The work is called “Hello Again” and comes from a paper on arXiv that is also tied to ACM CCS ’26. Windows Hello is the main sign-in method on more than one billion Windows 11 devices, and it allows PINs as short as four digits. A short PIN is only safe because the TPM, the security chip that guards keys, locks down after too many wrong guesses. Microsoft explains that the TPM protects against PIN brute-force attempts on lost or stolen devices, and the device locks after too many bad tries. BitLocker works the same way. Microsoft’s BitLocker countermeasures page says TPM anti-hammering is built to stop people from guessing a startup PIN. The whole design depends on the chip keeping an honest count of failed guesses. Hello Attack Bypasses Windows Hello and BitLocker Most modern x86 PCs use a firmware TPM, or fTPM, which runs inside the processor and has no private storage of its own. It saves its state, including the failed-guess count, on the SPI flash chip on the motherboard. If someone copies that saved state and writes it back later, the count goes back too. To stop this, newer boards use Replay Protected Monotonic Counters, or RPMC. These are counters inside the flash chip that can only move up. The researchers did the first practical security study of RPMC in real x86 PCs and found several weak spots. The first flaw is in Winbond flash chips. Winbond is the top NOR flash maker, with more than 25 percent of the market. The team found that a short voltage glitch makes the chip leak its HMAC key, the secret used to sign counter values. With that key in hand, they could forge any counter value they wanted. The second flaw is in AMD’s non-volatile controller. It never checks that a counter actually went up. A small board sitting between the processor and the flash chip can block the increase, say it worked, and the PC accepts the old state without noticing. AMD PCs without RPMC flash looked even weaker. On two AMD desktops, writing an old flash image back reset the fTPM’s lockout counters, and no special board was needed. The paper says these rollbacks work on AMD, Intel, and Pluton fTPM state. The researchers tested the idea on locked and encrypted hardware from start to finish. Each time the TPM locked them out, they rolled back the saved state and kept guessing. This brought a 4-digit Hello PIN down to 40 hours, and the BitLocker TPM+PIN protector fell the same way. Attack Setup A stolen Hello PIN also opens device-bound keys and Hello-based single sign-on at work, so the damage can reach company accounts and not only the laptop. AMD has published bulletin AMD-SN-7079 for the flaw. It tracks the issue as CVE-2026-43613 and gives it a CVSS score of 5.1. AMD says the Secure Processor firmware does not properly confirm that an RPMC increase finished, allowing someone with physical access to suppress counter updates. AMD notes that physical attacks sit outside its normal threat model. It adds that RPMC exists to stop exactly this kind of interposer trick, so it plans firmware fixes. Some target dates for affected Ryzen, EPYC, and Athlon lines are in November 2026. Until the fixes arrive, AMD tells users to keep systems under physical control and watch for signs of tampering. The Winbond key leak is a chip design problem, and the paper’s findings suggest that only new flash designs can close it. Other BitLocker Bypasses This is not the first time BitLocker’s physical protections have been tested this year. Cyber Security News covered the YellowKey BitLocker zero-day , which let someone with physical access skip BitLocker through the Windows Recovery Environment. We also reported on Microsoft’s YellowKey mitigation , tracked as CVE-2026-45585. Microsoft’s advice after YellowKey was to move from TPM-only mode to TPM+PIN. Hello Again shows why that advice needs a second step. A short PIN is only as strong as the lockout behind it. The GreatXML bug, which we covered in our GreatXML report , points to the same pattern of physical-access bypasses. The risk is real but narrow. It requires physical access, special tools, and time, so it mainly worries owners of lost or stolen laptops that carry valuable data. Longer PINs are the easiest fix, because each added digit multiplies the number of guesses needed. Microsoft’s guidance also suggests using a longer, enhanced alphanumeric PIN with BitLocker when strong protection is needed. Admins can raise the minimum PIN length in Group Policy, turn on enhanced startup PINs, and install AMD firmware updates once vendors release them. Companies that store sensitive data should also treat a stolen laptop as a possible data exposure, even when the drive was encrypted. What Are Leading Organizations Doing About AI and Cyber Risks? items.title: Microsoft’s AI Uncovers 99 Security Issues in Express, ImageMagick and Other Open-Source Projects
items.summary: Microsoft and GitHub sent 99 verified security reports to six open-source projects, including Express and ImageMagick, after an AI pilot identified thousands of potential vulnerabilities. In its Nov. 17 announcement, GitHub said maintainers had fixed 55 issues as of Nov. 15. However, only 14 of those fixes had made it into software releases. The other four projects, Caddy, AutoGPT, FastMCP, and Netty, also participated in the GitHub Secure Open Source Fund, with maintainers approving the scans before the pilot began. Microsoft’s Codename MDASH scanned the projects with an earlier version of the MAI Cyber model and suggested code fixes. A GitHub Security Lab AI tool removed duplicates, filtered out reports that didn’t hold up, and prioritized higher-impact issues. Seven Microsoft FORGE Lab researchers then manually reviewed the remaining findings. Microsoft had previously used MDASH to find Windows vulnerabilities . Codename MDASH AI Flags Thousands of Potential Flaws (source : Github ) Microsofts AI Uncovers 99 Security Issues GitHub sent the verified reports through its private vulnerability reporting system. Each report included evidence of the issue and a proposed patch. According to GitHub , maintainers could accept, modify, or replace suggested patches and decide when to release fixes without receiving raw scan results. Caddy fixed all 22 reported issues within a week, while ImageMagick’s two-person team also received 22 reports. One looked like a problem the team had seen before, but the report explained what was different and pointed to the relevant code. The team pushed a fix in 15 minutes. Those findings are separate from previously reported ImageMagick memory corruption flaws . Maintainers received 99 private reports (source: GitHub) AutoGPT’s team received a report about a newly added security check three days after it shipped. The maintainers went beyond the suggested patch, wrote their own fix within a day, and put it into production in less than a week. Express maintainers said the reports helped them cut through the noise from other vulnerability submissions. The pilot covered only six projects, and the human review took about two days per project. That makes the results an early test of how AI can help small teams, not proof that the approach can work at the same pace across thousands of repositories. The work also does not end when a maintainer writes a patch. Users need a release that contains the fix, and they still need to install it. GitHub plans to offer reviewed AI scans to all alums of its Secure Open Source Fund and deliver findings privately. For developers who rely on open-source packages, GitHub recommends enabling Dependabot alerts to catch known vulnerabilities in their dependencies. Once a public advisory is reviewed for the GitHub Advisory Database, Dependabot can notify repositories that use the affected package. Teams can then check the advisory against the version they actually run and confirm that their next update includes the fix. items.title: LABScon26 Replay | Governing Just-in-Time Intelligence: AI, Dual-Use Capabilities, and the Limits of Guardrails
items.summary: In his LABScon 26 talk, Mauro Vignati, Advisor on Digital Technologies of Warfare at the International Committee of the Red Cross (ICRC), argues that guardrails cannot address the deeper problem with frontier AI. Advanced cognitive capabilities are now distributed through the same on-demand, as-a-service model that has shaped industry, and later cybercrime, for seventy years. That model was designed for industrial efficiency, not for technology this powerful. Vignati traces the model back to Toyota’s post-war just-in-time production system, built on the principle that customers get only what they need and pay only for what they get. The IT needed to coordinate that system helped give rise to application service providers and eventually to software-as-a-service. Cybercriminals later adopted the same logic for crimeware and ransomware, and hacktivists for DDoS campaigns. In each case the people taking part needed no technical skill of their own. Model-as-a-service differs from its predecessors because the capability is dual-use at the source, supplied by private technology firms largely independent of who the end users are or what they intend. Vignati explains why criminals who tried to build their own AI systems have largely turned to wrapping commercial ones instead, leaving the legitimate economy to carry the cost of training and infrastructure. He then draws on cybernetics’ law of requisite variety, the principle that any system regulating another must match its complexity, to argue that AI governance has no simple fix. In its place he proposes a layered framework for deciding what a model can do, for whom and under what conditions. His warning is that as long as the industry keeps offering powerful general-purpose models, criminals and activists will continue to parasitise commercial services. For policymakers, AI providers and threat researchers, this talk offers a historical lens on how offensive capability spreads and a starting point for thinking about how to govern it. About the Author Mauro Vignati is Advisor on Digital Technologies of Warfare at the International Committee of the Red Cross (ICRC). His work focuses on the militarisation of digital space and AI, the exploitation of the cognitive domain as a means of confrontation, and the impact of digital technologies in armed conflict on civilians, critical infrastructure and society. He has more than 20 years of experience in cybersecurity and previously spoke at LABScon 2022. About LABScon This presentation was featured live at LABScon 2026, an immersive 3-day conference bringing together the world’s top cybersecurity minds, hosted by SentinelOne’s research arm, SentinelLABS. Keep up with all the latest on LABScon here.

items.title: Inside Secretless Analysis: from CI identity to project-scoped access
items.summary: The problem In March 2026, an attacker force-pushed version tags of aquasecurity/trivy-action , the GitHub Action for the Trivy security scanner, to malicious commits ( Aqua's write-up ). Pipelines that ran it while the tags were compromised had their secrets read from the runner's memory, and then the real scan ran as usual, so nothing looked wrong. A year earlier, the same technique hit tj-actions/changed-files and more than 23,000 repositories, that time printing secrets into build logs ( CVE-2025-30066 ). And compromised actions aren't the only route. The GhostAction campaign uses stolen developer accounts to push workflows whose only purpose is to send repository secrets to an attacker-controlled server. GitGuardian first reported it in September 2025, with 3,325 stolen secrets. In October 2026 it came back with about 1,900 compromised accounts and more than 30,000 targeted repositories. In between, the Shai-Hulud 2.0 npm worm pushed workflows that published every repository secret. A SonarQube token stored as a CI secret is exactly what these attacks harvest. What a stored token costs With token-based analysis, every repository needs the same setup: Generate a SonarQube token. Paste it into the repository secrets or CI/CD variables. Give the pipeline the organization and project keys. Then repeat it for the next repository, and for all of them at every rotation. The SonarQube admin can choose between two types of tokens. A personal access token is the easiest to create, but it carries all of its owner's permissions, far more than an analysis job needs. A scoped organization token, available on the Team and Enterprise plans, can be limited to one project, but it still has to be created, distributed, rotated and revoked. Sharing one token across repositories reduces that work but multiplies the impact of a leak. The real cost shows up during an incident like the examples mentioned above. You have to find every pipeline that uses the token, rotate it and redistribute it without breaking the build. All while the extent of the exposure is still being assessed. When designing Secretless Analysis for SonarQube Cloud, we didn't try to store tokens more safely. We stopped storing them altogether. Every single analysis now receives an ephemeral token, scoped strictly to that project, that expires in 30 minutes. No secret to manage, yet more secure than a stored token: that can sound like magic. This post demystifies it. We start with what changes in your pipeline, then open up the exchange behind it: how a CI job proves where it runs, how SonarQube Cloud turns that proof into access to exactly one project, and what this does and doesn't protect you against. Secretless Analysis is available for GitHub Actions on GitHub.com and for GitLab.com CI/CD, on every SonarQube Cloud plan, including the Free plan. What changes in your pipeline Secretless Analysis removes every step of that setup. There's no token to generate, store or rotate, and no keys to copy into the pipeline. Here is a complete GitHub Actions job for a repository bound to one SonarQube Cloud project, using the SonarQube auth action : ```yaml jobs: sonarqube: runs-on: ubuntu-latest permissions: contents: read id-token: write steps: - uses: actions/checkout@v6 with: fetch-depth: 0 - uses: SonarSource/sonarqube-auth-action@v1 id: auth - uses: SonarSource/sonarqube-scan-action@v8 with: args: > -Dsonar.organization=${{ steps.auth.outputs.organization }} -Dsonar.projectKey=${{ steps.auth.outputs.project-key }} ``` The id-token: write permission lets the job ask GitHub for an OIDC token. The auth action exchanges that OIDC token for a short-lived analysis token, makes it available to the scan step as SONAR_TOKEN , and outputs the organization and project keys that SonarQube Cloud resolved for this repository. Because nothing in it is repository-specific, the same workflow, or one shared reusable workflow, works unchanged across thousands of repositories . Onboarding a repository means binding it to a SonarQube Cloud project, with no new secret and no new pair of keys to maintain. The job targets the EU instance by default; add sonar-region: us to the auth step for the US instance. The region also sets the audience of the OIDC token, one of the checks described below. Everything that makes this safe happens inside that auth step. How does OIDC token exchange work in SonarQube Cloud? The mechanism is workload identity federation: one system that accepts an Identity established by another, then applies its own authorization policy. Two tokens are involved, which we'll call the OIDC token and the analysis token: Token Issued by What it says OIDC ID token GitHub Actions or GitLab.com "This job runs in repository X." Signed and short-lived. Analysis token SonarQube Cloud "The holder may submit analysis for project Y." Valid for 30 minutes. GitHub or GitLab vouches for where the job runs. SonarQube Cloud decides what it may do. The CI platform never chooses the SonarQube permissions. The exchange uses the OAuth 2.0 Token Exchange grant defined in RFC 8693 . RFC 8693 also allows additional response fields, which is how the organization and project keys come back with the token. Between the request and the response, SonarQube Cloud goes through three steps, each covered in its own section below: Step 1: Proving where the job runs GitHub and GitLab issue OIDC tokens as signed JSON Web Tokens. A GitHub token carries around thirty claims about the run; these are the ones the exchange relies on: { "iss": "https://token.actions.githubusercontent.com", "aud": "https://sonarcloud.io", "repository_id": "123456789", "jti": "example-job-token-id", "iat": 1781723841, "exp": 1781724141 } GitLab tokens carry the equivalent project_id . Anyone can write that JSON, so decoding it proves nothing. The signature is what counts, and the exchange checks it against the provider's published keys: Verification follows the JSON Web Signature standard ( RFC 7515 ), using public keys published as a JSON Web Key Set ( RFC 7517 ) and located through each provider's OpenID Connect Discovery document, at a URL we configure rather than derive from the token. We accept only RS256, and we cache the provider's keys and refresh them in the background, so key rotations on GitHub's or GitLab's side are picked up automatically. A valid signature isn't enough on its own: a token that GitHub signed for another service, or one that has expired, is still correctly signed. So the exchange also checks that: the issuer is the expected provider, the audience is the SonarQube Cloud region the job targets, the token is within its validity window, the token hasn't been exchanged before: each OIDC token, identified by its jti , can be exchanged only once, so a replayed token is rejected, the identity claims the exchange needs are present. Only then are the claims used to find a corresponding SonarQube project. Step 2: Deciding what the job may do A verified token proves which repository a job runs in. It doesn't say which SonarQube project that job can analyze. This is where authentication ends and authorization begins, and the CI platform has no say in it: the answer comes from the binding SonarQube Cloud keeps between each SonarQube project and its repository on the DevOps platform. The exchange looks up that binding by provider and signed repository ID, never by name . If a repository is deleted and recreated by someone else under the same name, a name-based rule would trust the newcomer; that's repo-jacking. An ID is assigned only once, so the recreated repository gets a new ID and no binding. The same goes for forks, which have their own IDs. One bound project: the project and organization are resolved without either key in the request. Several bound projects (a monorepo): the caller must pass a project key to pick one; the organization is still resolved automatically. ```yaml - uses: SonarSource/sonarqube-auth-action@v1 id: auth with: project-key: acme_billing-service ``` The candidates always come from the bindings, never from the request. Just as the CI platform doesn't choose the SonarQube permissions, neither does the caller. The caller can only narrow the set of bound projects; it can't enlarge it. A monorepo containing a billing service and a web application can get a token for either project, and a request for any other project fails. A binding is necessary but not sufficient. An organization administrator must also enable the Secretless Analysis feature at organization level. Until they do, no repository in the organization can exchange a token, bound or not. Step 3: A token for one project, for 30 minutes When every check passes, SonarQube Cloud issues an analysis token with a single permission: scan on the resolved project. It expires 30 minutes after it is issued. The analysis APIs enforce both limits: an expired token is rejected, and so is a request for any other project. Nothing about the token outlives the job. The next job goes through the same exchange and gets a fresh one. What this protects against, and what it doesn't Back to the attacks at the top of this post. There's nothing at rest to steal. GhostAction and Shai-Hulud collected secrets stored in repository settings. With Secretless Analysis, there is no SonarQube secret there. A personal access token exposes everything its owner can access. An analysis token can only submit analysis for the project bound to the repository it was issued for. There's nothing to clean up. No long-lived token needs to be rotated or redistributed after an incident, so there's nothing a rotation can miss. Like any CI credential, the analysis token is available to the code running in your job, including a compromised step like the Trivy action.
