items.summary_html:
The problem

In March 2026, an attacker force-pushed version tags of aquasecurity/trivy-action, the GitHub Action for the Trivy security scanner, to malicious commits (Aqua's write-up). Pipelines that ran it while the tags were compromised had their secrets read from the runner's memory, and then the real scan ran as usual, so nothing looked wrong.

A year earlier, the same technique hit tj-actions/changed-files and more than 23,000 repositories, that time printing secrets into build logs (CVE-2025-30066). And compromised actions aren't the only route. The GhostAction campaign uses stolen developer accounts to push workflows whose only purpose is to send repository secrets to an attacker-controlled server. GitGuardian first reported it in September 2025, with 3,325 stolen secrets. In October 2026 it came back with about 1,900 compromised accounts and more than 30,000 targeted repositories. In between, the Shai-Hulud 2.0 npm worm pushed workflows that published every repository secret.

A SonarQube token stored as a CI secret is exactly what these attacks harvest.

What a stored token costs

With token-based analysis, every repository needs the same setup:

  1. Generate a SonarQube token.
  2. Paste it into the repository secrets or CI/CD variables.
  3. Give the pipeline the organization and project keys.

Then repeat it for the next repository, and for all of them at every rotation.

The SonarQube admin can choose between two types of tokens. A personal access token is the easiest to create, but it carries all of its owner's permissions, far more than an analysis job needs. A scoped organization token, available on the Team and Enterprise plans, can be limited to one project, but it still has to be created, distributed, rotated and revoked. Sharing one token across repositories reduces that work but multiplies the impact of a leak.

The real cost shows up during an incident like the examples mentioned above. You have to find every pipeline that uses the token, rotate it and redistribute it without breaking the build. All while the extent of the exposure is still being assessed. 

When designing Secretless Analysis for SonarQube Cloud, we didn't try to store tokens more safely. We stopped storing them altogether. Every single analysis now receives an ephemeral token, scoped strictly to that project, that expires in 30 minutes.

No secret to manage, yet more secure than a stored token: that can sound like magic. This post demystifies it. We start with what changes in your pipeline, then open up the exchange behind it: how a CI job proves where it runs, how SonarQube Cloud turns that proof into access to exactly one project, and what this does and doesn't protect you against.

Secretless Analysis is available for GitHub Actions on GitHub.com and for GitLab.com CI/CD, on every SonarQube Cloud plan, including the Free plan.

What changes in your pipeline

Secretless Analysis removes every step of that setup. There's no token to generate, store or rotate, and no keys to copy into the pipeline. Here is a complete GitHub Actions job for a repository bound to one SonarQube Cloud project, using the SonarQube auth action:

```yaml
jobs:
  sonarqube:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    permissions:
      contents: read
      id-token: write
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v6
        with:
          fetch-depth: 0
      - uses: SonarSource/sonarqube-auth-action@v1
        id: auth
      - uses: SonarSource/sonarqube-scan-action@v8
        with:
          args: >
            -Dsonar.organization=${{ steps.auth.outputs.organization }}
            -Dsonar.projectKey=${{ steps.auth.outputs.project-key }}
```


The id-token: write permission lets the job ask GitHub for an OIDC token. The auth action exchanges that OIDC token for a short-lived analysis token, makes it available to the scan step as SONAR_TOKEN, and outputs the organization and project keys that SonarQube Cloud resolved for this repository.

Because nothing in it is repository-specific, the same workflow, or one shared reusable workflow, works unchanged across thousands of repositories. Onboarding a repository means binding it to a SonarQube Cloud project, with no new secret and no new pair of keys to maintain. The job targets the EU instance by default; add sonar-region: us to the auth step for the US instance. The region also sets the audience of the OIDC token, one of the checks described below.

Everything that makes this safe happens inside that auth step.

How does OIDC token exchange work in SonarQube Cloud?

The mechanism is workload identity federation: one system that accepts an Identity established by another, then applies its own authorization policy. Two tokens are involved, which we'll call the OIDC token and the analysis token:

Token

Issued by

What it says

OIDC ID token

GitHub Actions or GitLab.com

"This job runs in repository X." Signed and short-lived.

Analysis token

SonarQube Cloud

"The holder may submit analysis for project Y." Valid for 30 minutes.

GitHub or GitLab vouches for where the job runs. SonarQube Cloud decides what it may do. The CI platform never chooses the SonarQube permissions.

The exchange uses the OAuth 2.0 Token Exchange grant defined in RFC 8693. The auth action sends the OIDC token as the subject token (line breaks added, values not URL-encoded for readability):

```http
POST /authentication/token
Content-Type: application/x-www-form-urlencoded


grant_type=urn:ietf:params:oauth:grant-type:token-exchange
&subject_token=
&subject_token_type=urn:ietf:params:oauth:token-type:id_token
&audience=https://sonarcloud.io
```


And receives (simplified):

{
    "access_token": "sqco_...",
    "token_type": "Bearer",
    "expires_in": 1800,
    "issued_token_type": "urn:ietf:params:oauth:token-type:access_token",
    "organization": "acme",
    "project_key": "acme_billing-service"
  }


We chose a standard grant over a custom endpoint so that any OAuth-aware client can call it, and so that supporting another CI platform means trusting a new issuer rather than designing a new API. RFC 8693 also allows additional response fields, which is how the organization and project keys come back with the token.

Between the request and the response, SonarQube Cloud goes through three steps, each covered in its own section below:

Step 1: Proving where the job runs

GitHub and GitLab issue OIDC tokens as signed JSON Web Tokens. A GitHub token carries around thirty claims about the run; these are the ones the exchange relies on:

{
    "iss": "https://token.actions.githubusercontent.com",
    "aud": "https://sonarcloud.io",
    "repository_id": "123456789",
    "jti": "example-job-token-id",
    "iat": 1781723841,
    "exp": 1781724141
  }


GitLab tokens carry the equivalent project_id.

Anyone can write that JSON, so decoding it proves nothing. The signature is what counts, and the exchange checks it against the provider's published keys:

Verification follows the JSON Web Signature standard (RFC 7515), using public keys published as a JSON Web Key Set (RFC 7517) and located through each provider's OpenID Connect Discovery document, at a URL we configure rather than derive from the token. We accept only RS256, and we cache the provider's keys and refresh them in the background, so key rotations on GitHub's or GitLab's side are picked up automatically.

A valid signature isn't enough on its own: a token that GitHub signed for another service, or one that has expired, is still correctly signed. So the exchange also checks that:

  • the issuer is the expected provider,
  • the audience is the SonarQube Cloud region the job targets,
  • the token is within its validity window,
  • the token hasn't been exchanged before: each OIDC token, identified by its jti, can be exchanged only once, so a replayed token is rejected,
  • the identity claims the exchange needs are present.

Only then are the claims used to find a corresponding SonarQube project.

Step 2: Deciding what the job may do

A verified token proves which repository a job runs in. It doesn't say which SonarQube project that job can analyze. This is where authentication ends and authorization begins, and the CI platform has no say in it: the answer comes from the binding SonarQube Cloud keeps between each SonarQube project and its repository on the DevOps platform.

The exchange looks up that binding by provider and signed repository ID, never by name. If a repository is deleted and recreated by someone else under the same name, a name-based rule would trust the newcomer; that's repo-jacking. An ID is assigned only once, so the recreated repository gets a new ID and no binding. The same goes for forks, which have their own IDs.

For a repository that does match, the lookup has three outcomes:

  • No bound project: the exchange is rejected.
  • One bound project: the project and organization are resolved without either key in the request.
  • Several bound projects (a monorepo): the caller must pass a project key to pick one; the organization is still resolved automatically.
```yaml
      - uses: SonarSource/sonarqube-auth-action@v1
        id: auth
        with:
          project-key: acme_billing-service
```


The candidates always come from the bindings, never from the request. Just as the CI platform doesn't choose the SonarQube permissions, neither does the caller. The caller can only narrow the set of bound projects; it can't enlarge it. A monorepo containing a billing service and a web application can get a token for either project, and a request for any other project fails.

A binding is necessary but not sufficient. An organization administrator must also enable the Secretless Analysis feature at organization level. Until they do, no repository in the organization can exchange a token, bound or not.

Step 3: A token for one project, for 30 minutes

When every check passes, SonarQube Cloud issues an analysis token with a single permission: scan on the resolved project. It expires 30 minutes after it is issued. The analysis APIs enforce both limits: an expired token is rejected, and so is a request for any other project.

Nothing about the token outlives the job. The next job goes through the same exchange and gets a fresh one.

What this protects against, and what it doesn't

Back to the attacks at the top of this post.

  • There's nothing at rest to steal. GhostAction and Shai-Hulud collected secrets stored in repository settings. With Secretless Analysis, there is no SonarQube secret there.
  • A leaked token stops working quickly. tj-actions left secrets in build logs for about a day. An analysis token leaked the same way expires 30 minutes after it is issued, long before most people would find it.
  • A leaked token reaches one project. A personal access token exposes everything its owner can access. An analysis token can only submit analysis for the project bound to the repository it was issued for.
  • There's nothing to clean up. No long-lived token needs to be rotated or redistributed after an incident, so there's nothing a rotation can miss.

Like any CI credential, the analysis token is available to the code running in your job, including a compromised step like the Trivy action. The difference is what an attacker can do with it: submit analysis for one project, for at most 30 minutes after their code stops running, instead of holding a long-lived token until someone notices and rotates it. As with any pipeline, keep an eye on who can change workflow files, and treat repository bindings and the organization opt-in as security settings.

Try it and tell us

Enable Secretless Analysis in your organization settings, check that your repositories are bound, and replace your token-based job with the configuration above. The documentation covers all the details.

Secretless Analysis is available in all SonarQube Cloud plans today for GitHub and GitLab. We’re planning to bring the same mechanism to SonarQube Server in the near future.

If you are running your pipelines in a DevOps platform other than GitHub and GitLab or in a custom CI environment, tell us on the SonarSource Community which one you’d like to see supported next.

items.title: Java4Shell (CVE-2026-114938): Find affected Java in your container images
items.summary: What has been reported Calif , a security research firm, reported the flaw and named it Java4Shell. Calif reports it demonstrated remote code execution without logging in against several widely used Java products in their default configurations. Each exploit needs custom work, and a failed attempt can crash the Java process. Oracle, which assigned the CVE, rates it 8.1 (High) on CVSS 3.1. Red Hat’s preliminary score is 9.8 (Critical). The bug is in the optimized Base64 decoder of OpenJDK . On x86-64 processors that support AVX-512 VBMI, a crafted input can write past the end of a buffer. Java 17.0.6 and later, including 21, 25, and 27, are affected. Java 11, Java 17.0.5 and earlier, and standard Java 8 are not. Oracle lists one Java 8 exception: its performance build, 8u511b33-perf. Exploitation needs an Intel or AMD processor with AVX-512 VBMI, the accelerated decoder enabled (the default), and attacker-supplied data reaching Java's built-in Base64 decoder, for example in authentication headers, tokens, or uploads. ARM processors such as AWS Graviton are not affected. Find affected images with SonarQube container scanning Code analysis and dependency analysis will not show this flaw. It sits in the Java runtime underneath your code, not in your code or your declared libraries. Container scanning in SonarQube Advanced Security looks at the runtime itself. It matches each image against Linux distribution advisories and it re-checks images you have already scanned based on your organization's re-analysis settings so you do not need to scan them again. Debian, Ubuntu, and Alpine have already published their advisories for CVE-2026-114938. Red Hat has a security bulletin and is preparing updates. To check an image: Download the container scanner for your platform. Pull or build the image, then run sonar-container-scanner --organization --token . In SonarQube Cloud, open your organization and select Container images. Select an image to see its dependency risks, including CVE-2026-114938. What to know before you rely on it: Container scanning is available on SonarQube Cloud with SonarQube Advanced Security. It covers images built on Red Hat Enterprise Linux, Debian 11 and later, Rocky Linux, AlmaLinux, Ubuntu, and Alpine. It does not cover Amazon Linux. It sees the images you scan. It does not see Java on hosts outside containers. A JDK installed as a downloaded archive, rather than a distribution package, may not be matched. Debian and Ubuntu have not released fixed packages yet, so a finding shows exposure but may not name a fixed version. It shows exposure, not whether an attacker can reach the flaw. SonarQube Server does not have container scanning yet. Server customers with SonarQube Advanced Security can import an SBOM of an image for a similar check. Fixed builds Oracle fixed the flaw in its November 17 Critical Security Patch Update . The fixed Java SE builds are below. Oracle Java SE line Fixed build 17 17.0.21.1 21 21.0.13.1 25 25.0.5.1 27 27.0.1.1 Oracle's November update fixes other flaws too. Other OpenJDK distributions ship on their own schedules and use their own build numbers. Amazon Corretto has already released fixed builds . If you use another vendor’s JDK distribution, you will need to check for their updates. What to do now Find every Java runtime you run. Container scanning covers images. For everything else, check java -version on each host. On Linux, grep -m1 avx512vbmi /proc/cpuinfo prints a line only if the processor is in scope. Then check the less obvious places: Oracle Java SE and GraalVM, OpenJDK builds from other vendors, Linux packages such as openjdk-17, applications that bundle their own JDK, and the base image in each container build. Update to your vendor's fixed build as soon as it is available. Oracle's builds are in the table above. Other vendors use their own version numbers. Start with services reachable from the internet. Remove network exposure you do not need. Java programs that connect out to servers you do not control are also exposed. Restart the Java processes. Then confirm the running version, not only the installed package. Until you can patch, turn off the accelerated decoder. Add -XX:-UseBASE64Intrinsics to the Java options of each affected process and restart. Java then uses its standard Base64 code, and only Base64 encoding and decoding get slower. The flag is safe on ARM. Apply it only to Java 17 and later: Java 8 does not recognize the option and will not start with it. This is a mitigation, not a fix. Calif, which found the flaw, recommends it. You should still patch. After the restart, confirm the flag appears in the running process, not only in the config file. Running SonarQube? SonarQube Server and Community Build: add the one-line Java option from our Community advisory . It has exact steps for ZIP, Docker, Kubernetes and Helm, Data Center Edition, and scanners and CI agents. We will post confirmed patch versions and rebuilt Docker images in the same thread. SonarQube Cloud: we are rolling out the fix to the service. If you run SonarScanner in your own CI, apply the scanner steps in the advisory. For help, contact Sonar Support .
items.summary_html:
What has been reported

Calif, a security research firm, reported the flaw and named it Java4Shell. Calif reports it demonstrated remote code execution without logging in against several widely used Java products in their default configurations. Each exploit needs custom work, and a failed attempt can crash the Java process. Oracle, which assigned the CVE, rates it 8.1 (High) on CVSS 3.1. Red Hat’s preliminary score is 9.8 (Critical).

The bug is in the optimized Base64 decoder of OpenJDK. On x86-64 processors that support AVX-512 VBMI, a crafted input can write past the end of a buffer. Java 17.0.6 and later, including 21, 25, and 27, are affected. Java 11, Java 17.0.5 and earlier, and standard Java 8 are not. Oracle lists one Java 8 exception: its performance build, 8u511b33-perf.

Exploitation needs an Intel or AMD processor with AVX-512 VBMI, the accelerated decoder enabled (the default), and attacker-supplied data reaching Java's built-in Base64 decoder, for example in authentication headers, tokens, or uploads. ARM processors such as AWS Graviton are not affected.

Find affected images with SonarQube container scanning

Code analysis and dependency analysis will not show this flaw. It sits in the Java runtime underneath your code, not in your code or your declared libraries. Container scanning in SonarQube Advanced Security looks at the runtime itself.

It matches each image against Linux distribution advisories and it re-checks images you have already scanned based on your organization's re-analysis settings so you do not need to scan them again. Debian, Ubuntu, and Alpine have already published their advisories for CVE-2026-114938. Red Hat has a security bulletin and is preparing updates.

To check an image:

  1. Download the container scanner for your platform.
  2. Pull or build the image, then run sonar-container-scanner --organization --token .
  3. In SonarQube Cloud, open your organization and select Container images. Select an image to see its dependency risks, including CVE-2026-114938.

What to know before you rely on it:

  • Container scanning is available on SonarQube Cloud with SonarQube Advanced Security.
  • It covers images built on Red Hat Enterprise Linux, Debian 11 and later, Rocky Linux, AlmaLinux, Ubuntu, and Alpine. It does not cover Amazon Linux.
  • It sees the images you scan. It does not see Java on hosts outside containers.
  • A JDK installed as a downloaded archive, rather than a distribution package, may not be matched.
  • Debian and Ubuntu have not released fixed packages yet, so a finding shows exposure but may not name a fixed version.
  • It shows exposure, not whether an attacker can reach the flaw.

SonarQube Server does not have container scanning yet. Server customers with SonarQube Advanced Security can import an SBOM of an image for a similar check.

Fixed builds

Oracle fixed the flaw in its November 17 Critical Security Patch Update. The fixed Java SE builds are below.

Oracle Java SE line

Fixed build

17

17.0.21.1

21

21.0.13.1

25

25.0.5.1

27

27.0.1.1

Oracle's November update fixes other flaws too. Other OpenJDK distributions ship on their own schedules and use their own build numbers. Amazon Corretto has already released fixed builds. If you use another vendor’s JDK distribution, you will need to check for their updates.

What to do now
  1. Find every Java runtime you run. Container scanning covers images. For everything else, check java -version on each host. On Linux, grep -m1 avx512vbmi /proc/cpuinfo prints a line only if the processor is in scope. Then check the less obvious places: Oracle Java SE and GraalVM, OpenJDK builds from other vendors, Linux packages such as openjdk-17, applications that bundle their own JDK, and the base image in each container build.
  2. Update to your vendor's fixed build as soon as it is available. Oracle's builds are in the table above. Other vendors use their own version numbers.
  3. Start with services reachable from the internet. Remove network exposure you do not need. Java programs that connect out to servers you do not control are also exposed.
  4. Restart the Java processes. Then confirm the running version, not only the installed package.
  5. Until you can patch, turn off the accelerated decoder. Add -XX:-UseBASE64Intrinsics to the Java options of each affected process and restart. Java then uses its standard Base64 code, and only Base64 encoding and decoding get slower. The flag is safe on ARM. Apply it only to Java 17 and later: Java 8 does not recognize the option and will not start with it. This is a mitigation, not a fix. Calif, which found the flaw, recommends it. You should still patch.
  • After the restart, confirm the flag appears in the running process, not only in the config file.
Running SonarQube?

SonarQube Server and Community Build: add the one-line Java option from our Community advisory. It has exact steps for ZIP, Docker, Kubernetes and Helm, Data Center Edition, and scanners and CI agents. We will post confirmed patch versions and rebuilt Docker images in the same thread.

SonarQube Cloud: we are rolling out the fix to the service. If you run SonarScanner in your own CI, apply the scanner steps in the advisory. For help, contact Sonar Support.

items.title: Hackers Steal Exposed AWS Credentials From Docker Hub Images in Just 8 Seconds
items.summary: Automated bots used a decoy Amazon Web Services (AWS) access key just 7.86 seconds after researchers published the Docker Hub image containing it. That was the fastest case in a controlled Stony Brook University study, not the average. Still, the median time to the first AWS request was just 51.19 seconds, and all 100 keys in the first round were used within 15 minutes. The study did not report a break-in at Docker Hub. It showed how quickly a secret left inside a public image can be found and used. Researchers Billy Tsouvalas and Nick Nikiforakis published 300 test images across eight public container registries over four months. They planted AWS, OpenAI, and Anthropic API keys, along with decoy SSH and database credentials. In the first round alone, 100 unadvertised Docker Hub images were downloaded 58,819 times. The AWS keys inside them drew 66,321 requests from 3,842 distinct IP addresses. Those addresses indicate where requests came from, not how many attackers were involved. A container image packages an application and its files in layers. The researchers saw no signs that anyone ran the images in the first round, despite heavy use of the planted keys. That points to bots reading the image layers directly. It also explains why watching running containers would miss this kind of leak. A file removed in a later build step can still be present in an earlier layer. Exposed AWS Credentials From Docker Hub Images AWS logs showed that some requests checked whether a key worked, while others tried to list cloud resources or use paid services. The study’s first-round restrictions blocked attempts to consume AWS resources. Image instrumentation: Injection of dynamic lifecycle beacons, static honeytokens, and honeypot credentials(source: dl.acm ) However, requests made with planted OpenAI and Anthropic keys drained the researchers’ test balances. The difference illustrates why permissions matter. A separate investigation covered by Cyber Security News found 768 exposed corporate AWS credentials with full admin access . Scan the built image before uploading it, not just the source code. The scan should cover image layers and metadata because a clean project folder does not guarantee a clean image. If a build needs a password or token, use Docker BuildKit secret mounts to make it available only during the build step that needs it. Avoid putting secrets in Dockerfile ARG or ENV instructions. For applications running on AWS, prefer roles that issue temporary credentials with only the permissions the application needs. Parallel log streams aggregation diagram for deployment of instrumented image (source: dl.acm ) If an AWS key has already shipped in a public image, deactivate it immediately and replace it if the application still needs one. Removing the image does not invalidate a copied key. Review AWS CloudTrail logs from the time of publication for unfamiliar requests, permission changes, and unexpected resource creation. As Cyber Security News reported in its coverage of AWS key quarantine , automatic restrictions can block some actions without revoking the key. The researchers shared their findings with Docker, whose security team acknowledged the report. They proposed checking images for secrets before publication and limiting access to the public feed of new and updated images. For developers, the most useful change is one they can make now. Put the secret check before the upload, when a failed scan can still stop a leak. items.summary_html:
Automated bots used a decoy Amazon Web Services (AWS) access key just 7.86 seconds after researchers published the Docker Hub image containing it. That was the fastest case in a controlled Stony Brook University study, not the average.

Still, the median time to the first AWS request was just 51.19 seconds, and all 100 keys in the first round were used within 15 minutes. The study did not report a break-in at Docker Hub. It showed how quickly a secret left inside a public image can be found and used.

Researchers Billy Tsouvalas and Nick Nikiforakis published 300 test images across eight public container registries over four months. They planted AWS, OpenAI, and Anthropic API keys, along with decoy SSH and database credentials.

In the first round alone, 100 unadvertised Docker Hub images were downloaded 58,819 times. The AWS keys inside them drew 66,321 requests from 3,842 distinct IP addresses. Those addresses indicate where requests came from, not how many attackers were involved.

A container image packages an application and its files in layers. The researchers saw no signs that anyone ran the images in the first round, despite heavy use of the planted keys.

That points to bots reading the image layers directly. It also explains why watching running containers would miss this kind of leak. A file removed in a later build step can still be present in an earlier layer.

Exposed AWS Credentials From Docker Hub Images

AWS logs showed that some requests checked whether a key worked, while others tried to list cloud resources or use paid services. The study’s first-round restrictions blocked attempts to consume AWS resources.

Image instrumentation: Injection of dynamic lifecycle beacons, static honeytokens, and honeypot credentials(source: dl.acm )

However, requests made with planted OpenAI and Anthropic keys drained the researchers’ test balances. The difference illustrates why permissions matter. A separate investigation covered by Cyber Security News found 768 exposed corporate AWS credentials with full admin access.

Scan the built image before uploading it, not just the source code. The scan should cover image layers and metadata because a clean project folder does not guarantee a clean image.

If a build needs a password or token, use Docker BuildKit secret mounts to make it available only during the build step that needs it. Avoid putting secrets in Dockerfile ARG or ENV instructions. For applications running on AWS, prefer roles that issue temporary credentials with only the permissions the application needs.

Parallel log streams aggregation diagram for deployment of instrumented image (source: dl.acm )

If an AWS key has already shipped in a public image, deactivate it immediately and replace it if the application still needs one. Removing the image does not invalidate a copied key.

Review AWS CloudTrail logs from the time of publication for unfamiliar requests, permission changes, and unexpected resource creation. As Cyber Security News reported in its coverage of AWS key quarantine, automatic restrictions can block some actions without revoking the key.

The researchers shared their findings with Docker, whose security team acknowledged the report. They proposed checking images for secrets before publication and limiting access to the public feed of new and updated images. For developers, the most useful change is one they can make now. Put the secret check before the upload, when a failed scan can still stop a leak.

items.title: The Gentlemen Ransomware Gang Allegedly Claims to Have Breached NVIDIA
items.summary: The Gentlemen ransomware gang listed NVIDIA on its dark web leak site on November 18, 2026, but
items.summary_html:
The Gentlemen ransomware gang listed NVIDIA on its dark web leak site on November 18, 2026, but the post does not prove that the group broke into the chipmaker’s systems.

The listing shows a countdown and references ransom talks, but includes no sample files. NVIDIA has not publicly confirmed a breach, and there is no verified evidence that the group stole data or encrypted company systems.

The screenshot shows NVIDIA’s logo, its NVDA stock ticker, and a revenue figure of $303 billion with no reporting period. It also shows the words “DATA INFO – SOON” and a reference to Tox, a messaging service.

The countdown reads 237 hours, 50 minutes and 39 seconds, or just under 10 days. It does not say what will happen when the timer reaches zero.

NVIDIA Ransomware Listing

The company details in the post are not evidence of access to an internal network. The image does not show which systems the gang claims to have reached, what files it claims to hold, or when any intrusion may have occurred. Without that evidence, it is not clear whether the claim concerns NVIDIA’s own systems, a third party, or neither.

The Gentlemen emerged in 2025 and operates as a ransomware-as-a-service group, meaning affiliates use the group’s tools to carry out attacks. As Cyber Security News previously reported in its profile of The Gentlemen, the group uses double extortion: stealing data and threatening to publish it while also locking files. That history does not establish that either happened at NVIDIA.

Previous Cyber Security News coverage of the gang’s attacks cited a Sophos review of 15 incidents. In some cases, attackers disabled endpoint security tools and backup services before encrypting systems less than 24 hours after gaining access. Those findings describe past attacks, not the NVIDIA claim. The leak post offers no technical evidence that the same methods were used here.

Ransomware tracker Breach House indexed the NVIDIA listing on November 18 and marked its leak status as pending. Its record documents when the claim appeared, not whether the gang accessed NVIDIA’s systems.

The listing also follows NVIDIA’s November 12 announcement that Chief Financial Officer Colette Kress would serve as interim CEO after co-founder Jensen Huang resigned. No evidence links that leadership change to the ransomware claim.

A company disclosure or independently verified files could help establish whether data was taken and where it came from. Even a genuine sample would not, on its own, show how the data was obtained or whether ransomware ran on company systems. Until such evidence emerges, the countdown marks a deadline set by the gang, not proof of a breach.

items.title: Token-replay campaign hijacks 97 Microsoft 365 accounts as Huntress extends SOC response across Defender
items.summary: Huntress has expanded its Agentic Security Platform so that its 24/7 security operations centre (SOC) can investigate and respond to incidents raised across the wider Microsoft Defender suite, not only Defender for Endpoint and Defender Antivirus. The move follows a token-replay campaign that Huntress tracked between 14 July and 22 September 2026, which compromised 97 Microsoft 365 accounts across 79 organisations. The attackers used adversary-in-the-middle (AiTM) phishing to capture session tokens after victims had completed multi-factor authentication, then replayed those tokens to access accounts without a password or a further MFA prompt. Once inside, they registered rogue devices and authenticator apps and set up inbox rules to hide their activity. In one case, a hijacked mailbox was used to send a payroll-related email to an external accountant. Huntress Managed ITDR detected the activity first, and Microsoft Entra ID Protection flagged the same attacker infrastructure. Huntress says the campaign prompted it to rebuild its detection pipeline so that a single incident naming several accounts is attached to each affected identity. The identity angle is central to the update. Huntress reports that in a recent two-week period, 85% of medium- and high-severity Defender incidents it saw carried no device-related evidence at all, meaning endpoint-centric tooling would have missed them. Under the expanded integration, Huntress now ingests incident data from: Microsoft Defender for Identity Microsoft Defender for Office 365 (for example, phishing emails caught at the gateway) Microsoft Defender for Cloud Apps (for example, risky OAuth applications) Microsoft Entra ID Protection (for example, compromised-account verdicts) Huntress analysts correlate these signals, prioritise the queue, confirm whether a threat is active and respond, before sending customers a report on what happened and what action was taken. Incidents are attached to the endpoints involved, the identities named, or both. Analysts can also run advanced hunting queries against a customer’s own Microsoft tenant data, going back up to 30 days, to trace process trees, look for the same tooling on other devices, or review what an account did after a suspicious sign-in. Huntress applies its own per-tenant query limits so that its hunting does not exhaust the Microsoft API quota shared with other security tools. “Attackers don’t care how big a company is, and neither should the quality of its defence,” said Adam Bates, Vice President of Product Management at Huntress. Bates added that Huntress integrates with the Defender Suite because organisations of every size need defence in depth, and that Defender signal helped uncover the token-replay campaign. The capability is aimed at organisations licensed for Microsoft 365 E5 or Defender Suite for Business Premium that want round-the-clock response without building in-house capacity to triage Defender alerts. Existing customers whose Microsoft tenant and Defender for Endpoint are already connected to Huntress receive the expanded data automatically. Huntress also highlighted a new Adversary Infrastructure capability within Managed ITDR, which converts one organisation’s incident into a same-day Conditional Access block across eligible, opted-in Entra ID P1 tenants.

items.title: Who protects the antivirus? How we secure Malwarebytes itself
items.summary: An antivirus is also software, and it can have weaknesses of its own. That makes antivirus development particularly demanding. The product must safely handle files that may be hostile, run reliably across very different Windows environments, and resist attackers who try to abuse its privileges or shut it down completely. Imagine a piece of malware that can disable your antivirus and leave you unprotected. That’s exactly what we as engineers work to prevent. The attack surface of a privileged process You might wonder why vulnerabilities matter for a desktop application that runs locally. Our software runs with high privileges, so it has access to the entire system. That access is what lets it protect the system from exploits, data theft, and ransomware. It also makes our software an attractive target. An attacker who can disable our protection, or abuse it to gain those privileges, has a much easier path to taking over the system. Two layers, one critical boundary At a basic level, Malwarebytes has two layers: a user interface running as the signed-in user, and a background service running as SYSTEM. They communicate through COM (Component Object Model), a built-in Windows mechanism that lets one program call functions in another program, even one running in a separate process. The UI can’t do much on its own. When you add an exclusion, restore a file from quarantine, or pause real-time protection, the UI only asks, and the SYSTEM service does the work. Those are exactly the operations malware would like to perform: excluding its own folder from scanning or turning protection off. And malware doesn’t need our UI to act. Any process running as the same user can write its own COM client and call the same methods. So on every call, the service must answer two questions: who is really calling, and is this caller allowed to do this specific operation? This is just one small example of an attack surface we keep in mind and protect. An antivirus has many more, and every fix to any of them has to preserve protection, performance, and system stability. AI is making vulnerabilities cheaper to find Finding a vulnerability usually involves four stages, and AI now speeds up every one of them: Identifying possible weaknesses Preparing test code and an environment Running the tests Analyzing the results before trying again AI is a multiplier not just in development or business processes, but in finding vulnerabilities as well. AI can explain unfamiliar code, generate diagnostic programs, and interpret compiler errors, logs, and debugger output. That lets people attempt investigations that used to be beyond their skills or would have taken far longer, even though a model alone still can’t reliably compromise an antivirus. An experienced Windows engineer already understands privileges, process boundaries, and common security mistakes, and they know which assumptions to question. AI turns those questions into tests without the engineer having to write every variation by hand. It can build a diagnostic client and repeat the same test under different user accounts, integrity levels, and configurations, while the engineer decides whether the results show a real security failure. The next step is already here: agents that combine a model with code navigation, build tools, a debugger, and a test environment. They propose a hypothesis, generate a test, observe the result, and refine the investigation in a loop. The hard part is still verification: telling a suspicious pattern apart from a real weakness. But a few years ago, none of this was possible. The evidence is accumulating: In July 2025, Google reported that its AI agent Big Sleep discovered a critical SQLite flaw (CVE-2025-6965) that attackers already knew about. Google says this stopped attackers from exploiting it. Mozilla confirmed 22 security-sensitive bugs found through its collaboration with Anthropic and fixed by Firefox 148. Mozilla rated 14 bugs from the work high severity. HackerOne reported a record 46,947 vulnerability submissions in March 2026, 76% more than a year earlier, with the share of valid, exploitable findings holding steady at about 25%. In November 2026, OpenAI reported that an autonomous AI pipeline running an unreleased model built working root exploits for 948 unique Linux kernel local privilege escalation (LPE) vulnerabilities in a single scan. Vulnerabilities will be found in greater numbers and at greater speed, and teams need to be ready. Finding is only half the problem Discovering is easier, but fixing vulnerabilities still takes substantial engineering effort, and the industry is already feeling the gap. HackerOne’s 2026 report found that the backlog of valid, unresolved findings grew 131% in two years, even though critical issues are being resolved faster than before. If discovery speeds up and remediation doesn’t, the backlog grows, and open vulnerabilities present an opportunity for an attacker. For a security company, the goal is to get ahead of the pace of discovery, and that takes dedicated resources and focus. How we keep pace: prevent, detect, fix, learn The inter-process boundary from the example above is just one of many areas attackers may target, and new ones appear as the product grows. At Malwarebytes we approach security as a continuous engineering process. Prevent Security by design. Before writing code, we build a threat model for each new feature: how could it be attacked, what privileges can it reach, and where does it accept untrusted input? Each component gets only the privileges its job requires, so a flaw in one part can’t easily lead to a full system compromise. Zero trust between components. No component trusts another by default. Even our own processes must authenticate and be authorized on every privileged request, so a compromised or spoofed caller can’t ride on someone else’s trust. This is the per-call check the SYSTEM service runs in the two-layer example above. Minimize the attack surface. Every interface we expose is something an attacker could probe, so we expose as few as possible. Features that aren’t needed are turned off, and privileged operations are reachable only through well-defined, authenticated entry points. Secure development practices. Our engineers follow secure coding standards that define how to handle memory, untrusted input, and privileged operations, and which unsafe functions and patterns are not allowed. These rules are enforced in code review and by automated checks, not left to individual judgment. The compiler is part of our defense too: strict warning levels catch risky code at build time, and built-in protections such as stack protection, control-flow integrity, and address randomization make any remaining bugs much harder to exploit. Detect Static and dynamic analysis. Memory-safety bugs such as buffer overflows and use-after-free errors are among the most common causes of arbitrary code execution. Static analysis catches dangerous patterns before code runs; dynamic analysis catches memory and runtime errors as they happen in our test builds. An AI vulnerability scanner. We built an internal scanner using modern AI models for source code analysis. It reasons about context and follows untrusted data through the code. AI security review on every pull request. A dedicated AI agent reviews every pull request purely for security: unsafe memory handling, missing validation, privilege-boundary problems, and more. Engineers still do the regular review, but every change, however small, gets security attention. Fuzzing and hostile testing. Malware authors craft files to attack scanners, so our file parsers, unpackers, and inter-process communication (IPC) interfaces are tested with malformed data, huge data streams, and fuzzed input on every release build. Company-wide pipelines continuously scan our repositories for exposed secrets, vulnerable dependencies, and insecure configurations. Fix Structured triage. Every finding, whatever its source, is validated and reproduced. We then establish what an attacker would need to do to exploit it, give it a CVSS score, and assign an owner with a deadline based on that severity. Safe fixes. Let’s imagine an authorization vulnerability between layers is found. The obvious response is to add an additional check. In practice, that check is often tricky to get right. An antivirus is made up of many components that authenticate each other; some start at boot, and some run in the kernel. If one piece breaks, the whole product can fail. In a large codebase with years of history, even a small patch can cause a blue screen of death (BSOD), slow the system down, or break features for millions of users at once. A security fix has to preserve protection, performance, and stability. AI-assisted remediation. AI helps our engineers investigate suspicious code, test hypotheses about exploitability, and explore possible fixes. Engineers review every change to confirm it fixes the root problem without introducing regressions. Safe delivery. Fixes reach users through cryptographically signed updates, with critical security fixes released first. Learn A vulnerability isn’t closed when the patch is merged. For each fix, we add a regression test and put the triggering input into our fuzzing corpus. We search for the same bug pattern elsewhere in the code, analyze why the flaw was introduced, and update our scanner rules, fuzzing targets, and coding guidelines. We also track time to remediation, so we can make sure that fixes are shipped on time according to their severity. What this costs us Running Prevent, Detect, Fix, and Learn as a continuous loop isn’t free, and we accept the costs on purpose. The tradeoff on people is time. Security work takes roughly 10–20% of every sprint. We guard that time, so it isn’t pulled into new feature development. The tradeoff on AI review is noise. AI pipelines review pull requests, scan source code, and propose fixes, but an engineer still checks every finding and proposal. Each month, as the models and our process improve, the agent raises fewer false alarms. The tradeoff on testing is volume. Every fixed vulnerability gets its own tests, so the same flaw can’t quietly return. That’s more tests to write, run, and maintain, but a regression in a security fix is a flaw we’ve already paid for once. The tradeoff on runtime checks is execution time. Verifying who is calling across the boundary, locking down our files, folders, and processes, and hardening installs and updates all add a little work to every operation. We accept that overhead so every task runs securely. What this means for you You won’t see most of this work, but it protects you every day: Protection that holds up under attack. Malwarebytes is designed so that malware can’t switch it off, tamper with it, or turn its privileges against you. We protect every point where attackers might try, from how components talk to each other to our own files and processes. Fixes don’t trade one problem for another. Every security fix has to keep protection, performance, and stability intact. Fixes reach you safely. They arrive as cryptographically signed updates, with critical security fixes first. Fixed stays fixed. Each fix gets a regression test, and we look for the same bug elsewhere in the code. Security comes first AI has lowered the cost of finding vulnerabilities, for defenders and attackers alike, and that shift isn’t slowing down. For a product that runs with the highest privileges on a machine and protects millions of users, the only durable answer is to keep up with, and get ahead of, the discovery of flaws. That’s why at Malwarebytes we treat security as one continuous loop—prevent, detect, fix, and learn—where every finding makes the next release stronger. When your application protects other applications, its own security deserves the same attention as the threats it detects. “One of the best cybersecurity suites on the planet.” According to CNET. An antivirus is also software, and it can have weaknesses of its own. 

That makes antivirus development particularly demanding. The product must safely handle files that may be hostile, run reliably across very different Windows environments, and resist attackers who try to abuse its privileges or shut it down completely. 

Imagine a piece of malware that can disable your antivirus and leave you unprotected. That’s exactly what we as engineers work to prevent. 

The attack surface of a privileged process 

You might wonder why vulnerabilities matter for a desktop application that runs locally.  

Our software runs with high privileges, so it has access to the entire system. That access is what lets it protect the system from exploits, data theft, and ransomware. It also makes our software an attractive target. An attacker who can disable our protection, or abuse it to gain those privileges, has a much easier path to taking over the system.

At a basic level, Malwarebytes has two layers: a user interface running as the signed-in user, and a background service running as SYSTEM. They communicate through COM (Component Object Model), a built-in Windows mechanism that lets one program call functions in another program, even one running in a separate process.

Those are exactly the operations malware would like to perform: excluding its own folder from scanning or turning protection off. 

And malware doesn’t need our UI to act. Any process running as the same user can write its own COM client and call the same methods. So on every call, the service must answer two questions: who is really calling, and is this caller allowed to do this specific operation? 

This is just one small example of an attack surface we keep in mind and protect. An antivirus has many more, and every fix to any of them has to preserve protection, performance, and system stability. 

AI is making vulnerabilities cheaper to find 

Finding a vulnerability usually involves four stages, and AI now speeds up every one of them:

  • Identifying possible weaknesses
  • Preparing test code and an environment
  • Running the tests
  • Analyzing the results before trying again

AI is a multiplier not just in development or business processes, but in finding vulnerabilities as well. 

AI can explain unfamiliar code, generate diagnostic programs, and interpret compiler errors, logs, and debugger output. That lets people attempt investigations that used to be beyond their skills or would have taken far longer, even though a model alone still can’t reliably compromise an antivirus. 

An experienced Windows engineer already understands privileges, process boundaries, and common security mistakes, and they know which assumptions to question. AI turns those questions into tests without the engineer having to write every variation by hand. It can build a diagnostic client and repeat the same test under different user accounts, integrity levels, and configurations, while the engineer decides whether the results show a real security failure. 

The next step is already here: agents that combine a model with code navigation, build tools, a debugger, and a test environment. They propose a hypothesis, generate a test, observe the result, and refine the investigation in a loop. The hard part is still verification: telling a suspicious pattern apart from a real weakness. But a few years ago, none of this was possible. 

The evidence is accumulating: 

  • In July 2025, Google reported that its AI agent Big Sleep discovered a critical SQLite flaw (CVE-2025-6965) that attackers already knew about. Google says this stopped attackers from exploiting it. 
  • Mozilla confirmed 22 security-sensitive bugs found through its collaboration with Anthropic and fixed by Firefox 148. Mozilla rated 14 bugs from the work high severity. 
  • HackerOne reported a record 46,947 vulnerability submissions in March 2026, 76% more than a year earlier, with the share of valid, exploitable findings holding steady at about 25%. 
  • In November 2026, OpenAI reported that an autonomous AI pipeline running an unreleased model built working root exploits for 948 unique Linux kernel local privilege escalation (LPE) vulnerabilities in a single scan. 

Vulnerabilities will be found in greater numbers and at greater speed, and teams need to be ready. 

Finding is only half the problem 

Discovering is easier, but fixing vulnerabilities still takes substantial engineering effort, and the industry is already feeling the gap. HackerOne’s 2026 report found that the backlog of valid, unresolved findings grew 131% in two years, even though critical issues are being resolved faster than before. 

If discovery speeds up and remediation doesn’t, the backlog grows, and open vulnerabilities present an opportunity for an attacker.  

For a security company, the goal is to get ahead of the pace of discovery, and that takes dedicated resources and focus. 

How we keep pace: prevent, detect, fix, learn

The inter-process boundary from the example above is just one of many areas attackers may target, and new ones appear as the product grows. At Malwarebytes we approach security as a continuous engineering process. 

Prevent 

Security by design. Before writing code, we build a threat model for each new feature: how could it be attacked, what privileges can it reach, and where does it accept untrusted input? Each component gets only the privileges its job requires, so a flaw in one part can’t easily lead to a full system compromise. 

Zero trust between components. No component trusts another by default. Even our own processes must authenticate and be authorized on every privileged request, so a compromised or spoofed caller can’t ride on someone else’s trust. This is the per-call check the SYSTEM service runs in the two-layer example above. 

Minimize the attack surface. Every interface we expose is something an attacker could probe, so we expose as few as possible. Features that aren’t needed are turned off, and privileged operations are reachable only through well-defined, authenticated entry points. 

Secure development practices. Our engineers follow secure coding standards that define how to handle memory, untrusted input, and privileged operations, and which unsafe functions and patterns are not allowed. These rules are enforced in code review and by automated checks, not left to individual judgment. The compiler is part of our defense too: strict warning levels catch risky code at build time, and built-in protections such as stack protection, control-flow integrity, and address randomization make any remaining bugs much harder to exploit. 

Detect 

Static and dynamic analysis. Memory-safety bugs such as buffer overflows and use-after-free errors are among the most common causes of arbitrary code execution. Static analysis catches dangerous patterns before code runs; dynamic analysis catches memory and runtime errors as they happen in our test builds. 

An AI vulnerability scanner. We built an internal scanner using modern AI models for source code analysis. It reasons about context and follows untrusted data through the code. 

AI security review on every pull request. A dedicated AI agent reviews every pull request purely for security: unsafe memory handling, missing validation, privilege-boundary problems, and more. Engineers still do the regular review, but every change, however small, gets security attention. 

Fuzzing and hostile testing. Malware authors craft files to attack scanners, so our file parsers, unpackers, and inter-process communication (IPC) interfaces are tested with malformed data, huge data streams, and fuzzed input on every release build. 

Company-wide pipelines continuously scan our repositories for exposed secrets, vulnerable dependencies, and insecure configurations. 

Fix 

Structured triage. Every finding, whatever its source, is validated and reproduced. We then establish what an attacker would need to do to exploit it, give it a CVSS score, and assign an owner with a deadline based on that severity. 

Safe fixes. Let’s imagine an authorization vulnerability between layers is found. The obvious response is to add an additional check. In practice, that check is often tricky to get right. An antivirus is made up of many components that authenticate each other; some start at boot, and some run in the kernel. If one piece breaks, the whole product can fail. 

In a large codebase with years of history, even a small patch can cause a blue screen of death (BSOD), slow the system down, or break features for millions of users at once. A security fix has to preserve protection, performance, and stability. 

AI-assisted remediation. AI helps our engineers investigate suspicious code, test hypotheses about exploitability, and explore possible fixes. Engineers review every change to confirm it fixes the root problem without introducing regressions. 

Safe delivery. Fixes reach users through cryptographically signed updates, with critical security fixes released first. 

Learn 

A vulnerability isn’t closed when the patch is merged. For each fix, we add a regression test and put the triggering input into our fuzzing corpus. We search for the same bug pattern elsewhere in the code, analyze why the flaw was introduced, and update our scanner rules, fuzzing targets, and coding guidelines. We also track time to remediation, so we can make sure that fixes are shipped on time according to their severity. 

What this costs us 

Running Prevent, Detect, Fix, and Learn as a continuous loop isn’t free, and we accept the costs on purpose.  

The tradeoff on people is time. 

Security work takes roughly 10–20% of every sprint. We guard that time, so it isn’t pulled into new feature development. 

The tradeoff on AI review is noise. 

AI pipelines review pull requests, scan source code, and propose fixes, but an engineer still checks every finding and proposal. Each month, as the models and our process improve, the agent raises fewer false alarms. 

The tradeoff on testing is volume. 

Every fixed vulnerability gets its own tests, so the same flaw can’t quietly return. That’s more tests to write, run, and maintain, but a regression in a security fix is a flaw we’ve already paid for once. 

The tradeoff on runtime checks is execution time. 

Verifying who is calling across the boundary, locking down our files, folders, and processes, and hardening installs and updates all add a little work to every operation. We accept that overhead so every task runs securely. 

What this means for you

You won’t see most of this work, but it protects you every day: 

  • Protection that holds up under attack. Malwarebytes is designed so that malware can’t switch it off, tamper with it, or turn its privileges against you. We protect every point where attackers might try, from how components talk to each other to our own files and processes. 
  • Fixes don’t trade one problem for another. Every security fix has to keep protection, performance, and stability intact. 
  • Fixes reach you safely. They arrive as cryptographically signed updates, with critical security fixes first. 
  • Fixed stays fixed. Each fix gets a regression test, and we look for the same bug elsewhere in the code. 
Security comes first 

AI has lowered the cost of finding vulnerabilities, for defenders and attackers alike, and that shift isn’t slowing down. For a product that runs with the highest privileges on a machine and protects millions of users, the only durable answer is to keep up with, and get ahead of, the discovery of flaws. That’s why at Malwarebytes we treat security as one continuous loop—prevent, detect, fix, and learn—where every finding makes the next release stronger.  

When your application protects other applications, its own security deserves the same attention as the threats it detects. 

“One of the best cybersecurity suites on the planet.” 

According to CNET. Read their review →

items.summary: Java4Shell, tracked as CVE-2026-114938, is a heap overflow in Java's hardware-accelerated Base64 decoder. Researchers at Calif say it can let attackers without an account run code on Jira, Jenkins, Keycloak and other Java applications. Oracle and the OpenJDK project shipped fixes on Nov. 17, 2026, and CISA urged organizations to patch immediately. No exploitation in the wild has been reported. Patch it, but read the conditions before you rank it next to Log4Shell. The vulnerable code runs only on x86-64 servers whose processors support AVX-512 VBMI, so a server's exposure depends on its CPU as much as its Java version. The same container image can be vulnerable on one host and safe on the next, and that is the detail most patch plans will miss. Which Java versions and servers are affected? A server is exposed only when three conditions hold at once. 1. A vulnerable Java build. Java 17.0.6 and later on the 17 line, plus Java 21, 25 and 27 before the November fixes. Standard Java 8 and 11 don't contain the flawed code, but the Java SE 8 Performance Pack build 8u511b33-perf does, as do recent GraalVM builds. 2. The right CPU. The vulnerable path runs only on x86-64 chips with AVX-512 VBMI: Intel Xeon Ice Lake, Sapphire Rapids, Emerald Rapids and Granite Rapids, and AMD Zen 4 or newer. ARM64 servers, including AWS Graviton, don't run it. On Linux, this command should print all four flags if the chip qualifies: grep -m1 '^flags' /proc/cpuinfo | tr ' ' '\n' | grep -E '^(avx512f|avx512bw|avx512vbmi|bmi2)$' 3. A reachable decoder. An attacker has to get malformed Base64 into Java's standard decoder. Many servers decode Base64 before checking who you are, in HTTP Basic login headers, SAML artifacts and CSRF tokens, which is what makes the attack possible without a login. Calif reports pre-authentication code execution under default settings on Keycloak, Atlassian Jira, Atlassian Confluence, JFrog Artifactory, Jenkins and PingFederate, and with a login on Apache Kafka, Apache Solr, Elasticsearch, Gerrit and Spinnaker. It says the list is incomplete. Java build Fixed release Oracle Java SE 17 (17.0.6 and later) 17.0.21.1 Oracle Java SE 21 21.0.13.1 Oracle Java SE 25 25.0.5.1 Oracle Java SE 27 27.0.1.1 Amazon Corretto 17, 21, 25, 27 17.0.21.1.2, 21.0.13.1.2, 25.0.5.1.2, 27.0.1.1.4 Azul Zulu 17, 21, 25, 27 17.70.201, 21.54.201, 25.38.201, 27.30.201 Red Hat build of OpenJDK and RHEL 8, 9, 10 Not yet released as of Nov. 18 Products that bundle their own Java runtime, from CI servers to appliances, need an update from their vendor, not just a new system JDK. That routine miscalculates the output size when the input ends with an unexpected = padding character. Wiz gives the example of 64 A characters followed by a single = . Log4Shell could be triggered by almost any logged string on any hardware with a simple, reliable exploit. Java4Shell needs specific CPUs, a reachable Base64 decoder and target-specific exploitation work. A pre-auth crash is easy, though, so treat it as urgent. How can I mitigate Java4Shell without patching? Start the JVM with -XX:-UseBASE64Intrinsics to disable the vulnerable decoder path, or -XX:UseAVX=2 on x86-64 only. Java4Shell, tracked as CVE-2026-114938, is a heap overflow in Java's hardware-accelerated Base64 decoder. Patch it, but read the conditions before you rank it next to Log4Shell. The vulnerable code runs only on x86-64 servers whose processors support AVX-512 VBMI, so a server's exposure depends on its CPU as much as its Java version. The same container image can be vulnerable on one host and safe on the next, and that is the detail most patch plans will miss.

Which Java versions and servers are affected?

A server is exposed only when three conditions hold at once.

1. A vulnerable Java build. Java 17.0.6 and later on the 17 line, plus Java 21, 25 and 27 before the November fixes. Standard Java 8 and 11 don't contain the flawed code, but the Java SE 8 Performance Pack build 8u511b33-perf does, as do recent GraalVM builds.

2. The right CPU. The vulnerable path runs only on x86-64 chips with AVX-512 VBMI: Intel Xeon Ice Lake, Sapphire Rapids, Emerald Rapids and Granite Rapids, and AMD Zen 4 or newer. ARM64 servers, including AWS Graviton, don't run it. On Linux, this command should print all four flags if the chip qualifies:

grep -m1 '^flags' /proc/cpuinfo | tr ' ' '\n' | grep -E '^(avx512f|avx512bw|avx512vbmi|bmi2)$'

3. A reachable decoder. An attacker has to get malformed Base64 into Java's standard decoder. Many servers decode Base64 before checking who you are, in HTTP Basic login headers, SAML artifacts and CSRF tokens, which is what makes the attack possible without a login.

Calif reports pre-authentication code execution under default settings on Keycloak, Atlassian Jira, Atlassian Confluence, JFrog Artifactory, Jenkins and PingFederate, and with a login on Apache Kafka, Apache Solr, Elasticsearch, Gerrit and Spinnaker. It says the list is incomplete.

Java build Fixed release Oracle Java SE 17 (17.0.6 and later) 17.0.21.1 Oracle Java SE 21 21.0.13.1 Oracle Java SE 25 25.0.5.1 Oracle Java SE 27 27.0.1.1 Amazon Corretto 17, 21, 25, 27 17.0.21.1.2, 21.0.13.1.2, 25.0.5.1.2, 27.0.1.1.4 Azul Zulu 17, 21, 25, 27 17.70.201, 21.54.201, 25.38.201, 27.30.201 Red Hat build of OpenJDK and RHEL 8, 9, 10 Not yet released as of Nov. 18

Products that bundle their own Java runtime, from CI servers to appliances, need an update from their vendor, not just a new system JDK.

How Java4Shell works

When a method runs often enough, Java's JIT compiler swaps the standard Base64 decoding loop for a hand-tuned assembly routine, an "intrinsic," that uses AVX-512 VBMI instructions. That routine miscalculates the output size when the input ends with an unexpected = padding character. Wiz gives the example of 64 A characters followed by a single =.

The result is a write of 62 or 63 bytes past the end of the output array on the Java heap. Java does reject the malformed string, but only after the write has happened. That ordering is the whole bug: input validation in your application can't help, because the damage is done inside the decoder.

The overflowed bytes are fixed by the decoder, which is why early readings predicted a crash, not code execution. Calif's researchers got around that by arranging heap memory so the overflow enlarges a neighboring array. They then used that array to write chosen bytes and a second array to read memory back, a step they call JavaBleed, and worked from there to code execution.

There is no universal exploit. Each application needs its own memory layout and timing, and some attempts are sensitive to network delay. A failed attempt usually crashes the JVM, and an attacker can often try again.

One uncomfortable footnote: a pull request to OpenJDK on Sept. 9 described an overflow in the same decoder and included a triggering input. It was closed unmerged in early November after eight weeks of inactivity.

Is Java4Shell being exploited, and why do the scores disagree?

As of Nov. 18, 2026, no exploitation has been reported. The flaw isn't in CISA's Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog, Canada's Cyber Centre said it wasn't aware of attacks, and Calif is holding back its exploit code.

Independent labs have confirmed the dangerous part, though. Upwind reproduced the memory corruption on an Intel Ice Lake server on AWS until Java crashed. Blackpoint Cyber crashed a test Spring Boot app with about 28,300 malformed login requests in roughly 20 seconds, without logging in, and used the JavaBleed technique to read a secret from memory in all 30 local runs. Neither reproduced remote code execution.

That split explains the scores:

Source Score What it emphasizes Calif 9.2 (CVSS 4.0) Demonstrated pre-auth code execution on six apps Red Hat 9.8 (preliminary) No login required Amazon 8.8 JVM crash for unauthenticated users; code execution for low-privileged users in some environments Oracle / OpenJDK 8.1 (CVSS 3.1) No login required, but hard to exploit

The practical read: a pre-auth crash of any affected Java service is easy today. Reliable code execution takes per-target work, but the researchers have shown it can be done, and the triggering input has been public since September. Treat it as urgent.

How to fix and mitigate Java4Shell

  1. Find every affected runtime. Inventory Java 17 and later, including runtimes bundled inside products. Then check the CPU on each host with the command above. Mixed fleets and autoscaling groups can change exposure from one instance to the next.

  2. Patch. Install the fixed build for your distribution from the table above, then restart Java services and rebuild and redeploy container images so the running process actually uses it. Red Hat users need the workaround until Red Hat ships fixes.

  3. If you can't patch yet, turn off the vulnerable path. Start the JVM with -XX:-UseBASE64Intrinsics, which removes only the faster Base64 code. -XX:UseAVX=2 disables AVX-512 entirely, but use it only on x86-64, because Java on ARM64 won't start with it. Upwind warns that -XX:DisableIntrinsic=_base64_decodeBlock on its own stops Java from starting. Remove the flag once the fixed build is in.

  4. Reduce exposure at the edge. CISA recommends validating Base64 input at application boundaries, enforcing input-size limits and limiting unauthenticated access. A reverse proxy that buffers complete requests, as nginx does by default, blocks some attacks but not all.

  5. Hunt for attempts. Look for Base64 tokens of 32 characters or more that end in = and whose length isn't a multiple of four, especially in Authorization headers; bursts of IllegalArgumentException from java.util.Base64$Decoder; and unexplained hs_err_pid crash logs or restart storms. None of these proves a compromise, and their absence doesn't prove you're safe.

Standard Java 8 and 11 builds don't contain the vulnerable code. The exception is the Java SE 8 Performance Pack build 8u511b33-perf, which is affected; Oracle's latest Performance Pack build is 8u513.

No exploitation in the wild had been reported as of Nov. 18, 2026, and the flaw wasn't in CISA's Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog. Independent labs have reproduced crashes and memory reads but not remote code execution.

It's narrower. Log4Shell could be triggered by almost any logged string on any hardware with a simple, reliable exploit. Java4Shell needs specific CPUs, a reachable Base64 decoder and target-specific exploitation work. A pre-auth crash is easy, though, so treat it as urgent.
