items.title: Optimizing Kubernetes admission control: Where Kyverno’s CEL admission cost actually goes
items.summary: Kyverno’s CEL (Common Expression Language)-based engines exist to evaluate policy expressions. So when we profiled the admission path, we expected to find the bulk of the cost in CEL evaluation. It was not there. About 86% of what the engine allocated went into preparing the object for evaluation, and almost none of it into evaluating policy. We went looking because a public benchmark put Kyverno behind the alternatives. Those benchmarks measured the legacy ClusterPolicy JMESPath engine, which did have a real regression at the time, and the usual answer was to point people at the newer CEL-based engine instead. That answer was right but incomplete: we had not checked what the CEL engine itself was spending its time on. This post is about where that performance cost came from, why it grew with the number of policies you deploy, and what removing it did. The fix ships in Kyverno 1.19.2. Please read the limitations section before you quote any number here. And as always, run your own tests in your environments, for real-world accuracy. What the profile showed Kyverno’s CEL engines evaluate policies against a CEL activation: a set of variables your policy expressions can reference. One of those variables is request , the AdmissionRequest the API server sent, converted into the unstructured map form CEL understands. Here is a heap profile of the ValidatingPolicy engine handling admission requests, before and after the change, by share of total allocated bytes: Before, ConvertObjectToUnstructured accounted for 86.8% of everything the engine allocated. CEL evaluation itself barely registered. After, object conversion falls to 2.9%, and the largest single frame becomes evaluateWithData — the code that actually runs your policy expressions. The same pattern shows up in the MutatingPolicy engine, which was paying a smaller but still substantial version of the same cost: One caveat on reading those profiles: the post-fix benchmark completes more iterations in the same time because it is faster, so the two profiles have different absolute totals. Compare the shares, not the raw bytes. Per-request figures come from the benchmark table further down. Why: the same object, converted once per policy The API server sends the admitted object as raw JSON bytes. CEL cannot read bytes, so Kyverno parses them into the map form CEL understands before it can evaluate anything against them. That conversion happened inside the loop over matched policies rather than before it. With the Pod Security Standards set, roughly 16 policies match a typical Pod creation — so Kyverno parsed the same Pod 16 times, same input, same output, every time. The cost grew with your policy count and with the size of the object being admitted: O(policies) , where it should have been O(1). The object does not change between policies. There was never a reason to convert it more than once. The fix: convert once per request The change moves the conversion out of the per-policy loop. Kyverno builds the CEL request value once, before the loop starts, and every matched policy reuses it. Doing that without changing what policies see takes some care. The expensive part of the conversion is the admitted object itself, so Kyverno converts a copy of the request with that object temporarily blanked out — which leaves only cheap fields to walk — and splices the object back in afterwards. The same conversion code still produces the result, so the output matches what policies saw before rather than being a reimplementation that someone has to keep in sync by hand. Keeping policy behavior identical The first attempt used a single shared builder for every CEL engine. Testing caught that this quietly changed how policies behave, because the engines had never agreed on what request.object meant in the first place. Validating and generating policies saw the object exactly as the API server sent it. Mutating policies saw a normalized version. The two also disagreed about what an empty object looks like to CEL, which matters for operations like DELETE where one side is absent. Unifying them would have changed the result of expressions people already have deployed. That is a conversation worth having, but not one a performance fix should start on its own. So each engine keeps the contract it already had, sharing one fast implementation underneath. Equivalence tests pin this down: they run the original code as the reference and compare its output against the new one field by field, across every request type, so any drift fails the build. What changed The benchmark calls the engine directly with a roughly 50 KB Pod and a varying number of matched policies. It times the engine alone — building the request value, matching, and evaluating CEL. It does not include the webhook round trip, the API server, or etcd, so these are not end-to-end admission latencies. Matched policies Allocations before Allocations after Engine time before Engine time after 1 2,327 854 0.31 ms 0.10 ms 16 37,055 2,718 4.91 ms 0.16 ms 64 148,131 8,672 20.01 ms 0.36 ms The MutatingPolicy engine improves on the same curve, from 258,943 to 52,689 allocations and 10.59 ms to 2.97 ms at 64 policies. The slope is the point, not the headline multiple. Before the change, allocations grew about 63 times going from 1 policy to 64. After, about 10 times — and that residual growth is CEL evaluation, which is the work you deployed the policies to get. Object preparation is now constant per request instead of proportional to how many policies you run. Practically: adding policies to a Kyverno deployment used to carry a hidden per-policy serialization cost on top of the evaluation you asked for. It no longer does. Image verification too The image verification engine had the same pattern, with its own private copy of the conversion code, so it got the same fix. The gain there is memory rather than speed: image verification spends most of its time fetching signatures and attestations over the network, and that part does not change. How this compares to native admission policies With the per-policy tax gone, it is worth asking where Kyverno’s CEL engine actually sits against the API server’s own ValidatingAdmissionPolicy. Running the same 16 Pod Security Standards policies through both engines on one cluster, the answer depends on how many policies you enforce: At one policy, native is ahead: about 9.2 ms against Kyverno’s 12.8 ms. At the full 16-policy set, Kyverno is ahead: about 20 ms against native’s 29 ms. Those numbers were measured on Kyverno 1.19.0, which predates the change described above. The Kyverno side of that chart should now be better than shown; we have not re-run the comparison. The two engines pay their costs differently. Native dispatches each policy separately on the API server, so its cost grows with the number of policies you enforce. Kyverno pays once per request to receive the object over a webhook, and that cost is shared across however many policies then evaluate. With only a policy or two, native is ahead. Once you are running a realistic set, Kyverno matches it and can come out ahead. That framing only became accurate with this fix. Kyverno’s cost was not fixed per request before it — it was per policy, which is exactly why the curve looked the way it did. The CPU side is more one-sided. Under matched load, Kyverno’s engine used about 3.2 cores against the API server’s 8.2 for native. The surprise in the API server profile is that 67% of its CPU sits in the policy dispatch machinery while the actual CEL bytecode execution is about 5.5% — the cost is dispatching 16 policies and building an input for each, not evaluating them. And that load lands on the control plane, which you cannot scale horizontally the way you can scale a Kyverno deployment. Both numbers come from a single-host setup where the webhook hop is loopback and effectively free. On a real multi-node cluster that hop costs real latency on every Kyverno request, which narrows the latency gap and matters most at low policy counts. The CPU finding does not depend on topology. The legacy engine, briefly The benchmarks that prompted this work measured ClusterPolicy, the older non-CEL engine, so it is worth saying what happened there. We reproduced the regression across four releases, each on a fresh cluster, run in shuffled order over eight rounds so no version was systematically favored, and compared everything against 1.13.6. The regression is real — between 12% and 23% depending on load — and it appears between 1.16.4 and 1.17.0. That is where the engine started copying its entire evaluation context on every checkpoint, in order to fix a separate bug where one rule’s data could leak into the next. The fix keeps that guarantee but stops paying for it upfront: it takes a shallow snapshot and only copies a value when something actually writes to it. The benchmark returns to roughly its pre-regression level, and the rule isolation still holds, pinned by a test that fails on the old code. This ships in 1.19.2 alongside the CEL work, and only there. The legacy engine is on its way out, so the effort belongs in the engine replacing it. What this does not fix The engine still pays one JSON round-trip of the admitted object per request, to preserve the raw, un-normalized parse that request.object has always exposed. Evaluating against the typed object, or a cheaper representation, would remove even that — but it would change what policies see, so it needs its own design. Mutating policies thread full objects between policies rather than propagating a patch diff. A patch-only model is a substantially larger redesign and is not implemented. Tail latency under sustained load on a single replica is not addressed by any of this, and we have not re-measured it since. If you have seen Kyverno’s p95 swing widely between runs at high load, that is a separate problem and it is still open. Limitations Single machine. Everything here reproduces the relationship between configurations, not the absolute numbers you would see on a 32-core server. Most of this is a Go benchmark. The allocation and timing figures come from benchmarks driving the real engine loop, and the profiles come from those benchmark runs. They isolate the engine cleanly, and they exclude network, serialization at the webhook boundary, and etcd. The engine comparison uses loopback, so the webhook network hop is excluded, and dry-run, so the etcd write is excluded. The native side runs Kyverno’s generated policies, which is a faithful same-policy comparison rather than a hand-tuned native policy set. Side controllers were disabled in these runs. Only the admission controller was active. Reproduce it The harness is in the Kyverno repository under docs/perf-testing/: the version ladder, the pinned Pod Security Standards policy set, the k6 scripts, and the cluster setup. The engine benchmarks live beside the code they measure, in pkg/cel/policies/vpol/engine and pkg/engine/context. If you benchmark Kyverno and get a result you do not like, please publish it — with the method, the caveats, and the per-trial numbers. Conclusion Our mission at Kyverno is to be the best policy engine for Kubernetes and beyond. Admission control is a critical process in Kubernetes clusters, and a slow or misconfigured controller can impact cluster operations. Thanks to our community, we have fixed performance issues and added more tests. For future releases, we will be looking at improving concurrency and further optimization. Thanks to Mustafa Erdinç , whose comparison of different Kubernetes policy engines motivated this work. References #17572 — build the request activation once per admission request #17585 — hoist the request-map build in the image verification engine #17565 — reduce engine context checkpoint copy cost ___________________________________________________________________ This blog was originally posted on kyverno.io .

Please read the limitations section before you quote any number here. And as always, run your own tests in your environments, for real-world accuracy.

What the profile showed

Kyverno’s CEL engines evaluate policies against a CEL activation: a set of variables your policy expressions can reference. One of those variables is request, the AdmissionRequest the API server sent, converted into the unstructured map form CEL understands.

Here is a heap profile of the ValidatingPolicy engine handling admission requests, before and after the change, by share of total allocated bytes:

Before, ConvertObjectToUnstructured accounted for 86.8% of everything the engine allocated. CEL evaluation itself barely registered. After, object conversion falls to 2.9%, and the largest single frame becomes evaluateWithData — the code that actually runs your policy expressions.

The same pattern shows up in the MutatingPolicy engine, which was paying a smaller but still substantial version of the same cost:

One caveat on reading those profiles: the post-fix benchmark completes more iterations in the same time because it is faster, so the two profiles have different absolute totals. Compare the shares, not the raw bytes. Per-request figures come from the benchmark table further down.

Why: the same object, converted once per policy

The API server sends the admitted object as raw JSON bytes. CEL cannot read bytes, so Kyverno parses them into the map form CEL understands before it can evaluate anything against them.

That conversion happened inside the loop over matched policies rather than before it. With the Pod Security Standards set, roughly 16 policies match a typical Pod creation — so Kyverno parsed the same Pod 16 times, same input, same output, every time. The cost grew with your policy count and with the size of the object being admitted: O(policies), where it should have been O(1).

The object does not change between policies. There was never a reason to convert it more than once.

The fix: convert once per request

The change moves the conversion out of the per-policy loop. Kyverno builds the CEL request value once, before the loop starts, and every matched policy reuses it.

Doing that without changing what policies see takes some care. The expensive part of the conversion is the admitted object itself, so Kyverno converts a copy of the request with that object temporarily blanked out — which leaves only cheap fields to walk — and splices the object back in afterwards. The same conversion code still produces the result, so the output matches what policies saw before rather than being a reimplementation that someone has to keep in sync by hand.

Keeping policy behavior identical

The first attempt used a single shared builder for every CEL engine. Testing caught that this quietly changed how policies behave, because the engines had never agreed on what request.object meant in the first place.

Validating and generating policies saw the object exactly as the API server sent it. Mutating policies saw a normalized version. The two also disagreed about what an empty object looks like to CEL, which matters for operations like DELETE where one side is absent.

Unifying them would have changed the result of expressions people already have deployed. That is a conversation worth having, but not one a performance fix should start on its own. So each engine keeps the contract it already had, sharing one fast implementation underneath.

Equivalence tests pin this down: they run the original code as the reference and compare its output against the new one field by field, across every request type, so any drift fails the build.

What changed

The benchmark calls the engine directly with a roughly 50 KB Pod and a varying number of matched policies. It times the engine alone — building the request value, matching, and evaluating CEL. It does not include the webhook round trip, the API server, or etcd, so these are not end-to-end admission latencies.

Matched policiesAllocations beforeAllocations afterEngine time beforeEngine time after12,3278540.31 ms0.10 ms1637,0552,7184.91 ms0.16 ms64148,1318,67220.01 ms0.36 ms

The MutatingPolicy engine improves on the same curve, from 258,943 to 52,689 allocations and 10.59 ms to 2.97 ms at 64 policies.

The slope is the point, not the headline multiple. Before the change, allocations grew about 63 times going from 1 policy to 64. After, about 10 times — and that residual growth is CEL evaluation, which is the work you deployed the policies to get. Object preparation is now constant per request instead of proportional to how many policies you run.

Practically: adding policies to a Kyverno deployment used to carry a hidden per-policy serialization cost on top of the evaluation you asked for. It no longer does.

Image verification too

The image verification engine had the same pattern, with its own private copy of the conversion code, so it got the same fix. The gain there is memory rather than speed: image verification spends most of its time fetching signatures and attestations over the network, and that part does not change.

How this compares to native admission policies

With the per-policy tax gone, it is worth asking where Kyverno’s CEL engine actually sits against the API server’s own ValidatingAdmissionPolicy.

Running the same 16 Pod Security Standards policies through both engines on one cluster, the answer depends on how many policies you enforce:

At one policy, native is ahead: about 9.2 ms against Kyverno’s 12.8 ms. At the full 16-policy set, Kyverno is ahead: about 20 ms against native’s 29 ms.

Those numbers were measured on Kyverno 1.19.0, which predates the change described above. The Kyverno side of that chart should now be better than shown; we have not re-run the comparison.

The two engines pay their costs differently. Native dispatches each policy separately on the API server, so its cost grows with the number of policies you enforce. Kyverno pays once per request to receive the object over a webhook, and that cost is shared across however many policies then evaluate. With only a policy or two, native is ahead. Once you are running a realistic set, Kyverno matches it and can come out ahead.

That framing only became accurate with this fix. Kyverno’s cost was not fixed per request before it — it was per policy, which is exactly why the curve looked the way it did.

The CPU side is more one-sided. Under matched load, Kyverno’s engine used about 3.2 cores against the API server’s 8.2 for native. The surprise in the API server profile is that 67% of its CPU sits in the policy dispatch machinery while the actual CEL bytecode execution is about 5.5% — the cost is dispatching 16 policies and building an input for each, not evaluating them. And that load lands on the control plane, which you cannot scale horizontally the way you can scale a Kyverno deployment.

Both numbers come from a single-host setup where the webhook hop is loopback and effectively free. On a real multi-node cluster that hop costs real latency on every Kyverno request, which narrows the latency gap and matters most at low policy counts. The CPU finding does not depend on topology.

The legacy engine, briefly

The benchmarks that prompted this work measured ClusterPolicy, the older non-CEL engine, so it is worth saying what happened there.

We reproduced the regression across four releases, each on a fresh cluster, run in shuffled order over eight rounds so no version was systematically favored, and compared everything against 1.13.6.

The regression is real — between 12% and 23% depending on load — and it appears between 1.16.4 and 1.17.0. That is where the engine started copying its entire evaluation context on every checkpoint, in order to fix a separate bug where one rule’s data could leak into the next.

The fix keeps that guarantee but stops paying for it upfront: it takes a shallow snapshot and only copies a value when something actually writes to it. The benchmark returns to roughly its pre-regression level, and the rule isolation still holds, pinned by a test that fails on the old code.

This ships in 1.19.2 alongside the CEL work, and only there. The legacy engine is on its way out, so the effort belongs in the engine replacing it.

What this does not fix
  • The engine still pays one JSON round-trip of the admitted object per request, to preserve the raw, un-normalized parse that request.object has always exposed. Evaluating against the typed object, or a cheaper representation, would remove even that — but it would change what policies see, so it needs its own design.
  • Mutating policies thread full objects between policies rather than propagating a patch diff. A patch-only model is a substantially larger redesign and is not implemented.
  • Tail latency under sustained load on a single replica is not addressed by any of this, and we have not re-measured it since. If you have seen Kyverno’s p95 swing widely between runs at high load, that is a separate problem and it is still open.
Limitations
  • Single machine. Everything here reproduces the relationship between configurations, not the absolute numbers you would see on a 32-core server.
  • Most of this is a Go benchmark. The allocation and timing figures come from benchmarks driving the real engine loop, and the profiles come from those benchmark runs. They isolate the engine cleanly, and they exclude network, serialization at the webhook boundary, and etcd.
  • The engine comparison uses loopback, so the webhook network hop is excluded, and dry-run, so the etcd write is excluded.
  • The native side runs Kyverno’s generated policies, which is a faithful same-policy comparison rather than a hand-tuned native policy set.
  • Side controllers were disabled in these runs. Only the admission controller was active.
Reproduce it

The harness is in the Kyverno repository under docs/perf-testing/: the version ladder, the pinned Pod Security Standards policy set, the k6 scripts, and the cluster setup. The engine benchmarks live beside the code they measure, in pkg/cel/policies/vpol/engine and pkg/engine/context.

If you benchmark Kyverno and get a result you do not like, please publish it — with the method, the caveats, and the per-trial numbers.

Conclusion

Our mission at Kyverno is to be the best policy engine for Kubernetes and beyond. Admission control is a critical process in Kubernetes clusters, and a slow or misconfigured controller can impact cluster operations. Thanks to our community, we have fixed performance issues and added more tests. For future releases, we will be looking at improving concurrency and further optimization.

Thanks to Mustafa Erdinç, whose comparison of different Kubernetes policy engines motivated this work.

References
  • #17572 — build the request activation once per admission request
  • #17585 — hoist the request-map build in the image verification engine
  • #17565 — reduce engine context checkpoint copy cost

items.title: Keeper Security Launches Global Emergency Breach Response Service for Organisations Under Cyberattack
items.summary: Keeper Security has announced the launch of a global emergency breach response service designed to help organisations contain active cyberattacks by rapidly securing compromised identities, credentials and infrastructure. The new initiative allows organisations experiencing a breach to bypass traditional sales and procurement processes, connecting directly with Keeper’s Solution Engineering team to begin deploying its identity security platform within minutes. As cyberattacks become increasingly sophisticated, particularly with the emergence of AI-powered threats, the time between initial compromise and full administrative takeover can be extremely short. Attackers frequently exploit compromised credentials, unmanaged secrets and excessive privileges to move laterally through networks, maintain access and exfiltrate sensitive information. However, traditional software procurement cycles and lengthy deployment processes can delay organisations’ ability to respond effectively during an active incident. Keeper’s new emergency response portal aims to eliminate these delays by routing requests directly to technical specialists, enabling affected organisations to prioritise containment before addressing commercial arrangements. Quotes and billing discussions are deferred until the platform has been deployed and access to sensitive resources has been secured. “Seconds matter during an active breach, so organisations need immediate containment, not a sales pitch,” said Darren Guccione, CEO and Co-founder of Keeper Security. “Our priority is to provide breached organisations with the critical technology and engineering support required to lock down their environments and stop lateral movement. We will secure your organisation first and discuss the commercial details only after the threat is contained.” The service provides rapid access to KeeperPAM, the company’s identity security platform, which combines enterprise password and passkey management, secrets management, privileged session management and endpoint privilege management within a zero-trust and zero-knowledge architecture. According to Keeper, its cloud-native architecture enables organisations to deploy these capabilities in minutes, rather than the months potentially required by traditional privileged access management (PAM) solutions. Once deployed, security teams can revoke standing privileges, rotate compromised credentials and secure infrastructure secrets to restrict attackers’ access. These controls extend across both human and non-human identities, including service accounts and AI agents, helping organisations reduce the opportunities for attackers to maintain persistence within their networks. The platform also incorporates KeeperAI, which uses real-time threat detection to monitor privileged sessions and automatically terminate anomalous activity during incident response. “When an adversary is already inside your network, you do not have time to re-architect your infrastructure or deploy complex legacy software,” said Craig Lurey, CTO and Co-founder of Keeper Security. “You need to immediately establish a secure control plane, cut off the attacker’s access to privileged accounts or privileged access and gain total visibility into session activity. Keeper is built to deploy instantly and provide that definitive layer of control.” The launch reflects the growing importance of identity security in incident response, as organisations seek to limit the damage caused by credential compromise and unauthorised privileged access. Organisations experiencing an active cyberattack can request assistance through Keeper Security’s dedicated emergency breach response portal .

items.title: 6 Cybersecurity Lessons We Can Learn from the Biggest Data Breaches
items.summary: From global retailers to healthcare giants, some of the world’s biggest organisations have fallen victim to devastating cybersecurity attacks in in the last few months alone. The PHP incident affected millions across the world and attacks are now even targeting fridges to disrupt organisations and the public. With millions of people’s personal information compromised and businesses facing significant financial and reputational damage, these incidents serve as important reminders that no organisation is immune to cyber threats. But beyond the headlines, what can businesses actually learn from these incidents? Here are six key cybersecurity lessons from some of the biggest breaches in recent years. Cybersecurity is everyone’s responsibility In 2025, UK retailer Marks & Spencer (M&S) suffered a major cyberattack that disrupted its operations and resulted in customer data being stolen. The incident highlighted how cyberattacks can extend far beyond IT departments, affecting everything from customer experience to business continuity. Organisations must recognise that cybersecurity is a company-wide responsibility. Regular employee training, clear security policies and collaboration between departments are essential to reducing risk. Third-party security cannot be overlooked The 2024 ransomware attack on Change Healthcare, a subsidiary of UnitedHealth Group, became one of the largest healthcare data breaches in US history, affecting approximately 192.7 million people. The attack also disrupted healthcare payment and claims processing across the country, demonstrating how a single compromised organisation can have consequences throughout an entire industry. Businesses must thoroughly assess the security practices of their suppliers and partners, ensuring third-party vulnerabilities do not become their own. Insider threats deserve just as much attention In November 2025, South Korean e-commerce giant Coupang disclosed a major data breach involving a former employee. The incident involved unauthorised access to personal information associated with approximately 33 million customer accounts. The breach serves as a reminder that cyber threats do not always originate from external hackers. Organisations should implement strict access controls, regularly review employee permissions and ensure access is promptly revoked when employees leave the business. Strong access controls are essential The Change Healthcare attack also highlighted the risks associated with insufficient identity protection, with attackers reportedly gaining access through compromised credentials and a remote access system that lacked multi-factor authentication (MFA). While no single security measure can prevent every attack, enforcing MFA, monitoring unusual login activity and applying least-privilege access principles can significantly reduce an organisation’s exposure. Cyber resilience is about more than preventing attacks In September 2025, Jaguar Land Rover (JLR) experienced a significant cyber incident that forced the manufacturer to shut down systems and severely disrupted production and retail operations. The incident demonstrated that the consequences of a cyberattack can be felt long after the initial compromise. Businesses must prioritise resilience alongside prevention, developing tested incident response plans, reliable backups and recovery strategies that minimise disruption when an attack occurs. Communication is critical during a cyber crisis When a major breach occurs, the way an organisation communicates can have a lasting impact on its reputation. The M&S cyberattack demonstrated the importance of keeping customers informed, with the retailer publicly confirming that some personal data had been stolen and providing guidance to affected customers. Having a clear crisis communications strategy is therefore just as important as having a technical incident response plan. Cybersecurity and PR teams should work closely together to deliver timely, transparent and consistent messaging to customers, employees and other stakeholders. Effective communication may not undo the damage caused by a breach, but it can help organisations maintain trust and protect their reputation during an incredibly challenging period. Learning from the past to prepare for the future These high-profile incidents demonstrate that cybersecurity is no longer simply about protecting systems and data. It is about protecting people, maintaining business continuity and preserving trust. As cyber threats continue to evolve, organisations must learn from the mistakes and experiences of others. After all, when it comes to cybersecurity, preparation is far less costly than recovery.

items.title: France Is Blaming Iran for the Fridge Cyberattack
items.summary: Interesting : U.S. intelligence agencies have recently reached a “”ow confidence” assessment that Iran was responsible for the attacks in France, according to three U.S. officials who spoke on the condition of anonymity to discuss sensitive intelligence. A “low confidence” assessment generally means that there is some intelligence that points in a certain direction but is fragmented, and that the assessment could change as more information is collected. The agencies’ judgment on the French incidents linked those attacks to Iran generally and not to a specific group such as the Revolutionary Guards, two of the officials said. They added that Iran was also seen as probably responsible for other similar attacks around Europe, but that those investigations were in their early stages. Alternate link .

items.title: Filigran’s OpenCTI Surpasses 400 Integrations
items.summary: Filigran , known for open-source XTM Platform for agentic CTEM, today announced that OpenCTI now offers more than 400 integrations . The threat intelligence platform’s ecosystem spans commercial and open-source threat feeds, enrichment services, and the SIEM, EDR, and SOAR platforms security teams use every day. By embedding intelligence directly into these existing workflows, OpenCTI breaks down data silos and turns raw information into actionable defence right on the front line. That expansion is increasingly driven by the growing OpenCTI community . Community members now add an average of nine integrations per month, more than double the previous 12-month average. This accelerating momentum is reflected across the open-source project, which recently surpassed 10,000 GitHub stars after growing more than 30% this year. Because OpenCTI is open source, threat analysts and development engineers can build the connectors their own environments need, and every new contribution makes the platform more valuable for everyone else. According to Filigran’s State of Threat Management report, the single most important factor when evaluating cybersecurity tools is integration with existing security platforms. OpenCTI’s open architecture lets organisations choose the intelligence sources that fit their mission, from adversary and malware tracking to financial fraud and AI risk. The platform then pipes that intelligence directly into tools like Google SecOps, Microsoft Sentinel, CrowdStrike Falcon, Splunk, ServiceNow and more. Analysts get threat context inside their existing workflows, not in another standalone console. “Data in a silo is powerless, and no single vendor can connect it all,” said Samuel Hassine, CEO and co-founder of Filigran. “Our team builds and maintains the integrations organisations depend on, and the community reaches the places a vendor roadmap never will, like regional feeds, niche tools and specialised sources. When the people closest to the problem build the connections themselves, the platform keeps pace with a security landscape that never stops changing.” “Threat intelligence delivers the greatest value when it reaches the teams and systems responsible for acting on it,” said David Holmes, VP of Partnerships at Flashpoint, the world’s largest private provider of threat intelligence. “OpenCTI’s expanding integration ecosystem helps organisations break down information silos and bring critical threat context into their existing security workflows. Our partnership with Filigran reflects a shared commitment to making intelligence more accessible, actionable and effective in helping organisations stay ahead of emerging threats.” Intelligence where teams already work OpenCTI’s integrations push structured threat intelligence into the tools security teams already use and, in some cases, also ingest case findings back into OpenCTI. This means that security teams see adversary, malware and vulnerability context right inside their existing alerts, cases and workflows, enabling them to make faster decisions. The average OpenCTI deployment runs 29 integrations . Recent additions: Google SecOps SOAR: Exchanges threat intelligence and case data between platforms, reducing manual work across tools SigmaHQ: Imports thousands of community-maintained detection rules into OpenCTI to correlate with threat intelligence ServiceNow Vulnerability Response: Sends vulnerability intelligence from OpenCTI to ServiceNow to support remediation tracking Google Digital Threat Monitoring and Recorded Future Attack Surface Intelligence: Bring digital risk alerts and attack surface findings into OpenCTI as enriched incidents Palo Alto Cortex XDR: Pushes OpenCTI indicators to Palo Alto Cortex XDR as IOCs in real time, with severity, expiration and deletion handled automatically Contributors submit community connectors as pull requests on GitHub. Filigran engineers review the code and implementation before adding approved connectors to the library. The full catalog is available to Community and Enterprise Edition users; Enterprise Edition also supports one-click connector deployment. Security teams can browse the full OpenCTI integration catalog at hub.filigran.io . Developers who want to build and contribute a connector can find guidelines in the OpenCTI connectors repository on GitHub. To learn more, please visit the blog here . This follows a new guide from Filigran highlighting the many routes women take into cyber threat intelligence About Filigran Filigran builds the open-source XTM Platform for Agentic CTEM. On the XTM One agentic core, OpenCTI, OpenAEV and OpenCRQ help security teams know their threats, validate their defences and quantify cyber risk. Founded in 2022, Filigran’s platforms are trusted by more than 6,000 organisations worldwide. Learn more: Website – Blog – LinkedIn

In this article
  • Java4Shell can cause memory corruption and, in some applications, remote code execution
  • Exploitation depends on the Java runtime, processor and application
  • Most home users are unlikely to be affected, but organizations should patch promptly

A critical-sounding Java flaw is making headlines. Most consumers are unlikely to be affected, but companies running Jira, Confluence, Jenkins and similar tools have work to do.

On November 17, Oracle and the OpenJDK project shipped fixes for CVE-2026-114938, a memory-corruption bug in Java’s Base64 decoder. Security firm Calif discovered the flaw and named it Java4Shell. CISA urged organizations to patch immediately.

After a run of high-profile computer problems and security scares, it’s understandable that another vulnerability with a catchy name would set alarm bells ringing. But it’s important to separate the potential damage from the likelihood of being affected. This is a serious issue for organizations running vulnerable applications, not a reason for every home user to assume their computer is at risk.

It doesn’t help that organizations give out different CVSS scores for the same vulnerability.

  • Oracle rates it 8.1 under CVSS 3.1 and describes it as “difficult to exploit.”
  • Calif rates it 9.2 (Critical) under CVSS 4.0.

Meanwhile, there are currently no reports of abuse in the wild. Calif demonstrated remote code execution without logging in on default installations of Keycloak, Jira, Confluence, Artifactory, Jenkins and PingFederate. It also demonstrated post-login code execution on Kafka, Solr, Elasticsearch, Gerrit and Spinnaker.

Technical details

Base64 is a common way of representing binary data as text. It’s used in login protocols, file uploads and network messages. To decode it faster, OpenJDK uses special x86-64 CPU instructions.

The bug is in hand-written assembly code for that fast path. A short, malformed input can write 62 bytes past the end of a memory buffer.

For remote code execution, several conditions have to line up:

  1. The right processor. The flaw only affects x86-64 CPUs that support the AVX-512 VBMI instruction set. Examples include Intel Xeon from Ice Lake onward and AMD Zen 4 or newer. ARM64 chips aren’t affected.
  2. A recent OpenJDK-based Java. The flaw affects OpenJDK from 17.0.6 onward, and the distributions built on it.
  3. An exposed Java service. The attacker has to feed crafted data to a Java application that decodes it. Oracle notes it can only be exploited by supplying data to the affected APIs, such as through a web service. It can’t be exploited through untrusted Java Web Start applications or applets.
  4. A target-specific exploit. Calif says there is no universal exploit. Each chain needs a decoder route, a feedback path, a heap layout, and an application-specific action. The attack also works best with low, stable network latency, and Calif rented a VM in the same region as its target.

An ordinary home PC rarely runs a Java server that accepts Base64 input from the internet. Organizations running affected Java applications on vulnerable processors should patch promptly, since attackers may find narrow, application-specific paths to remote code execution.

“One of the best cybersecurity suites on the planet.” 

According to CNET. Read their review →

items.title: CVE-2026-114938: Java4Shell Flaw Enables Pre-Auth RCE in Major Java Applications
items.summary: A newly disclosed vulnerability tracked as CVE-2026-114938 and dubbed Java4Shell exposes certain Java environments to memory corruption, sensitive data disclosure, service crashes, and potentially remote code execution. The flaw resides in OpenJDK’s hardware-accelerated Base64 decoder and can be triggered remotely when attacker-controlled Base64 data reaches the vulnerable Java runtime. Calif researchers demonstrated pre-authentication RCE against widely deployed enterprise applications running default configurations, including Keycloak, Atlassian Jira, Atlassian Confluence, JFrog Artifactory, Jenkins, and PingFederate. Authenticated exploitation was also demonstrated against Apache Kafka Broker, Apache Solr, Elasticsearch, Gerrit, and Spinnaker, while sample Spring Boot and Apache Struts applications were successfully exploited as well. The vulnerability is highly dependent on the underlying hardware. The vulnerable accelerated decoder runs on x86-64 processors supporting AVX-512 VBMI, including Intel Xeon Ice Lake and newer server platforms and AMD Zen 4 or later systems. ARM64 systems are not known to be affected by this specific flaw. Calif assigned Java4Shell a CVSS 4.0 score of 9.2, Critical , while Oracle rates it 8.1, High under CVSS 3.1. Oracle released security updates on November 17, 2026, while several downstream Java vendors have been issuing their own patched builds on separate schedules. Organizations can leverage SOC Prime’s AI-Native Detection Intelligence Platform to accelerate threat hunting and detection engineering around emerging vulnerabilities and adapt relevant detection logic across SIEM, EDR, XDR, and Data Lake environments. Security teams can also use Prime Architect to transform emerging vulnerability intelligence into hunting queries, refine detection logic, and adapt behavioral detections to the telemetry available within their infrastructure. CVE-2026-114938 analysis CVE-2026-114938 affects OpenJDK 17 beginning with version 17.0.6 and subsequent Java 17 builds, as well as affected Java 21, 25, and 27 releases derived from the vulnerable OpenJDK code. Multiple downstream distributions inherit the issue, including Oracle Java SE, Amazon Corretto, Eclipse Temurin, Microsoft Build of OpenJDK, Azul Zulu, BellSoft Liberica, SAP SapMachine, and Red Hat OpenJDK. Standard Java 8 and Java 11 do not contain the vulnerable code path, although Oracle’s Java SE 8 Performance Pack build 8u511b33-perf is specifically listed as affected. The vulnerability originates in the optimized implementation of java.util.Base64.Decoder. On supported x86-64 CPUs, the JVM can automatically select AVX-512 VBMI accelerated instructions on supported x86-64 processors to improve Base64 decoding performance. Specially malformed Base64 input causes the decoder to miscalculate the amount of data that should be written to the destination buffer, resulting in a heap-based out-of-bounds write. According to Calif’s technical analysis, one malformed input pattern causes the accelerated routine to write approximately 62 bytes beyond the allocated output buffer. Java ultimately rejects the malformed Base64 value, but the memory corruption occurs before the validation failure stops processing. This behavior is particularly dangerous because Base64 decoding occurs throughout enterprise Java applications. HTTP Basic authentication headers, SAML artifacts, CSRF tokens, encoded file uploads, MIME content, and other application data may all pass through the standard Java decoder. Importantly, many of these operations can take place before a user is authenticated, creating pathways toward pre-authentication exploitation. Researchers initially faced an important limitation: the bytes written beyond the buffer are largely fixed rather than freely attacker-controlled. Calif developed an application-dependent exploitation technique that manipulates the JVM heap layout so the overflow corrupts neighboring arrays. By enlarging one array and using another to read memory, researchers created a memory disclosure primitive called JavaBleed , which could then be extended toward controlled memory modification and code execution. There is therefore no single universal Java4Shell exploit. Exploitation varies according to the application, its Base64 processing path, JVM heap layout, network conditions, and timing. Researchers noted that remote heap grooming can require repeated attempts and careful control over allocation behavior. Failed exploitation can instead terminate the JVM and cause application outages. The CVE-2026-114938 PoC publicly released by the researchers demonstrates the underlying memory corruption, while the weaponized application-specific exploit chains used to achieve RCE against major enterprise products have been withheld. Other security teams have independently reproduced memory corruption, JVM crashes, and memory disclosure, but some have not reproduced the full remote code execution chain. The hardware requirement significantly changes exposure assessment. A Java application running the same container image may be vulnerable on one server and unaffected on another depending on the CPU presented to the JVM. Known susceptible processor families include Intel Xeon Ice Lake, Sapphire Rapids, Emerald Rapids, and Granite Rapids, along with AMD Zen 4 and newer CPUs. ARM64 environments are not known to execute the vulnerable AVX-512 code path. Administrators can verify CPU capability on Linux by checking whether the processor exposes AVX-512 VBMI support. They should also run java -version inside the actual application environment, including containers and software packages that bundle private Java runtimes, rather than relying only on the system-wide Java installation. For CVE-2026-114938 detection, defenders should monitor application, JVM, web, authentication, and endpoint telemetry together. Potential indicators include unusual malformed Base64 input, repeated Base64 decoding exceptions, JVM crashes, unexpected Java process restarts, and suspicious child processes launched by Java services after inbound requests. Security teams should pay particular attention to Base64 tokens whose lengths or padding differ from expected application behavior, especially when they appear repeatedly in authentication endpoints or other unauthenticated request paths. Bursts of IllegalArgumentException errors involving java.util.Base64$Decoder may also indicate probing, although such events are not sufficient by themselves to confirm exploitation. To Detect CVE-2026-114938 exploitation beyond the initial memory-corruption attempt, defenders should correlate suspicious inbound requests with subsequent Java process behavior. Unexpected shell execution, new outbound network connections, file downloads, persistence creation, credential access, or unusual commands launched by a Java service should be treated as high-priority evidence of potential compromise. Traditional CVE-2026-114938 IOCs such as fixed attacker IP addresses, domains, or malware hashes are currently of limited value because the flaw is a vulnerability rather than a campaign tied to known malicious infrastructure. Behavioral detection and exposure assessment therefore provide stronger coverage than static blocklists. As of November 18, 2026, the Canadian Centre for Cyber Security and the reviewed security reports state that no active exploitation has been confirmed. The vulnerability was also not listed in CISA’s Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog when The Hacker News checked on November 18. However, public knowledge of the memory-corruption primitive significantly increases the urgency of patching internet-facing Java applications. Security professionals seeking further details for CVE-2026-114938 should track advisories from their specific Java vendor because downstream OpenJDK distributions, bundled application runtimes, containers, and commercial products may receive patches on different schedules. CVE-2026-114938 Mitigation The primary remediation is to update affected Java runtimes to a fixed release as soon as possible. Oracle issued its November 2026 security updates on November 17 and lists the following fixed Java SE builds: Java release Affected Oracle build Fixed build Java SE 17 17.0.6 through 17.0.21.1 Java SE 21 17.0.21.0.3 21.0.13.1 Java SE 25 Up to 21.0.13.0.3 25.0.5.1 Java SE 27 Up to 25.0.5.0.3 27.0.1.1 Java SE 8 Performance Up to 27.0.1.0.3 8u513 Performance Pack 8u511b33-perf Pack GraalVM users should likewise move to the corresponding November security releases. Downstream OpenJDK distributions use their own versioning and patch schedules, so organizations should verify fixes with the vendor supplying the JVM rather than assuming Oracle build numbers apply universally. At the time of writing, Amazon had released corrected Corretto builds and Azul had published updated Zulu releases, while Red Hat was still preparing fixes for affected RHEL and OpenJDK packages. That status can change quickly, making vendor advisories the authoritative source for patch availability. Organizations should inventory Java not only on traditional servers but also inside containers, vendor applications, appliances, CI/CD systems, identity infrastructure, and enterprise development platforms. Products that package their own JVM may need an application vendor update instead of replacing the runtime manually. After upgrading Java, restart affected services and verify that the running JVM actually uses the patched build. Containerized applications should be rebuilt and redeployed using an updated base image or vendor runtime. When immediate updates are impossible, administrators can temporarily disable the vulnerable accelerated decoder by starting affected JVMs with: -XX:-UseBASE64Intrinsics This is the preferred temporary workaround because it disables the hardware-accelerated Base64 implementation while leaving other AVX-512 optimizations available. An alternative is: -XX:UseAVX=2 This prevents the JVM from using AVX-512 entirely and therefore removes the vulnerable code path. This option should only be applied to x86-64 environments; ARM64 Java runtimes do not recognize the flag and may fail to start. Additional defensive measures should prioritize internet-facing Java applications, identity systems, authentication portals, CI/CD platforms, and development infrastructure because these environments commonly process attacker-controlled Base64 before authentication. Organizations should also monitor Java services for unexpected crashes or restarts during the remediation period. Because failed exploitation can terminate the JVM, repeated application failures combined with malformed inbound requests may warrant immediate incident-response investigation rather than being treated as ordinary availability issues. FAQ What is CVE-2026-114938 and how does it work? CVE-2026-114938, also known as Java4Shell, is a memory-corruption vulnerability in OpenJDK’s hardware-accelerated Base64 decoder. On x86-64 processors supporting AVX-512 VBMI, malformed Base64 input can cause the decoder to write beyond an allocated heap buffer. Researchers demonstrated that careful manipulation of neighboring heap objects can transform this corruption into memory disclosure and, for specific applications, remote code execution. When was CVE-2026-114938 first discovered? The precise date of the initial private discovery has not been publicly specified. Calif researcher Quang Luong discovered the flaw while auditing OpenJDK HotSpot with AI-assisted tooling and reported that identifying the bug took roughly one hour, followed by approximately two additional hours to develop an initial exploit. The vulnerability was publicly disclosed and patched on November 17, 2026. What is the impact of CVE-2026-114938 on systems? Successful exploitation can corrupt JVM memory, crash Java applications, expose sensitive information from process memory, or enable arbitrary code execution in the security context of the affected Java process. Calif demonstrated unauthenticated RCE against Keycloak, Jira, Confluence, Artifactory, Jenkins, and PingFederate, with additional authenticated attack paths against several other Java products. Can CVE-2026-114938 still affect me in 2026? Yes. An environment remains potentially exposed if it runs a vulnerable OpenJDK-derived runtime, executes on an x86-64 CPU supporting AVX-512 VBMI, and passes attacker-controlled Base64 data into Java’s standard decoder. Internet-facing applications and authentication services warrant particular attention. Standard Java 8 and Java 11 are not affected by this code path, while the specific Oracle Java 8 Performance Pack build identified by the vendor is vulnerable. How can I protect myself from CVE-2026-114938? Update affected Java runtimes using the security release provided by your Java or application vendor and restart all impacted services. Inventory bundled and containerized JVMs, not just system Java installations. If patching cannot be completed immediately, temporarily disable the Base64 intrinsic with -XX:-UseBASE64Intrinsics or disable AVX-512 on x86-64 systems with -XX:UseAVX=2, then remove the workaround after deploying a permanent fix.

items.title: Majority of Workplace AI Activity Takes Place Outside Enterprise Accounts
items.summary: New research from CultureAI has revealed that 81% of workplace AI interactions take place outside enterprise accounts, raising concerns about organisations’ ability to monitor AI usage and protect sensitive information. The AI security and governance company’s latest report, The Unmanaged Majority: What 1.7 million AI interactions reveal about enterprise control , analysed nearly 1.7 million AI interactions across 40 organisations over six months spanning Q2 and Q3 2026. The findings highlight a significant gap between how organisations believe employees are using AI and what is happening in practice, with sensitive information detected in approximately one in every seven prompts. AI Adoption Extends Far Beyond Approved Tools CultureAI identified 1,064 distinct AI applications across the organisations studied, with an average of 113 applications used per organisation. Nearly half of these applications appeared in just one organisation, while general-purpose chatbots accounted for only 6% of the total. Despite growing investment in enterprise AI licences and governance policies, just 19% of interactions took place through enterprise accounts. Almost half (47%) involved personal, free or unauthenticated accounts, while a further 34% took place through applications where the licence type could not be identified. The findings suggest that organisations relying solely on approved AI tools and enterprise licences may have limited visibility into how employees are using AI across their businesses. The research also found that blocking AI applications could have unintended consequences. In organisations that introduced restrictions, personal account usage increased by approximately 50%, suggesting employees were continuing to access AI tools through less visible channels. Sensitive Data Exposure Becomes Widespread The report identified 252,480 sensitive data detections across 100 different categories, highlighting the scale and variety of information being shared with AI applications. HR records and correspondence were detected in 90% of organisations, followed by company strategy information (85%), health conditions (82%), and legal case details and financial information (72%). Notably, credentials accounted for less than 1% of all sensitive data detections. Instead, disclosures involving company strategy, finance, HR, legal and health information outnumbered credential exposures by almost 30 to one. This presents a challenge for traditional data loss prevention (DLP) tools, which are typically designed to identify structured information such as passwords, account numbers and other recognisable data patterns. More contextual information, such as employee grievances, medical conditions, recruitment decisions and confidential business strategies, can be considerably harder to identify and protect. Growing Compliance Concerns The findings also raise questions about organisations’ ability to meet their regulatory and compliance obligations as workplace AI adoption accelerates. Under UK and EU GDPR, health information may qualify as special category data, requiring additional safeguards when processed. Meanwhile, certain high-risk AI systems used in recruitment and employment decisions will face requirements under the EU AI Act, including human oversight and record-keeping obligations, from December 2027. For legal professionals, sharing confidential or privileged information with external AI services can also create risks around client confidentiality and legal privilege. The report suggests that simply approving an AI platform or purchasing an enterprise licence is insufficient to address these challenges. Organisations must also consider what information employees are sharing and whether appropriate safeguards are in place. Visibility, Not Blocking, Is Key Commenting on the findings, Oliver Simonnet, Lead Cybersecurity Researcher at CultureAI, said: “AI is now firmly embedded in everyday working life, but our research shows a significant disconnect between how organisations believe AI is being used and what is actually happening. With 81% of AI interactions taking place outside enterprise accounts, it’s clear that traditional approaches to governance are failing to keep pace with employee behaviour.” Simonnet warned that organisations should not assume that introducing AI policies or approving specific applications automatically gives them control over employee activity. “Organisations cannot assume that approving an AI tool or introducing a policy automatically means they have control over how it is used. They need visibility into the applications employees are accessing, the accounts they are using and, crucially, the information being shared.” He added that restricting access to AI tools is unlikely to solve the problem, particularly when employees can turn to personal accounts to continue using them. “Restricting AI isn’t the answer. Where organisations blocked AI tools, personal account use rose by around half. The better route is to make secure use the easiest option. By continuously monitoring AI activity and applying appropriate safeguards, businesses can protect sensitive information without sacrificing the productivity benefits that make AI so valuable in the first place.” The findings underline the need for organisations to move beyond static approved-tool lists and adopt more continuous approaches to AI discovery, monitoring and data protection.

items.title: Behind the Power Outage: Unmasking a New Intrusion Vector in Enterprise Infrastructure Tools
items.summary: A UPS management feature that runs a script when the power fails gives an intruder a trusted, built-in way to execute code on a domain controller, dump Active Directory secrets and launch a persistent implant.

items.title: KQLs for Major brands compromised through Optimizely
items.summary: Investigating malicious connections, potential payload execution, and suspicious endpoint activity using KQL. Introduction On November 16, 2026, Report URI published an investigation revealing how attackers abused Optimizely Web to distribute malicious JavaScript through legitimate websites belonging to major global brands. According to the research, 178 organizations were affected. The malicious code was associated with several capabilities, including cryptocurrency address replacement, payment card skimming, information theft, and the delivery of iOS exploits such as Coruna and DarkSword. From a threat hunting perspective, this is particularly interesting: users could be exposed to malicious JavaScript simply by visiting a legitimate website. Let’s explore how Microsoft Defender XDR/Sentinel can help investigate this activity. Original research: https://blog.report-uri.com/worlds-largest-brands-infected-with-malware-via-optimizely/ 1. Identify connections to malicious infrastructure The first step is to identify devices communicating with the reported IoCs. DeviceNetworkEvents | where Timestamp > ago(3d) | where RemoteUrl contains "1688360.cc" or RemoteUrl contains "5vobauua3ojpklx.icu" or RemoteUrl contains "eil786npto9u5bq.icu" or RemoteUrl contains "webshell.lol" | project Timestamp, DeviceName, DeviceId, ActionType, RemoteUrl, RemoteIP, InitiatingProcessFileName | order by Timestamp desc 2. Identify the most affected devices Next, determine which devices generated the most connections and whether they contacted multiple malicious domains + which type of malicious URLs are ( PayLoad, Data Exfiltration, Screenshoot, others ). DeviceNetworkEvents | where Timestamp > ago(3d) | where RemoteUrl contains "1688360.cc" or RemoteUrl contains "5vobauua3ojpklx.icu" or RemoteUrl contains "eil786npto9u5bq.icu" or RemoteUrl contains "webshell.lol" | extend ActivityType=case(RemoteUrl contains "1688360.cc" and RemoteUrl contains "hit.php","Potential Cookie & Screenshot Exfiltration",RemoteUrl contains "1688360.cc" and RemoteUrl contains "card.php","Potential Card Data Exfiltration",RemoteUrl contains "1688360.cc" and RemoteUrl contains "track.js","Malicious JavaScript Payload",RemoteUrl contains "1688360.cc","Malicious Payload / Exfiltration Infrastructure",RemoteUrl contains "5vobauua3ojpklx.icu","iOS Exploit Router 1",RemoteUrl contains "eil786npto9u5bq.icu","iOS Exploit Router 2",RemoteUrl contains "webshell.lol","JavaScript Injection Infrastructure","Unknown") | summarize Connections=count(), FirstSeen=min(Timestamp), LastSeen=max(Timestamp), Domains=make_set(RemoteUrl,20), ActivityType=make_set(ActivityType,10) by DeviceName, DeviceId Repeated connections may indicate continued exposure, although they do not necessarily confirm compromise. 3. Investigate process activity after the connections Did the browser launch any additional processes shortly after contacting the malicious infrastructure? let Hits = DeviceNetworkEvents | where Timestamp > ago(3d) | where RemoteUrl contains "1688360.cc" or RemoteUrl contains "5vobauua3ojpklx.icu" or RemoteUrl contains "eil786npto9u5bq.icu" or RemoteUrl contains "webshell.lol" | project DeviceId, ConnectionTime=Timestamp, BrowserPID=InitiatingProcessId, BrowserCreationTime=InitiatingProcessCreationTime; Hits | join kind=inner (DeviceProcessEvents | project DeviceId, Timestamp, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessId, InitiatingProcessCreationTime) on DeviceId | where Timestamp between (ConnectionTime .. ConnectionTime + 10m) | where InitiatingProcessId == BrowserPID and InitiatingProcessCreationTime == BrowserCreationTime | project Timestamp, ConnectionTime, DeviceId, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName | order by Timestamp desc This can help identify unexpected browser-spawned processes, although JavaScript execution may occur entirely within the browser. 4. Look for potential payload downloads We can also investigate file creation events following suspicious connections but I had too many false positives. let Hits = DeviceNetworkEvents | where Timestamp > ago(3d) | where RemoteUrl contains "1688360.cc" or RemoteUrl contains "5vobauua3ojpklx.icu" or RemoteUrl contains "eil786npto9u5bq.icu" or RemoteUrl contains "webshell.lol" | project DeviceId, ConnectionTime=Timestamp; Hits | join kind=inner (DeviceFileEvents | where ActionType == "FileCreated" | project DeviceId, Timestamp, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256, FileOriginUrl, InitiatingProcessFileName) on DeviceId | where Timestamp between (ConnectionTime .. ConnectionTime + 2m) | project Timestamp, DeviceId, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256, FileOriginUrl, InitiatingProcessFileName 5. Investigate subsequent network activity Finally, we can examine additional connections initiated by the same process within five minutes. let Hits = DeviceNetworkEvents | where Timestamp > ago(3d) | where RemoteUrl contains "1688360.cc" or RemoteUrl contains "5vobauua3ojpklx.icu" or RemoteUrl contains "eil786npto9u5bq.icu" or RemoteUrl contains "webshell.lol" | project DeviceId, ConnectionTime=Timestamp, IOC=RemoteUrl, PID=InitiatingProcessId, ProcessCreationTime=InitiatingProcessCreationTime; Hits | join kind=inner (DeviceNetworkEvents | project DeviceId, Timestamp, RemoteUrl, RemoteIP, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessId, InitiatingProcessCreationTime) on DeviceId | where Timestamp between (ConnectionTime .. ConnectionTime + 5m) | where InitiatingProcessId == PID and InitiatingProcessCreationTime == ProcessCreationTime | project Timestamp, ConnectionTime, DeviceId, IOC, RemoteUrl, RemoteIP, InitiatingProcessFileName | order by Timestamp asc This may reveal additional suspicious destinations, but normal browser background traffic must be considered. ⚠️ Additional Queries 17/11/2026 Identify Compromised Websites Visited by Users Before the Malicious URLs The article highlights several affected organizations, including BBC, CNN, Zoom, GitLab, IKEA, and Ledger. We can correlate visits to these legitimate websites with subsequent connections to malicious domains to identify potential infection paths. let Sites = dynamic(["bbc.com","bbc.co.uk","cnn.com","zoom.com","zoom.us","gitlab.com","ledger.com","ikea.com","smartsheet.com","salesforce.com","zattoo.com"]); let Hits = materialize(DeviceNetworkEvents | where Timestamp between (datetime(2026-11-16) .. datetime(2026-11-18)) | where RemoteUrl has_any ("1688360.cc","5vobauua3ojpklx.icu","eil786npto9u5bq.icu") | project DeviceId, HitTime=Timestamp, MaliciousURL=RemoteUrl); DeviceNetworkEvents | where Timestamp between (datetime(2026-11-16) .. datetime(2026-11-18)) | where RemoteUrl has_any (Sites) | join kind=inner Hits on DeviceId | where Timestamp between ((HitTime - 2m) .. HitTime) | project Timestamp, DeviceName, LegitimateSite=RemoteUrl, MaliciousURL, HitTime, InitiatingProcessFileName | order by HitTime asc 6. Can we inspect the actual payload? One important limitation: DeviceNetworkEvents does not capture complete HTTP/HTTPS payloads. Even if we observe connections to malicious infrastructure, we cannot directly confirm whether JavaScript was executed or sensitive information was exfiltrated. Additional telemetry, such as proxy logs, browser artifacts, or packet captures with decryption, may be necessary. Final thoughts This campaign demonstrates how a trusted third-party JavaScript integration can become an effective attack vector. For threat hunters, identifying malicious connections is only the beginning. These KQL queries are intended as starting points for further investigation rather than production-ready detections. Original research: https://blog.report-uri.com/worlds-largest-brands-infected-with-malware-via-optimizely/ 🚨KQLs for Major brands compromised through Optimizely was originally published in Detect FYI on Medium, where people are continuing the conversation by highlighting and responding to this story.
items.summary_html:
Investigating malicious connections, potential payload execution, and suspicious endpoint activity using KQL.

Introduction

On November 16, 2026, Report URI published an investigation revealing how attackers abused Optimizely Web to distribute malicious JavaScript through legitimate websites belonging to major global brands. According to the research, 178 organizations were affected.

The malicious code was associated with several capabilities, including cryptocurrency address replacement, payment card skimming, information theft, and the delivery of iOS exploits such as Coruna and DarkSword. From a threat hunting perspective, this is particularly interesting: users could be exposed to malicious JavaScript simply by visiting a legitimate website.

Let’s explore how Microsoft Defender XDR/Sentinel can help investigate this activity.

Original research: https://blog.report-uri.com/worlds-largest-brands-infected-with-malware-via-optimizely/

1. Identify connections to malicious infrastructure

The first step is to identify devices communicating with the reported IoCs.

DeviceNetworkEvents 
| where Timestamp > ago(3d) 
| where RemoteUrl contains "1688360.cc" or RemoteUrl contains "5vobauua3ojpklx.icu" or RemoteUrl contains "eil786npto9u5bq.icu" or RemoteUrl contains "webshell.lol" 
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, DeviceId, ActionType, RemoteUrl, RemoteIP, InitiatingProcessFileName | order by Timestamp desc
2. Identify the most affected devices

Next, determine which devices generated the most connections and whether they contacted multiple malicious domains + which type of malicious URLs are ( PayLoad, Data Exfiltration, Screenshoot, others).

DeviceNetworkEvents 
| where Timestamp > ago(3d) 
| where RemoteUrl contains "1688360.cc" or RemoteUrl contains "5vobauua3ojpklx.icu" or RemoteUrl contains "eil786npto9u5bq.icu" or RemoteUrl contains "webshell.lol" 
| extend ActivityType=case(RemoteUrl contains "1688360.cc" and RemoteUrl contains "hit.php","Potential Cookie & Screenshot Exfiltration",RemoteUrl contains "1688360.cc" and RemoteUrl contains "card.php","Potential Card Data Exfiltration",RemoteUrl contains "1688360.cc" and RemoteUrl contains "track.js","Malicious JavaScript Payload",RemoteUrl contains "1688360.cc","Malicious Payload / Exfiltration Infrastructure",RemoteUrl contains "5vobauua3ojpklx.icu","iOS Exploit Router 1",RemoteUrl contains "eil786npto9u5bq.icu","iOS Exploit Router 2",RemoteUrl contains "webshell.lol","JavaScript Injection Infrastructure","Unknown") 
| summarize Connections=count(), FirstSeen=min(Timestamp), LastSeen=max(Timestamp), Domains=make_set(RemoteUrl,20), ActivityType=make_set(ActivityType,10) by DeviceName, DeviceId

Repeated connections may indicate continued exposure, although they do not necessarily confirm compromise.

3. Investigate process activity after the connections

Did the browser launch any additional processes shortly after contacting the malicious infrastructure?

let Hits = DeviceNetworkEvents | where Timestamp > ago(3d) 
| where RemoteUrl contains "1688360.cc" or RemoteUrl contains "5vobauua3ojpklx.icu" or RemoteUrl contains "eil786npto9u5bq.icu" or RemoteUrl contains "webshell.lol" 
| project DeviceId, ConnectionTime=Timestamp, BrowserPID=InitiatingProcessId, BrowserCreationTime=InitiatingProcessCreationTime;
 Hits 
| join kind=inner (DeviceProcessEvents 
| project DeviceId, Timestamp, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessId, InitiatingProcessCreationTime) on DeviceId 
| where Timestamp between (ConnectionTime .. ConnectionTime + 10m) 
| where InitiatingProcessId == BrowserPID and InitiatingProcessCreationTime == BrowserCreationTime 
| project Timestamp, ConnectionTime, DeviceId, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName | order by Timestamp desc

This can help identify unexpected browser-spawned processes, although JavaScript execution may occur entirely within the browser.

4. Look for potential payload downloads

We can also investigate file creation events following suspicious connections but I had too many false positives.

let Hits = DeviceNetworkEvents | where Timestamp > ago(3d) 
| where RemoteUrl contains "1688360.cc" or RemoteUrl contains "5vobauua3ojpklx.icu" or RemoteUrl contains "eil786npto9u5bq.icu" or RemoteUrl contains "webshell.lol" | project DeviceId, ConnectionTime=Timestamp; 
Hits 
| join kind=inner (DeviceFileEvents 
| where ActionType == "FileCreated" 
| project DeviceId, Timestamp, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256, FileOriginUrl, InitiatingProcessFileName) on DeviceId 
| where Timestamp between (ConnectionTime .. ConnectionTime + 2m) 
| project Timestamp, DeviceId, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256, FileOriginUrl, InitiatingProcessFileName
5. Investigate subsequent network activity

Finally, we can examine additional connections initiated by the same process within five minutes.

let Hits = DeviceNetworkEvents | where Timestamp > ago(3d) 
| where RemoteUrl contains "1688360.cc" or RemoteUrl contains "5vobauua3ojpklx.icu" or RemoteUrl contains "eil786npto9u5bq.icu" or RemoteUrl contains "webshell.lol" 
| project DeviceId, ConnectionTime=Timestamp, IOC=RemoteUrl, PID=InitiatingProcessId, ProcessCreationTime=InitiatingProcessCreationTime;
Hits 
| join kind=inner (DeviceNetworkEvents | project DeviceId, Timestamp, RemoteUrl, RemoteIP, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessId, InitiatingProcessCreationTime) on DeviceId 
| where Timestamp between (ConnectionTime .. ConnectionTime + 5m) 
| where InitiatingProcessId == PID and InitiatingProcessCreationTime == ProcessCreationTime
| project Timestamp, ConnectionTime, DeviceId, IOC, RemoteUrl, RemoteIP, InitiatingProcessFileName | order by Timestamp asc

This may reveal additional suspicious destinations, but normal browser background traffic must be considered.

⚠️ Additional Queries

17/11/2026 Identify Compromised Websites Visited by Users Before the Malicious URLs

The article highlights several affected organizations, including BBC, CNN, Zoom, GitLab, IKEA, and Ledger. We can correlate visits to these legitimate websites with subsequent connections to malicious domains to identify potential infection paths.

let Sites = dynamic(["bbc.com","bbc.co.uk","cnn.com","zoom.com","zoom.us","gitlab.com","ledger.com","ikea.com","smartsheet.com","salesforce.com","zattoo.com"]); let Hits = materialize(DeviceNetworkEvents 
| where Timestamp between (datetime(2026-11-16) .. datetime(2026-11-18)) 
| where RemoteUrl has_any ("1688360.cc","5vobauua3ojpklx.icu","eil786npto9u5bq.icu") 
| project DeviceId, HitTime=Timestamp, MaliciousURL=RemoteUrl); 
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp between (datetime(2026-11-16) .. datetime(2026-11-18)) 
| where RemoteUrl has_any (Sites) 
| join kind=inner Hits on DeviceId 
| where Timestamp between ((HitTime - 2m) .. HitTime) 
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, LegitimateSite=RemoteUrl, MaliciousURL, HitTime, InitiatingProcessFileName | order by HitTime asc
6. Can we inspect the actual payload?
One important limitation: DeviceNetworkEvents does not capture complete HTTP/HTTPS payloads.

Even if we observe connections to malicious infrastructure, we cannot directly confirm whether JavaScript was executed or sensitive information was exfiltrated. Additional telemetry, such as proxy logs, browser artifacts, or packet captures with decryption, may be necessary.

Final thoughts

This campaign demonstrates how a trusted third-party JavaScript integration can become an effective attack vector. For threat hunters, identifying malicious connections is only the beginning. These KQL queries are intended as starting points for further investigation rather than production-ready detections.

Original research: https://blog.report-uri.com/worlds-largest-brands-infected-with-malware-via-optimizely/

items.title: Most agents reach sensitive data with no verified DLP
items.summary: In October, Arrakis Security published its 2026 Autonomous Agents Threat Report, built on 12 weeks of telemetry from thousands of agents in its customers’ environments. It found that 70% of agents can reach sensitive systems, such as cloud storage, AI services, and marketing platforms, and 99.4% of those had no verified data loss prevention on that connection. Source: Arrakis Security, 2026 Autonomous Agents Threat Report , Oct. 2026. That is the DLP gap in numbers. This post compares DLP, DSPM, and a data security platform when the thing reaching your data is an agent. Part 1: Finding it a day later isn’t protecting it Both categories are adding agent features Vendors are extending DLP to agents. Cyera (August 2026), for example, says its endpoint product applies the same data protection controls wherever agents run, including desktop AI apps. DSPM vendors now map which data each agent can reach. Both are natural extensions, and both still work at the exit or on the map. The gap did not move Approach In the agent era What stays open DLP Watches or blocks data moving toward an agent or a device. Data already sitting still, and files it cannot read. DSPM Maps what an agent can reach and flags over-access. Fixing what it finds. The fix often lands in a ticket. Data security platform Finds the data, then encrypts, masks, or redacts it. The protection stays on the file when an agent copies it, and an agent without access to the key can’t read it. Stopping a transfer mid-send. Protection on the file covers what happens after it leaves. Speed widens the gap In October, CrowdStrike reported that a China-linked group it tracks as VAPOR PANDA ran an AI agent framework, ARTEX, against more than 200 organizations in 11 days. CrowdStrike confirmed intrusions at nine of them, and a human operator steered the agents only at decision points. A review queue is built for a person’s pace. These agents ran in parallel. Source: CrowdStrike, VAPOR PANDA threat report , Oct. 2026. A file that PK Protect has already encrypted doesn’t wait for anyone to respond to an alert. The protection is on the file however fast the agents move, and an agent that hasn’t been given access to the key can’t read it. Keys go only to the directory groups that need them, so a credential lifted from a config file or a cloud role doesn’t come with a key unless that identity was given one. Request your assessment

Source: Arrakis Security, 2026 Autonomous Agents Threat Report, Oct. 2026.

That is the DLP gap in numbers. This post compares DLP, DSPM, and a data security platform when the thing reaching your data is an agent.

Both categories are adding agent features

Vendors are extending DLP to agents. Cyera (August 2026), for example, says its endpoint product applies the same data protection controls wherever agents run, including desktop AI apps. DSPM vendors now map which data each agent can reach. Both are natural extensions, and both still work at the exit or on the map.

The gap did not move ApproachIn the agent eraWhat stays open DLPWatches or blocks data moving toward an agent or a device.Data already sitting still, and files it cannot read. DSPMMaps what an agent can reach and flags over-access.Fixing what it finds. The fix often lands in a ticket. Data security platformFinds the data, then encrypts, masks, or redacts it. The protection stays on the file when an agent copies it, and an agent without access to the key can’t read it.Stopping a transfer mid-send. Protection on the file covers what happens after it leaves.
Speed widens the gap

In October, CrowdStrike reported that a China-linked group it tracks as VAPOR PANDA ran an AI agent framework, ARTEX, against more than 200 organizations in 11 days. CrowdStrike confirmed intrusions at nine of them, and a human operator steered the agents only at decision points. A review queue is built for a person’s pace. These agents ran in parallel.
