items.title: Shadow AI Is Shipped to You, One Release Note at a Time
items.summary: Shadow AI is usually described as a people problem: an employee pasting company data into a chatbot nobody approved. That person exists, and the risk is growing: IBM’s Cost of a Data Breach Report 2026 found that incidents involving employee shadow AI more than doubled in a year, to 43% from 20%. But they are the more visible part of the problem. The larger part is less obvious. The software your organization already runs has been adding AI features release by release, and each of those features sends your data to a model. They arrived the way every other feature arrives, in a vendor update, described in a release note that nobody in security read. That is the shadow AI this piece is about. A working definition: shadow AI is any AI model your data reaches that security has not inventoried, whether an employee brought it in or a vendor shipped it in an update. You became an AI company without asking Count the SaaS products your organization runs. Now count how many of them shipped an AI feature in the last twelve months. The CRM added an assistant. The helpdesk added summarization. The search box quietly became semantic. The analytics platform now answers questions in natural language. Every one of those features means an LLM is being called with your data. Most of them arrived in a release note nobody in security read. Nothing was smuggled in. Nothing was unsanctioned. Enshittifiers groom us for scammers ( permalink ) We live in a scam economy: there's a presidential memecoin, a public health system run by a supplement peddler (who sold his trademark for "MAHA" to a pal before taking the job), and Spacex got to debut into the NASDAQ 100 and turn your retirement savings into exit liquidity for Musk's Emirati and tech oligarch cronies: https://prospect.org/2026/06/10/elon-musk-spacex-ipo-retirement-savings-index-funds-stock-market/#:~:text=The%20upcoming%20SpaceX,rake%20in%20millions. Then there's AI: voice cloning, deepfakes, and image-genned documents (including convincing IDs) have ushered in a golden age of account takeovers, identity theft and good, old-fashioned impersonation: https://www.404media.co/the-confessions-of-an-ai-fraud-kingpin-onlyfake-owner-nazarenko/ AI summarization is a priceless gift to fraudsters, who can comb through otherwise intractable mountains of breach data to customize precision-targeted spear-phishing campaigns for millions of potential victims at once. These summarization tools have a lot to summarize, thanks to a string of catastrophic breaches that saw (for example) the escape of the credit histories of nearly every person in America: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2017_Equifax_data_breach The companies involved in those breaches were not meaningfully punished. Quite the contrary, they were allowed to buy up and merge more of their competitors, combining these new divisions' creaking servers with their own spit-and-baling-wire frankensystems, even as they fired the people who had built and maintained those systems (in the name of "efficiency"). The commercial surveillance sector has repeatedly proven itself to be more interested in profits than security or accuracy, and yet we continue to entrust them with crucial public functions, including purging electoral rolls: https://mississippitoday.org/2026/11/10/u-s-senate-election-mississippi-andrew-goodman/ For margin-obsessed corporate leadership, IT cuts represent a unique hazard. When a manager fires the person who maintains the assembly line, the shop-floor quickly seizes up. But managers who fire IT staff inherit software that keeps chugging along long after the people who built it are gone…until it stops, and the company no longer knows how to restart it. This is one of the unique challenges of unionizing tech workers: when the tech workers go on strike, the scab software they wrote crosses the picket line on them: https://pluralistic.net/2026/11/07/aeiou-but-sometimes-why/#unrecognizable-playbook Tech debt has a long maturity: you can incur a lot of tech debt before the margin call comes and you find yourself in technological bankruptcy. Corporate management has spent decades playing IT Jenga, removing every available block, leaving behind a skeletal skyline of teetering towers that now routinely collapse: https://www.404media.co/breaking-everything/ The entire IT system is grossly overleveraged and technological bankruptcies are everywhere. This is very bad, because the USA hasn't had a new consumer privacy law since 1988 (when Congress banned disclosure of your VHS rental history), which means that these eggshell-thin servers are jammed with the most sensitive data imaginable about everyone, everywhere: https://pluralistic.net/2026/11/02/agony-verification/#great-turnbulls-ghost Far from breaking this cycle of overaccumulation and breach of sensitive data, the AI sector is accelerating it, claiming that a single person's "consent" to use pervert glasses, always-on mics, or other surveillance equipment can stand in for the consent of everyone they meet, see, or converse with: https://www.eff.org/deeplinks/2026/11/tech-companies-are-trying-shift-entire-concept-privacy-again This is the new normal: everything is broken, everything is breached. It's completely normal to wake up and read panicked headlines advising companies to shut off their servers until the latest showstopper bug can be patched. Half the email you get is from companies announcing new security protocols in the wake of a fresh data breach (the other half is from companies announcing changes to their terms of service to allow them to collect even more of your data, and to ban you from suing them when that data leaks): https://pluralistic.net/2026/10/26/abandon-hope/#all-ye-who-enter-here So it's also normal to get phone calls, emails and texts from your bank, employer, insurer and broker asking you to verify a transaction or requiring you to sign up for a new two-factor authentication system. What's more, it's normal for these entities to insist that you immediately install a new app or go through a new authentication process that is totally unlike any of the other ones you're already using. It's normal to log in to a service you use every day and be confronted with an entirely different login flow – a CAPTCHA unlike any you've ever seen, a requirement to visit a third-party site to complete an authentication step (which may involve taking selfies and transmitting copies of sensitive ID documents using an app from a company you've never heard of), an embedded widget that only works if you disable your browser's advanced privacy settings that prevent cross-site scripting and other horrors. We're told to hang up on anyone who calls us from our bank or credit-card issuer and to call them back using the number on the back of our cards. But when we call our banks, we get shunted to AI chatbots that "hallucinate" nonsensical advice for accessing our accounts. If we try to reach a human, we're stuck in lengthy hold queues whose soundtrack is a looping announcement scolding us for not using a faulty chatbot or the company's broken website to solve our problems. When a human does come on the line, they often seem to be improvising a new security protocol that was created five minutes before to deal with the latest state of exception. This is the security storm: a world of zero visibility, shifting gale-force winds, and blockages that impede your usual route and force you down unfamiliar paths every time you venture forth. It is the perfect environment for fraudsters. It's not just that fraudsters can impersonate anyone with AI voice-cloning or generate undetectable document forgeries: it's also the fact that your bank, HR department, insurer, credit card company and government have groomed you to expect a chaotic process that requires you to do something different every time you try to access a service. They've groomed you to turn off your browser's advanced protections. They've groomed you to ignore your carefully created, carefully saved random passwords in favor of clicking on links that get texted or emailed to you by third-party services you've never heard of. They've groomed you to expect cold-calls from outsource fraud prevention companies that don't know how to pronounce your bank's name. This isn't new. As far back as 2009, the cryptographer Ben Laurie was railing against "Verified by Visa," which required you to enter sensitive data into a page hosted on a domain that was separate from both your bank and the merchant you were paying, which Laurie called "Phished by Visa": https://web.archive.org/web/20090331094020/http://www.links.org/?p=591 No one listened to Laurie. Instead, the banks got worse . I've been a customer of HSBC subsidiary Firstdirect for nearly 20 years, and in that time, I've been told to make note of a "customer ID number," a "telephone passcode", eight password recovery answers, a "web username", a web password, a "digital secure key password", a "digital secure key PIN", and a regular PIN. Despite all this, I haven't been able to access my bank account for two months, ever since they "upgraded" their system to block app log-ins on mobile devices running the open, secure Android fork Graphene (Firstdirect doesn't use a standard two-factor authenticator; you have to use its app to generate a one-time PIN in addition to all those other authentication details every time you log in, even via a browser). When I spoke to Firstdirect about why they'd blocked Graphene, they told me that they "considered open source to be insecure." Talk about grooming for fraudsters: telling your customers that they should only trust systems that can't be independently inspected and validated is grossly irresponsible. (Don't worry, we're going to use the UK's excellent open banking system to switch back to the Co-Op Bank, which we left after it was mismanaged to the brink of bankruptcy and flogged to private equity; it's since been restructured as a co-op again:) https://www.banktrack.org/success/the_cooperative_bank_bought_back_into_mutual_ownership The perfect mark is someone who thinks they can't get scammed. The more technologically savvy and security conscious you are, the more you've encountered the incoherence of the official system and the less surprised you'll be when you're told to do something obviously insecure in order to complete a transaction: Boy, that stupid, dangerous requirement is even stupider and more dangerous than all the other stupid, dangerous things I've been forced to do this year. That's the story of Uri Bram, a technological sophisticate who edits Atoms vs Bits and nearly got scammed trying to buy an Amtrak ticket: https://www.atvbt.com/expected-incompetence-enables-fraud/ Bram tried to buy his Amtrak ticket on the web but found himself on a nonfunctional site that put him through a bizarre stopgap process that required him to enter his email address, click a link, log in to his Paypal account… Each step was more out-of-place than the last, but all of them had the eerie ring of plausibility, given the dysfunction of Bram's other interactions with giant, creaking companies like Amtrak. As Bram puts it: "Expected incompetence enables fraud." The corollary is that technological excellence makes fraud easier to spot and harder to pull off. Most of our anti-fraud measures demand that you be more vigilant and more discerning. We'd be much better off if we insisted that our official institutions invest in coherent, orderly practices that are thoughtfully designed, well maintained, and staffed by easily reached experts who can guide us through our problems. It's much harder to impersonate a system where you can get through to a thoroughly trained, in-house customer service rep in a few minutes than it is to impersonate a system that's typically worse than the fraudster's vibe-coded scam website, whose "customer service" has been replaced by broken chatbots. The ongoing collapse of all of our technology has created a permanent state of exception in which fraudsters' demands are no weirder than the ad-libbing our own essential institutions engage in every time we deal with them. The answer can't be to demand superhuman fraud-detection skills from the public: rather, we must demand excellence from our institutions: These summarization tools have a lot to summarize, thanks to a string of catastrophic breaches that saw (for example) the escape of the credit histories of nearly every person in America:

https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2017_Equifax_data_breach

The companies involved in those breaches were not meaningfully punished. Quite the contrary, they were allowed to buy up and merge more of their competitors, combining these new divisions' creaking servers with their own spit-and-baling-wire frankensystems, even as they fired the people who had built and maintained those systems (in the name of "efficiency").

The commercial surveillance sector has repeatedly proven itself to be more interested in profits than security or accuracy, and yet we continue to entrust them with crucial public functions, including purging electoral rolls:

https://mississippitoday.org/2026/11/10/u-s-senate-election-mississippi-andrew-goodman/

For margin-obsessed corporate leadership, IT cuts represent a unique hazard. When a manager fires the person who maintains the assembly line, the shop-floor quickly seizes up. But managers who fire IT staff inherit software that keeps chugging along long after the people who built it are gone…until it stops, and the company no longer knows how to restart it. This is one of the unique challenges of unionizing tech workers: when the tech workers go on strike, the scab software they wrote crosses the picket line on them:

https://pluralistic.net/2026/11/07/aeiou-but-sometimes-why/#unrecognizable-playbook

Tech debt has a long maturity: you can incur a lot of tech debt before the margin call comes and you find yourself in technological bankruptcy. Corporate management has spent decades playing IT Jenga, removing every available block, leaving behind a skeletal skyline of teetering towers that now routinely collapse:

https://www.404media.co/breaking-everything/

The entire IT system is grossly overleveraged and technological bankruptcies are everywhere. This is very bad, because the USA hasn't had a new consumer privacy law since 1988 (when Congress banned disclosure of your VHS rental history), which means that these eggshell-thin servers are jammed with the most sensitive data imaginable about everyone, everywhere:

https://pluralistic.net/2026/11/02/agony-verification/#great-turnbulls-ghost

Far from breaking this cycle of overaccumulation and breach of sensitive data, the AI sector is accelerating it, claiming that a single person's "consent" to use pervert glasses, always-on mics, or other surveillance equipment can stand in for the consent of everyone they meet, see, or converse with:

https://www.eff.org/deeplinks/2026/11/tech-companies-are-trying-shift-entire-concept-privacy-again

This is the new normal: everything is broken, everything is breached. It's completely normal to wake up and read panicked headlines advising companies to shut off their servers until the latest showstopper bug can be patched. Half the email you get is from companies announcing new security protocols in the wake of a fresh data breach (the other half is from companies announcing changes to their terms of service to allow them to collect even more of your data, and to ban you from suing them when that data leaks):

https://pluralistic.net/2026/10/26/abandon-hope/#all-ye-who-enter-here

So it's also normal to get phone calls, emails and texts from your bank, employer, insurer and broker asking you to verify a transaction or requiring you to sign up for a new two-factor authentication system. What's more, it's normal for these entities to insist that you immediately install a new app or go through a new authentication process that is totally unlike any of the other ones you're already using.

It's normal to log in to a service you use every day and be confronted with an entirely different login flow – a CAPTCHA unlike any you've ever seen, a requirement to visit a third-party site to complete an authentication step (which may involve taking selfies and transmitting copies of sensitive ID documents using an app from a company you've never heard of), an embedded widget that only works if you disable your browser's advanced privacy settings that prevent cross-site scripting and other horrors.

We're told to hang up on anyone who calls us from our bank or credit-card issuer and to call them back using the number on the back of our cards. But when we call our banks, we get shunted to AI chatbots that "hallucinate" nonsensical advice for accessing our accounts. If we try to reach a human, we're stuck in lengthy hold queues whose soundtrack is a looping announcement scolding us for not using a faulty chatbot or the company's broken website to solve our problems. When a human does come on the line, they often seem to be improvising a new security protocol that was created five minutes before to deal with the latest state of exception.

This is the security storm: a world of zero visibility, shifting gale-force winds, and blockages that impede your usual route and force you down unfamiliar paths every time you venture forth.

It is the perfect environment for fraudsters.

It's not just that fraudsters can impersonate anyone with AI voice-cloning or generate undetectable document forgeries: it's also the fact that your bank, HR department, insurer, credit card company and government have groomed you to expect a chaotic process that requires you to do something different every time you try to access a service.

They've groomed you to turn off your browser's advanced protections. They've groomed you to ignore your carefully created, carefully saved random passwords in favor of clicking on links that get texted or emailed to you by third-party services you've never heard of. They've groomed you to expect cold-calls from outsource fraud prevention companies that don't know how to pronounce your bank's name.

This isn't new. As far back as 2009, the cryptographer Ben Laurie was railing against "Verified by Visa," which required you to enter sensitive data into a page hosted on a domain that was separate from both your bank and the merchant you were paying, which Laurie called "Phished by Visa":

https://web.archive.org/web/20090331094020/http://www.links.org/?p=591

No one listened to Laurie. Instead, the banks got worse. I've been a customer of HSBC subsidiary Firstdirect for nearly 20 years, and in that time, I've been told to make note of a "customer ID number," a "telephone passcode", eight password recovery answers, a "web username", a web password, a "digital secure key password", a "digital secure key PIN", and a regular PIN.

Despite all this, I haven't been able to access my bank account for two months, ever since they "upgraded" their system to block app log-ins on mobile devices running the open, secure Android fork Graphene (Firstdirect doesn't use a standard two-factor authenticator; you have to use its app to generate a one-time PIN in addition to all those other authentication details every time you log in, even via a browser).

When I spoke to Firstdirect about why they'd blocked Graphene, they told me that they "considered open source to be insecure." Talk about grooming for fraudsters: telling your customers that they should only trust systems that can't be independently inspected and validated is grossly irresponsible.

(Don't worry, we're going to use the UK's excellent open banking system to switch back to the Co-Op Bank, which we left after it was mismanaged to the brink of bankruptcy and flogged to private equity; it's since been restructured as a co-op again:)

https://www.banktrack.org/success/the_cooperative_bank_bought_back_into_mutual_ownership

The perfect mark is someone who thinks they can't get scammed. The more technologically savvy and security conscious you are, the more you've encountered the incoherence of the official system and the less surprised you'll be when you're told to do something obviously insecure in order to complete a transaction: Boy, that stupid, dangerous requirement is even stupider and more dangerous than all the other stupid, dangerous things I've been forced to do this year.

That's the story of Uri Bram, a technological sophisticate who edits Atoms vs Bits and nearly got scammed trying to buy an Amtrak ticket:

https://www.atvbt.com/expected-incompetence-enables-fraud/

Bram tried to buy his Amtrak ticket on the web but found himself on a nonfunctional site that put him through a bizarre stopgap process that required him to enter his email address, click a link, log in to his Paypal account… Each step was more out-of-place than the last, but all of them had the eerie ring of plausibility, given the dysfunction of Bram's other interactions with giant, creaking companies like Amtrak. As Bram puts it: "Expected incompetence enables fraud."

The corollary is that technological excellence makes fraud easier to spot and harder to pull off. Most of our anti-fraud measures demand that you be more vigilant and more discerning. We'd be much better off if we insisted that our official institutions invest in coherent, orderly practices that are thoughtfully designed, well maintained, and staffed by easily reached experts who can guide us through our problems. It's much harder to impersonate a system where you can get through to a thoroughly trained, in-house customer service rep in a few minutes than it is to impersonate a system that's typically worse than the fraudster's vibe-coded scam website, whose "customer service" has been replaced by broken chatbots.

The ongoing collapse of all of our technology has created a permanent state of exception in which fraudsters' demands are no weirder than the ad-libbing our own essential institutions engage in every time we deal with them. The answer can't be to demand superhuman fraud-detection skills from the public: rather, we must demand excellence from our institutions:

https://www.nyc.gov/mayors-office/news/2026/07/mayor-mamdani-launches–public-interest-technology–pit–crew–t

items.title: Addressing Java4Shell CVE-2026-114938: upgrade guidance and Azure WAF mitigations
items.summary: Introduction On November 17, 2026, CVE-2026-114938 , also known as Java4Shell , a critical remote code execution (RCE) vulnerability affecting OpenJDK, was publicly disclosed. Under specific conditions, specially crafted Base64 input can trigger memory corruption in affected Java runtimes, potentially allowing unauthenticated attackers to execute arbitrary code. We strongly recommend that customers update the Java runtime used by their own applications to a patched version or update third-party Java-based applications to a version that includes the security fix, as applicable. Updating the affected Java runtime is the primary way to fully remediate this vulnerability. For further details, refer to Oracle's official security advisory . Azure Web Application Firewall (WAF) has developed mitigations designed to detect and block known HTTP-based exploitation patterns associated with this vulnerability, providing an additional layer of protection while customers apply the necessary security updates. These mitigations are intended to complement patching, not replace it. About CVE-2026-114938 CVE-2026-114938 is a memory-corruption vulnerability in OpenJDK's hardware-accelerated Base64 decoder. When an affected Java application processes specially crafted Base64 input, the vulnerability can cause heap memory corruption, potentially leading to application crashes, sensitive information disclosure, or remote code execution. The vulnerability primarily affects unpatched OpenJDK-based Java runtimes version 17.0.6 and later, including Java 21, 25, and 27, running on x86-64 processors supporting the AVX-512 VBMI instruction set. Exploitation requires attacker-controlled input to reach the vulnerable Base64 decoding functionality. ARM64 systems and x86-64 processors without AVX-512 VBMI support are not known to be affected. Recommended action: Update affected Java runtimes and third-party Java-based applications to versions containing the security fix as soon as possible. Treat Azure WAF mitigations as supplementary protection, not as a substitute for patching. Azure WAF protection If you are unable to upgrade your Java application to a patched version immediately, apply the following mitigations in the interim. Azure Front Door Since the vulnerability is exploited through malformed Base64 input, apply the following WAF custom rules based on where your application accepts Base64-encoded values in incoming HTTP requests: Request headers: Apply the request headers rule and specify the relevant header names (e.g., Cookie ). Request body: Apply the request body rule and specify the relevant HTTP POST argument name. Query string: Apply the query string rule. Authorization header: Apply the authorization header rule. If your application accepts Base64-encoded input in multiple parts of an HTTP request, apply all applicable rules to ensure comprehensive coverage. { "customRules": { "rules": [ { "name": "transforms": [ "Trim" ] } ] }, { "name": "Java4ShellB64Query", "priority": 12, "ruleType": "MatchRule", "action": "Block", "enabledState": "Enabled", "matchConditions": [ { "matchVariable":   • Request body: Apply the request body rule and specify the relevant HTTP POST argument name. 
  • Query string: Apply the query string rule. 
  • Authorization header: Apply the authorization header rule. 

If your application accepts Base64-encoded input in multiple parts of an HTTP request, apply all applicable rules to ensure comprehensive coverage.

items.title: Data Pipelines: Unlocking the Full Potential of Detection Engineering
items.summary: Practical Use Cases for Data Pipelines in Detection Engineering Back in 2023, I wrote about why you need Data Engineering Pipelines before an enterprise SIEM . It opened with the classic “Data is the new oil” line and a simple question: why are so many detection engineers still dealing with log data in its crude form? Crude logs mean the dirty job of cleaning, parsing and enriching data lands on the desk of SIEM and content engineers. Over and over again, for every new detection use case. Three years later, most of the pipeline discussions out there still revolve around one thing: cost. Licensing, storage, GB/day. You know the drill. Money is always a valid driver. However, shortening detection delivery time and improving the overall quality of detection output are directly tied to costs too. This is a follow-up with a focus on practical use cases where refined data, delivered by a pipeline, speeds up the implementation of Threat Detection use cases. The pipeline is not where the alerting decision is made. It’s where the dirty job gets done, so detection engineers can focus on the detection logic and advanced use cases (alert frameworks, detection models, etc). TLDR: in case you landed here for the detection takeaways only, skip to the “Category 1 — Advanced Parsing” section below! From 2023 to 2026: what has changed? In the original article, the main point was about the (log) data lifecycle: ingestion, transformation and consumption. Traditional SIEM architectures handled that in a very rudimentary fashion. Log shippers sending data to a SIEM index as the final destination. That’s it. Very little work was done to polish the data before it hit the SIEM storage layer, shifting the data quality problem to SIEM and content engineers. After all, the cruder the log, the longer the time-to-value. Decoupling ingestion, filtering and enrichment from the SIEM was supposed to leave the platform with a clear primary role: Security Analytics. So, are we there yet? Partially. Data pipelines became a product category on their own, and the SIEM market is clearly adapting to them. This article is sponsored by Axoflow , full disclosure at the end of the article. The most popular argument for them today is breaking log lock-in. With a routing and transformation layer in front of the SIEM, switching SIEMs no longer means re-plumbing thousands of servers and hundreds of log source types from scratch. A common setup I see working in the field: detection and triage stay in the SIEM, while the pipeline sits in front of it, forking archival data to cheaper storage. Still, notice how most of the market discussion is about where data goes and how much it costs. Not about accelerating detection use case delivery by providing refined, enriched data instead of raw data. That’s the gap I want to explore here. The obvious Use Cases Before getting into threat detection, let’s get the well-known use cases out of the way. Those are the ones you will find in any vendor deck, so I’m not going to spend much time on them. Pipeline unification: replacing the accumulated sprawl of SIEM agents, cloud forwarders, endpoint collectors and scripts with one centrally managed pipeline. Declarative config, central routing policies, and one view of health, drops and volume. Log normalization: consistent field names, formats and values across sources, so detection queries stop compensating for messy data (remember the FourToSixMapping blind spot?). Routing & reduction: sending the right data to the right destination. Security-relevant events go to the SIEM, the bulky compliance stuff goes to cheaper storage, and debug noise goes nowhere. Now, to the fun part. Data Pipeline Use Cases for Detection Engineers Each stage below is one category of use cases that can be outsourced from the Analytics stage to the Data Pipeline one. By the time an event reaches the SIEM, it’s refined: normalized, parsed, enriched and labeled. The detection logic still lives in the SIEM, it just has much less dirty work to do. Category 1 — Advanced Parsing Every SIEM problem starts with a poorly designed use case. And many poorly designed use cases start with poorly prepared data. If the data is not ready for questioning, the detection engineer ends up preparing it at search time. Every single query. Every single time. URLs A URL is not a string. It’s a bundle of attributes. Scheme, subdomain, registered domain, top-level domain, path, file extension, query parameters. Each one is a detection opportunity on its own. When the URL lands in the SIEM as one long field, every detection that needs one of those parts must extract it again, usually with a regex that someone wrote years ago and nobody dares to touch. Parsing it upstream enables things like: Prevalence by registered domain instead of by full hostname only (attackers love disposable subdomains). Flagging encoded or unusually long query parameters. Spotting executable or script file extensions being downloaded, regardless of where they sit in the path. Base64 Flag / PowerShell Decoding If you’ve read my article on malicious encoded PowerShell , you know spotting the encoded command is just the beginning. The actual payload only reveals itself once it’s decoded. So why not decoding it before it hits the SIEM? Actually, that idea expands beyond PS command lines to any base64-encoded string. Imagine if you are able to write detections on base64-flagged commands only? The decoded payload can be stored right next to the original command line. From there: Analysts can search it like any other field during triage and hunting. Pattern-based indicators (more on that later) match against the actual content, not against a Base64 blob. Nobody needs to decode the same command again at search time. Pro Tip: never replace the original value, enrich it. Keep the raw command line intact, unless it's really rubbish data (static log descriptions, debugging info, etc). Besides forensics needs, decoding logic can fail, and when it does, you want the original to fall back to. Category 2 — External IP Enrichment In What makes up a solid SIEM query? , enrichment is one of the core query components. Back then, the advice was to perform lookups only after aggregation, to avoid looking up every single event. That’s still good advice. But what if the event arrives already enriched? External IP addresses are the perfect candidate here. Practically every detection involving remote access, authentication or C2 traffic depends on knowing a bit more about the other side of the connection. ASN The Autonomous System Number (ASN) tells you who owns the network an IP address belongs to: a residential ISP, a cloud provider, a hosting company or a VPN service. That’s a far more stable attribute than the IP address itself. Attackers rotate IPs all the time, but they often stick to the same hosting providers. And it opens the door to some great use cases: Once an incident is identified, the ASN is already available. Analysts, hunters, and responders can quickly use the SIEM to identify other IP addresses in the logs that belong to the same ASN. Detection and hunting queries can use the ASN as an anchor for filtering or aggregation, potentially providing better visibility and more effective ways to identify related activity. Geolocation In my SPL2 if command article , I showed how even vendor-enriched sources such as Entra ID sign-in logs don’t always come with a location value. Filling that gap at search time means paying for a lookup on every IP, every time the query runs. Do it at ingestion time, and it’s paid once. Axoflow : How to enrich an IP address and decode URL in the pipeline Another often-overlooked aspect is temporal accuracy : IP allocations and geolocation mappings can change over time, meaning search-time enrichment may apply today’s attributes to historical events rather than reflecting the context at the time they occurred. (Un)Known IP addresses This is one of the most valuable. Every organization owns or trusts a set of public network ranges: corporate egress IPs, VPN concentrators, cloud tenants, partner networks, scanners. Those usually live in a spreadsheet somewhere, or worse, hard-coded as exceptions across dozens of detection rules. What if that list (CIDR values in a JSON or CSV file) is maintained in one place and applied upstream? Every event containing a public IP address then carries a simple label: known or unknown. Or even better, the name of the known range. Now any detection can leverage that golden data point without a single hard-coded exception. Update the list once, and every rule downstream follows. This enrichment provides immediate context to distinguish traffic involving known organizational or trusted networks from communication with unknown IP ranges. Category 3 — Entity Prevalence By now you know I love baselines. If not, check Baselines 101 and Data Prevalence: The Game Changer . Quick recap: prevalence tells you how often something happens; a baseline uses those frequencies to define what’s normal. Today, most teams compute that at the SIEM layer through scheduled searches that maintain lookup tables or summary indexes. It works, but it’s yet another job to design, schedule and keep healthy. What if the pipeline does the remembering? First Time Seen The simplest form of prevalence is a binary one: have we seen this before? There are two ideas here: Enrich the log's entities with prevalence info (more expensive) Update Entity Prevalence tables or lookups (preferable) The idea is to have a pipeline that flags once it sees a relevant entity (file hash, domain, IP) for the first time (idea 1) or update a data store where an entity prevalence can be looked up from the SIEM (idea 2). That enables anomaly indicators to be used within your detection logic or models. I explore the concept in more details in the following article: Data Prevalence: The Game Changer in Threat Detection & IR Pro Tip: Rare does not mean alert-able. ⚠️ Not all rare or anomalous events are alert-able! ⚠️ A first-time-seen label is context, not a verdict. Its value shows up when combined with other signals, as part of a detection model, or during triage when the analyst asks “was this seen before?” That’s one of the most common questions during triage, by the way. Prevalence: The catch Keeping state is not free. A few things to consider before getting excited: Cold start: on day one, everything is new. The state needs a learning period before the labels mean anything. Time window: how long does an entity stay “known”? That’s the Circadian Window discussion again, now applied to the pipeline. Distributed state: pipelines scale horizontally. If two workers process events from the same entity, they need to share the same memory. Cardinality: remembering every command line ever seen is a bad idea. Pick entities with reasonable cardinality. Notice something? A pipeline that remembers entities over time is starting to do something a SIEM is supposed to do. Hold that thought, we’ll come back to it. Category 4 — Alert Signaling This is where things get really interesting from a detection engineering standpoint. If the pipeline can parse, enrich and remember, it can also flag. Not a full-blown security alert, but an alert signal . IOC matching Automated IOC matching is a must-have, as I suggest a framework here . Nobody should be manually scanning logs for indicators from the latest CTI report. Matching at the pipeline means every event is checked as it flows, no scheduled searches scanning the same data over and over again. But here’s the limitation: a pipeline typically sees what’s flowing now. When a new IOC arrives today, the events from last month have already passed through. So stream matching doesn’t replace IOC retro-hunting. It complements it. Fresh events get matched in the stream; historical data gets swept at the SIEM or the data lake. Detection Model Indicators Labeling If you follow this blog, you know I keep saying atomic alerts sent straight to the SOC queue are a recipe for alert fatigue (or fat AI bills). The strongest signal shows up only after collecting and scoring multiple indicators, aggregating them by an alert entity (usually the target or the origin of the attack). Now, those indicators need to come from somewhere. Many of them are simple, pattern-based, atomic observations. Picking on suspicious PowerShell one-liners, for example, the presence of any of the following already raises a red flag: A double encoded payload. A download cradle pattern. A common obfuscation pattern. Each of those is a perfect candidate for labeling at the pipeline. The event gets tagged with the indicators it matches, and the detection model at the SIEM does what it’s good at: aggregating, scoring and deciding whether to alert or not. That’s precisely the idea behind the indicators in PowerShell.Exposed : an indicator is not a detection on its own, it’s input for one. The benefits: Write once, consume many: the same label feeds multiple detection models, hunting queries and dashboards. Searchable signals: analysts and hunters can pivot on labels instead of rewriting regexes. Lighter detections: the heavy pattern matching is done before the data is stored, not every time a detection runs. Pro Tip: treat pipeline labeling logic as detection content. Version it, peer-review it and test it, just like any other Detection-as-Code artifact. The Controversial Part: Who Is Eating Whom? Go back and look at Categories 3 and 4. Keeping state about entities over time, matching IOCs, labeling events with detection indicators. Is that still a pipeline? Or is it a SIEM in disguise? Are pipelines becoming SIEMs? The pipeline products are clearly moving up the stack. Search, storage, enrichment, even some sort of detection. From where they sit, it makes sense: they already see all the data. We’ve seen this movie before. Many products that promised to replace the SIEM ended up rebuilding SIEM features once they hit production. So that’s a move worth watching more closely over the coming years. Or are SIEMs absorbing pipelines? On the other side, SIEM vendors are adding native pipeline capabilities: filtering, routing, transformation and enrichment at ingestion time, sometimes even before the data leaves the customer’s network. And it’s not only the incumbents. New SIEM products are being designed with the pipeline built in from day one, not as an add-on. In the long run, pipeline features look like a checkbox in the SIEM feature list. A very important checkbox, but a checkbox nonetheless. But to be fair, there’s a strong argument for keeping the pipeline independent: leverage. The main reason pipelines broke log lock-in is that they sit outside the SIEM. If your SIEM vendor owns your pipeline too, the lock-in is back, just one layer earlier. So it’s a trade-off, as always. Convenience and tighter integration versus independence and negotiation power. Which side are you on? Closing Thoughts In 2023, the message was: you need data pipelines before an enterprise SIEM. In 2026, I’d add: stop treating them as plumbing only. A pipeline is where the dirty job gets outsourced. Data reaches the SIEM normalized, parsed, enriched and labeled, refined instead of crude, and detection engineers spend their time on detection logic, not on data preparation. Cost reduction is a great way to get the budget approved. Faster delivery of detection use cases is where the real return is. And whether the pipeline ends up inside the SIEM or the other way around, one thing doesn’t change: the less time spent cleaning crude data, the more time spent actually detecting threats. Did I miss any use case? Drop in the comments or reach out! About this article This article is sponsored by A xoflow , an autonomous security data layer, collecting, processing, routing, storing, and managing data, with in-stream detection in early access. Axoflow supported its production but had no editorial control over its content. All opinions, use cases and recommendations are my own, based on my experience as an independent Detection Engineering & Security Analytics SME. Data Pipelines: Unlocking the Full Potential of Detection Engineering was originally published in Detect FYI on Medium, where people are continuing the conversation by highlighting and responding to this story.

Keeping state is not free. A few things to consider before getting excited:

  • Cold start: on day one, everything is new. The state needs a learning period before the labels mean anything.
  • Time window: how long does an entity stay “known”? That’s the Circadian Window discussion again, now applied to the pipeline.
  • Distributed state: pipelines scale horizontally. If two workers process events from the same entity, they need to share the same memory.
  • Cardinality: remembering every command line ever seen is a bad idea. Pick entities with reasonable cardinality.

Notice something? A pipeline that remembers entities over time is starting to do something a SIEM is supposed to do. Hold that thought, we’ll come back to it.

Category 4 — Alert Signaling

This is where things get really interesting from a detection engineering standpoint.

If the pipeline can parse, enrich and remember, it can also flag. Not a full-blown security alert, but an alert signal.

IOC matching

Automated IOC matching is a must-have, as I suggest a framework here. Nobody should be manually scanning logs for indicators from the latest CTI report.

Matching at the pipeline means every event is checked as it flows, no scheduled searches scanning the same data over and over again.

But here’s the limitation: a pipeline typically sees what’s flowing now. When a new IOC arrives today, the events from last month have already passed through.

So stream matching doesn’t replace IOC retro-hunting. It complements it. Fresh events get matched in the stream; historical data gets swept at the SIEM or the data lake.

Detection Model Indicators Labeling

If you follow this blog, you know I keep saying atomic alerts sent straight to the SOC queue are a recipe for alert fatigue (or fat AI bills).

The strongest signal shows up only after collecting and scoring multiple indicators, aggregating them by an alert entity (usually the target or the origin of the attack).

Now, those indicators need to come from somewhere.

Many of them are simple, pattern-based, atomic observations. Picking on suspicious PowerShell one-liners, for example, the presence of any of the following already raises a red flag:

  • A double encoded payload.
  • A download cradle pattern.
  • A common obfuscation pattern.
Each of those is a perfect candidate for labeling at the pipeline.

The event gets tagged with the indicators it matches, and the detection model at the SIEM does what it’s good at: aggregating, scoring and deciding whether to alert or not.

That’s precisely the idea behind the indicators in PowerShell.Exposed: an indicator is not a detection on its own, it’s input for one.

The benefits:

  • Write once, consume many: the same label feeds multiple detection models, hunting queries and dashboards.
  • Searchable signals: analysts and hunters can pivot on labels instead of rewriting regexes.
  • Lighter detections: the heavy pattern matching is done before the data is stored, not every time a detection runs.

Pro Tip: treat pipeline labeling logic as detection content. Version it, peer-review it and test it, just like any other Detection-as-Code artifact.

The Controversial Part: Who Is Eating Whom?

Go back and look at Categories 3 and 4. Keeping state about entities over time, matching IOCs, labeling events with detection indicators.

Is that still a pipeline? Or is it a SIEM in disguise?

Are pipelines becoming SIEMs?

The pipeline products are clearly moving up the stack. Search, storage, enrichment, even some sort of detection. From where they sit, it makes sense: they already see all the data.

We’ve seen this movie before. Many products that promised to replace the SIEM ended up rebuilding SIEM features once they hit production.

So that’s a move worth watching more closely over the coming years.

Or are SIEMs absorbing pipelines?

On the other side, SIEM vendors are adding native pipeline capabilities: filtering, routing, transformation and enrichment at ingestion time, sometimes even before the data leaves the customer’s network.

And it’s not only the incumbents. New SIEM products are being designed with the pipeline built in from day one, not as an add-on.

In the long run, pipeline features look like a checkbox in the SIEM feature list. A very important checkbox, but a checkbox nonetheless.

But to be fair, there’s a strong argument for keeping the pipeline independent: leverage.

The main reason pipelines broke log lock-in is that they sit outside the SIEM. If your SIEM vendor owns your pipeline too, the lock-in is back, just one layer earlier.

So it’s a trade-off, as always. Convenience and tighter integration versus independence and negotiation power.

Which side are you on?

Closing Thoughts

In 2023, the message was: you need data pipelines before an enterprise SIEM.

In 2026, I’d add: stop treating them as plumbing only.

A pipeline is where the dirty job gets outsourced. Data reaches the SIEM normalized, parsed, enriched and labeled, refined instead of crude, and detection engineers spend their time on detection logic, not on data preparation.

Cost reduction is a great way to get the budget approved. Faster delivery of detection use cases is where the real return is.

And whether the pipeline ends up inside the SIEM or the other way around, one thing doesn’t change: the less time spent cleaning crude data, the more time spent actually detecting threats.

Did I miss any use case? Drop in the comments or reach out!

items.title: Google Reveals How Russian Hackers Used One Cloud Breach to Compromise Another US Organization
items.summary: Russian state-sponsored hackers broke into a U.S. organization’s Google Workspace environment in late 2025, stole its staff directory and cloud files, and used information from the breach to target a second U.S. organization in 2026. Google and Mandiant said the hackers posed as an employee of the first victim, turning a familiar professional identity into a way to steal cloud credentials from the second. Neither organization was named. In its November 17 case study, Google identified the group as COLD RELIC, previously tracked as COLDRIVER and also known as Star Blizzard or Callisto. The U.S. Justice Department has tied Callisto to Russia’s Federal Security Service, or FSB. Google’s researchers said they saw evidence of fresh phishing activity as recently as November 2026. Google Cloud researchers previously identified the group’s LOSTKEYS document theft malware in a separate 2025 campaign. The new report does not identify a malware payload in either U.S. breach. Instead, it shows how stolen credentials, unauthorized authentication methods, and convincing impersonation were enough to steal cloud files and reach another organization. Google Reveals How Russian Hackers Used One Cloud Breach The first intrusion began with stolen credentials for a Google Workspace Super Admin account. The attackers sent repeated multi-factor authentication (MFA) prompts until the user approved one, a tactic known as MFA fatigue. They signed in through a residential proxy near the victim, making the connection look geographically routine. Once inside, they registered a device model the organization had not seen before. With administrator access, the group downloaded the organization’s entire cloud drive, both by retrieving files directly and by sharing them with an attacker-controlled email account. The hackers also exported the staff directory, started a tenant-wide Google Workspace Customer Takeout export, and deleted security alerts. Some attacker-enrolled passkeys remained usable after password and session resets because responders had not revoked the passkeys themselves. Once removed from the first organization’s systems, the hackers used accounts impersonating its employees to approach staff and professional contacts. Social engineering conversation (Source – Google Cloud) That tactic fits a pattern seen in earlier Star Blizzard campaigns , where the group opened with what looked like ordinary professional correspondence. In the second U.S. breach, the conversation began on an encrypted messaging app, not in the victim’s work inbox. Previously targeted WhatsApp The group had previously targeted WhatsApp with malicious QR codes , but Google did not name the messaging app in this case. Investigators found a stronger link between the two breaches: a phishing redirect submitted to VirusTotal in June 2026 contained a reference to the first organization, matching the identity the hackers used in the chat. The phishing links targeted Microsoft Entra ID, which the second organization used for single sign-on to Google Workspace. That setup lets staff use their Microsoft identity to access Google services. After stealing login information, the hackers added an MFA device and downloaded files available to the compromised user. Unlike the first breach, Google did not report an organization-wide drive theft in the second. Indicators of compromise (IoCs):- Indicator or activity What defenders should look for MFA fatigue Repeated failed sign-ins or MFA challenges followed by a successful sign-in from the same IP Unauthorized device or passkey Device Registered or Passkey enrolled events after unusual sign-in activity Backup code use Backup code as the login challenge type from an unexpected network Tenant-wide export CUSTOMER_TAKEOUT_CREATED in Workspace Admin logs Bulk downloads or external sharing Spikes in Drive Download events or files marked shared_externally OAuth mail access An Authorize event granting broad mail access to an unapproved client Alert tampering or audit queries Unexpected Batch Delete Operation Performed or Investigation Query events Staff directory export User List Download from an unfamiliar device Sensitive file searches Item search performed events involving .pst , .bak , or credential-related terms Residential network examples AS5650 and AS20115 ; Google cites them as examples for network controls, not dedicated attacker infrastructure Note: IP addresses and domains are intentionally Qdefanged (e.g., [.] ) to prevent accidental resolution or hyperlinking. items.title: Betrayed Expectations: Malware Delivery via Common Brands
items.summary: By: Jacob Malimban, Intelligence Team In the first half of 2026, Cofense Intelligence observed a 239% rise in phishing campaigns that weaponize brand names to deliver malware onto corporate devices as compared to the first half of 2025. Adobe, the Social Security Administration, Docusign, the IRS, and Zoom are among the most abused. The names are familiar by design: employees who expect a routine document from a recognized sender appear more likely to click, and the borrowed credibility of those brands helps the emails slip past automated security filters. There are two primary ways that brands can be spoofed to deliver malware and abused legitimate remote access tools (RATs). The first is the initial phishing email. The brand spoofed in the email is what sets the expectation for the context of the campaign. For example, threat actors have used lures such as a refund sent by the IRS (Figure 5) and a benefits-themed document sent by the Social Security Administration (Figure 3). When a victim expects a file but does not realize the sender is malicious, they are likely to click on a phishing link. The second way a brand can be abused is through the filename. To trick victims, malware may be named “Social_Security_Administration_v02.4_EN_US.msi” (Figure 3) or “setup_Zoom.msi” (Figure 6), depending on the brand used in the phishing email. These malware files are often hosted on cloud services like Google or Amazon , which can bypass the organization’s security controls. What makes this threat category particularly difficult to manage is that the tools being delivered are not traditional malware. ConnectWise RAT, Datto RMM, SimpleHelp, and similar products are the same software that many IT departments use for legitimate remote support. Threat actors favor them precisely because standard security systems are built to trust them. Key Points In the first half of this year, 18% of all malware delivery campaigns impersonated new brands not seen before. Adobe is the most abused brand when delivering malware in the first half of 2026. The malware downloaded usually has a filename matching the phishing email branding, like “Adobe software update.msi”. Threat actors often abuse legitimate cloud services like Google or Amazon to distribute malware and bypass security controls. 94% of campaigns delivering malware abuse legitimate remote access tools (RATs). Brand Campaign Volume Malware delivering campaigns increased 239% in the first half of 2026 compared to the first half of 2025. The top five brands account for around 24% of all malware delivery campaign volume in the first half of this year. Figure 1: The relative proportion of brands spoofed in the first half of 2026. In the first half of 2026, Cofense Intelligence identified brands like Adobe, Social Security Administration, Docusign, IRS, and Zoom being abused in malware delivery campaigns. Docusign and Adobe are part of normal organizational operations. These brands follow the trends first identified in 2021 . Social Security Administration-spoofing and IRS-spoofing after April mark the trend of government themed phishing outside of the IRS tax season . Zoom has typically been abused to host documents with links to credential phishing pages—and rarely links to malware pages. Adobe Spoofing Campaigns Delivering Malware Adobe-spoofing phishing campaigns rank #1 by volume in the first half of 2026. Adobe-spoofing phishing emails delivering malware experienced an 18-fold increase when compared to the first half of 2025. Adobe-spoofing campaigns typically deliver ConnectWise RAT (44%), Datto RMM (16%), and GoTo RAT (7%). These software are technically legitimate remote access tools (RATs) but can be abused by threat actors to gain unauthorized administrative access. Figure 2: Adobe-spoofing website claiming a software update is necessary ( ATR 415874 ). In credential phishing, Adobe has been used to host documents with links to malicious websites. Typically, PDFs with shortened links or QR codes obfuscate the credential phishing pages. In Adobe-spoofing campaigns delivering malware, the email usually claims a document is available to view. After clicking on the phishing link and attempting to download the document, a website opens. The malicious website typically claims that Adobe Reader is out of date, and an update is necessary to see the PDF. Installing the file will deliver a legitimate RAT controlled by the threat actor . In these Adobe software update phishing campaigns, threat actors like to abuse tools such as ConnectWise’s ScreenConnect (ConnectWise RAT) and Datto RMM to take over the victim machine. For example, Figure 2 shows one website that claims Adobe Reader is out of date and downloads malware. Indicators of compromise (IOCs) for Figure 2 are listed in Active Threat Report (ATR) 415874 . ATRs contain the context for each threat actor campaign, allowing current and similar campaigns to be blocked. Social Security Administration Spoofing Campaigns Delivering Malware Social Security Administration-spoofing is the second highest by campaign volume. Campaign volume in the first half of 2025 is roughly equivalent to volume in the first half of 2026. SSA-spoofing typically delivers ConnectWise RAT (55%), SimpleHelp (12%), and Faronics Deploy (9%). Figure 3: Social Security Administration-spoofing email that bypasses email security technology to deliver ConnectWise RAT ( ATR 417484 ). In the United States, the Social Security Administration (SSA) becomes an important consideration near retirement age (at least age 62). For eligible members of the workforce, this pension information can dictate the lifestyle one lives after employment ends. Previous campaign iterations in Q4 2024 prioritized urgency and consequences when phishing. Current SSA-spoofing emails usually claim to provide information rather than demand it. Figure 3 shows an SSA download statement phishing email, one of the scams the SSA Office of the Inspector General warns about. If the phishing link is clicked, an SSA-spoofing website typically opens, and a file download starts. The file appears similar to those in the Docusign and Adobe sections. Some files act like benefit letters or document notifications. Others require a download file to be run because “Adobe Reader is out of date”. As usual, running the file will install a threat actor-controlled legitimate RAT . The RATs most commonly installed are ConnectWise RAT and SimpleHelp. The SSA-impersonation campaign delivering ConnectWise RAT has been going on since at least 2024. Docusign Spoofing Campaigns Delivering Malware Docusign-spoofing emails increased about 250% when comparing the first half of 2026 to the first half of 2025. Docusign-spoofing campaigns typically deliver ConnectWise RAT (34%), GoTo RAT (11%), Itarian RAT (5%), or some combination of the three. Figure 4: Docusign-spoofing file is a SuperOps RMM instance abused by the threat actor ( ATR 415883 ). Docusign is typically used by threat actors to host documents with links to redirect to malicious websites, usually Microsoft-spoofing credential phishing pages. This is because using trusted websites help bypass email security technologies, and abusing legitimate business tools helps malicious content mimic benign content. Docusign-branded emails are also useful for getting recipients to download fake documents. Downloading the fake document will deliver malware instead of the expected file. Threat actors will typically use the Docusign style for the email, the malware download website, and the filename. As seen in Figure 4, a malicious file is named like a Docusign attachment. Threat actors like to deliver legitimate RATs that they control , like ConnectWise RAT and GoTo RAT. IRS Spoofing Campaigns Delivering Malware IRS-spoofing email volume experienced a 10-fold increase when comparing the first half of 2026 to the first half of 2025. IRS-spoofing campaigns typically deliver ConnectWise RAT (50%), Tiflux RAT (13%), Splashtop (13%) or some combination of the three. Figure 5: IRS-spoofing, tax refund-themed phishing campaign delivering ConnectWise RAT ( ATR 415954 ). In the first half of 2025, IRS-spoofing campaigns delivering malware were most prevalent before the USA tax filing date on April 15. Now in the first half of 2026, threat actors continue to use the IRS brand in phishing emails past the tax filing deadline but with many themed about late filing deadlines. Well-developed phishing lures used after April 15 include a refund that has been processed or a tax filing extension being made available. As threat actors use current topics like Elon Musk and DOGE offering an IRS tax refund , IRS-spoofing campaigns are expected to increase. As with the general rise in threat-actor abused legitimate RATs , IRS-spoofing campaigns deliver similar malware in most cases. ConnectWise RAT is once again the most popular RAT to be abused in IRS-spoofing campaigns. There is also a multi-stage campaign where Tiflux RAT is first installed, then Tiflux RAT installs Splashtop and an UltraVNC utility. In earlier group-delivered malware campaigns , the malware was primarily purpose-built for threat actors and entirely malicious. In the case of Tiflux RAT and Splashtop, both are developed by legitimate organizations for IT operations. Unfortunately, the instances of Tiflux RAT and Splashtop delivered in these campaigns are controlled by threat actors. Zoom Spoofing Campaigns Delivering Malware Zoom-spoofing emails delivering malware increased over 100% when comparing the first half of 2026 to the first half of 2025. Zoom-spoofing campaigns typically deliver ConnectWise RAT (29%), TrustConnect (14%), and Atera (7%). Figure 6: A fake Zoom website that downloads an abused RAT ( ATR 416603 ). Legitimate Zoom links can prompt users to download the Zoom app to access the meeting. Threat actors frequently spoof Zoom and hijack this expected behavior to trick users into downloading malware instead. Zoom-spoofing phishing emails match the format of legitimate Zoom meeting emails, but the links will redirect to a malware download page instead of the legitimate Zoom site. The most prominent malware delivered is ConnectWise RAT again. TrustConnect and Atera are similar RATs abused by threat actors and delivered in Zoom-spoofing campaigns. Figure 6 shows a malicious Atera instance being downloaded from a threat actor’s website. Problems Caused by Legitimate Remote Access Tool Abuse As legitimate RATs are developed for enterprise use, abuse of these tools by threat actors may hide in plain sight. ConnectWise RAT is currently the most abused legitimate RAT, instead of NetSupport Manager RAT . When used for their intended purpose, legitimate remote access tools can reduce costs and improve efficiency. With legitimate RATs, IT professionals can easily maintain and monitor various devices across the organization without needing physical access to it. This elevated privilege becomes problematic when threat actors gain access to it. Legitimate RATs are just as capable of purpose-built malware in the hands of a threat actor. With PowerShell commands, additional malware payloads can be installed after the initial RAT infection. Threat actors have used ConnectWise RAT to deliver ransomware before. Organizations can find it hard to identify and contain legitimate RATs used by threat actors. Threat actors may even use the same RATs the organization uses, making context, continuous monitoring, and mitigative controls especially important. If the organization successfully contains one type of RAT, threat actors can easily use a different legitimate RAT for infections. In each of the brands spoofed in this report, threat actors already abuse various legitimate RATs. Conclusions This report shows five prominent brands spoofed by threat actors. Some key insights include malicious content nearly indistinguishable from legitimate brands, and the increasing abuse of legitimate remote administrative tools. These tactics by the threat actors can make it harder for both users and security analysts to determine if something is legitimate or not. Especially noteworthy are IRS-spoofing and Social Security Administration-spoofing phishing emails. IRS-spoofing emails will likely continue to increase even outside of tax filing season. Social Security Administration-spoofing emails already are not limited by a specific season. Page Break Mitigations Establish and enforce a software allowlist for remote access tools. Any remote access tool not on that list, including ConnectWise, SimpleHelp, Atera, and GoTo RAT, should be blocked from installing on corporate devices. Organizations that do not have an allowlist should at minimum block the digital certificates associated with remote access tools they do not use. Update employee security awareness training to reflect current lure themes, specifically Adobe document requests, SSA benefit notices, IRS refund emails, and Zoom meeting invitations. Employees who have been trained on real, current threats are more likely to pause before clicking. Simulation exercises should use these exact scenarios, not outdated generic examples. Blocking remote access tools and updating training are essential, but threat actors will keep finding new brands, filenames, and legitimate tools to abuse. Organizations need a way to respond quickly when a campaign reaches the inbox or an endpoint. To learn how Cofense Remediation can help your security team identify and remove these threats faster, visit https://cofense.com/pdr-platform .

The malicious website typically claims that Adobe Reader is out of date, and an update is necessary to see the PDF. Installing the file will deliver a legitimate RAT controlled by the threat actor. In these Adobe software update phishing campaigns, threat actors like to abuse tools such as ConnectWise’s ScreenConnect (ConnectWise RAT) and Datto RMM to take over the victim machine. For example, Figure 2 shows one website that claims Adobe Reader is out of date and downloads malware. Indicators of compromise (IOCs) for Figure 2 are listed in Active Threat Report (ATR) 415874. ATRs contain the context for each threat actor campaign, allowing current and similar campaigns to be blocked.

Social Security Administration Spoofing Campaigns Delivering Malware
  • Social Security Administration-spoofing is the second highest by campaign volume.
    • Campaign volume in the first half of 2025 is roughly equivalent to volume in the first half of 2026.
  • SSA-spoofing typically delivers ConnectWise RAT (55%), SimpleHelp (12%), and Faronics Deploy (9%).

Figure 3: Social Security Administration-spoofing email that bypasses email security technology to deliver ConnectWise RAT (ATR 417484).

In the United States, the Social Security Administration (SSA) becomes an important consideration near retirement age (at least age 62). For eligible members of the workforce, this pension information can dictate the lifestyle one lives after employment ends. Previous campaign iterations in Q4 2024 prioritized urgency and consequences when phishing. Current SSA-spoofing emails usually claim to provide information rather than demand it. Figure 3 shows an SSA download statement phishing email, one of the scams the SSA Office of the Inspector General warns about.

If the phishing link is clicked, an SSA-spoofing website typically opens, and a file download starts. The file appears similar to those in the Docusign and Adobe sections. Some files act like benefit letters or document notifications. Others require a download file to be run because “Adobe Reader is out of date”. As usual, running the file will install a threat actor-controlled legitimate RAT. The RATs most commonly installed are ConnectWise RAT and SimpleHelp. The SSA-impersonation campaign delivering ConnectWise RAT has been going on since at least 2024.

Docusign Spoofing Campaigns Delivering Malware
  • Docusign-spoofing emails increased about 250% when comparing the first half of 2026 to the first half of 2025.
  • Docusign-spoofing campaigns typically deliver ConnectWise RAT (34%), GoTo RAT (11%), Itarian RAT (5%), or some combination of the three.

Figure 4: Docusign-spoofing file is a SuperOps RMM instance abused by the threat actor (ATR 415883).

Docusign is typically used by threat actors to host documents with links to redirect to malicious websites, usually Microsoft-spoofing credential phishing pages. This is because using trusted websites help bypass email security technologies, and abusing legitimate business tools helps malicious content mimic benign content. Docusign-branded emails are also useful for getting recipients to download fake documents. Downloading the fake document will deliver malware instead of the expected file.

Threat actors will typically use the Docusign style for the email, the malware download website, and the filename. As seen in Figure 4, a malicious file is named like a Docusign attachment. Threat actors like to deliver legitimate RATs that they control, like ConnectWise RAT and GoTo RAT.

IRS Spoofing Campaigns Delivering Malware
  • IRS-spoofing email volume experienced a 10-fold increase when comparing the first half of 2026 to the first half of 2025.
  • IRS-spoofing campaigns typically deliver ConnectWise RAT (50%), Tiflux RAT (13%), Splashtop (13%) or some combination of the three.

Figure 5: IRS-spoofing, tax refund-themed phishing campaign delivering ConnectWise RAT (ATR 415954).

In the first half of 2025, IRS-spoofing campaigns delivering malware were most prevalent before the USA tax filing date on April 15. Now in the first half of 2026, threat actors continue to use the IRS brand in phishing emails past the tax filing deadline but with many themed about late filing deadlines. Well-developed phishing lures used after April 15 include a refund that has been processed or a tax filing extension being made available. As threat actors use current topics like Elon Musk and DOGE offering an IRS tax refund, IRS-spoofing campaigns are expected to increase.

As with the general rise in threat-actor abused legitimate RATs, IRS-spoofing campaigns deliver similar malware in most cases. ConnectWise RAT is once again the most popular RAT to be abused in IRS-spoofing campaigns. There is also a multi-stage campaign where Tiflux RAT is first installed, then Tiflux RAT installs Splashtop and an UltraVNC utility. In earlier group-delivered malware campaigns, the malware was primarily purpose-built for threat actors and entirely malicious. In the case of Tiflux RAT and Splashtop, both are developed by legitimate organizations for IT operations. Unfortunately, the instances of Tiflux RAT and Splashtop delivered in these campaigns are controlled by threat actors.

Zoom Spoofing Campaigns Delivering Malware
  • Zoom-spoofing emails delivering malware increased over 100% when comparing the first half of 2026 to the first half of 2025.
  • Zoom-spoofing campaigns typically deliver ConnectWise RAT (29%), TrustConnect (14%), and Atera (7%).

Figure 6: A fake Zoom website that downloads an abused RAT (ATR 416603).

Legitimate Zoom links can prompt users to download the Zoom app to access the meeting. Threat actors frequently spoof Zoom and hijack this expected behavior to trick users into downloading malware instead.

Zoom-spoofing phishing emails match the format of legitimate Zoom meeting emails, but the links will redirect to a malware download page instead of the legitimate Zoom site. The most prominent malware delivered is ConnectWise RAT again. TrustConnect and Atera are similar RATs abused by threat actors and delivered in Zoom-spoofing campaigns. Figure 6 shows a malicious Atera instance being downloaded from a threat actor’s website.

Problems Caused by Legitimate Remote Access Tool Abuse
  • As legitimate RATs are developed for enterprise use, abuse of these tools by threat actors may hide in plain sight.
  • ConnectWise RAT is currently the most abused legitimate RAT, instead of NetSupport Manager RAT.

When used for their intended purpose, legitimate remote access tools can reduce costs and improve efficiency. With legitimate RATs, IT professionals can easily maintain and monitor various devices across the organization without needing physical access to it. This elevated privilege becomes problematic when threat actors gain access to it.

Legitimate RATs are just as capable of purpose-built malware in the hands of a threat actor. With PowerShell commands, additional malware payloads can be installed after the initial RAT infection. Threat actors have used ConnectWise RAT to deliver ransomware before.

Organizations can find it hard to identify and contain legitimate RATs used by threat actors. Threat actors may even use the same RATs the organization uses, making context, continuous monitoring, and mitigative controls especially important. If the organization successfully contains one type of RAT, threat actors can easily use a different legitimate RAT for infections. In each of the brands spoofed in this report, threat actors already abuse various legitimate RATs.

Conclusions

This report shows five prominent brands spoofed by threat actors. Some key insights include malicious content nearly indistinguishable from legitimate brands, and the increasing abuse of legitimate remote administrative tools. These tactics by the threat actors can make it harder for both users and security analysts to determine if something is legitimate or not. Especially noteworthy are IRS-spoofing and Social Security Administration-spoofing phishing emails. IRS-spoofing emails will likely continue to increase even outside of tax filing season. Social Security Administration-spoofing emails already are not limited by a specific season.

 

Page Break

 


Mitigations
  • Establish and enforce a software allowlist for remote access tools. Any remote access tool not on that list, including ConnectWise, SimpleHelp, Atera, and GoTo RAT, should be blocked from installing on corporate devices. Organizations that do not have an allowlist should at minimum block the digital certificates associated with remote access tools they do not use.
  • Update employee security awareness training to reflect current lure themes, specifically Adobe document requests, SSA benefit notices, IRS refund emails, and Zoom meeting invitations. Employees who have been trained on real, current threats are more likely to pause before clicking. Simulation exercises should use these exact scenarios, not outdated generic examples.

Blocking remote access tools and updating training are essential, but threat actors will keep finding new brands, filenames, and legitimate tools to abuse. Organizations need a way to respond quickly when a campaign reaches the inbox or an endpoint.
