items.title: The Next Cyberattack Won’t Wait. Are You Ready?
items.summary: One day into the November Microsoft outage, Cofense Intelligence saw phishing emails posing as service notifications. The outage was real. The emails were designed to steal sign-in credentials. We published our findings on November 16. On November 17, CISA urged organizations to patch a critical Oracle Java vulnerability. Security teams should act on the patch guidance and keep email defenses running while they address it. Read our November 16 Flash Alert · Read CISA’s November 17 alert One campaign can look like many The FBI has warned that criminals use generative AI to make scams more convincing and easier to scale. In polymorphic phishing, different versions of the same campaign can land in different inboxes. AI can help attackers produce more of those variants. Even modern filters can miss a message that’s been designed to evade AI algorithms. For a security team, the work starts when the first report comes in. Removing that one message protects the person who reported it. Finding the other versions can protect employees who received a similar email and haven’t flagged it. That’s why teams need a way to investigate across inboxes. Why AI alone isn’t enough AI is essential to modern security. It processes volume and speed that no team could match by hand. But AI struggles with threats that don’t match previous patterns, and new lures are exactly what attackers are producing. Human analysts close that gap. They judge intent and context, and they respond to what automation hasn’t learned yet. Reports from employees and customers feed back into protection, so one organization’s report can help protect many others. In one recent case, a brand-new lure got past several automated systems, including AI-based ones. Employees at a Cofense Phishing Defense Center customer reported the lure, in turn giving Cofense analysts the opportunity to protect all of our customers from this threat. Speed and human judgment working together made the difference. Cofense has seen a 22% growth from 2025 to 2026 so far in non-Microsoft related branding being used in phishing attacks as AI allows Threat Actors to expand upon the types of threats they are able to create. Depending on the industry, between 39% and 49% of phishing subject lines included the recipient’s name or other personal details. It is becoming increasingly easy for threat actors to use AI to harvest employee information and use it in phishing campaigns. Find the campaign and remove it Say one employee reports a fake service alert. Start with that email, then check whether other inboxes received related versions. AI helps group similar messages for analyst review. An analyst confirms which emails are malicious so the team can remove them, including copies nobody reported. That’s the difference between closing one report and removing the campaign. See how Cofense Vision AI connects related messages What organizations can do now Walk through the steps below with the people who own email security, IT, and incident response. Start by checking who can remove a confirmed phish from multiple inboxes and how your team will coordinate if email is down. Have Cyber Security solutions that are able to be flexible in the everchanging landscape of cybercrime and AI. You should have human resources working in tandem with supervised AI to ensure that you aren't left waiting for AI security models to catch up. Map out alternative communication strategies for when you lose access to email or messaging platforms. Have and verify backups for all important company data. Ensure your internal Phishing Training programs are properly training your employees based on real life threats and targets weaknesses in your user base. Document clear lines of communication. Employees should know who to contact when verifying a request or transaction. They should also know which backup channels to use if they suspect the original source has been compromised. Don’t rely on a single layer of defense. No filter catches everything and attackers design campaigns to bypass them. Pair your automated security tools with detection and response to ensure that someone is finding what is slipping through. Treat legitimate remote access tools with the utmost scrutiny. Attackers often abuse legitimate remote monitoring and remote management (RMM) tools, such as ConnectWise/ScreenConnect, because those tools blend in with normal IT activity. Block any RMM or remote access software your organization doesn't officially use and closely monitor the ones you do. Patch with vetted updates. Apply tested patches for every known vulnerability. Prioritize anything actively exploited or facing the internet, like VPNs, firewalls, and remote access appliances. Shrink your attack surface. Review and remove old or unused accounts, services, appliances, and applications. Anything you don't need is just one more way in. Flag external email clearly. Use clear banners to warn users when a message comes from outside the organization. That simple visual cue helps users spot business email compromise (BEC) and impersonation attempts. How Cofense helps Cofense combines AI with human expertise to find and remove phishing from inboxes. Our Managed Phishing Defense team can help when your staff is stretched. If you’re a customer and want help reviewing your setup, contact Cofense Support. Read The Case for Human-Supervised AI · Request a demo · Contact Cofense · support@cofense.com

items.title: Critical Apache HTTP Server RCE Vulnerability Actively Exploited in Attacks
items.summary: Apache’s HTTP/2 module, mod_http2, has a critical flaw tracked as CVE-2026-119618 that reportedly allows unauthenticated remote code execution. Apache released version 2.4.71 on November 11 to fix the flaw, which it rates as critical, while Singapore’s CSA assigns it a high-severity CVSS 3.1 score of 8.1/10. Singapore’s CSA warned of active exploitation on November 17, 2026, urging administrators to patch immediately. It also noted that a public PoC was available but provided no details about victims or attack scale. Wiz Research had reported no known exploitation when it published its analysis on November 11. The later alert changes the urgency for administrators who have not yet applied the update. The bug sits in assign_headers(), a function in the module that handles HTTP/2 traffic. Apache says the function does not properly control how multiple threads access a shared resource. This creates a race condition, meaning the result depends on which task gets to the resource first. The bug can corrupt the heap, an area of memory the server uses while it runs. Apache HTTP Server RCE Exploitation A successful attack can turn that memory corruption into remote code execution (RCE), allowing an attacker to run commands with the web server process’s permissions. Apache credited Anthropic’s OSS Scanner, which reported the issue on October 26, and Google Cloud researchers Anthony Weems and Simon Scannell, who reported it independently on November 3. Cybersecurity News previously covered the Apache HTTP Server 2.4.71 patch and a separate Apache HTTP/2 code execution flaw fixed in May. The earlier fix does not protect servers from this vulnerability. The Apache security advisory lists versions 2.4.55 through 2.4.70 as affected when mod_http2 is enabled. It also lists standalone mod_h2 releases 2.0.8 through 2.0.42 as affected, including 2.0.42 itself. Servers configured to serve only HTTP/1.1 are not exposed to this flaw. Administrators should check the server’s active protocol settings rather than relying on the version number alone. Wiz found that 64% of the cloud environments it examined had resources running affected versions, while 51% had publicly exposed instances. Those figures do not account for whether HTTP/2 was enabled. They show where teams should check first, not how many environments could be exploited or how many were breached. Administrators should install Apache HTTP Server 2.4.71 or later, or apply a package their operating system vendor confirms contains the fix. If an update must wait, temporarily disable HTTP/2 by setting Protocols http/1.1 and checking that individual virtual hosts do not still allow h2 or h2c. After reloading the service, verify that the affected Apache listeners no longer accept HTTP/2. Start with internet-facing servers, but include internal deployments in the patch plan. For systems that were exposed before the update, keep relevant logs and review them for signs of compromise. Installing the fix closes the vulnerability, but it cannot tell you whether someone exploited it before the upgrade. Flipper Devices Launches Flipper One Linux-based Multi-tool With Advanced Network Security Tools
items.summary: Flipper Devices has launched a Kickstarter campaign for Flipper One, a portable Linux computer built for network testing, hardware projects, and security research. Backing starts at $399, with shipping estimated for July 2027. The campaign runs from November 17 through December 17, 2026, making this a crowdfunding launch rather than immediate retail availability. The device combines Wi-Fi 6E, two Gigabit Ethernet ports, and an expansion system for cellular modems, software-defined radios, and storage. Its main appeal is bringing several network tools into one standalone unit, giving researchers a portable platform for checking networks and building custom testing setups. Flipper One Linux Multi-tool Flipper One is not a replacement for Flipper Zero. Zero focuses on NFC, RFID, infrared, sub-GHz radio, and other direct hardware links. One targets IP networks and Linux applications. As covered in our earlier Flipper One report , the two products serve different tasks rather than forming a simple upgrade path. Flipper One Feature Comparison (Image Source: Kickstarter) Flipper One supports up to five network uplinks, with options for routing, failover, load balancing, firewall rules, and VPN tunnels. It can act as both a Wi-Fi client and hotspot. Two independent 1 Gbps Ethernet ports also let users place it between wired devices as a transparent bridge or traffic sensor. Its network scanner is designed to discover active hosts, identify open ports and services, and map network layouts. Flipper also describes passive monitoring that can detect network attacks and report unusual activity. These functions could help administrators find exposed services and investigate traffic, although their real value will depend on software quality and testing. According to the official product page , its MediaTek wireless hardware supports Wi-Fi 6E across the 2.4, 5, and 6 GHz bands, with monitor mode support. Flipper is still testing advanced wireless features. Packet injection appears among its development goals, so buyers should not treat every planned Wi-Fi testing function as finished. An eight-core Rockchip RK3576 processor runs Linux, user applications, and high-speed interfaces. A separate Raspberry Pi RP2350 microcontroller handles the screen, buttons, battery, power states, and boot control. The firmware documentation explains this split, which keeps core device controls separate from the Linux system. That separation matters when a custom Linux build fails or the main processor is switched off. Users retain access to the built-in interface instead of depending entirely on a working operating system. Flipper also supports charging and SSH access through one USB-C cable, while desktop mode combines display output, power, and USB peripherals through a compatible connection. Flipper One Desktop Mode (Image Source: Kickstarter) Flipper is working with Collabora to bring the RK3576 platform into mainline Linux. This approach aims to reduce reliance on vendor-specific board support packages that can become difficult to maintain. For researchers, upstream support offers a clearer path to kernel updates, code review, and custom builds without maintaining large private patches. However, the open-source claims need context. In its May development update , Collabora said a proprietary DDR training component remained in the boot chain. Hardware video decoding and the AI accelerator were also unfinished. Those findings describe development status at that time, not proof that every limitation remains today. The internal M.2 slot supports PCIe, USB, and SATA connections for compatible modems, radios, and SSDs. A 5G modem is required to use the built-in eSIM for cellular data. GPIO accessories offer another route for custom hardware. This extends the community-driven approach seen in Flipper Zero firmware development , but on a different computing platform. For security teams, Flipper One promises a compact network lab rather than an automatic hacking device. Buyers should separate announced features from tested performance and treat the delivery date as an estimate. Its strongest potential lies in combining open Linux software, wired traffic analysis, wireless monitoring, and expandable hardware in one field-ready design. items.title: Microsoft’s Agent Framework PyPI Package Hacked to Steal Azure and GitHub Credentials
items.summary: Hackers published two malicious versions of Microsoft’s agent-framework package on the Python Package Index (PyPI) on November 17, 2026. Versions 1.26.1 and 1.26.2 contained a credential stealer that could run during normal Python startup, even if an application never imported Agent Framework. The malware targeted Azure identities, GitHub credentials, and secrets used in automated builds. Wiz traced the first upload to 20:35 UTC and the second to about 21:08 UTC. Both versions were no longer available on PyPI by 21:30 UTC. Wiz identified 1.26.0 as the latest known clean release and put normal package traffic at about 41,000 downloads per week. It indicates the package’s overall use, not downloads of the malicious versions or the number of victims. Microsoft’s Agent Framework PyPI Compromised Both releases placed a .pth file in site-packages , the directory where Python stores installed libraries. Python processes these files during normal startup and can run executable lines in them. That meant an unrelated Python script could trigger the stealer simply by running in the affected environment. Cyber Security News documented a similar startup mechanism in its coverage of the elementary-data PyPI compromise . The two versions left different files behind. Version 1.26.1 used agent_framework_meta.pth and a collector named _telemetry.py . Version 1.26.2 restored the package’s original initializer and moved the malicious code into af_runtime_diag.py , triggered by af_runtime_diag.pth . A check limited to the first release’s files could therefore miss the second, even though both ran in the background and sent data to the same destination. Researchers found the malicious releases under the legitimate Microsoft-associated PyPI publisher, not under a lookalike name. Wiz found no matching python-1.26.1 tag or release in Microsoft’s GitHub repository and no malicious code on its main branch. The first malicious release also appeared only as a wheel, a ready-to-install Python package, rather than alongside a source archive and a matching agent-framework-core release. Those differences suggest it may have bypassed the usual build process, but the entry point remains unconfirmed Azure and GitHub Actions Credentials Socket’s analysis found that both versions searched environment variables, readable process data and local files for secrets. Targets included Azure CLI data, Azure DevOps agent credentials, Git credential stores, Docker and npm configuration, and application .env files. The stealer also tried to obtain fresh Azure managed identity and Azure DevOps tokens instead of relying only on credentials already stored on the system. Version 1.26.2 added requests for GitHub Actions OpenID Connect (OIDC) tokens in workflows that could issue them. OIDC lets a build job prove its identity without storing a cloud password. If Microsoft Entra ID trusts that workflow, a stolen token could be exchanged for Azure access within the permissions granted to that identity. An earlier Microsoft durabletask supply chain incident also targeted build and cloud credentials, but Wiz has not linked the two attacks. Both versions sent compressed, encoded data to a specific webhook[.]site address. Wiz said the destination used the service’s free tier and that no more than 50 requests were captured. That is not a count of affected systems or exposed credentials. A single accepted request could contain several working secrets, including cloud tokens and package registry credentials. Search dependency lockfiles, build logs, Python environments, container images, and package caches for either version. If you find one, isolate the affected host or runner and avoid starting Python in that environment to inspect it. Check proxy logs for the specific webhook path listed in Socket’s indicators. Then rebuild from a known-good image or dependency set and pin agent-framework to 1.26.0. Removal from PyPI does not remove copies already installed or cached. From a clean system, revoke or rotate credentials that were available to the affected environment. Review Azure sign-in and activity logs for unexpected use of managed identities and service connections. For GitHub Actions jobs that installed 1.26.2 with id-token: write , check the Entra ID trust settings and sign-ins for the linked application. items.summary_html:
Hackers published two malicious versions of Microsoft’s agent-framework package on the Python Package Index (PyPI) on November 17, 2026.

Versions 1.26.1 and 1.26.2 contained a credential stealer that could run during normal Python startup, even if an application never imported Agent Framework. The malware targeted Azure identities, GitHub credentials, and secrets used in automated builds.

Wiz traced the first upload to 20:35 UTC and the second to about 21:08 UTC. Both versions were no longer available on PyPI by 21:30 UTC. Wiz identified 1.26.0 as the latest known clean release and put normal package traffic at about 41,000 downloads per week. It indicates the package’s overall use, not downloads of the malicious versions or the number of victims.

Microsoft’s Agent Framework PyPI Compromised

Both releases placed a .pth file in site-packages, the directory where Python stores installed libraries. Python processes these files during normal startup and can run executable lines in them.

That meant an unrelated Python script could trigger the stealer simply by running in the affected environment. Cyber Security News documented a similar startup mechanism in its coverage of the elementary-data PyPI compromise.

The two versions left different files behind. Version 1.26.1 used agent_framework_meta.pth and a collector named _telemetry.py. Version 1.26.2 restored the package’s original initializer and moved the malicious code into af_runtime_diag.py, triggered by af_runtime_diag.pth.

A check limited to the first release’s files could therefore miss the second, even though both ran in the background and sent data to the same destination.

Researchers found the malicious releases under the legitimate Microsoft-associated PyPI publisher, not under a lookalike name. Wiz found no matching python-1.26.1 tag or release in Microsoft’s GitHub repository and no malicious code on its main branch.

The first malicious release also appeared only as a wheel, a ready-to-install Python package, rather than alongside a source archive and a matching agent-framework-core release. Those differences suggest it may have bypassed the usual build process, but the entry point remains unconfirmed

Azure and GitHub Actions Credentials

Socket’s analysis found that both versions searched environment variables, readable process data and local files for secrets. Targets included Azure CLI data, Azure DevOps agent credentials, Git credential stores, Docker and npm configuration, and application .env files. The stealer also tried to obtain fresh Azure managed identity and Azure DevOps tokens instead of relying only on credentials already stored on the system.

Version 1.26.2 added requests for GitHub Actions OpenID Connect (OIDC) tokens in workflows that could issue them. OIDC lets a build job prove its identity without storing a cloud password.

If Microsoft Entra ID trusts that workflow, a stolen token could be exchanged for Azure access within the permissions granted to that identity. An earlier Microsoft durabletask supply chain incident also targeted build and cloud credentials, but Wiz has not linked the two attacks.

Both versions sent compressed, encoded data to a specific webhook[.]site address. Wiz said the destination used the service’s free tier and that no more than 50 requests were captured. That is not a count of affected systems or exposed credentials. A single accepted request could contain several working secrets, including cloud tokens and package registry credentials.

Search dependency lockfiles, build logs, Python environments, container images, and package caches for either version. If you find one, isolate the affected host or runner and avoid starting Python in that environment to inspect it.

Check proxy logs for the specific webhook path listed in Socket’s indicators. Then rebuild from a known-good image or dependency set and pin agent-framework to 1.26.0. Removal from PyPI does not remove copies already installed or cached.

From a clean system, revoke or rotate credentials that were available to the affected environment. Review Azure sign-in and activity logs for unexpected use of managed identities and service connections.

For GitHub Actions jobs that installed 1.26.2 with id-token: write, check the Entra ID trust settings and sign-ins for the linked application.

items.title: Critical Java4Shell Flaw Lets Hackers Execute Code Without Authentication on OpenJDK Servers
items.summary: A critical flaw in OpenJDK’s Base64 decoder can let a remote attacker run code on an affected server without signing in. The vulnerability, dubbed Java4Shell and tracked as CVE-2026-114938, can also crash the Java Virtual Machine (JVM) or expose sensitive data held in its memory. Oracle released security updates on November 17, 2026, and the U.S. Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA) urged organizations to patch immediately. The flaw sits in HotSpot, the JVM that runs Java applications in many OpenJDK distributions. That differs from Log4Shell , which affected the Log4j logging library. Updating an application’s Java libraries will not replace a vulnerable runtime. Administrators need to identify the Java build each service actually runs, including any copy shipped by the application vendor. Security firm Calif rated Java4Shell 9.2 under CVSS 4.0, which puts it in the critical range. OpenJDK’s advisory lists a score of 8.1 under CVSS 3.1. The scores use different versions of the severity standard. Both describe a serious flaw, but neither means every Java server can be exploited. Exposure depends on the runtime, the processor, and how the application handles outside data. Calif researcher, Quang Luong, found the flaw while examining OpenJDK HotSpot with help from an AI coding tool. The disclosure follows Calif’s work on PHP2Shell and the emergency PHP patches . Both investigations found memory flaws in shared runtimes, but the PHP flaws and Java4Shell have different causes and require separate fixes. Base64 represents binary data as text so applications can pass it through systems that expect text. It is common in sign-in flows, file uploads, and network messages. On supported processors, HotSpot uses a faster decoder that handles several bytes at once. A mistake in that code can make the decoder write past the end of its allocated buffer before Java rejects the bad input. Rejecting it does not undo the memory damage. Java4Shell Exposes Java Applications Calif reported remote code execution without a login in default test setups of Keycloak, Atlassian Jira and Confluence, JFrog Artifactory, Jenkins and PingFederate. Its tests against Apache Kafka Broker, Apache Solr, Elasticsearch, Gerrit and Spinnaker required authentication. The researchers also demonstrated code execution in sample applications built with Apache Struts and Spring Boot. These results describe the setups Calif tested, not every installation of those products. The risk is not limited to servers that accept incoming requests. Calif also reported a client-side demonstration in which a Java program could be compromised after opening an encrypted TLS connection to a malicious server. The researchers compared the memory exposure to Heartbleed because a successful attack could reveal data already held by the process, such as session tokens or private keys. The two flaws do not share the same cause. The vulnerable decoder requires an x86-64 processor with AVX-512 VBMI support, a feature available on some Intel Xeon and newer AMD processors. ARM64 systems are not affected by this code path. The earlier Cybersecurity News report on the Java 17 flaw focused on that release line. The OpenJDK advisory now identifies fixes for Java 17, 21, 25 and 27. Oracle also lists a specific Java 8 Enterprise Performance Pack build and certain GraalVM builds as affected. There is no single exploit that works across all Java applications, according to Calif. WatchTowr also expects attacks to be tailored to individual products because the CPU, JDK, and the way the application uses Base64 all matter. The research demonstrations establish that code execution is possible, but they are not evidence of attacks against production systems. How to patch Java4Shell and Fix Versions Oracle’s fixed Java SE releases include 17.0.21.1, 21.0.13.1, 25.0.5.1 and 27.0.1.1. Organizations using Amazon Corretto, Eclipse Temurin, Azul Zulu, or another distribution should check their vendor’s advisory for the build that fixes this CVE. Product Affected build listed for this CVE Patched build or upgrade guidance Oracle Java SE 17 17.0.21.0.3 17.0.21.1 Oracle Java SE 21 21.0.13.0.3 21.0.13.1 Oracle Java SE 25 25.0.5.0.3 25.0.5.1 Oracle Java SE 27 27.0.1.0.3 27.0.1.1 Oracle Java 8 Enterprise Performance Pack 8u511b33-perf Install Oracle’s November 17 security update for the Enterprise Performance Pack. Verify the exact build in Oracle’s advisory. Oracle GraalVM for JDK 17 17.0.21.0.3 Install Oracle’s November 17 security update for GraalVM for JDK 17. Oracle GraalVM for JDK 21 21.0.13.0.3 Install Oracle’s November 17 security update for GraalVM for JDK 21. Oracle GraalVM Enterprise Edition 21.3.20.0.3 Install Oracle’s November 17 security update for GraalVM Enterprise Edition. CISA recommends patching internet-facing systems first and checking for runtimes bundled with third-party software, container images, and appliances. Those copies may not appear as separate entries in a software inventory. Where patching must wait, Calif recommends starting affected JVMs with -XX:-UseBASE64Intrinsics to turn off the optimized Base64 routines. Another option on x86-64 is -XX:UseAVX=2 , which disables AVX-512. Do not add the second flag to ARM startup settings because it can prevent Java from starting. CISA also recommends restricting unauthenticated access, validating Base64 input before it reaches the decoder, and enforcing input-size limits while teams prepare updates. These are temporary controls, not replacements for a patched runtime. After updating, restart each affected service or redeploy it with a rebuilt container image. Verify the version used by the running process rather than checking only the host’s default Java installation. CISA also recommends watching for unexpected JVM crashes, unapproved runtimes, and suspicious Java processes. A crash alone does not prove exploitation, but an unexplained crash on an exposed, unpatched system deserves investigation. What Are Leading Organizations Doing About AI and Cyber Risks? Find Out. items.title: Finding and closing gaps in security logging with AI
items.summary: A security incident is the worst time to discover that the logs you need were never collected. Even with a security information and event management (SIEM) in place, critical logging gaps can go unnoticed. Some tools may not send logs at all, while others may appear to be integrated but have collection or parsing issues that make their logs difficult to use during an investigation. With multiple tools, it can be a challenge to know what's missing or whether the logs you have are actually usable. At 1Password, finding these gaps meant manually comparing our tool inventory against SIEM log sources, one tool at a time. The process was time-consuming, difficult to keep up to date, and hard to scale as our environment evolved. We needed a more reliable way to identify gaps before they affected an investigation. We saw an opportunity to use AI to change how we identify security logging gaps and onboard new log sources. Instead of relying on time-consuming manual reviews, we built an approach that uses AI to uncover potential gaps and guide engineers through onboarding, while keeping critical decisions in human hands. Here's how we built it, what we learned, and where AI makes a difference. Collecting logs is only the beginning As 1Password adopts new tools, maintaining security visibility requires more than simply sending logs to the SIEM. We need to determine which logs matter for security, collect them, and ensure they contain the searchable information engineers need during an investigation. Even when logs are successfully ingested, important details can remain buried in unparsed text. Without proper parsing, engineers may struggle to search those details or build reliable detection rules. To address these challenges, we built an automated audit that compares our tool inventories against SIEM log sources and produces a prioritized report of potential logging gaps. For gaps we decide to close, we use AI skills: reusable instruction files that guide an AI tool through specific tasks, including required checks and approvals. These skills help engineers configure log collection and parsing pipelines, manage access controls, document integrations, and prepare detection rules. Engineers review every proposed action, keeping human oversight central to the onboarding process. Missing logs are only part of the problem The obvious gap is a tool whose logs we do not collect. The less obvious one is a source that appears to be onboarded because logs are arriving, but whose logs still cannot support the investigations or detection rules we need. Our audit looks for both. The first part compares the tools listed in our inventories with the log sources available in the SIEM. A tool with no matching logs is flagged as a potential coverage gap. The second checks whether existing log sources show signs of collection or parsing problems. Examples include a source that has stopped sending logs or logs whose activity details are not being extracted into searchable fields. These checks help identify sources that need attention even though an integration is already in place. These findings feed different decisions. A missing source might require a new pipeline to collect and deliver its logs. An existing source might need a parsing fix to correct how individual details are extracted from a log, such as who acted and what they did. Both belong in the same review. How AI helps find the logging gaps A scheduled workflow runs the audit automatically and produces a report for engineering review. It runs a Python script that requests vendor lists from our procurement system, reads our internal tool catalogs, queries the SIEM for log sources, and searches our ticketing system for related work. The script makes these requests directly through each system’s API. An AI model assesses which vendors are likely to have logs relevant to security monitoring and writes an explanation of each potential gap, why the logs would be valuable, and the recommended priority for onboarding them. The script handles data collection, comparison, and publication. This keeps the model focused on assessment while code handles repeatable operations. The AI model assesses vendor names using instructions focused on the potential value of their logs for monitoring identity, sensitive data, infrastructure, code, security controls, or administrative access. The audit then checks whether logs from the tools identified as security-relevant are available in the SIEM. Because names alone can be ambiguous, this assessment can miss tools and remains a limitation of the approach. The script builds a list of relevant tools from both inventories, standardizing names and removing duplicates from that list. It then compares that list with the names identifying tools in the SIEM logs. Matching accounts for naming differences, with safeguards against mistaking part of one tool’s name for a different tool. The result is an initial indication of coverage that an engineer can verify. The script also searches existing onboarding tickets so the report can show whether work to collect a tool’s logs is already underway. The script saves each report as a dated file and opens a pull request for review. Once merged, the file becomes part of the audit history, allowing comparison with reports from earlier runs. The report identifies tools whose logs are not currently ingested into the SIEM, as well as existing SIEM log sources with potential log collection or parsing issues. Our priority framework considers how useful the logs would be for detecting suspicious activity, investigating an incident, and proactively searching for signs of attacker activity. The workflow automatically sends a team notification with links to the report and audit run, along with a summary of potential gaps and log sources reviewed. A written review guide supports decisions about which findings need action. The report feeds planning; finding a gap does not trigger an emergency alert. Can we trust the audit report? An automated report can look convincing while silently omitting a tool, making completeness checks essential. The audit now stops if the vendor inventory or SIEM source list is empty, identifies tools without matching SIEM log sources, and verifies that every missing tool is assessed in the final report. Failed ticket searches are labeled “lookup failed” to distinguish them from searches that found no existing tickets. Consistency between runs matters too. The script chooses a consistent name for each tool and instructs the AI model to preserve it exactly, so findings can be matched to their history from earlier audits. The model also receives the previous priority for each finding, and a change needs new evidence. We reuse saved assessments when the supporting information and report instructions remain unchanged, with periodic refreshes. Changes to the instructions trigger fresh analysis. We save previous vendor classifications, tool assessments, and gap history in a cache, so each run can build on earlier work. Keeping this history makes it possible to inspect earlier assessments and correct them when needed. Which logging gaps should we close first? Before starting an integration, an engineer verifies that the reported gap exists. A tool may already send logs under a name the audit did not recognize, or the inventory may still list a tool that is no longer used. Before a finding becomes an onboarding project, we check three things: the gap is real, the vendor can deliver useful audit logs, and the expected security value justifies prioritizing the work alongside the team’s other commitments. For custom integrations, a classification skill reads the vendor's official audit log documentation and recommends a supported way to collect the logs, with a confidence rating. It can also identify cases our pipeline tooling cannot support. This happens before ticket creation, so we avoid generating a full onboarding plan for a source we cannot collect. The reviewer considers how much damage a compromise could cause, what we can already monitor, which suspicious activities we could detect, and the effort needed to add the logs. During report review, an engineer may prioritize repairing an existing source over collecting logs from another tool, especially if the repair would restore visibility into important activity. False gaps require a correction in the underlying inventory. Otherwise, the next audit simply asks the same question again. Putting AI to work on log onboarding For an approved source, a skill creates an onboarding plan in our ticketing system with standard tasks. Each task identifies which skill to use, explains the work it performs, and includes manual instructions as a fallback. The workflow covers choosing how to collect the logs, gathering access and configuration details, building the pipeline, making logs searchable, and restricting access. It also documents what the logs contain, how they are collected, and how engineers can find them in the SIEM. The later steps prepare the repository structure and review process for managing detection rules as code. A detection-seeding skill then examines the available logs and identifies detection opportunities, creating tasks for engineers to develop and review the proposed rules. A coordinating skill, the orchestrator, reads the onboarding plan and checks task status against evidence. For a task marked complete, it verifies the relevant result: infrastructure changes have merged, logs are arriving and searchable in the SIEM, or the log inventory has been updated with the collection method and instructions for finding the new source’s logs. The orchestrator proposes one next action for an engineer to approve. Each skill retains its own approval requirements, and the orchestrator pauses at tasks that require manual work. An engineer reviews and applies infrastructure changes and configures the credentials used in production. That onboarding boundary involves decisions with lasting consequences. An engineer needs to review which resources will be created or changed and decide whether the logs contain sensitive information that requires restricted access. When is a log source really ready? The skills check live evidence at several points in the workflow. When building a pipeline that collects logs through a vendor API, the pipeline-builder skill first makes a live request to that API. It confirms authentication, the response structure, the timestamp field, whether the API returns logs from oldest to newest or newest to oldest, and which vendor account or tenant the logs belong to. It uses real sample logs to map details into the fields our monitoring expects. Each proposed detection idea must be grounded in logs available in the SIEM and fields engineers can query. A successful deployment or an absence of alarms does not establish that log collection is working. Validation needs to follow logs through the pipeline and confirm that they are searchable. For teams building similar automation, this is a useful distinction: infrastructure status and evidence of log delivery answer different questions. The routing skill checks the configuration that determines whether incoming logs become searchable in the SIEM. This matters because successful delivery to the platform does not always mean the logs are available for monitoring. Reviewing that configuration before making changes also helps preserve integrations already in use. Access controls belong in the onboarding process before new logs become searchable. An engineer reviews the sample logs for sensitive information and decides who should be able to read them. Considering access at this stage helps avoid exposing sensitive logs while restrictions are still being arranged. At the detection stage, a skill checks a standard set of activities worth monitoring, including granting administrator access, creating access tokens, exporting data, and changing security settings. It records whether each is already covered by a detection rule, needs a new detection rule, lacks the necessary logs, or still needs verification. Only a confirmed detection gap becomes a detection task. If the logs are missing, we need to collect them first. We now have a recurring comparison of company tool inventories against SIEM log coverage, together with a documented workflow for collecting missing logs and preparing detection rules. The audit preserves history between runs, and the interactive workflow checks evidence before advancing. There are still limits. A name match in the SIEM does not prove that logs capture every activity we need to monitor. A source that produces logs infrequently may need an additional check before being treated as missing. Human review remains part of interpreting the report. Would your logs be ready for an incident? A useful starting point is to compare the tools your organization uses with the logs your security team can actually search. Investigating the differences helps establish where coverage is missing and which gaps deserve attention. From there, the audit and onboarding approach described in this post provides a repeatable path from identifying a gap to collecting the logs and preparing detection rules, with AI assisting the work and engineers reviewing the changes. During an incident, the logs available to investigators shape what they can establish about the activity involved. Finding missing logs, verifying that they can be searched, and building detection rules gives teams a stronger foundation for identifying and investigating threats before an incident puts that visibility to the test. A security incident is the worst time to discover that the logs you need were never collected.

Even with a security information and event management (SIEM) in place, critical logging gaps can go unnoticed. Some tools may not send logs at all, while others may appear to be integrated but have collection or parsing issues that make their logs difficult to use during an investigation. With multiple tools, it can be a challenge to know what's missing or whether the logs you have are actually usable.

At 1Password, finding these gaps meant manually comparing our tool inventory against SIEM log sources, one tool at a time. The process was time-consuming, difficult to keep up to date, and hard to scale as our environment evolved. We needed a more reliable way to identify gaps before they affected an investigation.

We saw an opportunity to use AI to change how we identify security logging gaps and onboard new log sources. Instead of relying on time-consuming manual reviews, we built an approach that uses AI to uncover potential gaps and guide engineers through onboarding, while keeping critical decisions in human hands. Here's how we built it, what we learned, and where AI makes a difference.

Collecting logs is only the beginning

As 1Password adopts new tools, maintaining security visibility requires more than simply sending logs to the SIEM. We need to determine which logs matter for security, collect them, and ensure they contain the searchable information engineers need during an investigation. Even when logs are successfully ingested, important details can remain buried in unparsed text. Without proper parsing, engineers may struggle to search those details or build reliable detection rules.

To address these challenges, we built an automated audit that compares our tool inventories against SIEM log sources and produces a prioritized report of potential logging gaps. For gaps we decide to close, we use AI skills: reusable instruction files that guide an AI tool through specific tasks, including required checks and approvals. These skills help engineers configure log collection and parsing pipelines, manage access controls, document integrations, and prepare detection rules. Engineers review every proposed action, keeping human oversight central to the onboarding process.

Missing logs are only part of the problem

The obvious gap is a tool whose logs we do not collect. The less obvious one is a source that appears to be onboarded because logs are arriving, but whose logs still cannot support the investigations or detection rules we need.

Our audit looks for both.

The first part compares the tools listed in our inventories with the log sources available in the SIEM. A tool with no matching logs is flagged as a potential coverage gap.

The second checks whether existing log sources show signs of collection or parsing problems. Examples include a source that has stopped sending logs or logs whose activity details are not being extracted into searchable fields. These checks help identify sources that need attention even though an integration is already in place.

These findings feed different decisions. A missing source might require a new pipeline to collect and deliver its logs. An existing source might need a parsing fix to correct how individual details are extracted from a log, such as who acted and what they did. Both belong in the same review.

How AI helps find the logging gaps

A scheduled workflow runs the audit automatically and produces a report for engineering review. It runs a Python script that requests vendor lists from our procurement system, reads our internal tool catalogs, queries the SIEM for log sources, and searches our ticketing system for related work. The script makes these requests directly through each system’s API. An AI model assesses which vendors are likely to have logs relevant to security monitoring and writes an explanation of each potential gap, why the logs would be valuable, and the recommended priority for onboarding them. The script handles data collection, comparison, and publication. This keeps the model focused on assessment while code handles repeatable operations.

The AI model assesses vendor names using instructions focused on the potential value of their logs for monitoring identity, sensitive data, infrastructure, code, security controls, or administrative access. The audit then checks whether logs from the tools identified as security-relevant are available in the SIEM. Because names alone can be ambiguous, this assessment can miss tools and remains a limitation of the approach.

The script builds a list of relevant tools from both inventories, standardizing names and removing duplicates from that list. It then compares that list with the names identifying tools in the SIEM logs. Matching accounts for naming differences, with safeguards against mistaking part of one tool’s name for a different tool. The result is an initial indication of coverage that an engineer can verify. The script also searches existing onboarding tickets so the report can show whether work to collect a tool’s logs is already underway.

The script saves each report as a dated file and opens a pull request for review. Once merged, the file becomes part of the audit history, allowing comparison with reports from earlier runs. The report identifies tools whose logs are not currently ingested into the SIEM, as well as existing SIEM log sources with potential log collection or parsing issues. Our priority framework considers how useful the logs would be for detecting suspicious activity, investigating an incident, and proactively searching for signs of attacker activity.

The workflow automatically sends a team notification with links to the report and audit run, along with a summary of potential gaps and log sources reviewed. A written review guide supports decisions about which findings need action. The report feeds planning; finding a gap does not trigger an emergency alert.

Can we trust the audit report?

An automated report can look convincing while silently omitting a tool, making completeness checks essential. The audit now stops if the vendor inventory or SIEM source list is empty, identifies tools without matching SIEM log sources, and verifies that every missing tool is assessed in the final report. Failed ticket searches are labeled “lookup failed” to distinguish them from searches that found no existing tickets.

Consistency between runs matters too. The script chooses a consistent name for each tool and instructs the AI model to preserve it exactly, so findings can be matched to their history from earlier audits. The model also receives the previous priority for each finding, and a change needs new evidence. We reuse saved assessments when the supporting information and report instructions remain unchanged, with periodic refreshes. Changes to the instructions trigger fresh analysis.

We save previous vendor classifications, tool assessments, and gap history in a cache, so each run can build on earlier work. Keeping this history makes it possible to inspect earlier assessments and correct them when needed.

Which logging gaps should we close first?

Before starting an integration, an engineer verifies that the reported gap exists. A tool may already send logs under a name the audit did not recognize, or the inventory may still list a tool that is no longer used.

Before a finding becomes an onboarding project, we check three things: the gap is real, the vendor can deliver useful audit logs, and the expected security value justifies prioritizing the work alongside the team’s other commitments.

For custom integrations, a classification skill reads the vendor's official audit log documentation and recommends a supported way to collect the logs, with a confidence rating. It can also identify cases our pipeline tooling cannot support. This happens before ticket creation, so we avoid generating a full onboarding plan for a source we cannot collect.

The reviewer considers how much damage a compromise could cause, what we can already monitor, which suspicious activities we could detect, and the effort needed to add the logs. During report review, an engineer may prioritize repairing an existing source over collecting logs from another tool, especially if the repair would restore visibility into important activity.

False gaps require a correction in the underlying inventory. Otherwise, the next audit simply asks the same question again.

Putting AI to work on log onboarding

For an approved source, a skill creates an onboarding plan in our ticketing system with standard tasks. Each task identifies which skill to use, explains the work it performs, and includes manual instructions as a fallback.

The workflow covers choosing how to collect the logs, gathering access and configuration details, building the pipeline, making logs searchable, and restricting access. It also documents what the logs contain, how they are collected, and how engineers can find them in the SIEM. The later steps prepare the repository structure and review process for managing detection rules as code. A detection-seeding skill then examines the available logs and identifies detection opportunities, creating tasks for engineers to develop and review the proposed rules.

A coordinating skill, the orchestrator, reads the onboarding plan and checks task status against evidence. For a task marked complete, it verifies the relevant result: infrastructure changes have merged, logs are arriving and searchable in the SIEM, or the log inventory has been updated with the collection method and instructions for finding the new source’s logs.

The orchestrator proposes one next action for an engineer to approve. Each skill retains its own approval requirements, and the orchestrator pauses at tasks that require manual work. An engineer reviews and applies infrastructure changes and configures the credentials used in production.

That onboarding boundary involves decisions with lasting consequences. An engineer needs to review which resources will be created or changed and decide whether the logs contain sensitive information that requires restricted access.

When is a log source really ready?

The skills check live evidence at several points in the workflow.

When building a pipeline that collects logs through a vendor API, the pipeline-builder skill first makes a live request to that API. It confirms authentication, the response structure, the timestamp field, whether the API returns logs from oldest to newest or newest to oldest, and which vendor account or tenant the logs belong to. It uses real sample logs to map details into the fields our monitoring expects. Each proposed detection idea must be grounded in logs available in the SIEM and fields engineers can query.

A successful deployment or an absence of alarms does not establish that log collection is working. Validation needs to follow logs through the pipeline and confirm that they are searchable. For teams building similar automation, this is a useful distinction: infrastructure status and evidence of log delivery answer different questions.

The routing skill checks the configuration that determines whether incoming logs become searchable in the SIEM. This matters because successful delivery to the platform does not always mean the logs are available for monitoring. Reviewing that configuration before making changes also helps preserve integrations already in use.

Access controls belong in the onboarding process before new logs become searchable. An engineer reviews the sample logs for sensitive information and decides who should be able to read them. Considering access at this stage helps avoid exposing sensitive logs while restrictions are still being arranged.

At the detection stage, a skill checks a standard set of activities worth monitoring, including granting administrator access, creating access tokens, exporting data, and changing security settings. It records whether each is already covered by a detection rule, needs a new detection rule, lacks the necessary logs, or still needs verification. Only a confirmed detection gap becomes a detection task. If the logs are missing, we need to collect them first.

We now have a recurring comparison of company tool inventories against SIEM log coverage, together with a documented workflow for collecting missing logs and preparing detection rules. The audit preserves history between runs, and the interactive workflow checks evidence before advancing.

There are still limits. A name match in the SIEM does not prove that logs capture every activity we need to monitor. A source that produces logs infrequently may need an additional check before being treated as missing. Human review remains part of interpreting the report.

Would your logs be ready for an incident?

A useful starting point is to compare the tools your organization uses with the logs your security team can actually search. Investigating the differences helps establish where coverage is missing and which gaps deserve attention. From there, the audit and onboarding approach described in this post provides a repeatable path from identifying a gap to collecting the logs and preparing detection rules, with AI assisting the work and engineers reviewing the changes.

During an incident, the logs available to investigators shape what they can establish about the activity involved. Finding missing logs, verifying that they can be searched, and building detection rules gives teams a stronger foundation for identifying and investigating threats before an incident puts that visibility to the test.

items.title: Podman Desktop 1.31 Release
items.summary: Podman Desktop 1.31 Release Podman Desktop 1.31 is now available. Click here to download it ! The new version of Podman Desktop is here with upgrades that speed up and secure your daily container workflow—featuring customizable bundled extensions, one-click image updates, a guided Windows Hyper-V setup, and important security patches: Extension management : Override bundled extensions with installed replacements, update bundled extensions directly from the catalog, and configure auto-updates per extension — complete with "Update available" links and accurate lifecycle status indicators. Container image updates: Update a single image or a bulk selection at once, with live progress tracking and cancellation in the task manager. Guided Hyper-V setup on Windows: Configure Hyper-V for Podman from Settings > Resources without running Podman Desktop as an administrator. Using existing volumes in Run Image page: Attach pre-created volumes directly from the Run Image page when launching a container. Manage macOS settings with MDM: Administrators can now distribute default settings and enforce locked configurations across managed macOS devices using MDM preference plists. Release details ​ Extension management ​ Previously, bundled extensions such as Podman, Docker, Kind, and Compose could not be updated between Podman Desktop releases—running a patched or newer version required sideloading it without any guarantee it would take precedence. Now, an installed extension can declare that it overrides a bundled extension, and the loader automatically gives it priority. You can also update bundled extensions directly from the catalog, with a new Overrides badge on the extension card confirming that your version is the one running. Overriding bundled extensions is paired with granular control over automatic updates. You can now disable auto-updates for individual extensions from their details page. Whenever a newer version is waiting, an Update available link appears next to the version on both the extension card and the details page so you can apply the update manually. Lifecycle status indicators have also been refreshed across the UI to align with the updated look and placement of these controls on both extension cards and details pages Container image updates ​ Updating an image to a newer remote build no longer requires walking through the manual Pull Image flow and re-entering the tag—you can now check for and pull image updates directly from the UI. Single image update: Trigger an update action directly from the upper-right corner of the Image Details page; Podman Desktop checks the local digest against the remote manifest and pulls the newer version only if an update exists. Bulk images update: Select multiple images from the Images list and run the update action across the entire batch at once, automatically skipping any images that are already up to date. Non-blocking task tracking: Image update checks and pulls run in the background as cancellable tasks in the task manager, ensuring large downloads never lock up the UI. Guided Hyper-V setup on Windows ​ On Windows systems with Podman 6.0.0 or later, Podman Desktop now checks podman system hyperv-prep --status to verify whether your account belongs to the Hyper-V Administrators group. When preparation has not yet been applied, a Podman: Prepare Hyper-V action appears on the Podman provider card in Settings > Resources . Triggering it requests a one-time administrator confirmation (UAC) to run podman system hyperv-prep in the background, hides the action once complete, and reminds you to sign out or restart Windows for the changes to take effect. Once preparation is complete, you no longer need to run Podman Desktop as an administrator to create a Hyper-V VM. Using existing volumes in Run Image page ​ Previously, configuring volume mounts on the Run Image page was restricted to host path binds, with no direct way to select a pre-created named volume without manually typing or remembering its path string. Podman Desktop 1.31 adds a flexible source-type selector to each mount row, making it easier to attach persistent storage. Source-type selection: Each mount row now includes a dropdown allowing you to switch between Host path and Existing volume . Engine-filtered volume dropdown: When Existing volume is selected, the host path input swaps for a dropdown populated from your available volumes, automatically filtered to match the target image's engine and sorted by name. The dropdown displays reader-friendly short names while submitting the full identifier as the bind source, making it effortless to select pre-created data volumes without copying and pasting long strings. Manage macOS settings with MDM ​ Podman Desktop now supports macOS Mobile Device Management (MDM) by reading managed preference files ( .plist , in either XML or binary format) at startup and merging them with existing JSON configurations. Administrators can deploy device-wide defaults and enforce restrictions using a locked array at /Library/Managed Preferences/io.podman_desktop.PodmanDesktop.plist , or supply account-specific startup overrides via per-user plists at /Library/Managed Preferences/ /io.podman_desktop.PodmanDesktop.plist . By combining the roles of default-settings.json and locked.json into standard macOS managed preference files, IT teams can natively standardize and lock Podman Desktop settings across their macOS fleets. Security hardening ​ This release includes fixes for multiple security vulnerabilities reported through Dependabot. Updated direct and transitive dependencies address known CVEs and help keep Podman Desktop's container and extension workflows secure. Other improvements ​ Catalog filters : The extension catalog now understands is:featured and not:featured in its search, so you can narrow results to featured extensions ( #19616 ). Catalog search placement : Search moved below the tabs, and the Install Custom dialog now closes as soon as the installation starts ( #19889 , #19621 ). Settings navigation : SettingsNavItem supports key shortcuts, and preferences search matches both the setting key and its display name ( #19204 ). Registries settings : The registries page now exposes labeled regions for screen reader users ( #19679 ). Task toast notifications : Enabled by default, so long-running work reports back when it finishes ( #19845 ). Community Thank You ​ 🎉 We’d like to say a big thank you to everyone who contributed their first pull request to Podman Desktop in this release: DeviceDidWhat in docs(website): remove /extend page and redirect to /docs/extensions ewerton336 in fix(container): keep Tty and OpenStdin when creating containers through libpod taljeon in fix(renderer): compact factory property descriptions Community Meeting ​ If you would like to discuss any of the new features, issues or other topics, please join us at the monthly community meeting that takes place every 4th Thursday of the month . Here are the meeting details . Final Notes ​ The complete list of issues fixed in this release is available here . Get the latest release from the Downloads section of the website. Visit the GitHub repository to report issues or contribute. items.summary_html:
Podman Desktop 1.31 Release

Podman Desktop 1.31 is now available. Click here to download it!

The new version of Podman Desktop is here with upgrades that speed up and secure your daily container workflow—featuring customizable bundled extensions, one-click image updates, a guided Windows Hyper-V setup, and important security patches:

  • Extension management: Override bundled extensions with installed replacements, update bundled extensions directly from the catalog, and configure auto-updates per extension — complete with "Update available" links and accurate lifecycle status indicators.
  • Container image updates: Update a single image or a bulk selection at once, with live progress tracking and cancellation in the task manager.
  • Guided Hyper-V setup on Windows: Configure Hyper-V for Podman from Settings > Resources without running Podman Desktop as an administrator.
  • Using existing volumes in Run Image page: Attach pre-created volumes directly from the Run Image page when launching a container.
  • Manage macOS settings with MDM: Administrators can now distribute default settings and enforce locked configurations across managed macOS devices using MDM preference plists.
Release details​ Extension management​

Previously, bundled extensions such as Podman, Docker, Kind, and Compose could not be updated between Podman Desktop releases—running a patched or newer version required sideloading it without any guarantee it would take precedence. Now, an installed extension can declare that it overrides a bundled extension, and the loader automatically gives it priority. You can also update bundled extensions directly from the catalog, with a new Overrides badge on the extension card confirming that your version is the one running.

Overriding bundled extensions is paired with granular control over automatic updates. You can now disable auto-updates for individual extensions from their details page. Whenever a newer version is waiting, an Update available link appears next to the version on both the extension card and the details page so you can apply the update manually. Lifecycle status indicators have also been refreshed across the UI to align with the updated look and placement of these controls on both extension cards and details pages

Container image updates​

Updating an image to a newer remote build no longer requires walking through the manual Pull Image flow and re-entering the tag—you can now check for and pull image updates directly from the UI.

Single image update: Trigger an update action directly from the upper-right corner of the Image Details page; Podman Desktop checks the local digest against the remote manifest and pulls the newer version only if an update exists. Bulk images update: Select multiple images from the Images list and run the update action across the entire batch at once, automatically skipping any images that are already up to date. Non-blocking task tracking: Image update checks and pulls run in the background as cancellable tasks in the task manager, ensuring large downloads never lock up the UI.

Guided Hyper-V setup on Windows​

On Windows systems with Podman 6.0.0 or later, Podman Desktop now checks podman system hyperv-prep --status to verify whether your account belongs to the Hyper-V Administrators group. When preparation has not yet been applied, a Podman: Prepare Hyper-V action appears on the Podman provider card in Settings > Resources. Triggering it requests a one-time administrator confirmation (UAC) to run podman system hyperv-prep in the background, hides the action once complete, and reminds you to sign out or restart Windows for the changes to take effect. Once preparation is complete, you no longer need to run Podman Desktop as an administrator to create a Hyper-V VM.

Using existing volumes in Run Image page​

Previously, configuring volume mounts on the Run Image page was restricted to host path binds, with no direct way to select a pre-created named volume without manually typing or remembering its path string. Podman Desktop 1.31 adds a flexible source-type selector to each mount row, making it easier to attach persistent storage.

Source-type selection: Each mount row now includes a dropdown allowing you to switch between Host path and Existing volume.

Engine-filtered volume dropdown: When Existing volume is selected, the host path input swaps for a dropdown populated from your available volumes, automatically filtered to match the target image's engine and sorted by name. The dropdown displays reader-friendly short names while submitting the full identifier as the bind source, making it effortless to select pre-created data volumes without copying and pasting long strings.

Manage macOS settings with MDM​

Podman Desktop now supports macOS Mobile Device Management (MDM) by reading managed preference files (.plist, in either XML or binary format) at startup and merging them with existing JSON configurations.

Administrators can deploy device-wide defaults and enforce restrictions using a locked array at /Library/Managed Preferences/io.podman_desktop.PodmanDesktop.plist, or supply account-specific startup overrides via per-user plists at /Library/Managed Preferences//io.podman_desktop.PodmanDesktop.plist. By combining the roles of default-settings.json and locked.json into standard macOS managed preference files, IT teams can natively standardize and lock Podman Desktop settings across their macOS fleets.

Security hardening​

This release includes fixes for multiple security vulnerabilities reported through Dependabot. Updated direct and transitive dependencies address known CVEs and help keep Podman Desktop's container and extension workflows secure.

Other improvements​
  • Catalog filters: The extension catalog now understands is:featured and not:featured in its search, so you can narrow results to featured extensions (#19616).
  • Catalog search placement: Search moved below the tabs, and the Install Custom dialog now closes as soon as the installation starts (#19889, #19621).
  • Settings navigation: SettingsNavItem supports key shortcuts, and preferences search matches both the setting key and its display name (#19204).
  • Registries settings: The registries page now exposes labeled regions for screen reader users (#19679).
  • Task toast notifications: Enabled by default, so long-running work reports back when it finishes (#19845).
Community Thank You​

🎉 We’d like to say a big thank you to everyone who contributed their first pull request to Podman Desktop in this release:

  • DeviceDidWhat in docs(website): remove /extend page and redirect to /docs/extensions
  • ewerton336 in fix(container): keep Tty and OpenStdin when creating containers through libpod
  • taljeon in fix(renderer): compact factory property descriptions
Community Meeting​

If you would like to discuss any of the new features, issues or other topics, please join us at the monthly community meeting that takes place every 4th Thursday of the month. Here are the

meeting details

.

Final Notes​

The complete list of issues fixed in this release is available here.

Get the latest release from the Downloads section of the website. Visit the GitHub repository to report issues or contribute.
